title: 12.17.10 Negative-line-bundle quotients
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: The simplest examples of the curvature criterion come from negative line bundles. Dividing the complement of the zero section of a negative line bundle over $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ by a dilation produces a principal elliptic bundle, and the logarithm of the fiber norm gives a connection form whose curvature is a multiple of a Kähler form on the base. Take $B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, let $\omega _1,\omega _2$ be the pullbacks of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one, and put \[  \begin{gathered} \Omega =a\omega _1+b\omega _2,\quad a,b\in \mathbb N_{>0},\qquad L=\mathcal O(-a,-b),\\ X=L^\times /\langle v\mapsto \rho v\rangle ,\quad 0<\rho <1, \end{gathered}  \] where $L^\times $ is the total space of $L$ with the zero section removed. Equip $L$ with the Hermitian norm induced by the standard norms on the tautological bundles of the two factors. Let $r=\log \| v\| ^2$ and set $\eta =\partial r$. Proposition 12.17.11 . 3E19D4A0EA58 The quotient $X$ is a compact complex threefold, and the projection to $B$ is a principal elliptic fibration. For $g=\pi ^*\Omega +s\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta $, $s>0$, 86B14E8734DC 12.17.12 \begin{equation}  v_-(g)=24\pi s ab\log (1/\rho ). \end{equation} Every Hermitian form on $X$ satisfies the endpoint bound of theorem 12.17.7 over its full set of normalized Gauduchon currents. The manifold has $H^2(X,\mathbb R)\ne 0$ and admits no balanced or pluriclosed metric. In particular, it is not diffeomorphic to a Hopf threefold $(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \lambda z\rangle $, $0<|\lambda |<1$. Proof. In product coordinates, the squared norm of the standard local frame of $L$ is $(1+|z_1|^2)^ a(1+|z_2|^2)^ b$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=\pi ^*\Omega ,\qquad \mathrm d\eta =2\pi \mathrm i\pi ^*\Omega .  \] Dilation changes $r$ by a constant, so $\eta $ descends to $X$. The function $r$ changes by the nonzero constant $\log \rho ^2$ under the generator, so the action is free and properly discontinuous; the unit circle bundle, which is compact, times a fundamental interval for $r$ maps onto $X$, which is therefore compact. Each fiber is $\mathbb C^*/\rho ^{\mathbb Z}$. Its logarithmic coordinate has periods $\log \rho $ and $2\pi \mathrm i$, and the curvature $F=2\pi \mathrm i\Omega $ has real part $0$ and imaginary part $2\pi \Omega $; hence \[  A_ E=4\pi \log (1/\rho ),\qquad Q=4\pi ^2\Omega ^2>0, \qquad \int _ B\Omega ^2=2ab.  \] Theorem 12.17.7 now gives ( 12.17.12 ) and the endpoint bound, and excludes pluriclosed metrics. To prove $H^2(X,\mathbb R)\ne 0$, put $A=\eta +\bar\eta $ and $B_1=\mathrm i(\eta -\bar\eta )$. Then $\mathrm dA=0$ and $\mathrm dB_1=-4\pi \pi ^*\Omega $. Suppose that $\pi ^*(\omega _1-\omega _2)=\mathrm d\zeta $ for a real one-form $\zeta $. Averaging $\zeta $ over the compact group of elliptic translations, we may assume $\zeta $ invariant, so that \[  \zeta =\pi ^*\xi +(\pi ^*f)A+(\pi ^*j)B_1  \] for a one-form $\xi $ and functions $f,j$ on $B$. The components of $\mathrm d\zeta $ with one vertical and one horizontal direction must vanish, which gives $\mathrm df=\mathrm dj=0$. Thus \[  \omega _1-\omega _2=\mathrm d\xi -4\pi j\Omega .  \] Integrating over the two rulings gives $1=-4\pi ja$ and $-1=-4\pi jb$, which is impossible because $a,b>0$. A Hopf threefold as above is diffeomorphic to $S^5\times S^1$, whose second real cohomology vanishes. Finally, $\pi ^*\Omega =-\mathrm dB_1/(4\pi )$ is a nonzero semipositive exact form. Its integral against the closed positive square of a balanced metric would vanish by Stokes' theorem and be strictly positive by positivity. Hence no balanced metric exists. $\square$

title: 12.17.13 A Calabi–Eckmann family without LCK metrics
search_title: A Calabi–Eckmann family without LCK metrics
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: A Hermitian metric $\Omega $ is locally conformally Kähler , or LCK, if $\mathrm d\Omega =\vartheta \wedge \Omega $ for a closed real one-form $\vartheta $, its Lee form; such metrics are studied in section 23.2 . The quotients of the preceding subsection resemble Hopf manifolds. A second family shows that the curvature criterion also applies on manifolds that carry no LCK metric at all. Let $\tau =A+\mathrm iB_0$, where $A<0$ and $B_0>0$, and let $\mathbb C$ act holomorphically on $(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )^2$ by \[  t\cdot (z,w)=(\mathrm e^ t z,\mathrm e^{\tau t}w).  \] Write $X_\tau $ for the quotient and put $r_1=\log |z|^2$, $r_2=\log |w|^2$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto ([z],[w])$ descends to a projection $\pi :X_\tau \to \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$; let $\omega _1,\omega _2$ be the pullbacks to the base of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one. Proposition 12.17.14 . 119B81D2AF8F The quotient $X_\tau $ is a compact complex threefold diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^3$, and $\pi $ is a principal elliptic fibration over $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$. The form $\eta =\tau \partial r_1-\partial r_2$ descends to $X_\tau $, and for \[  g=\pi ^*(\omega _1+\omega _2)+s\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta , \qquad s>0,  \] one has D04D662546BA 12.17.15 \begin{equation}  v_-(g)=48\pi ^2sB_0. \end{equation} Every Hermitian form $h\geq c g$, with $c>0$, satisfies \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm dV)} \leq c^{-1}(48\pi ^2sB_0)^{-1/3}.  \] There is no balanced, pluriclosed or LCK metric on $X_\tau $. Proof. Every orbit contains a unique point with $|z|=|w|=1$: the required parameter is determined by \[  \operatorname {Re}t=-r_1/2,\qquad \operatorname {Im}t=(r_2-Ar_1)/(2B_0).  \] These smooth formulas identify $(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )^2$ with $\mathbb C\times (S^3\times S^3)$, so the action is free and proper, and $X_\tau $ is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^3$. To obtain holomorphic charts, choose a nonzero coordinate $z_ k$ of $z$ and a branch of its logarithm, and use the action to normalize $z_ k=1$; the functions $z_ l/z_ k$, $l\ne k$, and $w_ jz_ k^{-\tau }$ are then local holomorphic coordinates on the quotient. Changing the branch of the logarithm accounts for the periods along the fibers. Thus $X_\tau $ is a compact complex threefold. The invariant form $\eta $ vanishes on the generator $z\partial _ z+\tau w\partial _ w$ of the action, so it descends. On an elliptic fiber it equals $\mathrm d\chi $, where $\chi =\tau \log v_1-\log v_2$ in terms of fiber coordinates $(v_1z,v_2w)$; its period lattice is generated by $2\pi \mathrm i\tau $ and $-2\pi \mathrm i$. Hence $A_ E=8\pi ^2B_0$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \begin{aligned}  F& =2\pi \mathrm i(\tau \omega _1-\omega _2),&  \alpha & =-2\pi B_0\omega _1,\\  \beta & =2\pi (A\omega _1-\omega _2),&  Q& =-8\pi ^2A\, \omega _1\wedge \omega _2>0. \end{aligned}  \] Since $\int _ B(\omega _1+\omega _2)^2=2$, theorem 12.17.7 gives the lower mass, the endpoint bound and the absence of pluriclosed metrics. Moreover $\mathrm d\operatorname {Re}\eta =-2\pi B_0\pi ^*\omega _1$. This nonzero semipositive exact form excludes every balanced metric by the Stokes argument at the end of the preceding proof, and hence also every Kähler metric. The quotient is simply connected, so the Lee form of a hypothetical LCK metric would be exact, equal to $\mathrm df$; multiplying the metric by $\mathrm e^{-f}$ would then give a Kähler metric, a contradiction. In particular $X_\tau $ carries no Vaisman metric, that is, no LCK metric with parallel Lee form. $\square$ The curvature criterion controls bounded potentials and the full set of normalized Gauduchon currents in these threefolds. Curvature pairs of changing sign, primitive curvature pairs and higher-dimensional analogues are not covered by this argument.

title: 12.18 Geometric bounds and determinant concentration
text: By theorem 12.9.2 , the determinant densities of all normalized Gauduchon currents are bounded in the critical space $L^{n/(n-1)}$ exactly when the lower mass is positive. Together with the mass-invariance criterion of theorem 11.1.7 , this gives geometric sufficient conditions for the critical bound. The critical exponent cannot be raised, even for currents that are powers of Kähler forms in one fixed class. The same concentrating family shows that currents approaching the maximum of the determinant functional for a fixed smooth density need not satisfy any uniform higher integrability, although the maximizer itself is smooth. Throughout this section $n\geq 2$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive probability volume form. For a Hermitian form $h$, $k_ T$ denotes the determinant density relative to $\mathrm{d}V$ of a current $T\in \mathscr G_ h$, as in section 12.9 . Put $q=n/(n-1)$. Corollary 12.18.1 . 40D45A12B192 Suppose $g$ is a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, and put $V_ g=\int _ Xg^ n$. For every Hermitian form $h\geq cg$, $c>0$, \[  v_-(h)\geq c^ nV_ g,\qquad \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)} \leq c^{-1}V_ g^{-1/n}.  \] Equality holds in the determinant bound when $h=g$ and $c=1$. In particular, on a compact Kähler manifold or a compact complex surface, the critical norm is uniformly bounded over the normalized Gauduchon currents of each fixed Hermitian form. Proof. The identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=2g\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g+2\mathrm{d}g\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g$ shows that $\mathrm{d}g\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}g=0$, so theorem 11.1.7 gives $v_-(g)=V_ g$. The quotient in ( 12.15.5 ) is monotone and homogeneous in its numerator, so $h\geq cg$ implies $v_-(h)^{1/n}\geq cV_ g^{1/n}$. Theorem 12.9.2 turns these lower-mass bounds into the asserted determinant bounds, with equality when $h=g$. A Kähler form satisfies both differential identities. On a surface, theorem 11.4.2 gives a metric $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=0$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$ for degree reasons. By compactness, each fixed $h$ satisfies $h\geq cg$ for some $c>0$. $\square$ For a fixed smooth $F$, theorem 12.7.3 gives a unique maximizing current for the determinant functional $\mathfrak D_ F$ of ( 12.7.1 ), and this current is smooth and strictly positive, so its determinant density is bounded. The following construction shows that currents approaching this maximum satisfy no uniform bound on higher moments of their determinant densities. Proposition 12.18.2 . 89AE8B534538 Let $X=E^ n$, where $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ carries its flat area form of total area one, and write $\omega _ i$ for the pullback of this form from the $i$th factor. Set \[  h=\sum _{i=1}^ n\omega _ i,\qquad \mathrm{d}V=\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n,\qquad V=n!,\qquad \alpha =\frac{n-1}{n}.  \] For $F=0$, the unique maximizing current is $T_*=h^{n-1}/V$, with $k_{T_*}=V^{-1/n}$ and $\mathfrak D_0(T_*)=V^{-1/n}$. There are smooth strictly positive closed forms $S_\varepsilon \in \mathscr G_ h$, $0<\varepsilon <\min \{ 1/4,\mathrm e^{-1}\} $, such that \[  \| k_{S_\varepsilon }\| _{L^ q}=V^{-1/n},\qquad \mathfrak D_0(S_\varepsilon )\longrightarrow V^{-1/n},  \] while for every fixed finite $p>q$, 827DBF9602F3 12.18.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X k_{S_\varepsilon }^{p}\, \mathrm{d}V \geq C_{n,p}[\log (1/\varepsilon )]^{-\alpha p} \varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p}\longrightarrow +\infty . \end{equation} Their $L^\infty $ norms also diverge. Each $S_\varepsilon $ is the $(n-1)$st power of a Kähler form in the fixed class $V^{-1/(n-1)}[h]$, and has the same Bott–Chern, de Rham and Aeppli classes as $T_*$. No $S_\varepsilon $ attains the maximum of $\mathfrak D_0$. Proof. Put $H_ i=\bigwedge _{j\ne i}\omega _ j$. Expanding the wedge powers gives $h^{n-1}=(n-1)!\sum _ iH_ i$ and $h\wedge H_ i=\mathrm{d}V$. Thus $T_*=(1/n)\sum _ iH_ i$ is normalized, and the determinant formula gives $k_{T_*}=V^{-1/n}$. The smooth equation for $F=0$ is solved by the zero potential, since $h^ n=V\, \mathrm{d}V$; theorem 12.7.3 therefore gives the maximal value and the uniqueness of the maximizer. To construct $S_\varepsilon $, choose a nonnegative smooth function $\beta $ compactly supported in the unit disk in $\mathbb C$, of integral one, with $\beta \geq \beta _0>0$ on a disk of radius $r_0\in (0,1)$. On an embedded disk in the first elliptic factor put $b_\varepsilon (z)=\varepsilon ^{-2}\beta (z/\varepsilon )$, extended by zero; it has integral one. For $0<t<1$, set \[  \begin{gathered} f_{\varepsilon ,t}=1-t+tb_\varepsilon ,\qquad a=V^{-1/(n-1)},\\ \gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}=a(f_{\varepsilon ,t}\omega _1+\omega _2+\cdots +\omega _ n), \qquad T_{\varepsilon ,t}=\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}^{n-1}. \end{gathered}  \] The form $\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}$ is strictly positive, and it is closed because $f_{\varepsilon ,t}$ depends only on the first factor, which has real dimension two. Direct expansion gives A89800F03DB4 12.18.4 \begin{equation}  T_{\varepsilon ,t}=\frac1n\left(H_1+f_{\varepsilon ,t}\sum _{i=2}^ nH_ i\right), \qquad k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}=V^{-1/n}f_{\varepsilon ,t}^{\alpha }. \end{equation} Since $\int _ Xf_{\varepsilon ,t}\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, the trace integral is one, so $T_{\varepsilon ,t}\in \mathscr G_ h$, and $\| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _{L^ q}=V^{-1/n}$ because $\alpha q=1$. The mean-zero function $f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1$ has a smooth real potential $\psi $ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =(f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1)\omega _1$; for example, the mean-zero Fourier series solving $\Delta \psi =4\pi (f_{\varepsilon ,t}-1)$ in the area-one coordinates. Consequently $\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}-ah=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\psi )$. Since $T_*=(ah)^{n-1}$, the closed form $R=\sum _{j=0}^{n-2}\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}^{n-2-j}\wedge (ah)^ j$ satisfies \[  T_{\varepsilon ,t}-T_*=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\psi R).  \] This proves all the assertions about classes, including the case $n=2$, where $R=1$. Jensen's inequality and $f_{\varepsilon ,t}\geq 1-t$ give \[  V^{-1/n}(1-t)^\alpha \leq \mathfrak D_0(T_{\varepsilon ,t}) =V^{-1/n}\int _ Xf_{\varepsilon ,t}^{\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}V <V^{-1/n},  \] where the inequality is strict because $f_{\varepsilon ,t}$ is nonconstant and $0<\alpha <1$. On the product of the disk of radius $r_0\varepsilon $ with the other factors, we have $f_{\varepsilon ,t}\geq t\beta _0\varepsilon ^{-2}$, and this set has volume $\pi r_0^2\varepsilon ^2$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  \int _ Xk_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}^ p\, \mathrm{d}V & \geq V^{-p/n}\pi r_0^2\beta _0^{\alpha p}t^{\alpha p} \varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p},\\  \| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _\infty & \geq V^{-1/n}\beta _0^\alpha t^\alpha \varepsilon ^{-2\alpha }. \end{split}  \] Now take $t=1/\log (1/\varepsilon )$, which lies in $(0,1)$ by the restriction on $\varepsilon $, and $S_\varepsilon =T_{\varepsilon ,t}$. Then $\mathfrak D_0(S_\varepsilon )$ converges to its maximum, while both lower bounds diverge for $p>q$ because $\alpha p>1$. All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. $\square$ If instead $t\in (0,1)$ is kept fixed in the same construction, then $\int _ Xk_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}^ p\, \mathrm{d}V\geq C_{n,p,t}\varepsilon ^{2-2\alpha p}$ and $\| k_{T_{\varepsilon ,t}}\| _\infty \geq C_{n,t}\varepsilon ^{-2\alpha }$. Thus there are no uniform bounds on higher moments, either over the full normalized cone or along a maximizing sequence for one smooth density. Every member of these families attains the supremum $V^{-1/n}$ of the critical norm in corollary 12.18.1 , whereas the maximum of $\mathfrak D_0$ is attained only by $T_*$.

For $0<t<1$, set \[  \begin{gathered} f_{\varepsilon ,t}=1-t+tb_\varepsilon ,\qquad a=V^{-1/(n-1)},\\ \gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}=a(f_{\varepsilon ,t}\omega _1+\omega _2+\cdots +\omega _ n), \qquad T_{\varepsilon ,t}=\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}^{n-1}. \end{gathered}  \] The form $\gamma _{\varepsilon ,t}$ is strictly positive, and it is closed because $f_{\varepsilon ,t}$ depends only on the first factor, which has real dimension two. text: Here $v_-(h)$ and $v_+(h)$ denote the infimum and supremum of $\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ over bounded $h$-psh potentials $w$. Theorem 12.18.13 . BDB7ADF7845B On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z))^ n$, $n\geq 2$, there are positive metrics $\omega _\varepsilon $ in a fixed Kähler class, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, with fixed complete current and determinant-measure families and fixed endpoint ( 12.18.9 ), while their least relative eigenvalue equals $\varepsilon $. They have uniformly bounded smooth coefficients and global potentials, and \[  v_-(\omega _\varepsilon )=v_+(\omega _\varepsilon )=n!>0.  \] The manifold has a global holomorphic volume form and $c_1=0$. Every displayed metric is already balanced and pluriclosed. Proof. Write $z_ j=x_ j+iy_ j$, $\beta _ j=(i/2)dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j=dx_ j\wedge dy_ j$, $\beta =\sum _ j\beta _ j$, $V=n!$, and $\mathrm dV=\beta ^ n/V$. Set \[  u_\varepsilon =\frac{1-\varepsilon }{4\pi }\cos (4\pi x_1), \qquad a_\varepsilon =1-(1-\varepsilon )\cos (4\pi x_1).  \] For a function of $x_1$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(u''/(4\pi ))\beta _1$. Hence \[  \omega _\varepsilon =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \beta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j.  \] These are globally periodic smooth positive closed forms with $\varepsilon \leq a_\varepsilon \leq 2-\varepsilon $ and $\omega _\varepsilon \leq 2\beta $. Their minimum relative eigenvalue is $\varepsilon $. They converge smoothly to a semipositive form losing rank on $\{ x_1\in \tfrac 12\mathbb Z\} $. All fixed-order smooth norms of the coefficients and potentials are uniformly bounded. Theorem 12.18.8 proves equality of the entire current data and the exact norm at every $\varepsilon $. Since $\omega _\varepsilon $ is closed, theorem 11.1.7 gives mass $V$ for every bounded $\omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential. The explicit formula also gives $\int _ X\omega _\varepsilon ^ n=V$, since $a_\varepsilon $ has mean one. Thus both extrema over bounded potentials equal $V$. The global form $dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dz_ n$ trivializes the canonical bundle; closed positive metrics are balanced and pluriclosed. $\square$

title: 12.18.14 The same obstruction for nonclosed pluriclosed metrics

text: Theorem 12.18.15 . 17E4315391CC On the fixed torus above, fix $0<\tau <1/2$. There is a positive nonclosed pluriclosed metric $h_\tau $ and a family $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon >0$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/2$, with identical actual current sets and intrinsic determinant-measure families. For any fixed smooth positive probability volume their entire-family endpoint is \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_{\Omega _\varepsilon }} \int _ X|p|\, \Gamma _0(T) =V_\tau ^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n(\mathrm dV)},\qquad V_\tau =n!(1-\tau ^2/2).  \] Both bounded-potential masses equal $V_\tau $. All fixed-order smooth coefficient and potential norms are uniformly bounded, while \[  \min _ X\lambda _{\min }(\Omega _\varepsilon \mid \beta )=\varepsilon , \qquad d\Omega _\varepsilon =dh_\tau \ne 0.  \] The flat $\beta $ is a fixed balanced metric on this same manifold with $c_1=0$; each $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is pluriclosed. Proof. With the torus coordinates above set $s=\sin (2\pi x_1)$ and \[  \xi =\frac i2(dz_1\wedge d\bar z_2+dz_2\wedge d\bar z_1) =dx_1\wedge dy_2+dx_2\wedge dy_1, \qquad h_\tau =\beta +\tau s\xi .  \] The first relative Hermitian block is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1& \tau s\\ \tau s& 1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, so positivity follows from $|\tau s|<1$. Moreover \[  dh_\tau =2\pi \tau \cos (2\pi x_1) dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dy_1\ne 0.  \] Because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ is proportional to $dz_1\wedge d\bar z_1$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s\xi )=0$. The first two-coordinate metric is thus pluriclosed, and its square is top degree on that complex surface. Expanding with the remaining closed curve factors proves \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_\tau ^ j)=0\quad (1\leq j\leq n-1),\qquad \int _ X h_\tau ^ n=n!\int _0^1(1-\tau ^2\sin ^2(2\pi x_1))dx_1 =V_\tau .  \] Use the same $u_\varepsilon $ and $a_\varepsilon $ as in Theorem 12.18.13 , now with $\varepsilon \leq 1/2$. Then \[  \Omega _\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \beta _1+ \sum _{j\geq 2}\beta _ j+\tau s\xi , \qquad a_\varepsilon =\varepsilon +2(1-\varepsilon )s^2.  \] The first block of $\Omega _\varepsilon -\varepsilon \beta $ has diagonal entries $2(1-\varepsilon )s^2$ and $1-\varepsilon $, and determinant \[  \bigl [2(1-\varepsilon )^2-\tau ^2\bigr ]s^2\geq 0.  \] It is positive semidefinite; the remaining diagonal entries are $1-\varepsilon $. Hence $\Omega _\varepsilon \geq \varepsilon \beta $, with equality in the least eigenvalue at $s=0$. Also $\Omega _\varepsilon \leq 3\beta $, all fixed-order smooth norms are uniformly bounded, and the smooth semipositive limit loses rank at $s=0$. Since $d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, the exterior derivative is the displayed fixed nonzero $dh_\tau $. The lower-power expansion in the proof of theorem 12.18.8 applies to $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $; it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega _\varepsilon ^ j)=0$ for $j\leq n-1$, in particular pluriclosedness. Its volume is $V_\tau $, either by integrating the displayed determinant or by theorem 11.1.7 . That theorem also gives mass $V_\tau $ for every bounded $\Omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential, so both mass extrema equal $V_\tau $. Theorem 12.18.8 applied to $h_\tau $ gives equality of the entire current and measure sets and their exact endpoint for every $p\in L^ n$. The balanced trace is fixed as well: \[  \int _ X\Omega _\varepsilon \wedge \beta ^{n-1}=n!.  \] The off-diagonal term has zero trace and the mean of $a_\varepsilon $ equals one. The global holomorphic volume form gives $c_1=0$. The manifold itself is already Kähler, so these nonclosed metrics show that the complete determinant profile and positive bounded-potential mass extrema can stay fixed while the least relative eigenvalue tends to zero. The coexistence problem of 24.4.22 remains open. $\square$

Expanding with the remaining closed curve factors proves \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h_\tau ^ j)=0\quad (1\leq j\leq n-1),\qquad \int _ X h_\tau ^ n=n!\int _0^1(1-\tau ^2\sin ^2(2\pi x_1))dx_1 =V_\tau .  \] Use the same $u_\varepsilon $ and $a_\varepsilon $ as in Theorem 12.18.13 , now with $\varepsilon \leq 1/2$. Then \[  \Omega _\varepsilon =a_\varepsilon \beta _1+ \sum _{j\geq 2}\beta _ j+\tau s\xi , \qquad a_\varepsilon =\varepsilon +2(1-\varepsilon )s^2.  \] The first block of $\Omega _\varepsilon -\varepsilon \beta $ has diagonal entries $2(1-\varepsilon )s^2$ and $1-\varepsilon $, and determinant \[  \bigl [2(1-\varepsilon )^2-\tau ^2\bigr ]s^2\geq 0.  \] It is positive semidefinite; the remaining diagonal entries are $1-\varepsilon $. Hence $\Omega _\varepsilon \geq \varepsilon \beta $, with equality in the least eigenvalue at $s=0$. Also $\Omega _\varepsilon \leq 3\beta $, all fixed-order smooth norms are uniformly bounded, and the smooth semipositive limit loses rank at $s=0$. Since $d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, the exterior derivative is the displayed fixed nonzero $dh_\tau $. The lower-power expansion in the proof of theorem 12.18.8 applies to $\Omega _\varepsilon =h_\tau +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $; it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega _\varepsilon ^ j)=0$ for $j\leq n-1$, in particular pluriclosedness. Its volume is $V_\tau $, either by integrating the displayed determinant or by theorem 11.1.7 . That theorem also gives mass $V_\tau $ for every bounded $\Omega _\varepsilon $-plurisubharmonic potential, so both mass extrema equal $V_\tau $. Theorem 12.18.8 applied to $h_\tau $ gives equality of the entire current and measure sets and their exact endpoint for every $p\in L^ n$. The balanced trace is fixed as well: \[  \int _ X\Omega _\varepsilon \wedge \beta ^{n-1}=n!.  \] The off-diagonal term has zero trace and the mean of $a_\varepsilon $ equals one. The global holomorphic volume form gives $c_1=0$. The manifold itself is already Kähler, so these nonclosed metrics show that the complete determinant profile and positive bounded-potential mass extrema can stay fixed while the least relative eigenvalue tends to zero. The coexistence problem of 24.4.22 remains open. $\square$

title: 12.18.16 Concentration at exact maximizers for varying roots
search_title: Concentration at exact maximizers for varying roots
text: Sharp determinant bounds also need not give uniform integrability of the determinant powers or preserve maximizers under weak current limits. Theorem 12.18.17 . 6072DDDAB57F On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^ n$, let $\beta _ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$, $\beta =\sum _ j\beta _ j$, $V=n!$ and $\mathrm dV=\beta ^ n/V$. There are smooth positive closed $A_\varepsilon =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon $, $0<\varepsilon <1$, and $T_\varepsilon =A_\varepsilon ^{n-1}/V \in \mathscr G_\beta $ satisfying \[  \int _ X k_{T_\varepsilon }^{n/(n-1)}\mathrm dV=V^{-1/(n-1)}.  \] Each $T_\varepsilon $ is an actual dual maximizer for a specified unit $L^ n$ root. The potentials $w_\varepsilon $ have uniformly bounded oscillation and converge uniformly to a continuous canonical $\beta $-psh $w_0$. The currents converge weakly to $T_0=(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0)^{n-1}/V\in \mathscr G_\beta $, but $\Gamma _0(T_0)=0$. The power densities above are not uniformly integrable. Nevertheless every $w_\varepsilon $, including $w_0$, has bounded-potential Monge–Ampère mass $V$. Proof. Put $r=1-\varepsilon $ and \[  P_ r(x)=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos (2\pi x)+r^2},\qquad f_\varepsilon =\varepsilon +(1-\varepsilon )P_ r.  \] The positive periodic Poisson kernel has mean one and Fourier series \[  P_ r=1+2\sum _{m\geq 1}r^ m\cos (2\pi mx).  \] Define \[  w_\varepsilon =-\frac{2(1-\varepsilon )}{\pi } \sum _{m\geq 1}\frac{r^ m\cos (2\pi mx_1)}{m^2}.  \] For fixed $\varepsilon >0$ this is smooth. Differentiation gives $w_\varepsilon ''=4\pi (f_\varepsilon -1)$, and hence \[  A_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (x_1)\beta _1+ \sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\varepsilon >0.  \] It is closed, and $\int A_\varepsilon ^ n=V$. Theorem 12.18.8 and the smooth-root formula give \[  k_{T_\varepsilon }=V^{-1/n}f_\varepsilon ^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad k_{T_\varepsilon }^{n/(n-1)} =V^{-1/(n-1)}f_\varepsilon .  \] Thus the displayed power integral attains the upper bound over all currents, not a bound for a selected family. More precisely, $p_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon ^{1/n}$ has $L^ n$ norm one, and $\int p_\varepsilon k_{T_\varepsilon }\mathrm dV=V^{-1/n}$, so $T_\varepsilon $ attains the original entire-family dual supremum for this varying root. No common fixed density is asserted. The Fourier series bounds $|w_\varepsilon |\leq \pi /3$ and implies uniform convergence to \[  w_0=-\frac2\pi \sum _{m\geq 1}\frac{\cos (2\pi mx_1)}{m^2}.  \] This limit is continuous and canonically $\beta $-psh by distributional positivity of $A_0=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0$. The probability measures $P_ r(x_1)dx_1$ converge weakly to the periodic Dirac mass at $x_1=0$, as follows from their Fourier coefficients $r^{|m|}$. Thus \[  A_0=\delta _{x_1=0}\beta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\beta _ j,  \] where the Dirac measure is tensored with Lebesgue measure in the remaining real coordinates. Its bounded local products are genuine Bedford–Taylor products. Locally the first-coordinate current $\beta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0$ is pulled back from one complex coordinate, so its powers of degree at least two vanish in the bounded-product recursion. The remaining factors are smooth and closed. Multilinear expansion therefore contains at most one first-coordinate factor; the same expansion for $A_\varepsilon $ passes directly to the distributional limit. Consequently $T_\varepsilon \to T_0=A_0^{n-1}/V$ weakly. This current is positive, closed and normalized by $\int \beta \wedge T_0=1$. In its positive coefficient matrix the absolutely continuous part is proportional to the first diagonal matrix below; the singular part on $x_1=0$ is proportional to the second: \[  \operatorname {diag}(1,0,\ldots ,0),\qquad \operatorname {diag}(0,1,\ldots ,1).  \] Their ranks are respectively one and $n-1$, both less than $n$. With a measure dominating these mutually singular parts, formula ( 12.18.7 ) therefore gives $\Gamma _0(T_0)=0$. This is not the Monge–Ampère measure of $w_0$, which has total mass $V$ by theorem 11.1.7 . Away from $x_1=0$, $f_\varepsilon \to 0$ pointwise; its integral against $\mathrm dV$ remains one. Thus the positive power densities are not uniformly integrable: almost-everywhere convergence to zero and uniform integrability would force their fixed positive integrals to vanish. In particular $T\mapsto \int k_ T^{n/(n-1)}\mathrm dV$ is not continuous under these weak current limits, even with uniformly convergent continuous potentials. The intrinsic measures themselves satisfy $\Gamma _0(T_\varepsilon )\to 0$ in total mass; this follows from their uniform $L^{n/(n-1)}$ bound by splitting off arbitrarily small neighborhoods of $x_1=0$. The discontinuity concerns their power integrals , not that last measure limit. $\square$ The maximizing root varies with $\varepsilon $. This construction concerns the complete dual profile and the critical power integral; it does not give a sequence of exact maximizers for one fixed smooth density.

title: 12.19 Vanishing lower mass
text: By ( 12.15.5 ), the lower mass $v_-(h)$ vanishes as soon as there are Gauduchon metrics $\eta $ whose degrees $\int _ Xh\wedge \eta ^{n-1}$ stay bounded while their volumes $\int _ X\eta ^ n$ tend to infinity. We construct such metrics on a compact threefold. Writing $\Gamma =\eta ^2$, the volume of $\eta $ is a determinant integral of the coefficient matrix of the positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed form $\Gamma $. The construction first concentrates the trace of a normalized form $\Gamma $ in one direction near a hypersurface, and then adds an average of compact rational curves that fills the two complementary directions. The degree stays bounded, while the determinant, and hence the volume of the positive root, becomes large. The smooth equation then converts these metrics into potentials whose masses tend to zero. Theorem 12.19.1 . 38D9206B1A2F There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ such that, for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, there are smooth real functions $u_ j$ satisfying \[  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad \int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on this manifold.

title: Theorem 12.19.1
text: Theorem 12.19.1 . 38D9206B1A2F There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ such that, for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, there are smooth real functions $u_ j$ satisfying \[  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0,\qquad \int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on this manifold. of theorem 12.19.1 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and choose $A>0$ with $h\leq A\omega $. Let $\eta _ j$ be the positive root of $\Gamma _ j$, so that $\eta _ j^2=\Gamma _ j$. These metrics are Gauduchon, and \[  P_ j=\int _ Xh\wedge \eta _ j^2\leq AC_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\eta _ j^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Set $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ and solve the smooth equation in the background $h$: \[  h_ j=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad h_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)\mu _ j, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0.  \] Since $D_{\mu _ j}(\eta _ j)=R_ j^{2/3}$, using $\eta _ j$ as a test in theorem 12.2.3 gives \[  0<\int _ Xh_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)=\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h) \leq \frac{P_ j^3}{R_ j^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The potentials $u_ j$ are smooth, hence bounded, so $v_-(h)=0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.19.4
text: Lemma 12.19.4 . 669B72559DF9 For $\delta >0$ put \[  C_\delta =\sup \left\{ \int _ XB_\delta \wedge \Theta : \Theta >0,\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Theta =0,\  \int _ X\omega \wedge \Theta =1\right\} ,  \] the supremum being taken over smooth real $(2,2)$-forms $\Theta $. These numbers are finite and tend to infinity as $\delta \downarrow 0$. Proof. For fixed $\delta $, choose a constant $M_\delta >0$ with $B_\delta \leq M_\delta \omega $; this shows that $C_\delta \leq M_\delta $. Suppose instead that $C_{\delta _ l}\leq C$ along a sequence $\delta _ l\to 0$. Then $\int _ X(C\omega -B_{\delta _ l})\wedge \Theta \geq 0$ for every admissible $\Theta $, and in particular for the squares of Gauduchon metrics. By theorem 11.6.1 , there are quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ such that \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\geq B_{\delta _ l},\qquad \sup _ Xv_ l=0.  \] By theorem 5.25.2 , a subsequence converges in $L^1$ to a $C\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $v$, not identically $-\infty $. Since $\delta ^{-2}p(\zeta /\delta )\sigma _\zeta $ is an approximate identity in the variable $\zeta $, \[  B_{\delta _ l}\rightharpoonup \chi [\zeta =0],\qquad C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \chi [\zeta =0].  \] On a coordinate ball where $\chi =1$, add to $v$ a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function whose complex Hessian dominates $C\omega $. The resulting plurisubharmonic function has a current that dominates $[\zeta =0]$, so its Lelong number is at least one at every point of an open subset of this hypersurface. Smooth corrections do not change Lelong numbers, so the same holds for $v$. Siu's analyticity theorem, recalled in 5.34.2 , shows that $Z=\{ \nu (v,\cdot )\geq 1\} $ is an analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset because $v$ is not identically $-\infty $. Let $\widetilde Z$ be the inverse image of $Z$ in $\Omega $. It contains an open subset of $H_0\cap \Omega $, where $H_0=\{ w_0=z_0\} $. This surface is a projective plane with two points removed, so it is connected and irreducible, and the identity principle gives $H_0\cap \Omega \subset \widetilde Z$. Since $\widetilde Z$ is invariant under $g$, also \[  H_ k\cap \Omega \subset \widetilde Z,\qquad H_ k=\{ w_0=q^ kz_0\} , \qquad k\in \mathbb Z.  \] Now use the chart $z_1=1$ near the point $[0:1:1:0]\in \Omega $. There $H_ k$ is the graph $z_0=q^{-k}w_0$. For each fixed $(w_0,w_1)$ near $(1,0)$, every local holomorphic defining function of $\widetilde Z$ vanishes at the distinct values $z_0=q^{-k}w_0$, which tend to zero as $k\to +\infty $. The one-variable identity theorem makes each defining function vanish identically on a polydisk. Thus $\widetilde Z$ contains a nonempty open subset of the connected manifold $\Omega $, contradicting properness. Hence no subsequence of $C_\delta $ stays bounded as $\delta \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 12.19.6 Averaging the trace and compact curves
search_title: Averaging the trace and compact curves
text: A large pairing with $B_{\delta _ j}$ means that $\Theta _ j$ has a large coefficient in one direction, but possibly only on a small set. Averaging by translations spreads this coefficient over a whole product region of size comparable to $\delta _ j$ in the vertical direction. A second average, this time of compact rational curves, fills the two complementary directions, which is needed for a lower bound on a determinant. Fix $j$ and write $\delta =\delta _ j$. For complex parameters $a,b,\tau $, the automorphisms \[  T_{a,b,\tau }[z_0:z_1:w_0:w_1] =[z_0:z_1+az_0:\mathrm{e}^{\tau }w_0: \mathrm{e}^{\tau }(w_1+bw_0)]  \] of $\Omega $ commute with $g$, and in the product chart they act by $(x,y,\zeta )\mapsto (x+a,y+b,\zeta +\tau )$.  Average $T_{a,b,\tau }^*\Theta _ j$ against the probability density \[  3^{-4}p(a/3)p(b/3)(3\delta )^{-2}p(\tau /(3\delta )) \sigma _ a\wedge \sigma _ b\wedge \sigma _\tau ,  \] and denote the result by $\widehat\Theta _ j$. It is smooth, strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. The parameters range in a fixed compact set of automorphisms, so $(T_{a,b,\tau }^{-1})^*\omega \leq C\omega $ with one constant $C$, and a change of variables gives E994975CCA57 12.19.7 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\omega \wedge \widehat\Theta _ j\leq C. \end{equation} Let $F_ j$ be the coefficient of $\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y$ in the restriction of $\Theta _ j$ to the slices $\{ \zeta =\text{constant}\} $, and let $\widehat F_ j$ be the corresponding coefficient of $\widehat\Theta _ j$. Positivity gives $F_ j\geq 0$, and since the translations preserve $\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y$, $\widehat F_ j$ is an average of translates of $F_ j$. At a point of \[  V_ j=\{ |x|,|y|<1/4,\  |\zeta |<\delta /4\} ,  \] every translation carrying it into $\operatorname {supp}B_\delta $ has $|a|,|b|\leq 5/4$ and $|\tau |\leq 5\delta /4$. On this range the first two averaging factors are bounded below by a positive constant, and the third by a positive constant times $\delta ^{-2}$. On the other hand, $\chi \leq 1$ and $p$ is bounded, so the number $J_ j$ of ( 12.19.5 ) is at most a constant times $\delta ^{-2}$ times the integral of $F_ j$ over $\operatorname {supp}B_\delta $. Comparing the two integrals gives 79DFF8AF8DCA 12.19.8 \begin{equation}  \widehat F_ j\geq cJ_ j\quad \hbox{on }V_ j, \end{equation} with $c>0$ independent of $j$. The second average fills the two horizontal directions. Put \[  f(a,b)=p(4(a-1))p(b/2),\qquad \rho _ j(\tau )=4\delta ^{-2}p(2\tau /\delta ).  \] For parameters in the supports of these functions and $|u|\leq 1/16$, consider the holomorphic maps $\iota _{\tau ,u,a,b}:\mathbb P^1\to X$ defined by BE92C16DAFFD 12.19.9 \begin{equation}  \iota _{\tau ,u,a,b}[z_0:z_1] =[z_0:z_1:\mathrm{e}^{\tau }(z_0+uz_1): \mathrm{e}^{\tau }(az_1+bz_0)]\in X. \end{equation} For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1/16$, average their integration currents against \[  \rho _ j(\tau )f(a,b)\varepsilon ^{-2}p(u/\varepsilon ) \sigma _\tau \wedge \sigma _ a\wedge \sigma _ b\wedge \sigma _ u,  \] and call the result $T_{j,\varepsilon }$. Define $T_{j,0}$ in the same way, but with $u=0$ and without the integral over $u$. Lemma 12.19.10 . 40DB573E7C1E For $\varepsilon >0$, the form $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is smooth on $X$, semipositive and closed, and \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge T_{j,\varepsilon }\leq C'  \] with $C'$ independent of $j$ and $\varepsilon $. For each fixed $j$, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ converges smoothly to $T_{j,0}$ on compact subsets of the product chart as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. In this chart 3DC335D33654 12.19.11 \begin{equation}  T_{j,0}=\rho _ j(\zeta )\sigma _\zeta \wedge K_ f,\qquad K_ f=\int _\mathbb Cf(a,y-ax)\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } (\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x)\wedge (\mathrm{d}\bar y-\bar a\, \mathrm{d}\bar x)\, \sigma _ a, \end{equation} and on $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $ the form $K_ f$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of $\sigma _ x+\sigma _ y$. Proof. On the parameter supports, $|a-bu|\geq 3/4-2/16=5/8$. Hence the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1& u\\ b& a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is uniformly invertible, and the projective line ( 12.19.9 ) lies in $\Omega $. Distinct deck translates of this line are disjoint: equality at a point fixes $[z_0:z_1]$, and invertibility of the matrix then forces the deck scalar to be one. Thus each map is an embedding onto a compact rational curve in $X$. The evaluation map from $\mathbb P^1$ times the open parameter domain to $X$ is a holomorphic submersion. Indeed, after fixing a projective gauge, variations of $u$ and $a$ span the two $w$-coordinates at points with $z_1\ne 0$, variations of $\tau $ and $b$ span them at points with $z_1=0$, and the coordinate on $\mathbb P^1$ supplies the remaining direction. For $\varepsilon >0$, the average is the integral along the fibers of this submersion of a smooth compactly supported parameter density, which proves smoothness. As an average of closed positive integration currents, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is closed and semipositive. All curve parameters lie in one compact subset of the domain where the matrix is invertible, so the $\omega $-areas of the curves are uniformly bounded. The weights in $\tau $ and $u$ have mass one, and the weight in $(a,b)$ has a fixed finite mass. This proves the degree bound. When $u=0$, the curve is given in the product chart by $\zeta =\tau $ and $y=ax+b$. Integrating in $b$ and $\tau $ yields ( 12.19.11 ); the $(1,1)$-factor there is the integration current of the graph of $y=ax+b$. On $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $, the density $f(a,y-ax)$ is bounded below by a positive constant for $a$ in a fixed small disk about $1$. The covectors $\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x$, for $a$ in that disk, have no common nonzero annihilator, so integrating their squared absolute values and using compactness of the unit sphere in the $(x,y)$-directions gives the asserted lower bound. For general $u$, the curve is given by \[  \zeta =\tau +\log (1+ux),\qquad y=\frac{ax+b}{1+ux}.  \] On a fixed compact subset of the chart, $1+ux$ stays away from zero for all sufficiently small $u$. Solving for the parameters gives $\tau =\zeta -\log (1+ux)$ and $b=(1+ux)y-ax$. Regarding $\rho _ j$ as a smooth function on $E$, this change of variables also applies near the boundary of its support. The Jacobians, the density coefficients and any fixed number of their derivatives depend smoothly on $u$. Averaging against the approximate identity in $u$ therefore gives local $C^\infty $ convergence. This convergence is needed only for each fixed $j$; it is not uniform in $j$. $\square$

text: Lemma 12.19.10 . 40DB573E7C1E For $\varepsilon >0$, the form $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is smooth on $X$, semipositive and closed, and \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge T_{j,\varepsilon }\leq C'  \] with $C'$ independent of $j$ and $\varepsilon $. For each fixed $j$, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ converges smoothly to $T_{j,0}$ on compact subsets of the product chart as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. In this chart 3DC335D33654 12.19.11 \begin{equation}  T_{j,0}=\rho _ j(\zeta )\sigma _\zeta \wedge K_ f,\qquad K_ f=\int _\mathbb Cf(a,y-ax)\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } (\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x)\wedge (\mathrm{d}\bar y-\bar a\, \mathrm{d}\bar x)\, \sigma _ a, \end{equation} and on $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $ the form $K_ f$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of $\sigma _ x+\sigma _ y$. Proof. On the parameter supports, $|a-bu|\geq 3/4-2/16=5/8$. Hence the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1& u\\ b& a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is uniformly invertible, and the projective line ( 12.19.9 ) lies in $\Omega $. Distinct deck translates of this line are disjoint: equality at a point fixes $[z_0:z_1]$, and invertibility of the matrix then forces the deck scalar to be one. Thus each map is an embedding onto a compact rational curve in $X$. The evaluation map from $\mathbb P^1$ times the open parameter domain to $X$ is a holomorphic submersion. Indeed, after fixing a projective gauge, variations of $u$ and $a$ span the two $w$-coordinates at points with $z_1\ne 0$, variations of $\tau $ and $b$ span them at points with $z_1=0$, and the coordinate on $\mathbb P^1$ supplies the remaining direction. For $\varepsilon >0$, the average is the integral along the fibers of this submersion of a smooth compactly supported parameter density, which proves smoothness. As an average of closed positive integration currents, $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ is closed and semipositive. All curve parameters lie in one compact subset of the domain where the matrix is invertible, so the $\omega $-areas of the curves are uniformly bounded. The weights in $\tau $ and $u$ have mass one, and the weight in $(a,b)$ has a fixed finite mass. This proves the degree bound. When $u=0$, the curve is given in the product chart by $\zeta =\tau $ and $y=ax+b$. Integrating in $b$ and $\tau $ yields ( 12.19.11 ); the $(1,1)$-factor there is the integration current of the graph of $y=ax+b$. On $\{ |x|,|y|\leq 1/4\} $, the density $f(a,y-ax)$ is bounded below by a positive constant for $a$ in a fixed small disk about $1$. The covectors $\mathrm{d}y-a\, \mathrm{d}x$, for $a$ in that disk, have no common nonzero annihilator, so integrating their squared absolute values and using compactness of the unit sphere in the $(x,y)$-directions gives the asserted lower bound. For general $u$, the curve is given by \[  \zeta =\tau +\log (1+ux),\qquad y=\frac{ax+b}{1+ux}.  \] On a fixed compact subset of the chart, $1+ux$ stays away from zero for all sufficiently small $u$. Solving for the parameters gives $\tau =\zeta -\log (1+ux)$ and $b=(1+ux)y-ax$. Regarding $\rho _ j$ as a smooth function on $E$, this change of variables also applies near the boundary of its support. The Jacobians, the density coefficients and any fixed number of their derivatives depend smoothly on $u$. Averaging against the approximate identity in $u$ therefore gives local $C^\infty $ convergence. This convergence is needed only for each fixed $j$; it is not uniform in $j$. $\square$

title: 12.19.12 The volume of the positive root
search_title: The volume of the positive root
text:
The two averages contribute complementary blocks of the coefficient matrix of a $(2,2)$-form: the translated forms give a large vertical entry, and the curves give a positive horizontal block. A Schur-complement estimate combines them into a lower bound for the volume of the positive root. In the coframe $(x,y,\zeta )$ put $\mathrm{d}V_0=\sigma _ x\wedge \sigma _ y\wedge \sigma _\zeta $. For a real $(1,1)$-form $\xi $, let $H_\xi $ be its coefficient matrix in this normalization. A real $(2,2)$-form $\Theta $ corresponds to a Hermitian matrix $Q_\Theta $, which we call its cofactor matrix, by \[  \xi \wedge \Theta =\operatorname {tr}(H_\xi Q_\Theta )\, \mathrm{d}V_0.  \] Strict positivity of $\Theta $ is equivalent to $Q_\Theta >0$. If $\eta ^2=\Theta $ and $H=H_\eta $, expanding the wedge products gives \[  Q_\Theta =2(\det H)H^{-1},\qquad \eta ^3=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}(\det Q_\Theta )^{1/2}\, \mathrm{d}V_0.  \] Conversely, these formulas uniquely recover a smooth positive $H$ from $Q_\Theta >0$; this is the three-dimensional case of the root construction used in the proof of theorem 11.6.1 . We write $\Theta ^{3/2}=\eta ^3$. Lemma 12.19.13 . BD9C00A32F59 There are smooth strictly positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(2,2)$-forms $\Gamma _ j$ such that \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \Gamma _ j\leq C_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\Gamma _ j^{3/2}\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Proof. Write the cofactor matrix of $\widehat\Theta _ j$ in block form, with a $2\times 2$ Hermitian block $A_ j$ in the $(x,y)$-directions and a column $\kappa _ j\in \mathbb C^2$: \[  Q_ j=\begin{pmatrix} A_ j

& \kappa _ j

\\ \kappa _ j^*

& \widehat F_ j

\end{pmatrix}.  \] The cofactor matrix of $T_{j,0}$ has the form $\operatorname {diag}(B_ j,0)$. Let $I_2$ denote the $2\times 2$ identity matrix. The lower bound for $K_ f$ and the definition of $\rho _ j$ give a constant $c_0>0$ such that $B_ j\geq c_0\delta _ j^{-2}I_2$ on $V_ j$. Since $Q_ j>0$, the Schur complement $A_ j-\kappa _ j\kappa _ j^*/\widehat F_ j$ is positive definite, and \[  \det \bigl (Q_ j+\operatorname {diag}(B_ j,0)\bigr ) =\widehat F_ j\det \left(B_ j+A_ j- \frac{\kappa _ j\kappa _ j^*}{\widehat F_ j}\right) \geq \widehat F_ j\det B_ j,  \] by monotonicity of the determinant on positive Hermitian matrices. Combining the root formula with ( 12.19.8 ), we obtain \[  (\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0})^{3/2} \geq c\delta _ j^{-2}\sqrt{J_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V_0 \quad \hbox{on }V_ j.  \] The smaller region $W_ j=\{ |x|,|y|<1/8,\  |\zeta |<\delta _ j/8\} $ has $\mathrm{d}V_0$-volume equal to a fixed positive constant times $\delta _ j^2$. Consequently \[  I_ j=\int _{W_ j}(\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0})^{3/2} \geq c_1\sqrt{J_ j}>c_1j^2.  \] For this fixed $j$, lemma 12.19.10 gives smooth convergence of $T_{j,\varepsilon }$ to $T_{j,0}$ on the closure of $W_ j$. The cofactor matrix of $\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,0}$ is positive definite there, so the integrand of the root volume depends continuously on these smooth coefficients. We can therefore choose $0<\varepsilon _ j\leq 1/16$ so small that \[  \int _{W_ j}(\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,\varepsilon _ j})^{3/2} \geq I_ j/2.  \] Set $\Gamma _ j=\widehat\Theta _ j+T_{j,\varepsilon _ j}$. It is smooth, strictly positive and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. Its degree is bounded by ( 12.19.7 ) and lemma 12.19.10 , whereas its root volume is at least $c_1j^2/2$. $\square$ of theorem 12.19.1 . Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and choose $A>0$ with $h\leq A\omega $. Let $\eta _ j$ be the positive root of $\Gamma _ j$, so that $\eta _ j^2=\Gamma _ j$. These metrics are Gauduchon, and \[  P_ j=\int _ Xh\wedge \eta _ j^2\leq AC_2,\qquad R_ j=\int _ X\eta _ j^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Set $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ and solve the smooth equation in the background $h$: \[  h_ j=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0,\qquad h_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)\mu _ j, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ j=0.  \] Since $D_{\mu _ j}(\eta _ j)=R_ j^{2/3}$, using $\eta _ j$ as a test in theorem 12.2.3 gives \[  0<\int _ Xh_ j^3=c_ h(\mu _ j)=\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h) \leq \frac{P_ j^3}{R_ j^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The potentials $u_ j$ are smooth, hence bounded, so $v_-(h)=0$. $\square$

title: 12.19.14 Consequences for dimension and equations
text: The example occurs in the smallest possible dimension: on a surface, comparison with a Gauduchon metric gives positive lower mass. Products with projective spaces carry the threefold degeneration to every higher dimension, and a product with the Hopf threefold produces, in addition, unbounded upper mass. Corollary 12.19.15 . 435BD74C27A9 Every Hermitian form on a compact complex manifold of dimension at most two has positive lower mass. In every dimension $n\geq 3$ there is a connected compact complex manifold on which every Hermitian form has zero lower mass. Proof. In dimension one the mass is $\int _ Xh>0$, and the surface case is corollary 12.18.1 . In higher dimensions we use the monotonicity and the homogeneity of degree $n$ of $v_-$, which follow directly from ( 12.15.5 ), to pass from a split metric to every Hermitian metric. For $n=3$ this is theorem 12.19.1 . For $n>3$, take the product of the threefold $X$ with $\mathbb P^{n-3}$, let $\kappa $ be a Fubini–Study form on the projective factor, and consider the split metric $h_0=\omega +\kappa $, with pullbacks understood. For the potentials $u_ j$ given by the theorem for the background $\omega $, \[  \int _{X\times \mathbb P^{n-3}}(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n =\binom n3\left(\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3\right) \left(\int _{\mathbb P^{n-3}}\kappa ^{n-3}\right) \longrightarrow 0.  \] For another Hermitian form $h$, choose $A$ with $h\leq Ah_0$. Monotonicity and homogeneity give $v_-(h)\leq A^ n v_-(h_0)=0$. $\square$ Corollary 12.19.16 . 940F7BB9270C In every dimension $n\geq 6$ there is a connected compact complex manifold with \[  v_-(h)=0,\qquad v_+(h)=+\infty  \] for every Hermitian form $h$. Proof. Take the product of the threefold above with the Hopf threefold of section 23.1 , with a split metric. Potentials pulled back from the first factor make the masses tend to zero, while the smooth potentials of theorem 23.1.1 , pulled back from the second factor, make them tend to infinity. In each case the product integral is $\binom 63$ times the product of the two factor masses. The metric comparison in the preceding proof handles the lower mass for every Hermitian form, and the metric independence in proposition 13.14.15 handles the upper mass. Products with projective spaces give every higher dimension by the same expansion of wedge powers. $\square$ Finally, fix a smooth positive probability measure $\mu $ on the threefold $X$. The smooth equation still gives $\mathcal V_\mu (h)>0$ for each Hermitian form $h$. With $\mathscr M$ and $\lambda _*$ as in subsection 12.15.3 , theorem 12.15.4 gives \[  \inf _{\nu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\nu (h)=0, \qquad \lambda _*(h)=0.  \] Thus even a smooth strictly positive background can have vanishing infimum over densities. For the metrics $\eta _ j$ and numbers $R_ j,P_ j$ in the proof of theorem 12.19.1 , the measures $\mu _ j=\eta _ j^3/R_ j$ satisfy $\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h)\leq P_ j^3/R_ j^2\to 0$. Hence the densities $\mu _ j/\mu $ cannot be uniformly bounded above: a bound $\mu _ j\leq M\mu $ would give $\mathcal V_{\mu _ j}(h)\geq M^{-1}\mathcal V_\mu (h)>0$, by the comparison of denominators in the proof of proposition 12.15.1 . The example also shows that the endpoint estimate in theorem 12.9.2 fails for the full family of normalized Gauduchon currents: the supremum of the $L^{3/2}$ norms of their determinant densities is infinite, although every subcritical $L^ q$ norm, $1<q<3/2$, remains uniformly bounded by theorem 12.9.1 . For the same fixed background, theorem 12.9.7 , corollary 12.9.10 give uniform $L^\infty $ bounds for the exact maximizers and their adjoint probabilities in a small $C^{2,\alpha }$ family of smooth densities. A larger sufficient family is given by theorem 12.9.18 : uniformly comparable smooth solution forms yield uniform bounds for both densities, without derivative bounds on the varying Hessian. Endpoint estimates for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities remain open.

title: 12.19.17 A balanced metric and a finite upper mass
search_title: A balanced metric and a finite upper mass
text: Although every Hermitian form on the threefold of theorem 12.19.1 has zero lower mass, the metric $\omega $ of ( 12.19.3 ) is balanced and has finite upper mass. A direct calculation expresses the loss of mass under a potential as a vertical Dirichlet energy along the elliptic fibers. The same calculation shows that the degeneration cannot be realized by potentials that are the sum of a periodic function of $t$ and a function on the base: their masses stay above $8$. Put $D=\mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, so that $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$. Proposition 12.19.18 . 94417AD14985 On the threefold $X$ of theorem 12.19.1 , the Hermitian form $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta \geq 0, \qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi .  \] For every smooth real function $u$, 9E38044EBFA0 12.19.19 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =24\pi -6\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta . \end{equation} Consequently $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. In particular, $X$ has the bounded mass property, while $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Proof. Although $t$ is defined only on the covering space $\Omega $, both $\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ descend to $X$. The Fubini–Study potentials $\log \| z\| ^2$ and $\log \| w\| ^2$ give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\beta -\alpha $. The forms $\alpha ,\beta $ are closed, and $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0$ since each is pulled back from a curve. As $D^2=0$, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}D=-\mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha ),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-(\beta -\alpha )^2=2\alpha \wedge \beta ,  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2) =-2(\alpha +\beta +D)\wedge \mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0.  \] In the last identity, the term involving $D$ contains $\mathrm{d}t$ twice, and $(\alpha +\beta )\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0$. Thus $\omega $ is balanced, hence Gauduchon, and the formula for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ follows from that for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D$. On a fiber, write $\zeta =a+\mathrm{i}b$, where both real periods are $2\pi $. There $t=2a$ plus a constant, so \[  D|_ E=\frac1\pi \, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}b, \qquad \int _ ED=4\pi .  \] Since $\omega ^3=6\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D$, fiber integration and the normalization of the Fubini–Study forms give $\int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi $. The identity ( 12.16.4 ) for Gauduchon metrics on threefolds, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta $, gives ( 12.19.19 ). Its last integral is nonnegative. Thus every smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential has mass at most $24\pi $, and the constant potential attains this value. Regularization of bounded potentials, as in the proof of theorem 12.15.4 , gives the same supremum over bounded potentials, so $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. The metric independence in proposition 13.14.15 then gives the bounded mass property of $X$. The assertion about the lower mass is theorem 12.19.1 . $\square$ For an admissible smooth $u$, equality in the upper-mass bound holds precisely when $u$ is constant along every elliptic fiber. Indeed, $\alpha \wedge \beta $ is a positive volume form in the base directions, so the nonnegative integral in ( 12.19.19 ) vanishes exactly when the derivative of $u$ along the fibers vanishes. The fibers are connected, and smooth local sections then show that $u$ is the pullback of a smooth function on $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$. For the potentials with masses tending to zero in theorem 12.19.1 , the same integral instead tends to $4\pi $. A function $f(t)$ descends to $X$ when $f$ is $4\pi $-periodic, since $t\circ g=t+4\pi $. Even after adding an arbitrary potential pulled back from the base, such functions leave a positive mass gap. The sharp gap follows from the bounds on the first two derivatives of $f$ imposed by positivity. Proposition 12.19.20 . 3290D6E85075 Let $\pi :X\to B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ be the elliptic fibration above, and put $L=4\pi $. Consider the smooth potentials \[  u=f(t)+\pi ^*v,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,  \] where $f:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ is smooth and $L$-periodic and $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$. The infimum of $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ over these potentials is $8$. Every such mass is strictly greater than $8$, and the infimum is approached already with $v=0$. Proof. Write $p=f'$, an $L$-periodic function with mean zero. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =(1-p)\alpha +(1+p)\beta +\pi ^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. On the complex plane $\ker \partial t$, the form $D$ vanishes and the projection to the base is an isomorphism. For each value of $t$ modulo $L$, every base point has a point above it with that value. Hence, writing $\alpha _ B,\beta _ B$ for the two Fubini–Study forms on $B$, the form $(1-p(s))\alpha _ B+(1+p(s))\beta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive on $B$ for every $s$. Integration over the two rulings gives $1-p>0$ and $1+p>0$. Thus $|p|<1$ and $p'>-1$; when $v=0$, these inequalities also suffice for strict positivity. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, both real periods are $2\pi $, $t=2x$ plus a constant, and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Hence $\int _ E F(t)D=\int _0^ L F(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ for every $L$-periodic function $F$. Only the derivative of $u$ along the fibers contributes to ( 12.19.19 ), and it equals $p(t)$ times the derivative of $t$. Fiber integration therefore gives 87EE58E6037C 12.19.21 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =6\left(L-\int _0^ L p(s)^2\, \mathrm{d}s\right). \end{equation} We now bound $\int _0^ Lp^2$. Suppose first that $p\not\equiv 0$, and put $m_+=\max p>0$, $m_-=-\min p>0$ and $r=m_++m_-<2$. The function $G(s)=(m_+-s)(s+m_-)$ is nonnegative on $[-m_-,m_+]$. Choose an interval $I$ of length at most $L$ that runs from a maximum point of $p$ forward to the next minimum point. Since $p'\geq -1$, we have $G(p)\geq -G(p)p'$. Using that $p$ has mean zero, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  m_+m_-L-\int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s & =\int _0^ L G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s\\ & =\int _{-m_-}^{m_+}G(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=\frac{r^3}{6}. \end{split}  \] As $m_+m_-\leq r^2/4$, it follows that \[  \int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s \leq \frac{Lr^2}{4}-\frac{r^3}{6}<L-\frac43,  \] where the last inequality holds because the middle expression is strictly increasing in $r\in (0,2]$, as $L>2$. The inequality $\int _0^ Lp^2<L-4/3$ holds trivially when $p=0$. Equation ( 12.19.21 ) now gives the strict lower bound $8$. To prove sharpness, put $a=(L-2)/2$ and define an $L$-periodic function $p_0$ by \[  p_0(s)= \begin{cases}  1,& 0\leq s<a,\\  1-(s-a),& a\leq s<a+2,\\  -1,& a+2\leq s<L. \end{cases}  \] It has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq 1$ and $\int _0^ L p_0^2\, \mathrm{d}s=L-4/3$. Its distributional derivative is $-1$ on the descending interval and zero on the two constant intervals, and it has a positive atom where the period closes up. Thus $p_0'\geq -1$ as distributions on the circle. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be a nonnegative smooth periodic approximate identity of integral one, and set $p_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )(p_0*\rho _\varepsilon )$ for $0<\varepsilon <1$. Then $p_\varepsilon $ is smooth, has mean zero, and \[  |p_\varepsilon |\leq 1-\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon '\geq -1+\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon \longrightarrow p_0\quad \hbox{in }L^2.  \] Its primitive $f_\varepsilon $ is smooth and periodic, so $u_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (t)$ is admissible. By ( 12.19.21 ), its mass tends to $8$. $\square$ Proposition 12.19.22 . 69BB70EA26D9 The threefold $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed Hermitian metric nor a closed Kähler current. Proof. By proposition 12.19.18 , the nonzero smooth semipositive $(2,2)$-form $\alpha \wedge \beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega /2)$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. If a Hermitian metric $\eta $ satisfied $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\eta \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\eta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0,  \] a contradiction. The first inequality holds because $\eta $ is positive in the vertical direction at every point. Similarly, if a closed positive current $T$ satisfied $T\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$, positivity and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  0<\varepsilon \int _ X\omega \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta \leq \int _ XT\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0.  \] Hence there is no closed Kähler current. $\square$ Since a compact complex manifold carries a closed Kähler current exactly when it belongs to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, as recalled in section 24.4 , the threefold $X$ lies outside this class. The example shows that a balanced metric does not guarantee positive lower mass, even together with bounded upper mass. The Hopf threefold, in contrast, has positive lower mass and infinite upper mass, so the two properties are logically independent, and the products in corollary 12.19.16 show that both can fail at once. In particular, in a theorem asserting solvability for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure, bounded mass alone cannot replace the hypothesis of positive lower mass.

title: Proposition 12.19.18
text: Proposition 12.19.18 . 94417AD14985 On the threefold $X$ of theorem 12.19.1 , the Hermitian form $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2)=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta \geq 0, \qquad \int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi .  \] For every smooth real function $u$, 9E38044EBFA0 12.19.19 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =24\pi -6\int _ X\mathrm{d}u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta . \end{equation} Consequently $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. In particular, $X$ has the bounded mass property, while $v_-(h)=0$ for every Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Proof. Although $t$ is defined only on the covering space $\Omega $, both $\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ descend to $X$. The Fubini–Study potentials $\log \| z\| ^2$ and $\log \| w\| ^2$ give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\beta -\alpha $. The forms $\alpha ,\beta $ are closed, and $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0$ since each is pulled back from a curve. As $D^2=0$, we obtain \[  \mathrm{d}D=-\mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha ),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=-(\beta -\alpha )^2=2\alpha \wedge \beta ,  \] \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega ^2) =-2(\alpha +\beta +D)\wedge \mathrm{d}t\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0.  \] In the last identity, the term involving $D$ contains $\mathrm{d}t$ twice, and $(\alpha +\beta )\wedge (\beta -\alpha )=0$. Thus $\omega $ is balanced, hence Gauduchon, and the formula for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ follows from that for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D$. On a fiber, write $\zeta =a+\mathrm{i}b$, where both real periods are $2\pi $. There $t=2a$ plus a constant, so \[  D|_ E=\frac1\pi \, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}b, \qquad \int _ ED=4\pi .  \] Since $\omega ^3=6\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D$, fiber integration and the normalization of the Fubini–Study forms give $\int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi $. The identity ( 12.16.4 ) for Gauduchon metrics on threefolds, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =2\alpha \wedge \beta $, gives ( 12.19.19 ). Its last integral is nonnegative. Thus every smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential has mass at most $24\pi $, and the constant potential attains this value. Regularization of bounded potentials, as in the proof of theorem 12.15.4 , gives the same supremum over bounded potentials, so $v_+(\omega )=24\pi $. The metric independence in proposition 13.14.15 then gives the bounded mass property of $X$. The assertion about the lower mass is theorem 12.19.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 12.19.20
text: Proposition 12.19.20 . 3290D6E85075 Let $\pi :X\to B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$ be the elliptic fibration above, and put $L=4\pi $. Consider the smooth potentials \[  u=f(t)+\pi ^*v,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,  \] where $f:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ is smooth and $L$-periodic and $v\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$. The infimum of $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$ over these potentials is $8$. Every such mass is strictly greater than $8$, and the infimum is approached already with $v=0$. Proof. Write $p=f'$, an $L$-periodic function with mean zero. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u =(1-p)\alpha +(1+p)\beta +\pi ^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+(1+p')D.  \] Positivity on the vertical line implies $p'>-1$. On the complex plane $\ker \partial t$, the form $D$ vanishes and the projection to the base is an isomorphism. For each value of $t$ modulo $L$, every base point has a point above it with that value. Hence, writing $\alpha _ B,\beta _ B$ for the two Fubini–Study forms on $B$, the form $(1-p(s))\alpha _ B+(1+p(s))\beta _ B+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive on $B$ for every $s$. Integration over the two rulings gives $1-p>0$ and $1+p>0$. Thus $|p|<1$ and $p'>-1$; when $v=0$, these inequalities also suffice for strict positivity. In a logarithmic fiber coordinate $x+\mathrm{i}y$, both real periods are $2\pi $, $t=2x$ plus a constant, and $D|_ E=\pi ^{-1}\mathrm{d}x\wedge \mathrm{d}y$. Hence $\int _ E F(t)D=\int _0^ L F(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$ for every $L$-periodic function $F$. Only the derivative of $u$ along the fibers contributes to ( 12.19.19 ), and it equals $p(t)$ times the derivative of $t$. Fiber integration therefore gives 87EE58E6037C 12.19.21 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =6\left(L-\int _0^ L p(s)^2\, \mathrm{d}s\right). \end{equation} We now bound $\int _0^ Lp^2$. Suppose first that $p\not\equiv 0$, and put $m_+=\max p>0$, $m_-=-\min p>0$ and $r=m_++m_-<2$. The function $G(s)=(m_+-s)(s+m_-)$ is nonnegative on $[-m_-,m_+]$. Choose an interval $I$ of length at most $L$ that runs from a maximum point of $p$ forward to the next minimum point. Since $p'\geq -1$, we have $G(p)\geq -G(p)p'$. Using that $p$ has mean zero, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  m_+m_-L-\int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s & =\int _0^ L G(p)\, \mathrm{d}s \geq -\int _ I G(p)p'\, \mathrm{d}s\\ & =\int _{-m_-}^{m_+}G(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=\frac{r^3}{6}. \end{split}  \] As $m_+m_-\leq r^2/4$, it follows that \[  \int _0^ L p^2\, \mathrm{d}s \leq \frac{Lr^2}{4}-\frac{r^3}{6}<L-\frac43,  \] where the last inequality holds because the middle expression is strictly increasing in $r\in (0,2]$, as $L>2$. The inequality $\int _0^ Lp^2<L-4/3$ holds trivially when $p=0$. Equation ( 12.19.21 ) now gives the strict lower bound $8$. To prove sharpness, put $a=(L-2)/2$ and define an $L$-periodic function $p_0$ by \[  p_0(s)= \begin{cases}  1,& 0\leq s<a,\\  1-(s-a),& a\leq s<a+2,\\  -1,& a+2\leq s<L. \end{cases}  \] It has mean zero, $|p_0|\leq 1$ and $\int _0^ L p_0^2\, \mathrm{d}s=L-4/3$. Its distributional derivative is $-1$ on the descending interval and zero on the two constant intervals, and it has a positive atom where the period closes up. Thus $p_0'\geq -1$ as distributions on the circle. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be a nonnegative smooth periodic approximate identity of integral one, and set $p_\varepsilon =(1-\varepsilon )(p_0*\rho _\varepsilon )$ for $0<\varepsilon <1$. Then $p_\varepsilon $ is smooth, has mean zero, and \[  |p_\varepsilon |\leq 1-\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon '\geq -1+\varepsilon , \qquad p_\varepsilon \longrightarrow p_0\quad \hbox{in }L^2.  \] Its primitive $f_\varepsilon $ is smooth and periodic, so $u_\varepsilon =f_\varepsilon (t)$ is admissible. By ( 12.19.21 ), its mass tends to $8$. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.19.22
text: Proposition 12.19.22 . 69BB70EA26D9 The threefold $X$ admits neither a pluriclosed Hermitian metric nor a closed Kähler current. Proof. By proposition 12.19.18 , the nonzero smooth semipositive $(2,2)$-form $\alpha \wedge \beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega /2)$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. If a Hermitian metric $\eta $ satisfied $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0$, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0<\int _ X\eta \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\eta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta =0,  \] a contradiction. The first inequality holds because $\eta $ is positive in the vertical direction at every point. Similarly, if a closed positive current $T$ satisfied $T\geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$, positivity and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  0<\varepsilon \int _ X\omega \wedge \alpha \wedge \beta \leq \int _ XT\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\frac12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0.  \] Hence there is no closed Kähler current. $\square$

title: 12.20 Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary
search_title: Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary
section: 12.20 Orders of degeneration at the nef boundary
text: If $\theta $ is nef and $h$ is Hermitian, the volumes $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$ are positive and, by theorem 12.11.1 , decrease to $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. When this limit is zero, the rate of decay measures how degenerate $\theta $ is at the nef boundary. For a closed nef class on a compact Kähler manifold, choosing $h$ Kähler makes the volume of the perturbation the intersection polynomial $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n$, so it decays like an integral power of $\epsilon $ determined by the numerical dimension. For a nonclosed nef background the logarithmic rate of decay can be fractional, and it need not converge. We therefore define lower and upper orders of degeneration as lower and upper limits of this rate. Changing the probability measure or the perturbing metric only introduces bounded factors, so the orders are invariants of the background. Let $X$ again be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\mu $ a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$. Let $\theta $ be nef and let $h$ be Hermitian. For $0<\epsilon <1$, put \[  a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon ) =\frac{\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)}{\log \epsilon }.  \] The logarithm is finite because $\theta +\epsilon h$ belongs to $\mathscr P$, so that its volume is positive. Proposition 12.20.1 . EBFCF76A5A51 The limits \[  \underline a(\theta )=\liminf _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon ), \qquad \overline a(\theta )=\limsup _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )  \] are independent of $\mu $ and $h$, and satisfy \[  0\leq \underline a(\theta )\leq \overline a(\theta )\leq n.  \] They are unchanged when $\theta $ is replaced by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, with $f$ smooth, or by $r\theta $, with $r>0$. If $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )>0$, both limits are zero. Proof. Since $\theta $ is pseudoeffective, monotonicity and homogeneity give \[  \epsilon \lambda _\mu (h) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) \leq \lambda _\mu (\theta +h), \qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] Thus there are constants $c,C>0$ such that \[  c\epsilon ^ n\leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)\leq C, \qquad 0<\epsilon \leq 1.  \] Taking logarithms and dividing by the negative number $\log \epsilon $ shows that the quotients $a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )$ stay bounded as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, and that their lower and upper limits lie in $[0,n]$. By proposition 12.15.1 , changing the smooth probability measure multiplies the volume by a factor between two fixed positive constants. The resulting error in the logarithm is bounded, and after division by $\log \epsilon $ it tends to zero. For another Hermitian metric $h'$, choose constants $c_2\geq c_1>0$ with $c_1h\leq h'\leq c_2h$. Then \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +c_1\epsilon h) \leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h') \leq \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +c_2\epsilon h).  \] For any fixed $t>0$ and small $\epsilon $, \[  \frac{\log \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +t\epsilon h)}{\log \epsilon } =a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;t\epsilon ) \frac{\log (t\epsilon )}{\log \epsilon }.  \] The last factor tends to one and the first is bounded, while the rescaling $\epsilon \mapsto t\epsilon $ does not change lower and upper limits as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence the left side has the same lower and upper limits as $a_{\mu ,h}(\theta ;\epsilon )$. Dividing the preceding inequalities by $\log \epsilon <0$ reverses them, and taking lower and upper limits proves independence of the metric. Invariance under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes follows from that of $\mathcal V_\mu $. For scaling, homogeneity gives \[  \mathcal V_\mu (r\theta +\epsilon h) =r^ n\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +(\epsilon /r)h).  \] The bounded error $n\log r$ and the same rescaling argument prove scale invariance. Finally, if $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )>0$, then by theorem 12.11.1 the perturbed volumes lie between $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ and $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta +h)$ for $0<\epsilon \leq 1$, so both limits are zero. $\square$ We call $\underline a(\theta )$ and $\overline a(\theta )$ the lower and upper orders of degeneration of the nef background $\theta $. When they agree, their common value is the common order , and we then also say that $\theta $ has this order. The two orders can differ, and a common order can be irrational. Even when both are zero, the volume can tend to zero, at a logarithmic rate. The elliptic examples in section 12.21 exhibit each of these behaviors. Closed nef classes on Kähler manifolds, in contrast, degenerate polynomially. Proposition 12.20.2 . 883742E77C19 Suppose $X$ is Kähler, $\theta $ is closed and nef, and $h$ is Kähler. Set \[  r=\max \left\{ 0\leq k\leq n: \int _ X\theta ^ k\wedge h^{n-k}>0\right\} .  \] Then \[  \underline a(\theta )=\overline a(\theta )=n-r.  \] Thus $n$ minus the common order is the numerical dimension of the closed nef class of $\theta $. Proof. All the intersection numbers in the definition of $r$ are nonnegative. Indeed, the mixed integrals against $h$ of smooth positive representatives of $\theta +\delta h$ are positive, agree with the cohomological integrals by closed Stokes, and converge to the stated numbers as $\delta \downarrow 0$. The number for $k=0$ is $\int _ Xh^ n>0$, so $r$ is well defined. By the closed nef formula following theorem 12.11.1 , \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) =\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n =\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk\epsilon ^{n-k} \int _ X\theta ^ k\wedge h^{n-k}.  \] As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, the leading nonzero term is a positive constant times $\epsilon ^{n-r}$, and taking the logarithmic quotient proves the assertion. By proposition 12.20.1 , the result holds for every Hermitian perturbation, not only for Kähler ones. $\square$ The orders can also be computed on the non-Kähler Hopf threefold $X$ of section 23.1 . Keep its forms $\omega =\alpha +\beta $, where $\alpha \geq 0$ is closed of rank two, $\beta \geq 0$ has rank one, $\alpha ^3=\beta ^2=0$, and $\int _ X\omega ^3=6$. Take $\theta =\alpha $, $h=\omega $, and $\mu _0=\omega ^3/6$. The metric \[  \Omega _\epsilon =\alpha +\epsilon \omega =(1+\epsilon )\alpha +\epsilon \beta  \] is strictly positive. Its volume is \[  \Omega _\epsilon ^3=\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2\omega ^3 =6\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2\mu _0.  \] Hence the zero potential solves the smooth normalized equation, and \[  \mathcal V_{\mu _0}(\alpha +\epsilon \omega ) =6\epsilon (1+\epsilon )^2, \qquad \underline a(\alpha )=\overline a(\alpha )=1.  \] By proposition 12.20.1 , the same orders are obtained for every smooth positive probability measure and every Hermitian perturbation. Each perturbed metric nevertheless has infinite upper mass. If $V_ j$ are the smooth potentials of theorem 23.1.1 , then \[  \Omega _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\epsilon V_ j) =\alpha +\epsilon (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)>0,  \] and monotonicity of the determinant of positive matrices gives \[  \int _ X\bigl (\Omega _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\epsilon V_ j)\bigr )^3 \geq \epsilon ^3\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_ j)^3\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus a finite order of degeneration at the boundary coexists with infinite upper mass at every positive perturbation.
