title: 18.29 Partial kernels and quotient equilibrium
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. Throughout this chapter, $L$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$. In a local holomorphic frame $e$ write $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\chi }$; the curvature form $c_1(L,h)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form, independent of the frame, as in section 19.8 . A quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, the selecting potential, selects in each tensor power $L^ m$ the holomorphic sections $s$ for which $|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-m\varphi }$ is locally integrable. A partial Bergman kernel is the Bergman kernel of this space of sections for a Hilbert norm defined by a continuous weight: the singular function $\varphi $ decides which sections occur, but it does not enter their norms. On a compact Kähler manifold, if $\varphi $ is $c_1(L,h)$-plurisubharmonic with positive non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère mass, the normalized kernel measures converge to the Monge–Ampère measure of a partial envelope. The competitors defining this envelope have multiplier ideals contained in those of $\varphi $ at every positive real weight, and lie below the continuous weight on the set where the norm is computed. The envelope is the largest of these $c_1(L,h)$-plurisubharmonic functions. This chapter studies how much of this equilibrium theory survives when $X$ is not Kähler, and when the selecting potential is plurisubharmonic only with respect to a Hermitian form unrelated to the curvature of $L$. One direction of the Kähler argument is local and works on every compact complex manifold. A Bernstein–Markov estimate, which follows from the submean inequality, keeps the partial Fubini–Study potentials below the weight, and Lelong-number estimates on local modifications keep their limits within the multiplier-ideal class of $\varphi $. Together these bound every limit of the potentials by the partial envelope. A matching lower bound requires global sections approximating the envelope, and this is where the Kähler hypothesis enters. If $X$ admits a modification from a compact Kähler manifold, the relative canonical bundle with a Jacobian metric makes the selected spaces upstairs and downstairs isometric, and the Kähler theorem gives convergence of the kernel measures on $X$ itself. Fibrations show what can happen without such a modification. On a holomorphic submersion with compact connected fibers, every section of a pulled-back line bundle is constant along the fibers and descends to the base. Probability measures on the fibers make this descent an isometry, so the kernel measures on the total space are lifts of kernel measures on the base. Their limit, the quotient equilibrium measure, is the lift of the equilibrium measure of the base, and it appears at the growth rate $m^{\dim B}$ of the section spaces rather than at $m^{\dim X}$. On the Hopf manifold it is a Hermitian Monge–Ampère measure; in dimension three this gives a nonzero limit on a manifold without the bounded mass property. A selecting potential that is plurisubharmonic only with respect to a Hermitian form need not descend, but the sections it selects still do, so its singularities act only through a vanishing condition on the base. For isolated logarithmic poles, for poles along a section over a base divisor, and for anisotropic singularities controlled by integrability along the fibers, this condition differs from a multiplier-ideal condition on the base by a bounded number of vanishing orders. Such shifts cost only $O(m^{\dim B-1})$ sections, and for point poles and for poles along a section over a divisor the kernel measures still converge to a quotient equilibrium measure. The price is a loss of information: moving a pole along its fiber changes the multiplier ideals on $X$ but leaves every kernel unchanged. Explicit point and divisor models on projective bases compute the limits through binomial tails, and a change of the integration volume separates the base equilibrium measure from the conditional fiber probabilities carried by its lift. Two mechanisms control the explicit models that follow: the local metric weight determines the scale of evaluation, and the number of selected sections determines the mass of the kernel measure. When vanishing orders grow sublinearly in $m$, an entire-function model gives a Gaussian transition on a shrinking scale. Transferring it to a compact curve requires a uniform local comparison of norms and a global $L^2$ correction preserving the vanishing order; the remainder of the smooth weight moves the center of the transition. In two dimensions, competing monomials at a fixed curvature zero can already introduce a logarithmic factor into the scale of the full kernel. The section count also distinguishes selections with similar potential limits. A Newton polytope gives a graded monomial family whose growth constraint determines an envelope and whose lattice points determine the limiting mass. For a lower-dimensional polytope, concentration of the monomial norms gives a positive limit carried by real tori, although the higher curvature powers of the envelope vanish. Multiplier-ideal spaces need not form a graded family: rounding at critical divisors can make the leading count oscillate between even and odd degrees, while at the base points of a pencil three neighboring monomial bands contribute to a single positive limit. Convergence of the potentials therefore needs to be separated from convergence of the normalized measures. We use the following notation from earlier chapters. For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$, we write $u\preceq v$ if $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ if $u\preceq v\preceq u$ (definition 16.7.1 ); we write $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ if $\mathcal I(ku)\subseteq \mathcal I(kv)$ for every real $k>0$, and $u\sim _{\mathcal I}v$ if these ideals are equal for every $k>0$ (section 5.33 ). For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 18.4.1 , and $V_\theta $ is the upper envelope of all nonpositive $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions, which has minimal singularities (section 5.40 ). The non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is written $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, or $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ when its mass may be infinite (theorem 13.14.3 ).

title: 18.31 A local Bernstein–Markov estimate
text:
A Bernstein–Markov estimate compares the supremum norm of sections on a weighted compact set with an integral norm, up to an exponential loss in the degree whose rate can be made arbitrarily small. It is what keeps partial Fubini–Study potentials below the weight in the limit. For a smooth positive volume and a continuous weight on the whole manifold, it follows from the submean inequality. For a compact set $K\subseteq X$ and $w\in C(K)$, write \[  \| s\| _{m,w,K}=\sup _ K |s|_{h^ m}\mathrm{e}^{-mw/2}.  \] A probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ is Bernstein–Markov for $(K,w)$ if, for every $\epsilon >0$, there is a constant $C_\epsilon $ such that \[  \| s\| _{m,w,K}\leq C_\epsilon \mathrm{e}^{\epsilon m} \left(\int _ K|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw}\, \mathrm{d}\mu ight)^{1/2}  \] for all $m\geq 1$ and all $s\in H^0(X,L^ m)$. If $K$ is non-pluripolar, the supremum norm is a norm: the zero set of a nonzero section is an analytic hypersurface, hence pluripolar, and cannot contain $K$. The Bernstein–Markov inequality then shows that the integral \[  \| s\| _{m,w,\mu }^2=\int _ K|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw}\, \mathrm{d}\mu  \] is also a norm on $H^0(X,L^ m)$, and in particular on every selected space $V_ m$. The definitions of section 18.30 therefore apply with $(X,v,
u )$ replaced by $(K,w,\mu )$. We write $B_{m,w,\varphi ,\mu }$ for the resulting partial Bergman kernel on $K$ and $ eta _ m^{(r)}=(r!/m^ r)B_{m,w,\varphi ,\mu }\, \mu $ for the partial kernel measure; the extremal formula and the total mass $r!N_ m/m^ r$ hold as before. Proposition 18.31.1 . 5E124FAEA311 Let $v\in C(X)$. Every smooth positive probability measure on $X$ is Bernstein–Markov for $(X,v)$. Proof. Let $
u $ be a smooth positive probability measure, and fix $\epsilon >0$. Cover $X$ by finitely many coordinate charts on which $L$ has holomorphic frames, and choose relatively compact open subsets of these charts that still cover $X$. In a frame $e$ write $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\chi }$ and $s=f e^{\otimes m}$, so that $|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv}=|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m(\chi +v)}$. By compactness and uniform continuity of the finitely many functions $\chi +v$, there is a radius $\delta >0$ with the following property: every point $x$ lies in one of the smaller sets, the coordinate ball $B(x,\delta )$ lies in the corresponding chart, and the oscillation of $\chi +v$ on $B(x,\delta )$ is at most $2\epsilon $. On these balls the density of $
u $ with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure is bounded below by a positive constant independent of $x$. The submean inequality for the holomorphic function $f$ on $B(x,\delta )$ therefore gives \[   egin{split}  |s(x)|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv(x)} & =|f(x)|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m(\chi +v)(x)}\ & \leq C_\delta \mathrm{e}^{2\epsilon m} \int _{B(x,\delta )}|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m(\chi +v)}\, \mathrm{d}
u \ & \leq C_\delta \mathrm{e}^{2\epsilon m}\| s\| _{m,v,
u }^2, \end{split}  \] with $C_\delta $ independent of $x$ and $m$. Taking the supremum over $x$ and then the square root gives the Bernstein–Markov inequality with $C_\epsilon =C_\delta ^{1/2}$. $\square$ For a general compact set $K$ and weight $w\in C(K)$, the Bernstein–Markov property is not automatic, and we assume it explicitly whenever it is needed.

title: 18.32 Partial envelopes on a weighted compact set

section: 18.32 Partial envelopes on a weighted compact set
text: Two constraints act on limits of partial Fubini–Study potentials. The continuous weight is an obstacle on the set where sections are measured, and the selecting potential imposes a multiplier-ideal constraint on the whole manifold. The partial envelope is the largest potential satisfying both. Since an obstacle on a non-pluripolar compact set bounds every competitor globally, the partial envelope lies below a translate of the multiplier-ideal envelope of the selecting potential; conversely, a translate of that envelope lying below the obstacle is a competitor. The partial envelope therefore differs from the multiplier-ideal envelope by a bounded function. Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and non-pluripolar, and let $w\in C(K,\mathbb R)$. Recall that theorem 5.37.3 characterizes the order $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ by Lelong numbers on local modifications. As in section 5.40 , an inequality holds quasi-everywhere if it holds outside a pluripolar set. The partial envelope of $\varphi $ with obstacle $w$ on $K$ is B5A5A1951FC8 18.32.1 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta ,K}[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}(w) & =\Bigl (\sup \bigl \{ a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ): a\preceq _{\mathcal I}\varphi ,\\ & \hspace{52pt}a\leq w\text{ quasi-everywhere on }K\bigr \} \Bigr )^*. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Theorem 18.32.2 . 04BABC8924B6 The function $E=E_{\theta ,K}[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}(w)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and it is the largest member of its defining family. Let $q=P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}$, and let $C$ be a constant as in lemma 5.40.1 , so that $\sup _ Xa\leq C$ for every $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq w$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. Then \[  q+\min _ Kw\leq E\leq q+C.  \] In particular, $E\sim q$ and \[  E\sim _{\mathcal I}\varphi .  \] Proof. By theorem 18.4.2 , $q\leq 0$ and $q\sim _{\mathcal I}\varphi $. Hence $q+\min _ Kw$ belongs to the defining family. Lemma 5.40.1 bounds the entire family above by $C$, so its regularized supremum $E$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and $E\geq q+\min _ Kw$. For the upper bound, let $a$ be a member of the family. Since $\sup _ Xa\leq C$, proposition 18.4.4 , proposition 18.4.6 give \[  a-C\leq a-\sup _ Xa\leq P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_\theta [\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}=q.  \] Taking the regularized supremum over $a$ proves $E\leq q+C$. The Bernstein–Markov inequality keeps the partial Fubini–Study potentials below the weight on $K$, up to an error that becomes arbitrarily small as the degree grows. The multiplier-ideal constraint survives in the limit because, on a fixed local modification, the Lelong numbers of the potentials fall short of those of the selecting potential by at most $O(m^{-1})$. To pass the obstacle condition to $L^1$ limits when $K$ has zero smooth volume, we compare the potentials with the envelope of the obstacle alone, which is defined on all of $X$. Now take $	heta =c_1(L,h)$, assume $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and let $\mu $ be a Bernstein–Markov probability measure for $(K,w)$, with $K$ and $w$ as in section 18.32 . Use the selected spaces $V_ m$ and their dimensions $N_ m$ from section 18.30 . Choose an orthonormal basis $s_1,\ldots ,s_{N_ m}$ of $V_ m$ for the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,w,\mu }$ of section 18.31 , and define the partial Fubini–Study potential \[  U_ m= rac1m\log \sum _{j=1}^{N_ m}|s_ j|_{h^ m}^2 \quad (N_ m>0).  \] Set $U_ m\equiv -\infty $ if $N_ m=0$. When $N_ m>0$, the local expression in a holomorphic frame, as in the proof of proposition 19.8.3 , shows that $U_ m\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and that $U_ m$ has analytic singularities. On $K$ it satisfies $\mathrm{e}^{m(U_ m-w)}=B_{m,w,\varphi ,\mu }$. Let $\pi :Y	o W$ be a local smooth modification of an open set $W\subseteq X$, let $y\in Y$, and write $J_\pi $ for the local holomorphic Jacobian determinant of $\pi $. Each $s_ j$ lies in $V_ m$, so lemma 5.38.10 applies to its local coefficient. Since the Lelong number of the logarithm of a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic functions is the minimum of their vanishing orders, and the smooth metric contributes nothing, we obtain \[  
u (U_ m\circ \pi ,y) \geq 
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y) - rac{n+\operatorname {ord}_ yJ_\pi }{m} \qquad (N_ m>0).  \] Theorem 18.33.1 . 336ACC796329 The potentials $U_ m$ with $N_ m>0$ form a relatively compact subset of $L^1(X)$. Let $U$ be the $L^1$ limit of a sequence $U_{m_ j}$ with $N_{m_ j}>0$ and $m_ j	o \infty $. Then $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, \[  U\preceq _{\mathcal I}\varphi ,  \] and $U\leq w$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. Consequently \[  \left(\limsup _{m	o \infty }U_ might)^* \leq E_{	heta ,K}[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}(w).  \] If only finitely many selected spaces are nonzero, the left-hand side is identically $-\infty $. Proof. Step 1: compactness. The extremal formula for the kernel and the Bernstein–Markov inequality give, for every $\epsilon >0$ and with $C_\epsilon \geq 1$, \[  U_ m\leq w+\delta _{m,\epsilon }\quad \hbox{on }K, \qquad \delta _{m,\epsilon }=2\epsilon + rac{2\log C_\epsilon }{m}.  \] No factor depending on $N_ m$ occurs, because the extremal formula is a supremum over single sections of unit norm. Let $U_{m_ j}	o U$ in $L^1(X)$, with $m_ j	o \infty $. Fix a local smooth modification $\pi :Y	o W$ of an open set $W\subseteq X$, and a point $y\in Y$. By lemma 5.43.19 , $U_{m_ j}\circ \pi 	o U\circ \pi $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Upper semicontinuity of Lelong numbers (lemma 5.38.7 ) and the order bound before the theorem give \[  
u (U\circ \pi ,y) \geq \limsup _ j
u (U_{m_ j}\circ \pi ,y) \geq 
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y).  \] Since $\pi $ and $y$ are arbitrary, the local valuative characterization in theorem 5.37.3 gives $U\preceq _{\mathcal I}\varphi $. Since $K$ may have zero smooth volume, the inequality on $K$ in Step 1 does not pass directly to $L^1$ limits. We therefore use the envelope of the obstacle alone. u }$ on the whole manifold from section 18.30 , with selecting potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. Fix $m$ with $N_ m>0$ and a basis of $V_ m$, and let $G_ m(v)$ be the Gram matrix of this basis for $\| \cdot \| _{m,v,
u }$, a positive definite Hermitian matrix. The determinant functional is \[  \mathcal F_ m^{(r)}(v) =- rac{r!}{m^{r+1}} \log  rac{\det G_ m(v)}{\det G_ m(0)}.  \] A change of basis multiplies both determinants by the same positive factor, so $\mathcal F_ m^{(r)}$ does not depend on the basis. title: 18.34.3 Dependence on the continuous weight
text:
When only the continuous weight changes, the selected space stays the same, and the two norms are related by a multiplication operator compressed to that space. Inverting this operator expresses the new reproducing vectors through the old ones. As a consequence the kernel itself, and not only the determinant functional, depends analytically on the weight. Keep $m\geq 1$, the selecting potential $\varphi $, the metric $h$ and the probability measure $
u $ fixed as in section 18.30 , and write $B_ v=B_{m,v,\varphi ,
u }$ and $ eta _ v= eta _ m^{(r)}$ for the kernel and the kernel measure at the weight $v$. Let $P_ v$ be the orthogonal projection of the weighted $L^2$ space of measurable sections of $L^ m$, with the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,v,
u }$, onto $V_ m$, and let \[  Z_ m=\{ x\in X:s(x)=0	ext{ for every }s\in V_ m\}   \] be the common zero set of the selected sections. At each $x\in X$ choose a covector of unit length on the fiber $(L^ m)_ x$; it defines a complex-linear evaluation $\ell _ x:V_ m	o \mathbb C$. Let $k_{v,x}\in V_ m$ be its Riesz vector, so that $\ell _ x(s)=\langle s,k_{v,x}angle _{m,v,
u }$ for all $s\in V_ m$. Then 389325A12314 18.34.4  egin{equation}  B_ v(x)=\mathrm{e}^{-mv(x)}\ell _ x(k_{v,x}) =\mathrm{e}^{-mv(x)}\| k_{v,x}\| _{m,v,
u }^2. \end{equation} These values do not depend on the phase of the chosen covector. Proposition 18.34.5 . 81FC6A666EC9 The map $v\mapsto B_ v$ from $C(X,\mathbb R)$ to $C(X,\mathbb R)$ is real analytic. The map $v\mapsto  eta _ v$ is real analytic with values in the finite signed measures on $X$, equipped with the total variation norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$. If $V_ m=\{ 0\} $, both maps vanish identically. Proof. If $V_ m=\{ 0\} $ there is nothing to prove. Fix a real weight $v_0$. For $f\in C(X,\mathbb C)$ define an operator on $V_ m$ by \[  T(f)s=P_{v_0}(\mathrm{e}^{-mf}s).  \] Since the exponential series converges in the uniform norm, $T$ is an entire function of $f$ with values in the endomorphisms of $V_ m$. Since $P_{v_0}$ is a contraction, \[  \| T(f)-I\| \leq \mathrm{e}^{m\| f\| _\infty }-1.  \] Hence, for $m\| f\| _\infty <\log (3/2)$, we have $\| T(f)-I\| <1/2$, so the Neumann series for $T(f)^{-1}$ converges in operator norm and $\| T(f)^{-1}\| \leq 2$. For real $f$, the operator $T(f)$ is selfadjoint and represents the new inner product: \[  \langle s,uangle _{m,v_0+f,
u } =\langle T(f)s,uangle _{m,v_0,
u }.  \] In particular it is positive definite, bounded below by $\mathrm{e}^{-m\| f\| _\infty }I$. The Riesz identity therefore gives \[  k_{v_0+f,x}=T(f)^{-1}k_{v_0,x}.  \] For complex $f$ the right-hand side is still a holomorphic function of $f$. Consequently \[  f\longmapsto \mathrm{e}^{-m(v_0(x)+f(x))} \ell _ x igl (T(f)^{-1}k_{v_0,x} igr )  \] is a holomorphic extension of $f\mapsto B_{v_0+f}(x)$. Evaluations on the finite-dimensional space $V_ m$ are uniformly bounded over the compact manifold $X$, so the linear map $A\mapsto [x\mapsto \ell _ x(Ak_{v_0,x})]$ from the endomorphisms of $V_ m$ to $C(X)$ is bounded; it is well defined because the phases of $\ell _ x$ and $k_{v_0,x}$ cancel. Hence the extension is holomorphic as a map with values in $C(X)$. Finally, $B\mapsto (r!/m^ r)B
u $ is a bounded linear map into finite measures with the total variation norm, which proves the assertion about $ eta _ v$. At points of $Z_ m$ the Riesz vector is zero, so the argument includes the common zero set. $\square$ Now let $I\subset \mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $t\mapsto v_ t$ be a smooth curve in $C(X,\mathbb R)$. The complete exponential Bell polynomials are \[  \mathcal B_ j(x_1,\ldots ,x_ j) =\sum _{\sum _{\ell =1}^ j\ell n_\ell =j} j!\prod _{\ell =1}^ j  rac{(x_\ell /\ell !)^{n_\ell }}{n_\ell !}, \qquad j\geq 1,  \] where the sum runs over nonnegative integers $n_1,\ldots ,n_ j$. Write $\mathcal B_ j(-mv_ t)$ for $\mathcal B_ j$ evaluated at the first $j$ derivatives of $-mv_ t$ with respect to $t$, so that $\partial _ t^ j\mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t}=\mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t}\mathcal B_ j(-mv_ t)$ by Faà di Bruno's formula. Define operators on $V_ m$ by \[  \mathcal T_{t,j}u=-P_{v_ t} igl (\mathcal B_ j(-mv_ t)u igr ), \qquad u\in V_ m.  \] For $k\geq 1$, let $\Lambda _ k$ be the set of compositions of $k$, that is, of ordered tuples $\alpha =(\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ p)$ of positive integers with sum $k$, and set $\alpha !=\prod _{j=1}^ p\alpha _ j!$. Theorem 18.34.6 . F82E8E685FEA For every $k\geq 1$, 59C2D7B608B5 18.34.7  egin{equation}  \partial _ t^ k k_{v_ t,x} =\sum _{\alpha \in \Lambda _ k} rac{k!}{\alpha !} \mathcal T_{t,\alpha _ p}\cdots \mathcal T_{t,\alpha _1}k_{v_ t,x}. \end{equation} Suppose moreover that $s\geq 1$, that $J\Subset I$ is a compact interval, and that constants $A,R>0$ satisfy \[  \sup _{t\in J}\| \partial _ t^ jv_ t\| _\infty \leq AR^ j(j!)^ s\qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Then there are constants $C,L>0$, depending only on the fixed data and on $m,r,J,A,R,s$, such that 1BF37D25A2C8 18.34.8  egin{equation}  \sup _{t\in J} \left(\| \partial _ t^ kB_{v_ t}\| _\infty +\| \partial _ t^ k eta _{v_ t}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}ight) \leq CL^ k(k!)^ s\qquad (k\geq 0). \end{equation} Thus the kernel and the kernel measure are of Gevrey class $s$ in the parameter. Proof. The derivative formula. By proposition 18.34.5 , $k_{v_ t,x}$ depends smoothly on $t$, for any fixed norm on $V_ m$. Since $H(a)-I=O(|a|)$, truncating the Neumann series of $H(a)^{-1}$ after $k$ powers leaves a remainder $O(|a|^{k+1})$. Expanding the truncated series to order $k$ in $a$ gives ( 18.34.7 ), with its ordered products and coefficients $k!/\alpha !$. Only a finite Taylor jet of the smooth curve is used. Gevrey bounds. For nonnegative integers $n_\ell $ with $\sum \ell n_\ell =j$, \[  \prod _{\ell =1}^ j(\ell !)^{(s-1)n_\ell } \leq (j!)^{s-1}.  \] The sum $\sum \prod _\ell (n_\ell !)^{-1}$ over these tuples is the coefficient of $z^ j$ in $\exp (z/(1-z))$, and evaluation at $z=1/2$ shows that it is at most $\mathrm{e}\, 2^ j$. Since $P_{v_ t}$ is a contraction, each ordered product in ( 18.34.7 ) has operator norm at most $L_0^ k(\alpha !)^ s$. There are $2^{k-1}$ compositions of $k$, and $\alpha !\leq k!$. Since $v_ t$ is uniformly bounded for $t\in J$, the norms $\| \cdot \| _{m,v_ t,
u }$ are uniformly equivalent, and the evaluations and Riesz vectors are bounded uniformly on $J	imes X$. Hence the $t$-derivatives of the unweighted diagonal $x\mapsto \ell _ x(k_{v_ t,x})$ are bounded in $C(X)$ by $C(2L_0)^ k(k!)^ s$. The factor $\mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t}$ satisfies bounds of the same Gevrey order, by the estimate for $\mathcal B_ j(-mv_ t)$. Leibniz's formula and $j!(k-j)!\leq k!$ then give ( 18.34.8 ) for $B_{v_ t}$, and the bounded linear map $B\mapsto (r!/m^ r)B
u $ gives the bound in total variation. $\square$ Corollary 18.34.9 . 7733E1B20E7B Let $v_ t=v+tq$ with $v,q\in C(X,\mathbb R)$. For $x
otin Z_ m$, the probability measure F73FC2DA9CA6 18.34.10  egin{equation}  \mathrm{d}\sigma _{t,x}(y) = rac{|k_{v_ t,x}(y)|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t(y)}}{\| k_{v_ t,x}\| _{m,v_ t,
u }^2}\, \mathrm{d}
u (y) \end{equation} satisfies CDF008B0B2C7 18.34.11  egin{equation}   rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log B_{v_ t}(x) =m\left(\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _{t,x}-q(x)ight). \end{equation} On $Z_ m$ the kernel and all its $t$-derivatives vanish. Moreover, $\int _ X\partial _ tB_{v_ t}\, \mathrm{d}
u =0$. Proof. Since $\mathcal T_{t,1}u=mP_{v_ t}(qu)$, the case $k=1$ of ( 18.34.7 ) gives $\partial _ tk_{v_ t,x}=mP_{v_ t}(qk_{v_ t,x})$. Applying the fixed evaluation $\ell _ x$ and the Riesz identity gives \[  \partial _ t\ell _ x(k_{v_ t,x}) =m\int _ Xq|k_{v_ t,x}|_{h^ m}^2 \mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t}\, \mathrm{d}
u .  \] Dividing by the positive number $\ell _ x(k_{v_ t,x})=\| k_{v_ t,x}\| _{m,v_ t,
u }^2$ and differentiating the factor $\mathrm{e}^{-mv_ t(x)}$ in ( 18.34.4 ) proves ( 18.34.11 ); the density in ( 18.34.10 ) has integral one by the definition of the norm. At points of $Z_ m$ the evaluations and Riesz vectors vanish for every weight. Finally, differentiating the identity $\int _ XB_{v_ t}\, \mathrm{d}
u =N_ m$ in $C(X)$ proves the last assertion. For constant $q$ the right-hand side of ( 18.34.11 ) vanishes, in accordance with the invariance of the kernel under adding a constant to the weight. $\square$ The uniform norm on the weights is essential in these results, because it controls the weight on the whole region of integration. The next example shows that real-analytic dependence of the weight on a parameter at each interior point of a domain does not suffice. Example 18.34.12 . 5DA140DF64C6 On the unit disk $D\subset \mathbb C$ with Euclidean area $\mathrm{d}A$, let $K_ t$ be the Bergman kernel of the Hilbert space of holomorphic functions $f$ on $D$ with the norm $(\int _ D|f|^2ho _ t\, \mathrm{d}A)^{1/2}$, where \[  ho _ t(z)=1+ rac{t^2}{(1-|z|^2)^2+t^2},\qquad t\in \mathbb R.  \] The weights $-\log ho _ t$ are bounded and depend real analytically on $(z,t)\in D	imes \mathbb R$, but 8F78E08AD393 18.34.13  egin{equation}  K_ t(0,0)=  egin{cases}  [\pi (1+|t|\arctan (1/|t|))]^{-1},& t
e 0,\  \pi ^{-1},& t=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} In particular, $K_ t(0,0)=\pi ^{-1}-|t|/2+O(t^2)$, so $K_ t(0,0)$ is not differentiable at $t=0$. Proof. The density $ho _ t$ is radial and lies between one and two. By radial symmetry, the constant functions are orthogonal to the holomorphic functions vanishing at the origin, so the reproducing value at the center is the reciprocal of $\int _ Dho _ t\, \mathrm{d}A$. Polar coordinates and the substitution $a=1-r^2$ give, for $t
e 0$, \[  \int _ Dho _ t\, \mathrm{d}A =\pi \int _0^1\left(1+ rac{t^2}{a^2+t^2}ight)\mathrm{d}a =\pi  igl (1+|t|\arctan (1/|t|) igr ).  \] For $t=0$ the integral is $\pi $. This proves ( 18.34.13 ) and the expansion. For every $t
e 0$ we have $\| \log ho _ t\| _{L^\infty (D)}=\log 2$, whereas $ho _0=1$. Thus the curve $t\mapsto \log ho _ t$ is not continuous at $t=0$ for the uniform norm, and the example does not contradict proposition 18.34.5 . $\square$ Throughout these estimates the degree $m$ and the selected space were fixed, and the constants depend on $m$. A limit envelope need not even be differentiable in the weight, as the corner in example 16.28.40 shows; differentiating limits would require estimates uniform in $m$.

title: Proposition 18.34.18
text: Proposition 18.34.18 . 4920A08E02F1 For $q,v,w\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, write $\operatorname {osc}_ Xq=\sup _ Xq-\inf _ Xq$. Then 5CBC01E88DA5 18.34.19 \begin{equation}  D\mu _ v[q]=m(\mathcal Q_ vq-q)\mu _ v, \qquad \| D\mu _ v[q]\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \frac m2\operatorname {osc}_ Xq. \end{equation} Consequently E8E6AD8629D0 18.34.20 \begin{equation}  \| \mu _ w-\mu _ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 2\tanh \left(\frac m4\operatorname {osc}_ X(w-v)\right). \end{equation} These bounds do not depend on $N_ m$. In particular, let $v_ m,w_ m\in C(X,\mathbb R)$ along a sequence of degrees with nonzero selected spaces. If $m\operatorname {osc}_ X(w_ m-v_ m)\to 0$, then the two sequences of normalized kernel probabilities have the same weak, or total variation, limit whenever one of them converges in that topology. Proof. The formula for $D\mu _ v[q]$ follows from corollary 18.34.9 , since $N_ m$ does not depend on the weight. For the bound, put $g=q-\mathcal Q_ vq$, $A=\{ g>0\} $ and $p=\mu _ v(A)$. Since $\mathcal Q_ v$ preserves integrals, $g$ has mean zero, and selfadjointness gives \[  \int _ Ag\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ v =\langle q,(I-\mathcal Q_ v)\mathbf1_ A\rangle _{L^2(\mu _ v)}.  \] The function $(I-\mathcal Q_ v)\mathbf1_ A$ is nonnegative on $A$ and nonpositive on its complement, almost everywhere, and its integral is zero. Subtracting $\inf _ Xq$ from $q$ does not change the pairing, which is therefore at most \[  \operatorname {osc}_ Xq \bigl (p-\langle \mathbf1_ A,\mathcal Q_ v\mathbf1_ A\rangle \bigr ).  \] Positivity of $\mathcal Q_ v$, applied to $\mathbf1_ A-p$, gives $\langle \mathbf1_ A,\mathcal Q_ v\mathbf1_ A\rangle \geq p^2$: since $\mathcal Q_ v$ fixes constants and preserves integrals, $\langle \mathbf1_ A-p,\mathcal Q_ v(\mathbf1_ A-p)\rangle =\langle \mathbf1_ A,\mathcal Q_ v\mathbf1_ A\rangle -p^2$. As $g$ has mean zero, it follows that \[  \| g\| _{L^1(\mu _ v)} =2\int _ Ag\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ v \leq 2\operatorname {osc}_ Xq\, p(1-p) \leq \tfrac 12\operatorname {osc}_ Xq.  \] The total variation norm of a signed measure is the integral of the absolute value of its density, so $\| D\mu _ v[q]\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=m\| g\| _{L^1(\mu _ v)}$, and ( 18.34.19 ) follows. For the global estimate, take $q=w-v$, $v_ t=v+tq$, $\mu _ t=\mu _{v_ t}$ and $\mathcal Q_ t=\mathcal Q_{v_ t}$ for $0\leq t\leq 1$, and put $a=m\operatorname {osc}_ Xq$. For a Borel set $E$, the function $p_ t=\mu _ t(E)$ is differentiable, because integration against $\mathbf1_ E$ is a bounded linear functional for the total variation norm, and selfadjointness gives \[  p'_ t=-m\langle q,(I-\mathcal Q_ t)\mathbf1_ E\rangle _{L^2(\mu _ t)}.  \] The function $(I-\mathcal Q_ t)\mathbf1_ E$ has positive and negative parts whose integrals both equal $p_ t-\langle \mathbf1_ E,\mathcal Q_ t\mathbf1_ E\rangle $. Bounding $q$ above and below on the supports of these parts, and applying positivity to $\mathbf1_ E-p_ t$ as before, we obtain \[  |p'_ t|\leq a\bigl (p_ t-\langle \mathbf1_ E,\mathcal Q_ t\mathbf1_ E\rangle \bigr ) \leq ap_ t(1-p_ t).  \] All the kernels $B_{v_ t}$ are positive exactly off the common zero set $Z_ m$, so the probabilities $\mu _ t$ are mutually absolutely continuous. Hence, if $p_0$ is zero or one, then $p_ t=p_0$ for all $t$. Otherwise $0<p_ t<1$ for all $t$, and integration gives \[  \left|\log \frac{p_1}{1-p_1}-\log \frac{p_0}{1-p_0}\right|\leq a.  \] Let $\sigma (z)=\mathrm{e}^ z/(1+\mathrm{e}^ z)$ be the logistic function. If $p_1\geq p_0$ and $z=\log (p_0/(1-p_0))$, then \[  p_1-p_0\leq \sigma (z+a)-\sigma (z) =\frac{\sinh (a/2)}{\cosh (z+a/2)+\cosh (a/2)} \leq \tanh (a/4).  \] The case $p_1\leq p_0$ is symmetric. Since $\mu _ w-\mu _ v$ has total mass zero, its total variation norm is $2\sup _ E|\mu _ w(E)-\mu _ v(E)|$, which proves ( 18.34.20 ). Under the hypothesis of the last assertion the right-hand side tends to zero, which gives the final statement. $\square$

text: Proposition 18.34.22 . 4F99D774A693 Put $\rho =\log (3/2)$. The map $f\mapsto \mu _{v+f/m}$ extends holomorphically to the ball $\{ f\in C(X,\mathbb C):\| f\| _\infty <\rho \} $, with values in complex measures of total variation at most three. For real $q\in C(X)$ and $k\geq 1$, 961FF4CC03F6 18.34.23 \begin{equation}  \left\| \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^ k}{\mathrm{d}t^ k}\right|_{t=0} \mu _{v+tq}\right\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 3k!\left(\frac{m\operatorname {osc}_ Xq}{2\rho }\right)^ k. \end{equation} The radius $\rho $ and the bound three do not depend on $m$, $N_ m$ or the real base weight $v$. Proof. On $V_ m$ use $T(f)=P_ v(\mathrm{e}^{-f}\, \cdot \, )$, the operator in the proof of proposition 18.34.5 for the perturbation $f/m$ of the weight $v$. That proof gives $\| T(f)^{-1}\| \leq 2$ on the ball. The extended measure has the density \[  \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-mv(x)-f(x)}}{N_ m} \ell _ x\bigl (T(f)^{-1}k_{v,x}\bigr )  \] with respect to $\nu $. By the Riesz identity at the weight $v$, its absolute value is at most $2\mathrm{e}^{\| f\| _\infty }B_ v(x)/N_ m\leq 3B_ v(x)/N_ m$, so its total variation is at most three. For a complex constant $c$ we have $T(f+c)=\mathrm{e}^{-c}T(f)$, and the resulting factor $\mathrm{e}^{c}$ cancels the factor $\mathrm{e}^{-c}$ in the density; thus adding constants to $f$ does not change the extension. If $q$ is constant, the measure does not depend on $t$, and all derivatives vanish. $\square$

title: 18.35 Partial kernels under a modification
text:
A modification identifies holomorphic sections, but it changes the integrability condition that defines multiplier ideals; the correction is a twist by the relative canonical bundle, through the Jacobian. If the relative canonical bundle carries the metric determined by two volume forms, the same Jacobian factor makes the identification of section spaces an isometry. The partial kernel measures downstairs are then exactly the pushforwards of those upstairs, and the convergence theorem on compact Kähler manifolds descends to every compact complex manifold that admits a Kähler modification. Let $\pi :Y	o X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds. We use the exceptional set $S\subset X$, its inverse image $D=\pi ^{-1}(S)\subset Y$, the relative canonical bundle $R_\pi $ and its Jacobian section $J_\pi $ from subsection 5.43.21 , together with the transformation of multiplier ideals in lemma 5.43.22 and the invariance of the multiplier-ideal order in lemma 5.43.23 . Proposition 18.35.1 . 609A9325CEC9 Let $	heta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For $v\in C(X)$ let $E_ X(v)=E_{	heta ,X}[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}(v)$ be the partial envelope with obstacle $v$ on the whole of $X$. Then \[  E_{\pi ^*	heta ,Y}[\varphi \circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}(v\circ \pi ) =E_ X(v)\circ \pi .  \] Moreover, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ the non-pluripolar measures satisfy \[  \pi _*\mathrm{MA}_{\pi ^*	heta }(u\circ \pi ) =\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)  \] as positive Borel measures, possibly of infinite total mass. Proof. By proposition 5.43.18 , $a\mapsto a\circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. For a continuous obstacle on the whole manifold, the quasi-everywhere and the pointwise obstacle conditions are equivalent, as recalled in section 5.40 , and since $\pi $ is surjective, $a\leq v$ on $X$ if and only if $a\circ \pi \leq v\circ \pi $ on $Y$. Together with lemma 5.43.23 , this identifies the two families of competitors. By theorem 18.32.2 , each partial envelope is the largest member of its family, which proves the envelope identity; no interchange of pullback and regularized supremum is needed. The map $\pi $ is a biholomorphism from $Y\setminus D$ onto $X\setminus S$, so locality of the non-pluripolar product identifies the two measures there. Neither measure charges the analytic sets $D$ and $S$. Testing against nonnegative Borel functions, or exhausting the complements by increasing compact sets, proves the pushforward identity, including the case of infinite total mass. $\square$ Choose smooth positive probability volumes $
u _ X$ on $X$ and $
u _ Y$ on $Y$. They determine a smooth Hermitian metric $h_ R$ on $R_\pi $ such that 7BB9F79BDB65 18.35.2  egin{equation}  |J_\pi |_{h_ R}^2\, 
u _ Y=\pi ^*
u _ X. \end{equation} Explicitly, let $f_ X$ and $f_ Y$ be the densities of $
u _ X$ and $
u _ Y$ in local coordinates. The local frame of $R_\pi $ given by the quotient of the coordinate canonical frames is given the squared norm $(f_ X\circ \pi )/f_ Y$. This function is smooth and strictly positive, also where $J_\pi $ vanishes, and the transformation rules of the coordinate densities show that it defines a metric. Equation ( 18.35.2 ) is an identity of smooth top-degree forms; it does not define the pullback of an arbitrary measure. Proposition 18.35.3 . u _ Y$, and define the kernels and kernel measures as in section 18.30 , with the fixed factor $(R_\pi ,h_ R)$ added. Then the identification $s\mapsto J_\pi \pi ^*s$, \[  H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )) \simeq H^0(Y,\pi ^*L^ m\otimes R_\pi \otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi \circ \pi )),  \] is an isometry for the continuous weighted norms. By ( 18.35.2 ) and the change of variables formula, \[  \int _ Y|J_\pi \pi ^*s|_{\pi ^*h^ m\otimes h_ R}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv\circ \pi }\, \mathrm{d}
u _ Y =\int _ X|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv}\, \mathrm{d}
u _ X.  \] The selecting potential has already determined the section spaces and does not enter the norms. Hence the identification maps an orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis, and summing the squared pointwise norms of the basis vectors gives the kernel formula, also at the zeros of $J_\pi $. Multiplying by $r!/m^ r$ and integrating a continuous function pulled back from $X$ proves the measure formula. $\square$

title: Proposition 18.35.1
text: Proposition 18.35.1 . 609A9325CEC9 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For $v\in C(X)$ let $E_ X(v)=E_{\theta ,X}[\varphi ]_{\mathcal I}(v)$ be the partial envelope with obstacle $v$ on the whole of $X$. Then \[  E_{\pi ^*\theta ,Y}[\varphi \circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}(v\circ \pi ) =E_ X(v)\circ \pi .  \] Moreover, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ the non-pluripolar measures satisfy \[  \pi _*\mathrm{MA}_{\pi ^*\theta }(u\circ \pi ) =\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)  \] as positive Borel measures, possibly of infinite total mass. Proof. By proposition 5.43.18 , $a\mapsto a\circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$. For a continuous obstacle on the whole manifold, the quasi-everywhere and the pointwise obstacle conditions are equivalent, as recalled in section 5.40 , and since $\pi $ is surjective, $a\leq v$ on $X$ if and only if $a\circ \pi \leq v\circ \pi $ on $Y$. Together with lemma 5.43.23 , this identifies the two families of competitors. By theorem 18.32.2 , each partial envelope is the largest member of its family, which proves the envelope identity; no interchange of pullback and regularized supremum is needed. The map $\pi $ is a biholomorphism from $Y\setminus D$ onto $X\setminus S$, so locality of the non-pluripolar product identifies the two measures there. Neither measure charges the analytic sets $D$ and $S$. title: Proposition 18.35.3
18.35.4 Convergence with a Kähler modification
text:
Through the Jacobian isometry, the equilibrium theorem on a compact Kähler manifold can be pushed down along a modification. The limit does not depend on the modification, because both the partial envelope and its non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure descend. Theorem 18.35.5 . B187DFAF6D97 Suppose that $X$ admits a modification from a compact Kähler manifold. Let $L	o X$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$, put $	heta =c_1(L,h)$, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (\varphi )(X)>0.  \] Then, for every $v\in C(X)$ and every smooth positive probability volume $
u _ X$, the partial kernel measures on $X$ satisfy \[   rac{n!}{m^ n}B_{m,v,\varphi ,
u _ X}\, 
u _ X ightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}_	heta (E_ X(v)).  \] The limit measure is finite and nonzero. Its total mass is \[  M=\lim _{m	o \infty } rac{n!}{m^ n} h^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )),  \] which does not depend on $v$ or $
u _ X$. The limit does not depend on the choice of Kähler modification. Proof. Choose a modification $\pi :Y	o X$ from a compact Kähler manifold $Y$, and a smooth positive probability volume $
u _ Y$ on $Y$. The pullback $\varphi \circ \pi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$, and by proposition 18.35.1 its non-pluripolar mass equals the given positive mass of $\varphi $. This mass is finite, by the theory of closed classes on compact Kähler manifolds. Apply [ Theorem 14.3.1 , SGPT ] on $Y$, with the line bundle $\pi ^*L$, the auxiliary twisting line bundle $R_\pi $, the continuous obstacle $v\circ \pi $ on $Y$ and the probability volume $
u _ Y$. Its Bernstein–Markov hypothesis follows from the proof of proposition 18.31.1 , since a fixed smooth auxiliary bundle only changes the local constants. The multiplier ideals and the continuous weighted norms in that theorem agree exactly with those of proposition 18.35.3 . The theorem gives \[   eta _{Y,m}^{(n)}ightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}_{\pi ^*	heta }  igl (E_{\pi ^*	heta ,Y}[\varphi \circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}(v\circ \pi ) igr ),  \] and the limit measure has finite positive mass. Now push this convergence forward to $X$, testing against continuous functions on $X$. By the kernel identity of proposition 18.35.3 and the envelope and pushforward identities of proposition 18.35.1 , this gives the asserted limit on $X$. Testing the constant function one shows that $n!N_ m/m^ n$ converges to the total mass of the limit, which proves the formula for $M$; the dimensions $N_ m$ involve neither $v$ nor the volumes. Finally, the limit is expressed entirely on $X$, so it does not depend on the modification. $\square$ Since $M>0$, the sections of $L$ grow at the maximal rate $m^ n$, so $X$ is Moishezon by corollary 19.9.17 . A Kähler modification also forces the bounded mass property, by lemma 19.9.12 ; the Jacobian identities, by contrast, hold for every modification of compact complex manifolds. When the section spaces grow more slowly than $m^ n$, the total mass identity shows that the kernel measures must instead be normalized by the growth degree of $N_ m$, as in section 18.36 . Corollary 18.35.6 . 9C43863CE5F1 Under the hypotheses of theorem 18.35.5 , let $M$ be the limit of the normalized dimensions in that theorem. The determinant functionals $\mathcal F_ m^{(n)}$ of section 18.34 converge pointwise on $C(X)$ to \[  \mathcal F(v)=\int _0^1\! \left(\int _ X v\, \mathrm{d}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E_ X(tv))ight)\mathrm{d}t.  \] This functional is concave and vanishes at zero, and for $v,w\in C(X,\mathbb R)$ and $c\in \mathbb R$, \[  \mathcal F(v+c)=\mathcal F(v)+Mc,\qquad |\mathcal F(v)-\mathcal F(w)|\leq M\| v-w\| _\infty .  \] Proof. Here $N_ m=\dim H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ))$. Integrate the first-variation formula of proposition 18.34.1 along the segment $t\mapsto tv$, $0\leq t\leq 1$. For each fixed $t$, the integrand converges by the theorem, and its absolute value is bounded by \[  \| v\| _\infty  rac{n!N_ m}{m^ n},  \] which is bounded in $m$ because it converges to $M\| v\| _\infty $. Dominated convergence on $[0,1]$ gives the formula; the limit integrand is measurable in $t$ as the pointwise limit of continuous functions. Concavity, the translation identity and the Lipschitz bound pass from $\mathcal F_ m^{(n)}$ to the pointwise limit, since $n!N_ m/m^ n	o M$. $\square$ This argument uses only weak convergence of measures along a segment of weights. It does not give a lower bound for the partial Fubini–Study potentials complementing theorem 18.33.1 ; such a bound would require the construction of sections approximating the envelope.

title: 18.36 Kernels on a fibration
text:
On a fibration with compact connected fibers, every section of a pulled-back line bundle is constant along the fibers and descends to the base. If probability measures are chosen on the fibers, this descent becomes an isometry, and the kernel measures on the total space are obtained from those on the base by integration along the fibers. Let $\pi :X	o B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds, with connected fibers. Write $n=\dim X$ and $q=\dim B\geq 1$. Let $A$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h_ A$, choose a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $B$, and set \[  (L,h)=(\pi ^*A,\pi ^*h_ A),\qquad \varphi =\pi ^*\psi .  \] For $y\in B$ write $X_ y=\pi ^{-1}(y)$. Choose a family of smooth positive probability measures $
u _ y$ on the fibers $X_ y$ that varies smoothly with $y$; for instance, restrict a smooth positive vertical volume density to the fibers and divide by its fiber integrals. For $F\in C(X)$ set \[  \mathcal A F(y)=\int _{X_ y}F\, \mathrm{d}
u _ y.  \] The function $\mathcal A F$ is continuous: a proper submersion is locally a smooth fiber bundle, the densities vary smoothly in a local trivialization, and $F$ is uniformly continuous on compact sets. For a finite positive Borel measure $\mu $ on $B$, define its lift $\mathcal L\mu $ by \[  \int _ X F\, \mathrm{d}\mathcal L\mu =\int _ B\mathcal A F\, \mathrm{d}\mu \qquad (F\in C(X)).  \] Since $\mathcal A$ is positive and $\mathcal A1=1$, the Riesz representation theorem makes $\mathcal L\mu $ a finite positive measure with the same total mass as $\mu $. Since $\mathcal AF$ is continuous, weak convergence of finite measures on $B$ implies weak convergence of their lifts. Proposition 18.36.1 . 7E88736EF73B Pullback of sections induces an isomorphism \[  H^0 igl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ) igr ) \simeq H^0 igl (X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ) igr ).  \] Let $K\subseteq B$ be closed and non-pluripolar, let $w\in C(K)$, and let $\mu $ be a Bernstein–Markov probability measure for $(K,w)$ on $B$. Set $K_ X=\pi ^{-1}(K)$, $w_ X=w\circ \pi $ and $\mu _ X=\mathcal L\mu $. Then pullback is an isometry from the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,w,\mu }$ on $B$ to the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,w_ X,\mu _ X}$ on $X$, the measure $\mu _ X$ is Bernstein–Markov for $(K_ X,w_ X)$, and the partial kernel measures on $B$ and $X$, normalized with the same integer $r$, satisfy \[   eta _{X,m}^{(r)}=\mathcal L igl ( eta _{B,m}^{(r)} igr ).  \] Proof. Let $s$ be a holomorphic section of $\pi ^*A^ m$. Over an open set of $B$ on which $A^ m$ is trivial, the coefficient of $s$ is a holomorphic function on the inverse image, and it is constant on each fiber, since the fibers are compact and connected. It is therefore the pullback of a function on the base, which is holomorphic because it is the composition of the coefficient with a local holomorphic section of the submersion. These local functions transform by the transition functions of $A^ m$, so they define a section of $A^ m$ whose pullback is $s$. This proves the identification without multiplier ideals. By lemma 5.37.7 , the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ on $X$ is generated by the pullbacks of the germs in $\mathcal I(m\psi )$. A pulled-back germ belongs to it exactly when the base germ belongs to $\mathcal I(m\psi )$: pullback gives one implication, and restriction to a local holomorphic section of $\pi $ gives the other. This identifies the selected spaces. Pointwise norms of corresponding sections agree and are constant along the fibers. Since each $
u _ y$ has mass one, \[  \int _{K_ X}|\pi ^*s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw_ X}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ X =\int _ K|s|_{h_ A^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw}\, \mathrm{d}\mu .  \] The supremum norms on $K_ X$ and $K$ also agree, because $\pi $ is surjective. Thus the Bernstein–Markov inequality transfers from $(K,w,\mu )$ to $(K_ X,w_ X,\mu _ X)$, and the integral norms on $X$ are nondegenerate. Pulling back an orthonormal basis gives $B_{X,m}=B_{B,m}\circ \pi $ on $K_ X$, where each kernel is set to zero outside its weighted set. Integrating a continuous test function first along the fibers proves the identity of measures. $\square$

title: Proposition 18.36.1
text: Proposition 18.36.1 . 7E88736EF73B Pullback of sections induces an isomorphism \[  H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) \simeq H^0\bigl (X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )\bigr ).  \] Let $K\subseteq B$ be closed and non-pluripolar, let $w\in C(K)$, and let $\mu $ be a Bernstein–Markov probability measure for $(K,w)$ on $B$. Set $K_ X=\pi ^{-1}(K)$, $w_ X=w\circ \pi $ and $\mu _ X=\mathcal L\mu $. Then pullback is an isometry from the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,w,\mu }$ on $B$ to the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,w_ X,\mu _ X}$ on $X$, the measure $\mu _ X$ is Bernstein–Markov for $(K_ X,w_ X)$, and the partial kernel measures on $B$ and $X$, normalized with the same integer $r$, satisfy \[  \beta _{X,m}^{(r)}=\mathcal L\bigl (\beta _{B,m}^{(r)}\bigr ).  \] Proof. Let $s$ be a holomorphic section of $\pi ^*A^ m$. Over an open set of $B$ on which $A^ m$ is trivial, the coefficient of $s$ is a holomorphic function on the inverse image, and it is constant on each fiber, since the fibers are compact and connected. It is therefore the pullback of a function on the base, which is holomorphic because it is the composition of the coefficient with a local holomorphic section of the submersion. These local functions transform by the transition functions of $A^ m$, so they define a section of $A^ m$ whose pullback is $s$. This proves the identification without multiplier ideals. By lemma 5.37.7 , the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ on $X$ is generated by the pullbacks of the germs in $\mathcal I(m\psi )$. A pulled-back germ belongs to it exactly when the base germ belongs to $\mathcal I(m\psi )$: pullback gives one implication, and restriction to a local holomorphic section of $\pi $ gives the other. This identifies the selected spaces. Pointwise norms of corresponding sections agree and are constant along the fibers. Since each $\nu _ y$ has mass one, \[  \int _{K_ X}|\pi ^*s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw_ X}\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ X =\int _ K|s|_{h_ A^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mw}\, \mathrm{d}\mu .  \] The supremum norms on $K_ X$ and $K$ also agree, because $\pi $ is surjective. Thus the Bernstein–Markov inequality transfers from $(K,w,\mu )$ to $(K_ X,w_ X,\mu _ X)$, and the integral norms on $X$ are nondegenerate. Pulling back an orthonormal basis gives $B_{X,m}=B_{B,m}\circ \pi $ on $K_ X$, where each kernel is set to zero outside its weighted set. Integrating a continuous test function first along the fibers proves the identity of measures. $\square$

title: 18.36.2 The quotient equilibrium measure
text: On a Kähler base, the partial kernel measures converge to the Monge–Ampère measure of the partial envelope. Since lifting is continuous, the kernel measures on the total space converge to the lift of this measure, with the normalization given by the dimension of the base. Keep the submersion and the weighted compact set $(K,w,\mu )$ above. Assume that $B$ is Kähler, put $\theta =c_1(A,h_ A)$, and take $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ with positive non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère mass. Write $B_{B,m}$ and $B_{X,m}$ for the partial Bergman kernels on $K$ and $K_ X$, put $\mu _ X=\mathcal L\mu $, and let \[  E=E_{\theta ,K}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(w)  \] be the partial envelope of section 18.32 . We call $\mathcal L(\mathrm{MA}_\theta (E))$ the quotient equilibrium measure of these data on $X$. Theorem 18.36.3 . 87C196C13DDE Under these hypotheses, \[  \frac{q!}{m^ q}B_{X,m}\, \mu _ X \rightharpoonup \mathcal L\bigl (\mathrm{MA}_\theta (E)\bigr ).  \] If $n>q$, then $(n!/m^ n)B_{X,m}\, \mu _ X\to 0$ in total variation. Proof. Apply [ Theorem 14.3.1 , SGPT ] on the compact Kähler manifold $B$, with trivial auxiliary twisting line bundle. Its hypotheses are exactly our assumptions: $\psi $ has positive mass, $K$ is closed and non-pluripolar, $w$ is continuous, and $\mu $ is a Bernstein–Markov probability measure. It gives \[  \frac{q!}{m^ q}B_{B,m}\, \mu \rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}_\theta (E).  \] By proposition 18.36.1 , the corresponding measures on $X$ are the lifts of these measures, and lifting preserves weak convergence; this proves the first assertion. In particular the $q$-normalized total masses are bounded, and multiplying them by $(n!/q!)m^{q-n}\to 0$ proves the last assertion when $n>q$. $\square$

title: 18.36.4 The Hopf equilibrium measure
text: On the Hopf manifold, the quotient equilibrium measure is a Hermitian Monge–Ampère measure: the vertical part of the Hopf metric supplies the missing fiber direction. The constant relating the two measures combines the fiber probability with a coefficient of the top power. Use the Hopf manifold $X_ n$, $n\geq 2$, its projection $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$, the Fubini–Study form $\sigma $ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ with $\int \sigma ^{n-1}=1$, and the forms $\alpha =\pi ^*\sigma $, $\zeta $ and $\omega =\alpha +\zeta $ of section 21.14 ; recall that $\zeta ^2=0$ and that $\zeta $ has integral two on each fiber. Take $A=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, so that $\theta =\sigma $, and keep the selecting potential $\psi $ and the weighted data $(K,w,\mu )$ above. On each elliptic fiber put $\nu _ y=\zeta |_{X_ y}/2$. The lift of a base measure $\tau $ is then \[  \mathcal L\tau =\tfrac 12\pi ^*\tau \wedge \zeta ,  \] in the fiber-integration notation of section 21.14 . Since $E\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, theorem 21.14.4 gives $\mathcal L(\mathrm{MA}_\sigma (E))=(2n)^{-1}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*E)$, and theorem 18.36.3 becomes C843534C9B58 18.36.5 \begin{equation}  \frac{(n-1)!}{m^{n-1}}B_{X_ n,m}\, \mu _ X \rightharpoonup \frac{1}{2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*E). \end{equation} The factor $1/(2n)$ combines the fiber probability $1/2$ with the coefficient $n$ of $\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta $ in $\omega ^ n=(\alpha +\zeta )^ n$. The closed curvature form $\alpha $ alone gives nothing: by theorem 21.14.4 , descended potentials have zero Monge–Ampère measure with respect to $\alpha $, and the nonzero limit comes from the vertical form $\zeta $. For $n=3$ this gives a nonzero limit, with the normalization $2/m^2$, on a manifold without the bounded mass property (theorem 23.1.1 ). For a positive integer $k$, every $k\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function on $X_ n$ is pulled back from $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, by theorem 21.14.2 . An $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function, by contrast, can have an isolated pole, and then it does not descend. Its selected sections still descend, so the pole is recorded by a vanishing condition on the base. The next two sections determine this condition and its effect on the kernels.

title: 18.37 Isolated logarithmic poles on a fibration

section: 18.37 Isolated logarithmic poles on a fibration
text:
Return to a fibration with compact connected fibers, and let the selecting potential have isolated logarithmic poles on the total space. Every selected section descends to the base, and in large tensor powers it must vanish to a certain order at the images of the poles. This order is computed from integrability in all variables of the total space, so it differs from the order imposed by a pole of the same coefficient on the base by at most the fiber dimension. The jets in between span $O(m^{q-1})$ dimensions on a $q$-dimensional base. This is negligible after normalization by $m^ q$, so the kernel measures converge to the same quotient equilibrium measure as for the corresponding poles on the base. The comparison rests on the following elementary fact: for nested section spaces, the total variation of the difference of their kernel measures is the normalized codimension. Lemma 18.37.1 . 22D696DB398E Let $B$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $q\geq 1$, let $A	o B$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth Hermitian metric, let $v\in C(B)$, and let $
u $ be a smooth positive probability volume on $B$. For every integer $m\geq 1$ let $W_ m\subseteq V_ m\subseteq H^0(B,A^ m)$ be subspaces, both with the norm $\| \cdot \| _{m,v,
u }$, and put $d_ m=\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m$. Write $B_{V_ m,v}$, $B_{W_ m,v}$ for their kernels and $ eta _{V_ m,v}^{(q)}$, $ eta _{W_ m,v}^{(q)}$ for their kernel measures, defined as in section 18.30 with the space indicated by the subscript. Then \[   egin{gathered} B_{V_ m,v}-B_{W_ m,v}\geq 0,\ \|  eta _{V_ m,v}^{(q)}- eta _{W_ m,v}^{(q)}\| _{\mathrm{TV}} = rac{q!d_ m}{m^ q}. \end{gathered}  \] The determinant functionals of the two spaces, each normalized to vanish at the zero weight, satisfy \[  |\mathcal F_{V_ m}^{(q)}(v)-\mathcal F_{W_ m}^{(q)}(v)| \leq  rac{q!d_ m}{m^ q}\| v\| _\infty .  \] These statements include the case of zero-dimensional spaces. Proof. Extend an orthonormal basis of $W_ m$ to an orthonormal basis of $V_ m$ for the norm at the weight $v$. The difference of the kernels is the sum of the squared weighted evaluations of the $d_ m$ added basis vectors. It is nonnegative, and its integral against $
u $ is $d_ m$, which gives the total variation formula. For the determinant functionals, apply the first-variation formula of proposition 18.34.1 to each of the two fixed spaces, and integrate the difference along $t\mapsto tv$, $0\leq t\leq 1$. By what we have just proved, at each $t$ the difference of the kernel measures is positive with total mass $q!d_ m/m^ q$, so its integral against $v$ is at most $q!d_ m\| v\| _\infty /m^ q$ in absolute value. Since both functionals vanish at zero, this proves the last assertion. $\square$ Return to a submersion $\pi :X	o B$ and a pulled-back line bundle $L=\pi ^*A$ as in section 18.36 , and write $f=n-q$ for the fiber dimension. Fix distinct points $p_1,\ldots ,p_ N$ of $X$ and positive rational numbers $a_1,\ldots ,a_ N$. Proposition 18.37.3 . BEF6F7AD320C Pullback identifies the selected space $H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ with \[  V_ m=H^0\left(B,A^ m\otimes  igcap _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{r_{m,b}}ight).  \] The space \[  W_ m=H^0\left(B,A^ m\otimes  igcap _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}ight)  \] satisfies $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$ and \[  0\leq \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m \leq \sum _{b\in Z}\sum _{j=r_{m,b}}^{s_{m,b}-1}  inom {j+q-1}{q-1} =O(m^{q-1}),  \] where an empty inner sum is zero. The implied constant depends only on the points and their coefficients, not on $m$. Proof. Lemma 5.37.1 , applied with a point as center, gives \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi )_{p_ j}=\mathfrak m_{p_ j}^{\max \{ \lfloor ma_ jfloor -n+1,0\} };  \] away from the points $p_ j$ the ideal is the full structure sheaf. Every section of $L^ m$ descends to $B$, by the argument in proposition 18.36.1 . Near $p_ j$ choose submersion coordinates $(z,	au )$ with $\pi (z,	au )=z$. A pulled-back section has a local coefficient $g(z)$ that does not depend on $	au $, and its vanishing order at $(0,0)$ equals the vanishing order of $g$ at $z=0$. The conditions imposed by the points of one fiber are therefore vanishing conditions at the same base point, and the strongest of them is vanishing to order $r_{m,b}$. This proves the identification. For the dimension bound, map each section in $V_ m$ to its jets modulo $\mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}$ at the finitely many points $b\in Z$. The kernel of this map is $W_ m$, so local trivializations of $A^ m$ give an injection \[  V_ m/W_ m\hookrightarrow  igoplus _{b\in Z}\mathfrak m_ b^{r_{m,b}}/ \mathfrak m_ b^{s_{m,b}}.  \] Surjectivity of the jet map is not needed. In $q$ variables there are $ inom {j+q-1}{q-1}$ monomials of degree $j$, which gives the dimensions of these quotients. Finally $0\leq s_{m,b}-r_{m,b}\leq f$ and $s_{m,b}=O(m)$, which proves the bound, also when $q=1$ or $f=0$. $\square$ Equip $A$ with a smooth metric $h_ A$ and put $	heta =c_1(A,h_ A)$. Choose a smooth positive probability volume $
u _ B$ on $B$, smooth fiber probabilities as in section 18.36 , and the smooth positive volume $
u _ X=\mathcal L
u _ B$ on $X$. Use the pullback metric on $L$, and for $v\in C(B)$ use the weight $v\circ \pi $ in the norm on $X$. We write $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and $\mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}$ for the kernel measure and the determinant functional on $X$ defined by these data and the selecting potential $\varphi $. Theorem 18.37.4 . D9B0D46D42B2 Assume that $B$ is Kähler and that there is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,	heta )$ with positive non-pluripolar mass, locally bounded off $Z$, such that \[  \psi (z)=a_ b\log |z-b|^2+O(1)\quad \hbox{near each }b\in Z  \] in local coordinates $z$ on $B$. Let $E(v)=E_{	heta ,B}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(v)$. Then, for the selecting potential $\varphi $ of ( 18.37.2 ), \[   eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)} ightharpoonup \mathcal L igl (\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(v)) igr ).  \] More precisely, the total variation distance between $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and the lift of the kernel measure on $B$ selected by $\psi $ is $O(m^{-1})$. The determinant functionals satisfy \[  \mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}(v\circ \pi )\longrightarrow \int _0^1\! \left(\int _ B v\, \mathrm{d}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(tv))ight)\mathrm{d}t.  \] The normalized dimensions $q!N_ m/m^ q$ converge to the total mass of the limit measure, which is finite and positive. If $n>q$, the kernel measures with the normalization $n!/m^ n$ tend to zero in total variation. Proof. By lemma 5.37.1 in dimension $q$, the space of sections of $A^ m$ selected by $\psi $ on $B$ is the space $W_ m$ of proposition 18.37.3 . Corresponding sections in $V_ m$ and on $X$ have equal norms, since their pointwise norms and the continuous weight are pulled back from $B$ and every fiber probability has mass one. As in proposition 18.36.1 , pulling back an orthonormal basis shows that the kernel measure on $X$ is the lift of the kernel measure of $V_ m$ on $B$. By lemma 18.37.1 , proposition 18.37.3 , the $q$-normalized kernel measures of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ on $B$ differ by a positive measure of total mass $O(m^{-1})$, and so do their lifts. Apply theorem 18.35.5 on $B$, with the identity as Kähler modification; its hypotheses are among ours. It gives the convergence of the kernel measures of $W_ m$, and since the difference tends to zero, the asserted limit on $X$ follows. By the same lemma, the determinant functionals of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ differ by at most $O(m^{-1})\| v\| _\infty $. The isometric identification of the norms and corollary 18.35.6 on $B$ give the limit of the functionals. Testing the constant function one proves the assertion about the dimensions. Since the $q$-normalized masses are bounded, multiplying them by $(n!/q!)m^{q-n}$ proves the last assertion. $\square$ If $	heta >0$, lemma 5.37.2 , applied on $B$ with the Hermitian form $	heta $, constructs the required $\psi $ whenever the coefficients $a_ b$ are sufficiently small. Off the poles, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ then dominates a positive multiple of $	heta $, so the non-pluripolar mass of $\psi $ is positive; it is finite because $	heta $ is closed and $B$ is Kähler. The same lemma, applied on $X$ with a Hermitian form, constructs $\varphi $. If the fibers have positive dimension, such a function $\varphi $ does not descend to $B$, since it is finite at the other points of a fiber containing a pole. The section formula of proposition 18.37.3 also shows that the kernels cannot recover the singularities of the selecting potential. Moving an isolated pole within its fiber does not change any selected space, and neither does adding further poles in that fiber whose coefficients do not exceed the largest one. For the fixed pullback metric $h=\pi ^*h_ A$, continuous weight $v\circ \pi $ and lifted volume $
u _ X$, all kernels and determinant functionals are therefore the same in every degree. The multiplier ideals on $X$ are nevertheless different: for large weights, the ideal of one potential is a proper ideal at a point where the ideal of the other is the full local ring. Under the hypotheses of theorem 18.37.4 , this loss of information occurs together with a positive limit at the growth rate $m^ q$. In the closed theory, by contrast, the limit envelope has the multiplier-ideal type of the selecting potential (theorem 18.32.2 ); this property is lost when the selecting potential is plurisubharmonic only with respect to a Hermitian form.

title: 18.38 A point pole on the Hopf manifold

section: 18.38 A point pole on the Hopf manifold
text:
On the Hopf manifold the comparison of section 18.37 can be made completely explicit. A single point pole selects the homogeneous polynomials whose degree in affine coordinates centered at the image point is bounded below, and summing the squared norms of the normalized monomials expresses the kernel as a binomial tail. The exponential rate of this tail determines the limit of the Fubini–Study potentials, and its concentration determines the limit of the measures. The limit potential has a pole along the entire fiber through the original pole, which makes the loss of the point singularity explicit. We keep the notation of subsection 18.36.4 , with $q=n-1$, so that $\pi :X_ n	o \mathbb P^ q$. Use $L=L_1=\pi ^*\mathcal O(1)$ with its pulled-back Fubini–Study metric and the probability volume $
u _ X=\omega ^ n/(2n)$, which is the lift of $\sigma ^ q$ for the fiber probabilities $\zeta |_{X_ y}/2$. Let $p\in X_ n$ lie over $b=[1:0:\cdots :0]$. Conversely, if $w\preceq \psi _ a$, then \[  w(z)\leq a\log |z|^2+C \leq a\log (|z|^2+|\tau |^2)+C  \] near $p$. Away from $p$, the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded and $w$ is bounded above, so by compactness the inequality $w\circ \pi \leq \varphi +C$ holds globally. Thus $w\circ \pi \preceq \varphi $, which implies $w\circ \pi \preceq _{\mathcal I}\varphi $. Since lemma 5.38.11 also applies on the base, the map $u=w\circ \pi \mapsto w$ identifies the competitors on $X_ n$ with the competitors for $E_ a$ considered above. Their largest members therefore correspond under pullback. Finally, theorem 21.14.4 and the measure formula on the base give the last identity. $\square$

title: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor

section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text:
We now replace the isolated poles by a pole along the image of a holomorphic section of the fibration over a divisor of the base. The selected sections must then vanish to a certain order along that divisor. As for point poles, the normal variables in the fiber shift the integrability threshold only by a bounded amount, so this order differs from the order imposed by a divisorial pole on the base by a bounded number. Restriction sequences along the divisor show that each unit of vanishing order costs $O(m^{q-1})$ sections, and kernel convergence again reduces to the equilibrium theorem on the base. For the restriction sequences we need a bound for the dimensions of section spaces that is uniform over a range of twists growing linearly with $m$. Lemma 18.39.1 . EF14C0C90C6C Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0(M,E^ m\otimes F^ j)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j\in \mathbb Z,\  |j|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$, the manifold $M$ is a finite set and the dimension is at most its number of points. Let $d\geq 1$. Fix smooth Hermitian metrics on $E$ and $F$, a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$, and finitely many coordinate charts with holomorphic frames, together with smaller subcharts that still cover $M$. For $|j|\leq C_0m$, the local weight of the metric on $E^ m\otimes F^ j$ has second derivatives bounded by $Cm$. At a point $p$ of a smaller subchart, multiply the frame by the exponential of a holomorphic affine function to remove the constant and real-linear terms of this weight at $p$. The new weight vanishes at $p$ and is bounded by $Cm|z-p|^2$ on a fixed neighborhood. A ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about $p$ lies in the chart, with $\varepsilon >0$ independent of $p$, $m$ and $j$, and on this ball the weight is bounded. The submean inequality for the holomorphic coefficient of a section $s$ on this ball gives \[  |s(p)|^2\leq Cm^ d\int _ M|s|^2\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where all constants depend only on the fixed charts, metrics, volume and $C_0$. Evaluation at $p$ has a one-dimensional target, so for an $L^2$-orthonormal basis $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ of $H^0(M,E^ m\otimes F^ j)$ its squared norm is $\sum _{\ell =1}^ N|s_\ell (p)|^2\leq Cm^ d$. Integrating over $M$ gives $N\leq C\operatorname {Vol}(M)m^ d$. $\square$ Let $\pi :X	o B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds, with connected fibers of dimension $r\geq 1$, and suppose that $B$ is Kähler of dimension $q\geq 1$. Fix a holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h_ A$ whose curvature $	heta =c_1(A,h_ A)$ is positive. Let $Z\subset B$ be a nonempty smooth divisor, and suppose that $\pi $ has a holomorphic section $\sigma :Z	o X$ over $Z$; put $Y=\sigma (Z)$. Fix $c>0$ and a smooth metric $h_ Z$ on $\mathcal O_ B(Z)$, with curvature $\Theta _ Z$, such that $\alpha :=	heta -c\Theta _ Z>0$. Let $s_ Z$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ B(Z)$, and set $\psi =c\log |s_ Z|_{h_ Z}^2$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, chosen independently of $h_ A$. Suppose that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus Y$ and that, in submersion coordinates $(x,z',w_1,\ldots ,w_ r)$ near each point of $Y$, 145C74FFDD88 18.39.2  egin{equation}   egin{gathered} \varphi =c\log \left(|x|^2+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^2ight)+O(1),\ Z=\{ x=0\} ,\qquad Y=\{ x=w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} , \end{gathered} \end{equation} with a locally bounded remainder. Here $x$ and $z'$ are coordinates on the base, and the vector $z'$ of the $q-1$ tangential coordinates is absent when $q=1$. Theorem 18.39.3 . AE701AEF7FDE The function $\psi $ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic, with positive non-pluripolar mass \[  \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi )=\int _ B\alpha ^ q>0.  \] For every integer $m\geq 1$ put $\ell _ m=\lfloor mcfloor $ and $k_ m=\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} $. Under holomorphic descent, the spaces selected by $\varphi $ on $X$ and by $\psi $ on $B$ are \[   egin{split}  V_ m& :=H^0 igl (X,\pi ^*A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ) igr ) =H^0 igl (B,A^ m(-k_ m Z) igr ),\  W_ m& :=H^0 igl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ) igr ) =H^0 igl (B,A^ m(-\ell _ m Z) igr )\subseteq V_ m. \end{split}  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed data, such that \[  0\leq \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m\leq Cm^{q-1}.  \] For $q=1$ the difference is at most $r\, \# Z$ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\alpha +c[Z]\geq 0$. The divisorial measure identity ( 11.41.2 ), applied with the residual form $\alpha >0$ and the bounded part zero, gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi )=\alpha ^ q$, which proves the mass formula. Every section of $\pi ^*A^ m$ descends by proposition 18.36.1 . In the $r+1$ normal variables $(x,w)$, lemma 5.37.1 gives \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi )=(x,w_1,\ldots ,w_ r)^{k_ m}.  \] The local coefficient $g(x,z')$ of a pulled-back section does not depend on $w$. Expanding $g$ in powers of $x$, we see that $g$ lies in this ideal exactly when the coefficients of $x^ j$ vanish for $j<k_ m$, that is, when $x^{k_ m}$ divides $g$. This is an identity of germs in all tangential variables, so it holds at every point of $Z$. Outside $Y$ the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded. On the base, the same lemma in the single normal variable $x$ gives $\mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B(-\ell _ mZ)$. These facts prove the two identities and the inclusion. For $k_ m\leq j<\ell _ m$, the restriction sequence along $Z$, \[   egin{split}  0& \longrightarrow A^ m(-(j+1)Z)\longrightarrow A^ m(-jZ)\ & \longrightarrow  igl (A^ m(-jZ) igr )|_ Z\longrightarrow 0, \end{split}  \] shows that passing from vanishing order $j$ to order $j+1$ along $Z$ loses at most $h^0(Z,(A^ m(-jZ))|_ Z)$ dimensions. Apply lemma 18.39.1 on $Z$ with $E=A|_ Z$ and $F=\mathcal O_ B(-Z)|_ Z$; since $0\leq j\leq cm$, each loss is at most $Cm^{q-1}$, uniformly in $j$. There are at most $r$ steps, which proves the estimate. When $q=1$, the divisor $Z$ is a finite set and each restriction space has dimension $\# Z$, which gives the last assertion directly. $\square$ We call $\psi $ the reference potential , $W_ m$ the reference spaces , and $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m$ the defect ; the same terms are used for the analogous comparisons below. The following example shows that the order $m^{q-1}$ in theorem 18.39.3 is sharp. Example 18.39.4 . FE69C8A3CBBF For all integers $q,r,k\geq 1$ and every real $0<c<k$, the hypotheses above are satisfied on $X=\mathbb P^ q	imes \mathbb P^ r$ with $B=\mathbb P^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)$, for suitable choices made in the proof. For $q\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m = rac{r(k-c)^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2}),  \] and for $q=1$ it equals $\min \{ r,\lfloor mcfloor \} $ for every $m$. Proof. Use homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ q]$ on the base and $[W_0:\cdots :W_ r]$ on the fiber. Let $Z=\{ Z_0=0\} $ and $Y=Z	imes \{ [1:0:\cdots :0]\} $, and let $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ be the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have top integrals one. Define \[  R_ B= rac{|Z_0|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ q|Z_ i|^2},\qquad R_ F= rac{\sum _{j=1}^ r|W_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ r|W_ j|^2},\qquad \varphi =c\log (R_ B+R_ F),\quad \psi =c\log R_ B.  \] The function $\varphi $ is smooth off $Y$ and satisfies ( 18.39.2 ). Over a common denominator, the numerator of $R_ B+R_ F$ is \[  \sum _{j=0}^ r|Z_0W_ j|^2+\sum _{i=0}^ q\sum _{j=1}^ r|Z_ iW_ j|^2,  \] whose logarithm is plurisubharmonic in each affine chart. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -c(\omega _ B+\omega _ F)$. Choose an integer $b\geq c$ and set $\omega =k\omega _ B+b\omega _ F$. This is a Hermitian form, and $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq (k-c)\omega _ B+(b-c)\omega _ F\geq 0$. On the base, $	heta =k\omega _ B$, $\Theta _ Z=\omega _ B$ and $\alpha =(k-c)\omega _ B>0$. Put $\ell _ m=\lfloor mcfloor $. Divisibility of homogeneous polynomials by powers of $Z_0$ gives the exact dimensions \[  \dim W_ m= inom {km-\ell _ m+q}{q},\qquad \dim V_ m= inom {km-\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} +q}{q}.  \] For large $m$, the two residual degrees differ by $r$ and equal $(k-c)m+O(1)$. Subtracting the two binomial coefficients, which are polynomials of degree $q$ in the residual degrees, gives the asserted leading coefficient and remainder. For $q=1$ the difference is $\ell _ m-\max \{ \ell _ m-r,0\} =\min \{ r,\ell _ m\} $ for every $m$. $\square$ The bounded shift of divisorial order thus has negligible normalized codimension. To compare the kernels under the hypotheses of theorem 18.39.3 , fix a smooth positive probability volume $
u _ B$ on $B$, smooth fiber probabilities, and the lifting map $\mathcal L$ of section 18.36 , and put $
u _ X=\mathcal L
u _ B$. Use the pullback metric on $\pi ^*A$ and, for a real function $v\in C(B)$, the weight $v\circ \pi $ in the norm on $X$. Write $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ and $\mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}$ for the kernel measure and the determinant functional on $X$, as in section 18.37 , and \[  E(v)=E_{	heta ,B}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(v).  \] Corollary 18.39.5 . 115614FB1F9D The total variation distance between the kernel measure $ eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)}$ selected by $\varphi $ on $X$ and the lift of the kernel measure selected by $\psi $ on $B$ is $O(m^{-1})$. In particular, \[   eta _{X,m,v\circ \pi ,\varphi }^{(q)} ightharpoonup \mathcal L igl (\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(v)) igr ).  \] The determinant functionals, normalized to vanish at the zero weight, satisfy \[  \mathcal F_{X,m}^{(q)}(v\circ \pi )\longrightarrow \int _0^1\left(\int _ Bv\, \mathrm{d}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (E(tv))ight)\mathrm{d}t.  \] With the normalization $(q+r)!/m^{q+r}$ given by the dimension of $X$, the kernel measures tend to zero in total variation. Proof. As in proposition 18.36.1 , fiber integration identifies the norm on $X$ with the norm on $V_ m\subseteq H^0(B,A^ m)$, so the kernel measure on $X$ is the lift of the kernel measure of $V_ m$ on $B$. By lemma 18.37.1 , theorem 18.39.3 , the latter differs from the kernel measure of $W_ m$ by a positive measure of total mass $q!(\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m)/m^ q=O(m^{-1})$, and so do the lifts. Since $B$ is Kähler and $\psi $ has positive non-pluripolar mass, the equilibrium theorem used in the proof of theorem 18.36.3 applies to $W_ m$ and gives the weak limit. By lemma 18.37.1 , the determinant functionals of $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ differ by at most $O(m^{-1})\| v\| _\infty $, and corollary 18.35.6 , applied on $B$ with the identity modification, gives the limit of the functionals; its dominated convergence bound is $\| v\| _\infty $ times the bounded sequence of $q$-normalized dimensions. Finally, the $q$-normalized masses are bounded, so multiplying them by $(q+r)!m^{-r}/q!$ proves the last assertion. $\square$ Thus the selecting potentials of ( 18.39.2 ) admit the approximation asked for in 24.10.2 , whenever the curvature margin $	heta -c\Theta _ Z$ is positive.

title: 18.39.6 A bounded divisorial band from fiber integrability
