section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: The comparison of theorem 18.39.3 does not need the exact local form ( 18.39.2 ). It suffices to bound the selecting potential from below by a divisorial pole on all of $X$, and from above by an anisotropic model in a single chart over the divisor. The lower bound gives the inclusion of the reference spaces into the selected spaces. The upper bound forces vanishing along the divisor to an order that falls short of the reference order by a bounded amount: separate powers of the normal variables replace the shift by the fiber dimension with a weighted shift. The selecting potential may then be singular along a positive-dimensional subset of a fiber, and it need not descend to the base. Let $\pi :X\to B$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion of connected compact complex manifolds with connected fibers of dimension $f\geq 1$, and let $B$ be Kähler of dimension $q\geq 1$. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, a holomorphic line bundle $A$ on $B$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$, and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Write $\theta =c_1(A,h)$, and use holomorphic descent to regard the selected spaces as subspaces of $H^0(B,A^ m)$: \[  V_ m=H^0\bigl (X,\pi ^*A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi )\bigr ) \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m),\qquad m\geq 1.  \] Let $D\subset B$ be a nonempty smooth connected reduced divisor. Fix a smooth metric $H_ D$ on $\mathcal O_ B(D)$, and write $s_ D$ for its canonical section and $\eta =c_1(\mathcal O_ B(D),H_ D)$ for its curvature. Lemma 18.39.7 . BBA6C67F74CF Let $r\geq 1$ and $\ell \geq 0$ be integers, let $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ be positive integers, and let $P>0$. The function \[  |z|^{2\ell }\left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)^{-P}  \] of $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^ r$ is locally integrable near the origin if and only if \[  \frac{\ell +1}{p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\frac1{b_ j}>P.  \] In the case of equality, the integral diverges logarithmically. Proof. After integrating over the angles, substitute $x_0=|z|^{2p}$ and $x_ j=|w_ j|^{2b_ j}$. Up to a positive constant, the integral becomes \[  \int (x_0+\cdots +x_ r)^{-P}x_0^{(\ell +1)/p-1} \prod _{j=1}^ r x_ j^{1/b_ j-1}\, \mathrm dx_0\cdots \mathrm dx_ r  \] over a box near the origin. This box contains a small simplex $\{ \sum _ jx_ j<\delta \} $ and is contained in a larger one. On either simplex use the coordinates $\rho =\sum _ jx_ j$ and $x_ j=\rho y_ j$. The integral over $y$ is finite and positive, because all its exponents exceed $-1$, and the integral over $\rho $ is \[  \int _0^\delta \rho ^{(\ell +1)/p+\sum b_ j^{-1}-P-1}\, \mathrm d\rho .  \] This gives the threshold and the logarithmic divergence at equality. Bounded factors in the weight, holomorphic units and additional tangential variables do not affect this local test. $\square$ Theorem 18.39.8 . A79139E2A3C6 Suppose that $c>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-c\eta >0, \qquad \varphi \geq c\log \| \pi ^*s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X  \] for a constant $C$. Suppose further that there is one submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D$, with coordinates \[  \pi (z,t,w,v)=(z,t),\quad D=\{ z=0\} ,\quad t\in \mathbb C^{q-1},\quad w\in \mathbb C^ r,\quad v\in \mathbb C^{f-r},  \] where $1\leq r\leq f$, on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+C'  \] for positive integers $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ and a constant $C'$. Put \[  a=p\sum _{j=1}^ r b_ j^{-1},\quad L_ m=\lfloor mc\rfloor ,\quad K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor mc-a\rfloor ,0\} ,\quad \psi =u+c\log \| s_ D\| _{H_ D}^2.  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$, its non-pluripolar mass is $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  W_ m:=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0(B,A^ m(-L_ mD))\subseteq V_ m \subseteq H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD)).  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})=o(m^ q)$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\lceil a\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +c[D]$. Off $D$, locality identifies the non-pluripolar top power with $\beta ^ q$; the non-pluripolar product puts no mass on $D$, and neither does the smooth measure $\beta ^ q$. Hence $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, whose mass is finite and positive because $\beta >0$ and $B$ is compact. The one-variable integrability condition $\ell +1>mc$ gives $\mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B(-L_ mD)$, also when $mc$ is an integer. Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C''$. Hence integrability on the base gives integrability of the pullback in every bounded submersion chart, which proves $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For the upper inclusion, take a nonzero section in $V_ m$ and let $\ell $ be its vanishing order along $D$; note that $D$ is irreducible, being smooth and connected. In the polydisk of the upper bound, the coefficient of the section is $z^\ell g(z,t)$, where $g(0,t)$ does not vanish identically on the open subset of $D$, since otherwise the identity theorem would increase the order along $D$. Shrink the polydisk about a point with $w=0$ at which $g(0,t)\ne 0$, so that $g$ becomes a holomorphic unit. The upper bound on $\varphi $ and lemma 18.39.7 then force $\ell +1>mc-a$. For an integer $\ell \geq 0$ this is equivalent to $\ell \geq K_ m$, which proves the upper inclusion. Since $\lfloor mc\rfloor -\lfloor mc-a\rfloor \leq \lceil a\rceil $, we have $0\leq L_ m-K_ m\leq \lceil a\rceil $. Use the restriction sequences along $D$ from the proof of theorem 18.39.3 for $K_ m\leq j<L_ m$. Each step loses at most $h^0(D,(A^ m(-jD))|_ D)$ dimensions, and by lemma 18.39.1 this is at most $Cm^{q-1}$, uniformly for $0\leq j\leq cm$. Since the number of steps is bounded, the estimate follows. For $q=1$ the connected divisor $D$ is a single point, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$ Corollary 18.39.9 . 094794C14195 Keep the positivity condition $\beta >0$ of theorem 18.39.8 . Suppose that a nonempty compact smooth submanifold $Z\subset \pi ^{-1}(D)$ projects submersively onto $D$, and that near every point of $Z$ there are coordinates as in that theorem in which \[  Z=\{ z=w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} ,\qquad \varphi =\frac cp\log \left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)+O(1),  \] with fixed $c,p,b_ j$. Suppose also that $\varphi $ is locally bounded outside $Z$. Then $\varphi $ satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 18.39.8 , so its conclusions hold, and moreover \[  V_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-K_ mD))\qquad (m\geq 1).  \] Proof. The local model is bounded below by $c\log |z|^2$ up to a constant. Near points of $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ outside $Z$, the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, so the same lower bound holds there; away from $\pi ^{-1}(D)$ both functions are locally bounded. By compactness, finitely many charts give the global lower bound. The upper bound holds in any chart of the model. Conversely, if a section is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, its residual coefficient is bounded and holomorphic in each chart of the model, and the strict inequality $K_ m+1>mc-a$ together with lemma 18.39.7 gives integrability there. Outside $Z$ the function $\varphi $ is locally bounded, which proves the reverse inclusion. $\square$ Such exact models exist with pole sets of positive dimension inside the fibers. Let $B$ be projective, let $A$ be ample, and let $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ f$ with $\pi $ the first projection. Mark a point $o_ j$ in each of the first $r$ factors $\mathbb P^1$ of the fiber, and let $E_ j\subset X$ be the inverse image of $o_ j$. With smooth metrics on the corresponding line bundles, put \[  Q=\| \pi ^*s_ D\| ^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\| s_{E_ j}\| ^{2b_ j}, \qquad \varphi =\lambda \log Q,\qquad c=p\lambda .  \] The common zero set of the terms of $Q$ is $D\times \{ o_1\} \times \cdots \times \{ o_ r\} \times (\mathbb P^1)^{f-r}$. Near it, the positive factors of the metrics give exactly the local model of corollary 18.39.9 , and $\varphi $ is smooth elsewhere. The inequality $Q\geq \| \pi ^*s_ D\| ^{2p}$ gives the global lower bound. Locally, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log Q$ is bounded below by a convex combination of the negatives of the smooth curvature forms of the terms; hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log Q\geq -C_0\omega $ for a constant $C_0$, first off the common zero set and then across it, after a quadratic correction, by the extension theorem for plurisubharmonic functions. Since $A$ is ample, there is $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. For sufficiently small $\lambda >0$ we then have $\lambda C_0\leq 1$, so that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-p\lambda \eta >0$. Thus the exact series of the corollary also occurs when $r<f$. Example 18.39.10 . EB221EFD409A Let $B=\mathbb P^ q$ with a hyperplane $D$, let $A=\mathcal O_ B(1)$, and let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ be the Fubini–Study forms normalized to have total mass one, and use the corresponding metrics on the divisor line bundles. For a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$ set \[  \varphi =\tfrac 14\log \bigl (\| s_ D\| ^4+\| s_ o\| ^6\bigr ),\qquad \omega =\omega _ B+\omega _ F.  \] Then $p=2$, $b_1=3$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$, and the reference potential $\psi =\tfrac 12\log \| s_ D\| ^2$ has mass $2^{-q}$. The spaces $V_1$ and $W_1$ agree, and for every $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =\binom {\lceil m/2\rceil +q}{q-1} \sim \frac{2^{1-q}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}.  \] For $q=1$ the defect is exactly one for every $m\geq 2$. Proof. Locally, the complex Hessian of the logarithm of a sum of two squared norms of holomorphic sections is bounded below by a convex combination of the negatives of their curvature forms. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\tfrac 12\omega _ B-\tfrac 34\omega _ F$ off the pole set, and across it by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Thus $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The pole set is $D\times \{ o\} $, along which $\varphi $ has the exact local model of corollary 18.39.9 . Here $u=0$, $\beta =\tfrac 12\omega _ B$, and $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$, while $K_1=L_1=0$. The spaces $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ therefore correspond to homogeneous polynomials of degrees $m-L_ m+1$ and $m-L_ m$, and since $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, the difference of their dimensions is the displayed binomial coefficient. $\square$ In this example $\varphi $ is finite on most of each fiber over $D$ and equals $-\infty $ on a proper subset of it, so $\varphi $ differs from every pullback of a function on $B$ by an unbounded amount. For $p=b_ j=1$ and $r=f$, the shift $a=f$ is the shift by the fiber dimension found in theorem 18.39.3 . Theorem 18.39.8 thus gives sufficient conditions for the approximation asked for in 24.10.2 ; we do not know which other fiber singularities admit such an approximation. The assumption $f\geq 1$ excludes only a trivial case. If the fibers have dimension zero, then $\pi $ is a covering, since $X$ is compact and $\pi $ is a submersion, and hence a biholomorphism, since the fibers are connected. If, in addition, the descended selecting potential is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic with finite positive mass, taking it as $\psi $ gives $V_ m=W_ m$.

title: Lemma 18.39.7
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Lemma 18.39.7 . BBA6C67F74CF Let $r\geq 1$ and $\ell \geq 0$ be integers, let $p,b_1,\ldots ,b_ r$ be positive integers, and let $P>0$. The function \[  |z|^{2\ell }\left(|z|^{2p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r|w_ j|^{2b_ j}\right)^{-P}  \] of $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^ r$ is locally integrable near the origin if and only if \[  \frac{\ell +1}{p}+\sum _{j=1}^ r\frac1{b_ j}>P.  \] In the case of equality, the integral diverges logarithmically. Proof. After integrating over the angles, substitute $x_0=|z|^{2p}$ and $x_ j=|w_ j|^{2b_ j}$. Up to a positive constant, the integral becomes \[  \int (x_0+\cdots +x_ r)^{-P}x_0^{(\ell +1)/p-1} \prod _{j=1}^ r x_ j^{1/b_ j-1}\, \mathrm dx_0\cdots \mathrm dx_ r  \] over a box near the origin. This box contains a small simplex $\{ \sum _ jx_ j<\delta \} $ and is contained in a larger one. On either simplex use the coordinates $\rho =\sum _ jx_ j$ and $x_ j=\rho y_ j$. The integral over $y$ is finite and positive, because all its exponents exceed $-1$, and the integral over $\rho $ is \[  \int _0^\delta \rho ^{(\ell +1)/p+\sum b_ j^{-1}-P-1}\, \mathrm d\rho .  \] This gives the threshold and the logarithmic divergence at equality. Bounded factors in the weight, holomorphic units and additional tangential variables do not affect this local test. $\square$

text: Theorem 18.39.8 . title: 18.39.11 Several crossing base divisors
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Keep the submersion $\pi :X\to B$, the line bundle $(A,h)$, the selecting potential $\varphi $ and the descended spaces $V_ m$ of subsection 18.39.6 . Several divisorial singularities can be handled at once if the divisors cross normally. At their intersections the integrability test on the base separates in normal coordinates, and a bounded change of each divisorial order again costs only $O(m^{q-1})$ sections. For this we need the restriction estimate with all the divisorial twists at once. Lemma 18.39.12 . 46F892FF98FE Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0\left(M,E^ m\otimes \bigotimes _{i=1}^ NF_ i^{j_ i}\right)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j_ i\in \mathbb Z,\  |j_ i|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$ the dimension is at most the number of points of $M$. For $d\geq 1$, use fixed smooth metrics, a smooth positive volume form and finitely many framed charts as in the proof of lemma 18.39.1 . The local weight of the metric is $m\phi _ E+\sum _ i j_ i\phi _{F_ i}$, whose second derivatives are bounded by $Cm$ uniformly over the stated range. After its constant and real-linear terms at a point have been removed by a holomorphic affine change of frame, it is bounded by a fixed constant on a ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about that point. The submean inequality then gives $|s(x)|^2\leq Cm^ d\| s\| _{L^2}^2$, uniformly in $x$, $m$ and the integers $j_ i$. Since evaluation has a one-dimensional target, an orthonormal basis satisfies $\sum _\ell |s_\ell (x)|^2\leq Cm^ d$, and integration gives the estimate. The constants depend only on the fixed bundles, metrics, charts, volume and $C_0$. $\square$ Let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ be distinct nonempty smooth connected reduced divisors on $B$ whose union has simple normal crossings. For each $i$, choose a smooth metric $H_ i$ on $\mathcal O_ B(D_ i)$, and write $s_ i$ for the canonical section and $\eta _ i$ for the curvature. Theorem 18.39.13 . A7CF6A5A6A5C Suppose that $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi \geq \sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| \pi ^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ there is a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\ne i}D_ j$, with coordinates $(z_ i,t_ i,w_ i,v_ i)$ as in theorem 18.39.8 , on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac{c_ i}{p_ i}\log \left(|z_ i|^{2p_ i} +\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}|w_{ij}|^{2b_{ij}}\right)+C_ i, \qquad 1\leq r_ i\leq f,  \] where $p_ i$ and $b_{ij}$ are positive integers and $C_ i$ is a constant. Put \[  \begin{gathered} a_ i=p_ i\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}b_{ij}^{-1},\quad L_{m,i}=\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor ,\quad K_{m,i}=\max \{ \lfloor mc_ i-a_ i\rfloor ,0\} ,\\ \psi =u+\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{split}  W_ m& :=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right)\subseteq V_ m,\\  V_ m& \subseteq H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Off the divisors the non-pluripolar measure equals $\beta ^ q$, and neither measure charges their union. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, with finite positive total mass. Near a point of an intersection, the divisors through that point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes $\{ z_ i=0\} $. If a holomorphic germ is divisible by each corresponding $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, then it is divisible by their product; its residual coefficient is bounded, and since $L_{m,i}+1>mc_ i$, Fubini's theorem gives integrability. Conversely, integrability at generic nearby points of each coordinate hyperplane forces divisibility by $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, by the one-variable threshold, and the divisor of the germ then gives divisibility throughout the chart. This proves \[  \mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right).  \] Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integration in submersion coordinates gives $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For a nonzero section in $V_ m$, the polydisk over $D_ i$ on which the upper bound holds detects the generic vanishing order of the section along the irreducible divisor $D_ i$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 18.39.8 , together with the strict integrability threshold of lemma 18.39.7 , shows that this order is at least $K_{m,i}$. Imposing all these orders proves the upper inclusion. To compare dimensions, raise the orders from $(K_{m,i})_ i$ to $(L_{m,i})_ i$, one divisor and one unit at a time. At each step, the restriction sequence loses at most \[  h^0\left(D_ i,\left.A^ m\left(-\sum _ j n_ jD_ j\right)\right|_{D_ i}\right), \qquad 0\leq n_ j\leq mc_ j,  \] dimensions. By lemma 18.39.12 with $E=A|_{D_ i}$ and $F_ j=\mathcal O_ B(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$, this is $O(m^{q-1})$ uniformly over all steps, and there are at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. When $q=1$, the distinct connected divisors are points, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$ The upper bounds are required only away from the crossings; integrability at the crossings is controlled by the global lower bound. Exact models can nevertheless have fiber poles over the crossings, as in the following example, where different divisors use separate fiber coordinates. Example 18.39.14 . 411D2D5FFC5D Let $B=(\mathbb P^1)^ q$, $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_ B(1,\ldots ,1)$. For each $i$, let $D_ i\subset B$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of $B$, and let $E_ i\subset X$ be the inverse image of a marked point in the $i$th factor of the fiber. Use normalized Fubini–Study metrics on the corresponding line bundles, and write $\omega _{B,i},\omega _{F,i}$ for the pullbacks to $X$ of the normalized Fubini–Study forms on the $i$th factors of $B$ and of the fiber. Put \[  \begin{gathered} R_ i=\| \pi ^*s_ i\| ^2,\quad T_ i=\| s_{E_ i}\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\frac14\sum _{i=1}^ q\log (R_ i^2+T_ i^3),\\ \omega =\sum _ i(\omega _{B,i}+\omega _{F,i}),\qquad \psi =\frac12\sum _ i\log \| s_ i\| ^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and theorem 18.39.13 applies with $u=0$, $c_ i=1/2$, $p_ i=2$, $b_{i1}=3$ and $a_ i=2/3$. The reference potential $\psi $ has mass $q!/2^ q$. With $L_ m=\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, the selected and reference spaces are exactly \[  \begin{split}  V_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-K_ m,\ldots ,m-K_ m)\bigr ),\\  W_ m& =H^0\bigl (B,\mathcal O_ B(m-L_ m,\ldots ,m-L_ m)\bigr ). \end{split}  \] They agree for $m=1$, and for $m\geq 2$ the defect is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m =(\lceil m/2\rceil +2)^ q-(\lceil m/2\rceil +1)^ q.  \] For $q\geq 2$ this is $q2^{1-q}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2})$, and for $q=1$ it is exactly one. Proof. By the calculation in example 18.39.10 , the complex Hessian of each summand of $\varphi $ is bounded below by $-\tfrac 12\omega _{B,i}-\tfrac 34\omega _{F,i}$, also across its pole set by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Summing proves $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The global lower bound follows from $R_ i^2+T_ i^3\geq R_ i^2$. For the upper bound over $D_ i$, away from the other divisors, place the $i$th fiber coordinate at its marked point; all the other summands are smooth there. The residual is $\beta =\tfrac 12\sum _ i\omega _{B,i}>0$, whose top integral is $q!/2^ q$. The theorem gives the required generic orders along every $D_ i$. Conversely, near a point where several of the pairs $(R_ i,T_ i)$ vanish, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-m\varphi }$ is comparable to the product of the factors $(|z_ i|^4+|w_ i|^6)^{-m/4}$ in disjoint pairs of variables. A descended coefficient divisible by every $z_ i^{K_ m}$ has a bounded holomorphic residual. Each factor is integrable because $K_ m+1>m/2-2/3$, and Fubini's theorem gives integrability at the intersections; elsewhere the same argument uses fewer factors. This proves the identity for $V_ m$, and the theorem gives $W_ m$. A line bundle $\mathcal O_ B(d,\ldots ,d)$ with $d\geq 0$ has $(d+1)^ q$ independent sections, the products of monomials in the separate factors. Since $K_ m=L_ m-1$ for $m\geq 2$ and $m-L_ m=\lceil m/2\rceil $, subtraction gives the displayed defect and its leading term. $\square$ As before, the selecting potential takes finite values and the value $-\infty $ in the fibers over the divisors, so it does not descend. Theorem 18.39.13 extends the sufficient conditions for 24.10.2 to normal crossing divisors; it does not cover base ideals of other forms, and it gives no necessary conditions.

title: Lemma 18.39.12
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Lemma 18.39.12 . 46F892FF98FE Let $M$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $d\geq 0$, and let $E,F_1,\ldots ,F_ N$ be holomorphic line bundles on $M$. For each $C_0>0$ there is a constant $C_1$ such that \[  h^0\left(M,E^ m\otimes \bigotimes _{i=1}^ NF_ i^{j_ i}\right)\leq C_1m^ d \qquad (m\geq 1,\  j_ i\in \mathbb Z,\  |j_ i|\leq C_0m).  \] Proof. For $d=0$ the dimension is at most the number of points of $M$. For $d\geq 1$, use fixed smooth metrics, a smooth positive volume form and finitely many framed charts as in the proof of lemma 18.39.1 . The local weight of the metric is $m\phi _ E+\sum _ i j_ i\phi _{F_ i}$, whose second derivatives are bounded by $Cm$ uniformly over the stated range. After its constant and real-linear terms at a point have been removed by a holomorphic affine change of frame, it is bounded by a fixed constant on a ball of radius $\varepsilon m^{-1/2}$ about that point. The submean inequality then gives $|s(x)|^2\leq Cm^ d\| s\| _{L^2}^2$, uniformly in $x$, $m$ and the integers $j_ i$. Since evaluation has a one-dimensional target, an orthonormal basis satisfies $\sum _\ell |s_\ell (x)|^2\leq Cm^ d$, and integration gives the estimate. The constants depend only on the fixed bundles, metrics, charts, volume and $C_0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 18.39.13
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Theorem 18.39.13 . A7CF6A5A6A5C Suppose that $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (B,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi \geq \sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| \pi ^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C \quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ there is a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j\ne i}D_ j$, with coordinates $(z_ i,t_ i,w_ i,v_ i)$ as in theorem 18.39.8 , on which \[  \varphi \leq \frac{c_ i}{p_ i}\log \left(|z_ i|^{2p_ i} +\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}|w_{ij}|^{2b_{ij}}\right)+C_ i, \qquad 1\leq r_ i\leq f,  \] where $p_ i$ and $b_{ij}$ are positive integers and $C_ i$ is a constant. Put \[  \begin{gathered} a_ i=p_ i\sum _{j=1}^{r_ i}b_{ij}^{-1},\quad L_{m,i}=\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor ,\quad K_{m,i}=\max \{ \lfloor mc_ i-a_ i\rfloor ,0\} ,\\ \psi =u+\sum _{i=1}^ Nc_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ B\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty )$, and for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{split}  W_ m& :=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )\bigr ) =H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right)\subseteq V_ m,\\  V_ m& \subseteq H^0\left(B,A^ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. For $q=1$ this difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Off the divisors the non-pluripolar measure equals $\beta ^ q$, and neither measure charges their union. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q$, with finite positive total mass. Near a point of an intersection, the divisors through that point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes $\{ z_ i=0\} $. If a holomorphic germ is divisible by each corresponding $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, then it is divisible by their product; its residual coefficient is bounded, and since $L_{m,i}+1>mc_ i$, Fubini's theorem gives integrability. Conversely, integrability at generic nearby points of each coordinate hyperplane forces divisibility by $z_ i^{L_{m,i}}$, by the one-variable threshold, and the divisor of the germ then gives divisibility throughout the chart. This proves \[  \mathcal I(m\psi )=\mathcal O_ B\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right).  \] Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound implies $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integration in submersion coordinates gives $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For a nonzero section in $V_ m$, the polydisk over $D_ i$ on which the upper bound holds detects the generic vanishing order of the section along the irreducible divisor $D_ i$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 18.39.8 , together with the strict integrability threshold of lemma 18.39.7 , shows that this order is at least $K_{m,i}$. Imposing all these orders proves the upper inclusion. To compare dimensions, raise the orders from $(K_{m,i})_ i$ to $(L_{m,i})_ i$, one divisor and one unit at a time. At each step, the restriction sequence loses at most \[  h^0\left(D_ i,\left.A^ m\left(-\sum _ j n_ jD_ j\right)\right|_{D_ i}\right), \qquad 0\leq n_ j\leq mc_ j,  \] dimensions. By lemma 18.39.12 with $E=A|_{D_ i}$ and $F_ j=\mathcal O_ B(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$, this is $O(m^{q-1})$ uniformly over all steps, and there are at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. When $q=1$, the distinct connected divisors are points, and each restriction space has dimension one. $\square$

title: Example 18.39.14
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Example 18.39.14 . 411D2D5FFC5D Let $B=(\mathbb P^1)^ q$, $X=B\times (\mathbb P^1)^ q$ and $A=\mathcal O_ B(1,\ldots ,1)$. By the calculation in example 18.39.10 , the complex Hessian of each summand of $\varphi $ is bounded below by $-\tfrac 12\omega _{B,i}-\tfrac 34\omega _{F,i}$, also across its pole set by the extension theorem after a quadratic correction. Summing proves $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. The global lower bound follows from $R_ i^2+T_ i^3\geq R_ i^2$. For the upper bound over $D_ i$, away from the other divisors, place the $i$th fiber coordinate at its marked point; all the other summands are smooth there. The residual is $\beta =\tfrac 12\sum _ i\omega _{B,i}>0$, whose top integral is $q!/2^ q$. The theorem gives the required generic orders along every $D_ i$. Conversely, near a point where several of the pairs $(R_ i,T_ i)$ vanish, the density $\mathrm{e}^{-m\varphi }$ is comparable to the product of the factors $(|z_ i|^4+|w_ i|^6)^{-m/4}$ in disjoint pairs of variables. A descended coefficient divisible by every $z_ i^{K_ m}$ has a bounded holomorphic residual. Each factor is integrable because $K_ m+1>m/2-2/3$, and Fubini's theorem gives integrability at the intersections; elsewhere the same argument uses fewer factors. This proves the identity for $V_ m$, and the theorem gives $W_ m$. A line bundle $\mathcal O_ B(d,\ldots ,d)$ with $d\geq 0$ has $(d+1)^ q$ independent sections, the products of monomials in the separate factors. title: 18.39.15 Fiber integrability on a modified base
search_title: Fiber integrability on a modified base
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Keep $\pi :X\to B$, $(A,h)$, $\theta $, $\varphi $ and $V_ m$ as in subsection 18.39.6 . A singularity of higher codimension on the base can become divisorial after a modification of the base. By lemma 5.43.22 , the integrability test upstairs then applies to the pulled-back section multiplied by the Jacobian. This fixed factor shifts the divisorial orders, while the restriction estimate still bounds the number of lost sections. Let $\rho :Y\to B$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds, and form the fiber product and its projections \[  X'=X\times _ B Y,\qquad \pi ':X'\to Y,\qquad \mu :X'\to X.  \] In local submersion coordinates one sees that $X'$ is smooth, that $\pi '$ is a submersion with the same compact connected fibers as $\pi $, and that $\mu $ is a modification. Let $R_\rho $ and $J_\rho $ be the relative canonical bundle and the Jacobian section of $\rho $, as in subsection 5.43.21 . The coordinate Jacobian matrix of $\mu $ is that of $\rho $, extended by the identity in the fiber variables, so \[  R_\mu =\pi '^*R_\rho ,\qquad J_\mu =\pi '^*J_\rho .  \] Put $\varphi '=\varphi \circ \mu $ and $\theta '=\rho ^*\theta $. Choose distinct nonempty smooth connected reduced divisors $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ on $Y$ whose union has simple normal crossings, together with smooth metrics $H_ i$ on $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ i)$, canonical sections $s_ i$ and curvatures $\eta _ i$. Theorem 18.39.16 . 1FC6712A00F0 Suppose that $c_ i>0$ and $u\in C^\infty (Y,\mathbb R)$ satisfy \[  \beta =\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _ i c_ i\eta _ i>0, \qquad \varphi '\geq \sum _ i c_ i\log \| \pi '^*s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2-C.  \] Suppose that for each $i$ the function $\varphi '$ satisfies an anisotropic upper bound, with respect to $\pi '$, on a submersion polydisk over an open subset of $D_ i$ away from the other divisors, as in theorem 18.39.13 , with fixed $p_ i,b_{ij}$. Define $a_ i$, $L_{m,i}$ and $K_{m,i}$ by the formulas of that theorem, and put \[  \psi '=u+\sum _ i c_ i\log \| s_ i\| _{H_ i}^2, \qquad M_ m=\rho ^*A^ m\otimes R_\rho .  \] Then there is a unique $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ with $\psi \circ \rho =\psi '$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\rho _*(\beta ^ q),\qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\int _ Y\beta ^ q\in (0,\infty ).  \] The map $T_ m(s)=J_\rho \rho ^*s$ identifies $H^0(B,A^ m)$ with $H^0(Y,M_ m)$, and for $W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi ))$, \[  \begin{split}  T_ m(W_ m)& =H^0\left(Y,M_ m\left(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right),\\  T_ m(W_ m)& \subseteq T_ m(V_ m) \subseteq H^0\left(Y,M_ m\left(-\sum _ iK_{m,i}D_ i\right)\right). \end{split}  \] Consequently $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$ and $\dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=O(m^{q-1})$. If $q=1$, the difference is at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ for every $m$. Proof. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi '=\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$. Thus $\psi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\rho ^*\theta )$, and proposition 5.43.18 gives the unique potential $\psi $ on $B$ with $\psi \circ \rho =\psi '$. On $Y$, locality off the union of the divisors and the fact that the non-pluripolar measure does not charge this union give $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta '}(\psi ')=\beta ^ q$. The measure identity in proposition 18.35.1 then gives the pushforward formula and the mass. Lemma 5.43.22 , applied first with weight zero and then with weight $m\psi $, gives the identification of the full section spaces and the formula for $T_ m(W_ m)$; here $\mathcal I(m\psi ')=\mathcal O_ Y(-\sum _ iL_{m,i}D_ i)$ by the integrability computation for simple normal crossings in the proof of theorem 18.39.13 . Since $u$ is bounded, the global lower bound gives $\varphi '\geq \psi '\circ \pi '-C'$. As $\rho \circ \pi '=\pi \circ \mu $ and $\mu $ is surjective, this descends to $\varphi \geq \psi \circ \pi -C'$, and integrability in bounded submersion charts proves $W_ m\subseteq V_ m$. For $s\in V_ m$, the transformation of multiplier ideals under $\mu $ gives \[  J_\mu \mu ^*s=\pi '^*T_ m(s) \in H^0\bigl (X',\pi '^*M_ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\varphi ')\bigr ).  \] Hence, in each polydisk where the upper bound holds, the descended coefficient of $T_ m(s)$ vanishes to order at least $K_{m,i}$ along $D_ i$, by lemma 18.39.7 and the argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 18.39.8 . This is the vanishing order of $T_ m(s)$, including the Jacobian factor, and it proves the upper inclusion. The chain of restrictions along the divisors on $Y$ has at most $\sum _ i\lceil a_ i\rceil $ steps. On $D_ i$, each target is $(\rho ^*A|_{D_ i})^ m$ twisted by powers of the bundles $\mathcal O_ Y(-D_ j)|_{D_ i}$ in a linear range and by the fixed bundle $R_\rho |_{D_ i}$. Including the latter in lemma 18.39.12 with exponent one, we see that every target has dimension $O(m^{q-1})$, uniformly. Summing gives the estimate. For $q=1$ each divisor is a point and every target has dimension one. $\square$ The theorem requires the modification and the divisorial data to be given, with a positive residual; it does not say which selecting potentials admit such data. In the following model with a point pole on the base, both the residual and the Jacobian correction are explicit. Example 18.39.17 . 17FFBB442DEB Let $q\geq 2$, $B=\mathbb P^ q$, $A=\mathcal O_ B(1)$, $p=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ and $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$. Use the normalized Fubini–Study forms $\omega _ B,\omega _ F$ and the corresponding metrics, and for a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$ put \[  R=\frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ q|Z_ j|^2},\quad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\tfrac 14\log (R^2+T^3),\quad \psi =\tfrac 12\log R.  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega _ B+\omega _ F)$, and $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\omega _ B)$ has mass $1-2^{-q}$. Let $\mathfrak m_ p$ be the ideal sheaf of $p$. The selected and reference spaces are exactly \[  \begin{gathered} V_ m=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ p^{k_ m}\bigr ),\qquad W_ m=H^0\bigl (B,A^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ p^{\ell _ m}\bigr ),\\ k_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor -q+1,0\} ,\qquad \ell _ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2\rfloor -q+1,0\} . \end{gathered}  \] Their defect vanishes for $m<2q$, and for $m\geq 2q$ it is \[  \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=\binom {\lfloor m/2\rfloor -1}{q-1} \sim \frac{2^{1-q}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}.  \] Proof. Over a common denominator, $R^2+T^3$ is a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients of sections of $\mathcal O_ X(2,3)$, divided by the corresponding metric factor. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\tfrac 12\omega _ B-\tfrac 34\omega _ F$, also across the common zero set by the extension theorem. Let $\rho :Y\to B$ be the blowup of $p$, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $\tau :Y\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $Y$ of the projection $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ q]\mapsto [Z_1:\cdots :Z_ q]$. Since $(\rho ,\tau )$ is an embedding, the forms \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _ B,\quad \gamma =\tau ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \beta =\tfrac 12(\alpha +\gamma )  \] satisfy $\beta >0$. The divisor bundle is $\mathcal O_ Y(E)=\rho ^*\mathcal O_ B(1)\otimes \tau ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{q-1}}(-1)$; its quotient metric has curvature $\alpha -\gamma $ and satisfies $R\circ \rho =\| s_ E\| ^2$. Thus the theorem applies with the single divisor $E$, $u=0$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$ and residual $\beta $. Along $E\times \{ o\} $ the pulled-back selecting potential has the exact local model $\tfrac 14\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1)$, and it is locally bounded elsewhere. If $T_ m(s)$ is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, where $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, then lemma 18.39.7 gives integrability in every chart of this model; this gives the inclusion opposite to the upper inclusion of the theorem. In the blowup coordinates $Z_1/Z_0=z$ and $Z_ j/Z_0=zt_ j$ for $j\geq 2$, the Jacobian of $\rho $ is $z^{q-1}$. Hence, if a section $s$ of $A^ m$ vanishes to order $d$ at $p$, then $T_ m(s)$ vanishes to order $d+q-1$ generically along $E$. The two divisorial thresholds $\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m$ therefore give exactly the orders $\ell _ m$ and $k_ m$ above. Homogeneous polynomials of degree $m$ realize every jet of total degree at most $m$ at $p$. For $m\geq 2q$ we have $k_ m=\ell _ m-1$, and the additional jets of degree $\ell _ m-1$ are spanned by $\binom {\ell _ m+q-2}{q-1}$ monomials, which gives the defect. For $m<2q$ both orders vanish. Finally, in cohomology $[\beta ]=\rho ^*c_1(A)-\tfrac 12[E]$. The intersection numbers containing both $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ and $[E]$ vanish, because $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ restricts to zero on $E$. The normal bundle of $E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ is $\mathcal O_ E(-1)$, so $\int _ Y[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, while $\int _ Y(\rho ^*c_1(A))^ q=1$. Expanding gives $\int _ Y\beta ^ q=1-2^{-q}$, which is the mass of $\psi $ by the theorem. $\square$ The selecting potential is finite at most points of the fiber over $p$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $(p,o)$, so again it does not descend, even up to a bounded function. The reference potential $\psi $ has a pole of codimension $q$ at $p$, and the Jacobian factor is what converts the divisorial orders along $E$ into vanishing orders at $p$.

Let $\rho :Y\to B$ be the blowup of $p$, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $\tau :Y\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $Y$ of the projection $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ q]\mapsto [Z_1:\cdots :Z_ q]$. Since $(\rho ,\tau )$ is an embedding, the forms \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _ B,\quad \gamma =\tau ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \beta =\tfrac 12(\alpha +\gamma )  \] satisfy $\beta >0$. The divisor bundle is $\mathcal O_ Y(E)=\rho ^*\mathcal O_ B(1)\otimes \tau ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{q-1}}(-1)$; its quotient metric has curvature $\alpha -\gamma $ and satisfies $R\circ \rho =\| s_ E\| ^2$. Thus the theorem applies with the single divisor $E$, $u=0$, $c=1/2$, $a=2/3$ and residual $\beta $. Along $E\times \{ o\} $ the pulled-back selecting potential has the exact local model $\tfrac 14\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1)$, and it is locally bounded elsewhere. If $T_ m(s)$ is divisible by $z^{K_ m}$, where $K_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m/2-2/3\rfloor ,0\} $, then lemma 18.39.7 gives integrability in every chart of this model; this gives the inclusion opposite to the upper inclusion of the theorem. In the blowup coordinates $Z_1/Z_0=z$ and $Z_ j/Z_0=zt_ j$ for $j\geq 2$, the Jacobian of $\rho $ is $z^{q-1}$. Hence, if a section $s$ of $A^ m$ vanishes to order $d$ at $p$, then $T_ m(s)$ vanishes to order $d+q-1$ generically along $E$. The two divisorial thresholds $\lfloor m/2\rfloor $ and $K_ m$ therefore give exactly the orders $\ell _ m$ and $k_ m$ above. Homogeneous polynomials of degree $m$ realize every jet of total degree at most $m$ at $p$. For $m\geq 2q$ we have $k_ m=\ell _ m-1$, and the additional jets of degree $\ell _ m-1$ are spanned by $\binom {\ell _ m+q-2}{q-1}$ monomials, which gives the defect. For $m<2q$ both orders vanish. Finally, in cohomology $[\beta ]=\rho ^*c_1(A)-\tfrac 12[E]$. The intersection numbers containing both $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ and $[E]$ vanish, because $\rho ^*c_1(A)$ restricts to zero on $E$. The normal bundle of $E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ is $\mathcal O_ E(-1)$, so $\int _ Y[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, while $\int _ Y(\rho ^*c_1(A))^ q=1$. Expanding gives $\int _ Y\beta ^ q=1-2^{-q}$, which is the mass of $\psi $ by the theorem. $\square$

title: 18.39.18 Semipositive residuals with positive volume
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Strict positivity of the residual $\beta $ was used only to make the reference potential $\psi $ plurisubharmonic with positive non-pluripolar mass; the estimates for the divisorial orders do not use it. The section comparison therefore holds for semipositive residuals with positive top integral. In particular, it does not require the residual class to contain a positive form. Corollary 18.39.19 . AF408F696ADF In each of theorem 18.39.8 , theorem 18.39.13 , theorem 18.39.16 , replace the condition $\beta >0$ by \[  \beta \geq 0,\qquad \int _ M\beta ^ q>0,  \] where $M=B$ in the first two theorems and $M=Y$ in the third, and keep all the other hypotheses. Then all the conclusions remain valid. The same replacement is valid in corollary 18.39.9 . Proof. In each case the reference current is $\beta +\sum _ i c_ i[D_ i]$, which is positive. Locality off the union of the divisors, together with the fact that the non-pluripolar measure does not charge this union, gives the non-pluripolar measure $\beta ^ q$ on $M$. Its mass is finite because $\beta $ is smooth and $M$ is compact, and positive by assumption. In the case of a modified base, the potential descends and its measure is $\rho _*(\beta ^ q)$, by the same descent and measure identities as before. The multiplier ideal on the base depends only on the logarithmic divisorial orders and the bounded smooth term. The lower inclusion uses the global lower bound for the selecting potential, and the upper inclusion uses the anisotropic threshold in a polydisk where the upper bound holds; neither uses strict positivity of $\beta $. The restriction estimates concern fixed line bundles, whatever their curvature, and the Jacobian and the fixed canonical twist in the case of a modified base are unchanged. Hence the inclusions and dimension bounds in all three proofs remain valid. The reverse inclusion for the exact anisotropic model uses only its local integrability test and the local boundedness off the pole set, so it also remains valid. $\square$ The condition on the top integral concerns the chosen reference: a semipositive residual may have zero top integral. Conversely, a semipositive residual with positive top integral need not become strictly positive after any smooth change of gauge. The following example shows this, with an exact computation of the selected spaces. Example 18.39.20 . C695A6659495 Let $q\geq 2$, let $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ be the blowup of $p=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, and let $E$ be its exceptional divisor. Let $\tau :B\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $B$ of the projection from $p$, and put \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^ q},\qquad \gamma =\tau ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \kappa =\alpha +\gamma >0,  \] where $\omega _{\mathbb P^ q}$ and $\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}}$ are the normalized Fubini–Study forms. Equip $\mathcal O_ B(E)=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(1)\otimes \tau ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{q-1}}(-1)$ with the quotient metric, whose curvature is $\eta =\alpha -\gamma $, and let $s_ E$ be its canonical section. For an integer $k\geq 1$, equip \[  A=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(E) \quad \hbox{with curvature}\quad \theta =k\alpha +\eta .  \] Let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with projection $\pi $ to $B$. For a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$, use the normalized Fubini–Study metric on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(o)$, and set \[  \begin{gathered} R=\| \pi ^*s_ E\| ^2,\quad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\quad \varphi =\tfrac 12\log (R^2+T^3),\quad \omega =\pi ^*\kappa +2\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\\ \psi =\log \| s_ E\| ^2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=(k\alpha )^ q,\qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=k^ q.  \] The residual $k\alpha $ cannot be made strictly positive by a smooth change of gauge. Nevertheless, for every $m\geq 1$ the selected and reference spaces coincide as subspaces of $H^0(B,A^ m)$: \[  V_ m=W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m) =s_ E^ m\rho ^*H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)), \qquad \dim V_ m=\binom {km+q}{q}.  \] Proof. Since $(\rho ,\tau )$ is an embedding, $\kappa >0$. The quotient metric satisfies \[  \| s_ E\| ^2=\rho ^*\left(\frac{\sum _{j=1}^ q|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ q|Z_ j|^2}\right),  \] as in example 18.39.17 . The same calculation over a common denominator, now with coefficient $1/2$, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -\pi ^*\alpha -\tfrac 32\omega _{\mathbb P^1}  \] off the pole set $E\times \{ o\} $, and across it by the extension theorem. Hence $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \pi ^*\gamma +\tfrac 12\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. Along the smooth pole set $E\times \{ o\} $, the function $\varphi $ has the exact local model $\tfrac 12\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1)$, and it is locally bounded elsewhere. It also satisfies the global lower bound $\varphi \geq \log R$. We may therefore take $c=1$, $u=0$, $p=2$, $b_1=3$ and $a=2/3$, with residual $\beta =\theta -\eta =k\alpha \geq 0$. Its top integral is $k^ q$, since the normalized Fubini–Study form has top integral one and $\rho $ is a modification. Corollary 18.39.19 , Corollary 18.39.9 therefore give \[  W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-mE)),\qquad V_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-(m-1)E)).  \] Let $t\geq 0$ be an integer. A section of $\rho ^*\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(tE)$, divided by $s_ E^ t$, gives a holomorphic section of $\mathcal O(km)$ on $\mathbb P^ q\setminus \{ p\} $, which extends across $p$ by Hartogs' theorem since $q\geq 2$. Pulling the extension back and multiplying by $s_ E^ t$ recovers the original section off $E$, hence everywhere by the identity theorem. Thus every section of $A^ m$ has the form $s_ E^ m\rho ^*s$, and the natural embeddings of $W_ m$ and $V_ m$ into $H^0(B,A^ m)$ both have this image. Its dimension is the number $\binom {km+q}{q}$ of monomials of degree $km$. Finally, let $C\subset E\simeq \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be a projective line; it is contracted by $\rho $. For every smooth real function $u$, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ C(k\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=0$, whereas a strictly positive form has positive integral over $C$. Changing the smooth metric on the divisor bundle changes the residual only by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a smooth function, so this proves the obstruction. Moreover, $\varphi $ is finite on most of each fiber over $E$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $o$ of that fiber, so it does not descend, even up to a bounded function. $\square$ Thus the selected and reference spaces agree, although the selecting potential does not descend and the reference has positive mass. The reason is that $E$ is a fixed component of every section of $A^ m$: all global sections vanish along $E$ to order $m$, more than the local integrability threshold requires. As before, the criterion presupposes the global bounds for the selecting potential and a residual with positive top integral; it does not produce them for arbitrary fiber singularities.

title: 18.39.21 Fixed exceptional orders and coefficient thresholds
search_title: Fixed exceptional orders and coefficient thresholds
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: In example 18.39.20 the fixed divisor $E$ absorbs the local integrability conditions. If the coefficient of the selecting potential increases, the selected sections must eventually also vanish at the point that was blown up. The following family shows when this happens, and when the mass of the reference potential vanishes. Keep the blowup $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ with $q\geq 2$, its exceptional divisor $E$, the extended projection $\tau $, the forms $\alpha ,\gamma ,\kappa $, and the quotient metric on $\mathcal O_ B(E)$ with curvature $\eta $ from that example, and write $x=\rho (E)$ for the point blown up. Let $k,e\geq 1$ be integers and equip \[  A_ e=\rho ^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ q}(k)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(eE), \qquad \theta =k\alpha +e\eta  \] with the product metric. Let $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$ with its projection $\pi $, let $o\in \mathbb P^1$, and let $R=\| \pi ^*s_ E\| ^2$ and $T=\| s_ o\| ^2$ as before. For positive integers $p,b$ and a real number $c>0$, put \[  \varphi _ c=\frac cp\log (R^ p+T^ b),\quad \omega _ c=c\pi ^*\kappa +(cb/p+1)\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\quad a=\frac pb,  \] and let $V_ m(c)\subseteq H^0(B,A_ e^ m)$ be the space selected by $\mathcal I(m\varphi _ c)$, regarded on $B$ by descent. Proposition 18.39.22 . F3005ECDDA69 For every $c>0$ we have $\varphi _ c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega _ c)$, and the selected space is \[  \begin{gathered} V_ m(c)=s_ E^{em}\rho ^*H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{v_ m}\bigr ),\\ v_ m=\max \{ \lfloor m(c-e)-a\rfloor ,0\} ,\qquad m\geq 1, \end{gathered}  \] where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the ideal sheaf of $x$. For $0<c\leq e+k$ put \[  d=\max \{ c,e\} ,\quad \delta =d-e,\quad \psi _ d=d\log \| s_ E\| ^2,\quad \ell _ m=\lfloor m\delta \rfloor .  \] Then $\psi _ d\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$ and \[  \begin{gathered} \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi _ d)=\bigl ((k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma \bigr )^ q, \qquad \int _ B\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi _ d)=k^ q-\delta ^ q. \end{gathered}  \] The reference spaces satisfy \[  \begin{split}  W_ m(c)& :=H^0\bigl (B,A_ e^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi _ d)\bigr )\\ & =s_ E^{em}\rho ^*H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{\ell _ m}\bigr ) \subseteq V_ m(c). \end{split}  \] If $0<c\leq e$, both spaces equal $H^0(B,A_ e^ m)$ for every $m$. If $e<c<e+k$, the defect and the leading term of the dimension are \[  \begin{gathered} \dim V_ m(c)-\dim W_ m(c) =\binom {\ell _ m+q-1}{q}-\binom {v_ m+q-1}{q}=O(m^{q-1}),\\ \dim V_ m(c)=\frac{k^ q-(c-e)^ q}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}), \end{gathered}  \] where $\binom {q-1}{q}=0$. At $c=e+k$ the reference $\psi _ d$ has zero mass and \[  \dim V_ m(e+k) =\frac{(\lceil a\rceil +1)k^{q-1}}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1}+O(m^{q-2}).  \] If $c>e+k$, the selected space is zero exactly when \[  m(c-e-k)\geq a+1;  \] in particular, it is zero for every $m\geq \lceil (a+1)/(c-e-k)\rceil $. Proof. As in example 18.39.20 , the norm identity writes $R^ p+T^ b$ over the common denominator for $\mathcal O(p,b)$ on $\mathbb P^ q\times \mathbb P^1$, pulled back to $X$, and its numerator is a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients. The lower bound for the complex Hessian of the logarithm of such a sum, together with the extension theorem across the pole set, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ c\geq -c\pi ^*\alpha -(cb/p)\omega _{\mathbb P^1}.  \] Thus $\omega _ c+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ c\geq c\pi ^*\gamma +\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. Hartogs' theorem, as in that example, shows that every global section of $A_ e^ m$ can be written uniquely as $s_ E^{em}\rho ^*s$ with $s\in H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km))$. If $s$ vanishes to order $j$ at $x$, this section vanishes to order $em+j$ generically along $E$. In a chart of the pole set, $\varphi _ c=(c/p)\log (|z|^{2p}+|w|^{2b})+O(1)$. The argument with a unit coefficient in the proof of theorem 18.39.8 and lemma 18.39.7 require \[  em+j+1>mc-a, \quad \hbox{equivalently}\quad j\geq \max \{ \lfloor m(c-e)-a\rfloor ,0\} .  \] Conversely, this divisorial order gives integrability in every chart of the pole set, and $\varphi _ c$ is locally bounded elsewhere. The vanishing order of $s$ at $x$ equals the generic vanishing order of $\rho ^*s$ along $E$, as the blowup coordinates of example 18.39.17 show. This proves the formula for $V_ m(c)$. For $0\leq \delta \leq k$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ d=(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma +d[E]\geq 0.  \] The non-pluripolar measure does not charge $E$, and it equals the top power of the smooth residual $(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma $. The class of this residual is $k\rho ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))-\delta [E]$. The mixed intersection numbers vanish and $\int _ B[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, as computed in example 18.39.17 , so its mass is $k^ q-\delta ^ q$. The divisorial ideal is $\mathcal I(m\psi _ d)=\mathcal O_ B(-\lfloor md\rfloor E)$. Since $em$ is an integer, $\lfloor md\rfloor =em+\ell _ m$, and the condition on $s$ is exactly $j\geq \ell _ m$. This gives the formula for $W_ m(c)$, and the inclusion follows from $\ell _ m\geq v_ m$. If $c\leq e$, both point orders are zero. For an integer $0\leq j\leq km+1$, homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$ realize every jet of total degree less than $j$ at $x$, and there are $\binom {j+q-1}{q}$ such jets. Hence \[  h^0\bigl (\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^ j\bigr ) =\binom {km+q}{q}-\binom {j+q-1}{q}.  \] For $e<c<e+k$ we have $0\leq v_ m\leq \ell _ m\leq km$ and $\ell _ m-v_ m\leq \lceil a\rceil $, and subtraction gives the exact defect. Each additional jet degree contributes $O(m^{q-1})$ monomials, which gives the bound, and $v_ m=m(c-e)+O(1)$ gives the leading term of $\dim V_ m(c)$. At $c=e+k$ we have $v_ m=\max \{ km-\lceil a\rceil ,0\} $. For large $m$, the allowed monomials have vanishing orders $km-\lceil a\rceil ,\ldots ,km$ at $x$, and each of these $\lceil a\rceil +1$ degrees has $k^{q-1}m^{q-1}/(q-1)!+O(m^{q-2})$ monomials, which proves the asymptotic formula. The residual is then $k\gamma $, whose top power vanishes. For $c>e+k$, a nonzero polynomial of degree $km$ vanishes at $x$ to order at most $km$. Hence $V_ m(c)=0$ exactly when $v_ m>km$, which is equivalent to $m(c-e-k)-a\geq 1$. $\square$ For $0<c<e+k$ the reference $\psi _ d$ has positive mass and the defect is $O(m^{q-1})$, so this family admits the approximation asked for in 24.10.2 . At $c=e+k$ the reference mass vanishes and the growth degree of the selected spaces drops to $q-1$; beyond this threshold the selected spaces eventually vanish.

The vanishing order of $s$ at $x$ equals the generic vanishing order of $\rho ^*s$ along $E$, as the blowup coordinates of example 18.39.17 show. This proves the formula for $V_ m(c)$. For $0\leq \delta \leq k$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ d=(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma +d[E]\geq 0.  \] The non-pluripolar measure does not charge $E$, and it equals the top power of the smooth residual $(k-\delta )\alpha +\delta \gamma $. The class of this residual is $k\rho ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))-\delta [E]$. The mixed intersection numbers vanish and $\int _ B[E]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$, as computed in example 18.39.17 , so its mass is $k^ q-\delta ^ q$. The divisorial ideal is $\mathcal I(m\psi _ d)=\mathcal O_ B(-\lfloor md\rfloor E)$. Since $em$ is an integer, $\lfloor md\rfloor =em+\ell _ m$, and the condition on $s$ is exactly $j\geq \ell _ m$. This gives the formula for $W_ m(c)$, and the inclusion follows from $\ell _ m\geq v_ m$. If $c\leq e$, both point orders are zero. For an integer $0\leq j\leq km+1$, homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$ realize every jet of total degree less than $j$ at $x$, and there are $\binom {j+q-1}{q}$ such jets. Each additional jet degree contributes $O(m^{q-1})$ monomials, which gives the bound, and $v_ m=m(c-e)+O(1)$ gives the leading term of $\dim V_ m(c)$. At $c=e+k$ we have $v_ m=\max \{ km-\lceil a\rceil ,0\} $. title: 18.39.23 A semipositive residual with nonzero defect
search_title: A semipositive residual with nonzero defect
section: 18.39 Singularities along a section over a divisor
text: Blowing up two points instead of one, we obtain a residual that is semipositive, cannot be made strictly positive, and still has positive top integral. Unlike the example with one blown-up point, the gap between the two divisorial thresholds now produces a nonzero defect of the largest possible order $m^{q-1}$. Counting the spaces requires the following elementary interpolation of jets at several points. Lemma 18.39.24 . 822490631827 Let $x_1,\ldots ,x_ N$ be distinct points of $\mathbb P^ q$, $q\geq 1$, and let $d,j_1,\ldots ,j_ N$ be nonnegative integers with $\sum _ i j_ i\leq d+1$. Then the map from $H^0(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(d))$ to the jets of order less than $j_ i$ at the points $x_ i$ is surjective. In particular, \[  h^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(d)\otimes \bigcap _ i\mathfrak m_{x_ i}^{j_ i}\right) =\binom {d+q}{q}-\sum _ i\binom {j_ i+q-1}{q},  \] where $\binom {q-1}{q}=0$. Proof. We may discard the points with $j_ i=0$; if no point remains, the target is zero. Choose an affine chart containing all the remaining points, and use the corresponding trivialization of $\mathcal O(d)$. For each pair $i\ne k$ choose an affine linear function $L_{ik}$ vanishing at $x_ k$ and nonzero at $x_ i$, and set \[  Q_ i=\prod _{k\ne i}L_{ik}^{j_ k}.  \] Given a jet $b_ i$ at $x_ i$, divide it by the invertible jet of $Q_ i$ at $x_ i$, and let $T_ i$ be the Taylor polynomial of degree at most $j_ i-1$ of the quotient. Then $Q_ iT_ i$ has the jet $b_ i$ at $x_ i$ and vanishes to order at least $j_ k$ at every other point $x_ k$, and its degree is at most $\sum _ kj_ k-1\leq d$. Hence $\sum _ iQ_ iT_ i$, homogenized to degree $d$, realizes all the prescribed jets. In $q$ variables there are $\binom {j_ i+q-1}{q}$ monomials of total degree less than $j_ i$, which gives the dimension formula. $\square$ Example 18.39.25 . 47ABA9EAB173 Let $q\geq 2$ and let $\rho :B\to \mathbb P^ q$ be the blowup of the two points $x_1=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ and $x_2=[0:1:0:\cdots :0]$, with exceptional divisors $E_1,E_2$. Let $\tau _ i:B\to \mathbb P^{q-1}$ be the extension to $B$ of the projection from $x_ i$. With the normalized Fubini–Study forms, put \[  \alpha =\rho ^*\omega _{\mathbb P^ q},\qquad \gamma _ i=\tau _ i^*\omega _{\mathbb P^{q-1}},\qquad \kappa =\alpha +\gamma _1+\gamma _2>0.  \] Equip $\mathcal O_ B(E_ i)=\rho ^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes \tau _ i^*\mathcal O(-1)$ with the quotient metric, whose curvature is $\eta _ i=\alpha -\gamma _ i$, and let $s_ i$ be its canonical section. Equip \[  A=\rho ^*\mathcal O(2)\otimes \mathcal O_ B(E_1+E_2), \qquad \theta =2\alpha +\eta _1+\eta _2  \] with the product metric. On $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with projection $\pi $ and a point $o\in \mathbb P^1$, set \[  \begin{gathered} R_ i=\| \pi ^*s_ i\| ^2,\qquad T=\| s_ o\| ^2,\\ \varphi =\log (R_1^2+T^3)+\log (R_2^2+T^3),\\ \omega =4\pi ^*\kappa +7\omega _{\mathbb P^1},\\ \psi =2\log \| s_1\| ^2+2\log \| s_2\| ^2, \qquad \beta =\gamma _1+\gamma _2. \end{gathered}  \] Then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta )$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\psi )=\beta ^ q,\qquad \int _ B\beta ^ q=2^ q-2>0.  \] No smooth change of gauge makes $\beta $ strictly positive. Nevertheless, writing $V_ m$ and $W_ m$ for the selected and reference spaces as before, their images in $H^0(B,A^ m)$ are, for every $m\geq 1$, \[  \begin{aligned}  V_ m& =s_1^ ms_2^ m\rho ^*H^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(2m) \otimes \mathfrak m_{x_1}^{m-1}\mathfrak m_{x_2}^{m-1}\right),\\  W_ m& =s_1^ ms_2^ m\rho ^*H^0\left(\mathbb P^ q,\mathcal O(2m) \otimes \mathfrak m_{x_1}^{m}\mathfrak m_{x_2}^{m}\right). \end{aligned}  \] The defect and the common leading term of the dimensions are \[  \begin{gathered} \dim V_ m-\dim W_ m=2\binom {m+q-2}{q-1} \sim \frac{2}{(q-1)!}m^{q-1},\\ \dim V_ m=\frac{2^ q-2}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}),\qquad \dim W_ m=\frac{2^ q-2}{q!}m^ q+O(m^{q-1}). \end{gathered}  \] Proof. The map $(\rho ,\tau _1,\tau _2)$ is an embedding: away from the exceptional divisors $\rho $ is already an embedding, and along $E_ i$ the map $\tau _ i$ separates the tangent directions of $E_ i$ while $\rho $ detects the normal direction. Hence $\kappa >0$. The identity for the quotient metric is the one-point identity of example 18.39.20 , applied at each center. For each $i$, the calculation over a common denominator writes $R_ i^2+T^3$ as a sum of squared moduli of holomorphic coefficients over the metric denominator for $\mathcal O(2,3)$. Together with the extension theorem across the pole set, this gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq -4\pi ^*\alpha -6\omega _{\mathbb P^1}.  \] It follows that $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 4\pi ^*\beta +\omega _{\mathbb P^1}\geq 0$. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta +2[E_1]+2[E_2]\geq 0.  \] The non-pluripolar product does not charge the divisors and equals $\beta ^ q$. The class of $\beta $ is $2H-[E_1]-[E_2]$, where $H=\rho ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. As in example 18.39.17 , $H^ q=1$, the mixed intersection numbers involving $H$ and some $[E_ i]$ vanish, and $[E_ i]^ q=(-1)^{q-1}$; moreover, the two exceptional divisors are disjoint. Expanding gives $\int _ B\beta ^ q=2^ q-2$. Let $C$ be the strict transform of the line through $x_1$ and $x_2$. Both maps $\tau _ i$ are constant on $C$, so $\int _ C\beta =0$. By Stokes' theorem, $\int _ C(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=0$ for every smooth real function $u$, whereas a strictly positive form has positive integral over $C$. This proves the obstruction, although the top integral is positive. The selecting potential satisfies $\varphi \geq \pi ^*\psi $. Its pole set is the disjoint union of the sets $E_ i\times \{ o\} $. Near either of them the other summand is smooth, and \[  \varphi =\log (|z|^4+|w|^6)+O(1),\qquad E_ i=\{ z=0\} ,\quad o=\{ w=0\} .  \] Thus $c_ i=p_ i=2$, $b_{i1}=3$ and $a_ i=2/3$. By theorem 18.39.13 , corollary 18.39.19 , $W_ m=H^0(B,A^ m(-2m(E_1+E_2)))$, and $V_ m$ is contained in $H^0(B,A^ m(-(2m-1)(E_1+E_2)))$; for an integer $\ell $, the strict local integrability condition $\ell +1>2m-2/3$ means $\ell \geq 2m-1$. Conversely, by lemma 18.39.7 , divisibility by these orders gives integrability in every chart of the pole set, and off the pole set the selecting potential is locally bounded. This proves equality for $V_ m$. Dividing a section of $A^ m$ by $s_1^ ms_2^ m$ gives a section of $\mathcal O(2m)$ away from the two centers, which extends across them by Hartogs' theorem since $q\geq 2$. The pullback of the extension, multiplied by $s_1^ ms_2^ m$, agrees with the original section everywhere, by the identity theorem. If the extended section vanishes to order $j_ i$ at $x_ i$, the corresponding section of $A^ m$ vanishes to order $m+j_ i$ generically along $E_ i$. The two divisorial conditions therefore give exactly the vanishing orders at $x_1$ and $x_2$ displayed in the statement. Since the two point ideals have disjoint supports, their product equals their intersection. Apply lemma 18.39.24 with $d=2m$ and orders $(m,m)$ or $(m-1,m-1)$; in both cases their sum is at most $d+1$. This gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \dim W_ m& =\binom {2m+q}{q}-2\binom {m+q-1}{q},\\  \dim V_ m& =\binom {2m+q}{q}-2\binom {m+q-2}{q}. \end{aligned}  \] Pascal's identity gives the exact defect, and the leading terms give both growth laws. For $m=1$ the vanishing orders for $V_1$ are zero, and the defect is already two. For $q=2$ the dimensions are $\dim W_ m=(m+1)^2$ and $\dim V_ m=m^2+4m+1$. $\square$ In this example the residual $\beta $ has zero integral over the curve $C$, so no smooth change of gauge makes it positive, and yet its top integral is positive. Thus the bound $O(m^{q-1})$ of corollary 18.39.19 cannot be improved to $o(m^{q-1})$ for semipositive residuals either. As in the previous examples, the selecting potential is finite on most of each fiber over $E_ i$ and equals $-\infty $ at the point $o$ of that fiber, so it does not descend, even up to a bounded function.

18.40.5 The domination envelope
text:
We first compute the envelope on the base, using the affine chart $Z_0
e 0$. Set $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$, $s=|z|^2$, $l=k-c$, $s_0=l/c$ and $C=k\log k-c\log c-l\log l$. In this chart the reference weight of $A$ is $\phi _ A=k\log (1+s)$. Put \[  F_0(z)=  egin{cases}  k\log (1+s),& s\leq s_0,\  l\log s+C,& s\geq s_0. \end{cases}  \] As a function of $\log s$, $F_0$ is increasing and convex: its derivative increases to $l$ and then stays constant. Hence $F_0$ is plurisubharmonic. The two branches match to first order at $s=s_0$, and the tangent-line inequality gives $F_0\leq \phi _ A$. On a chart $Z_ j
e 0$ with $j\geq 1$, write $x=Z_0/Z_ j$ and denote the remaining ratios by $\zeta $. Near $Z$ the corresponding weight is \[  F_ j=c\log |x|^2+l\log (1+|\zeta |^2)+C.  \] Therefore $F_0$ and the $F_ j$ define a global plurisubharmonic metric weight $F$ on $A$, with a divisor pole of coefficient $c$ along $Z$ and a smooth remainder. Let $v\leq \phi _ A$ be a competing plurisubharmonic weight, that is, $v=\phi _ A+u$ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,	heta )$ and $u\leq 0$, and suppose that $v\leq c\log |x|^2+O(1)$ near $Z$. Write $v_0$ for its expression in the chart $Z_0
eq 0$. The obstacle gives $v_0\leq F_0$ on $\{ s\leq s_0\} $. On each complex line $z=t\xi $ with $|\xi |=1$, either $v_0(t\xi )\equiv -\infty $, or $v_0(t\xi )-l\log |t|^2$ is subharmonic on $|t|>\sqrt{s_0}$ and bounded above near infinity. In the coordinate $1/t$ the puncture at infinity is then removable, and the maximum principle bounds this difference by its boundary bound $C$. Varying $\xi $ proves $v\leq F$ on $B$. Consequently $F=\phi _ A+u_ c$ is the largest such weight, and its contact set $\{ F=\phi _ A\} $ is $D_ c$. We now return to $X$. By proposition 5.43.5 , every $\pi ^*	heta $-plurisubharmonic function has the form $u\circ \pi $ for a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $B$. Restriction to the local section $w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0$ shows that $u\circ \pi \preceq \varphi $ implies $u\leq c\log |x|^2+O(1)$ near $Z$. Conversely, this divisorial bound and the inequality $|x|^2\leq |x|^2+\sum _ j|w_ j|^2$ give the domination $u\circ \pi \leq \varphi +O(1)$ near $Y$. A finite cover of $Y$ gives one constant there. On the compact complement of a smaller neighborhood of $Y$, the function $\varphi $ is bounded below and $u\leq 0$, so one constant works on all of $X$. The two competitor families therefore correspond to each other, which proves $\mathcal P(\varphi )=u_ c\circ \pi $. The pole of this envelope fills $\pi ^{-1}(Z)$, although $\varphi $ is finite on $\pi ^{-1}(Z)\setminus Y$.

title: 18.40.6 Binomial kernels
text:
For a fixed integer $j\geq 0$, set $d=km$, $t_{m,j}=\max \{ \ell _ m-j,0\} $ and $\mathcal H_ m^{(j)}=H^0(B,\mathcal O(d)(-t_{m,j}Z))$. The choices $j=0$ and $j=r$ give $W_ m$ and $V_ m$. Give these spaces the reference norm defined by the Fubini–Study metric, zero continuous weight and the volume $
u _0=\omega _ B^ q$. For a binomial random variable $\operatorname {Bin}(d,R)$ with $d$ trials and success probability $R$, their kernels are 1480BE1C8578 18.40.7  egin{equation}  B_{m,j}^0(R)=A_ dQ_{m,j}(R),\qquad A_ d= inom {d+q}{q},\qquad Q_{m,j}(R)=\mathbb P\{ \operatorname {Bin}(d,R)\geq t_{m,j}\} . \end{equation} To see this, apply the monomial norm formula ( 18.38.3 ) in degree $d$. Invariance under the coordinate circle actions makes the monomials orthogonal, and the selection keeps exactly those in which $Z_0$ has exponent at least $t_{m,j}$. Summing over the other exponents with the multinomial identity gives ( 18.40.7 ). Counting the selected monomials gives $\dim \mathcal H_ m^{(j)}= inom {d-t_{m,j}+q}{q}=C_ cm^ q+O(m^{q-1})$. We next bound the tails from below. Write $D(v\mid R)=v\log (v/R)+(1-v)\log ((1-v)/(1-R))$ for the relative entropy, and put $b=\lfloor dafloor =\ell _ m$. text: In the compact models above, the vanishing orders are proportional to the tensor degree. To see the transition when the order grows more slowly, we pass to a model space of entire functions. There the local metric fixes the scale of the full kernel, while the selecting ideal creates a second, larger radius. Grouping the monomials according to the residues of their degrees expresses the transition at that radius through Poisson tails. In this section $r$ and $q$ denote new integers. Fix an integer $r\geq 1$. On $\mathbb C$, with coordinate $z=x+\mathrm{i}y$ and area measure $\mathrm{d}A=\mathrm{d}x\, \mathrm{d}y$, put $\phi (z)=|z|^{2r}$. For a real $m>0$, let $H_{m,r}$ be the Hilbert space of entire functions with norm \[  \| f\| _{m,r}^2=\int _{\mathbb C}|f|^2\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }\, \mathrm{d}A.  \] For an integer $q\geq 0$, let $H_{m,r}^{(q)}$ consist of the functions vanishing to order at least $q$ at zero. Since the weight is bounded below on each fixed disk, the local submean and Cauchy inequalities bound point and jet evaluations, so this subspace is closed. Write $K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,w)$ for its reproducing kernel, holomorphic in $z$ and antiholomorphic in $w$, and put \[  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z)=\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi (z)}K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,z).  \] Thus the ideal $(z^ q)$ selects the functions, while the smooth weight determines the norm. We use $\Gamma (a)=\int _0^\infty t^{a-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\, \mathrm{d}t$ for $a>0$. Proposition 18.41.1 . 85EDCA2D872C For every $m>0$ and integer $q\geq 0$, 33E9A1B502F8 18.41.2 \begin{equation}  K_{m,r}^{(q)}(z,w)=\frac r\pi \sum _{k=q}^\infty \frac{m^{(k+1)/r}(z\bar w)^ k}{\Gamma ((k+1)/r)}. \end{equation} The series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on compact sets. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$, EF4D2AABC4A8 18.41.3 \begin{equation}  m^{-1/r}B_{m,r}^{(q)}(m^{-1/(2r)}\zeta ) =\frac r\pi \mathrm{e}^{-|\zeta |^{2r}} \sum _{k=q}^\infty \frac{|\zeta |^{2k}}{\Gamma ((k+1)/r)}. \end{equation} Consequently, if $m$ tends to infinity through positive integers and $q=q_ m\to \infty $, the left side tends to zero uniformly on compact $\zeta $-sets. Proof. The monomials are orthogonal by rotational invariance. For every integer $k\geq 0$, polar integration with radial variable $\rho $ and the substitution $t=m\rho ^{2r}$ give \[  \| z^ k\| _{m,r}^2=2\pi \int _0^\infty \rho ^{2k+1}\mathrm{e}^{-m\rho ^{2r}}\, \mathrm{d}\rho =\frac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\Gamma ((k+1)/r).  \] For an entire function $f(z)=\sum _{k\geq 0}a_ kz^ k$, Parseval's identity on circles and Tonelli's theorem yield $\| f\| _{m,r}^2=\sum _{k\geq 0}|a_ k|^2\| z^ k\| _{m,r}^2$. Thus the normalized monomials form an orthonormal basis, and those with $k\geq q$ form an orthonormal basis of the selected subspace. This proves ( 18.41.2 ). By Stirling's formula, the reciprocal Gamma coefficients decay faster than every fixed geometric progression, even after multiplication by any fixed power of $k$; this gives uniform convergence on compact sets together with all derivatives. Substituting $z=w=m^{-1/(2r)}\zeta $ gives ( 18.41.3 ). On a disk $|\zeta |\leq R$ of fixed radius, the series in ( 18.41.3 ) is bounded by the tail, from the index $q$ on, of the convergent series with $|\zeta |$ replaced by $R$. This tail tends to zero as $q\to \infty $, proving the last assertion. $\square$ For $r=1$ and $q=0$ the density is the constant $m/\pi $. For general $r$ and $q=0$ its value at zero is $rm^{1/r}/(\pi \Gamma (1/r))$, whereas it vanishes at zero when $q>0$. The scale $m^{-1/(2r)}$ therefore describes fixed vanishing orders, but a growing order requires a further rescaling.

title: 18.41.4 A uniform tail estimate
section: 18.41 Degenerate curvature and growing vanishing orders
text: Grouping the monomial degrees by their residues modulo $r$ expresses the kernel through weighted Poisson tails. The estimate of Gamma ratios below removes those weights, with an error independent of the vanishing threshold. Write $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb E$ for probability and expectation. For $T>0$, let $N_ T$ be a Poisson random variable with parameter $T$, so that $\mathbb P(N_ T=\ell )=\mathrm{e}^{-T}T^\ell /\ell !$ for integers $\ell \geq 0$. For a real $0<\alpha \leq 1$, define \[  w_{\alpha ,T}(\ell )=T^{\alpha -1}\frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )}.  \] All constants in the next lemma may depend on $\alpha $, but not on $T$. Lemma 18.41.5 . 44E50E6CAEB1 There is a constant $C_\alpha >0$ such that, for $T\geq 1$, \[  \mathbb E\bigl |w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)-1\bigr |\leq C_\alpha T^{-1/2}.  \] Proof. Recall that $\mathbb E N_ T=T$ and $\operatorname {Var}(N_ T)=T$. Stirling's formula, applied to the ratio of Gamma functions, gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )} & =\ell ^{1-\alpha }(1+O_\alpha (\ell ^{-1}))& & \quad (\ell \to \infty ),\\  \frac{\Gamma (\ell +1)}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha )} & \leq C_\alpha (\ell +1)^{1-\alpha }& & \quad (\ell \geq 0). \end{aligned}  \] The second bound follows from the first after the constant is increased to account for finitely many small integers. Since $0\leq 1-\alpha <1$, it implies \[  w_{\alpha ,T}(\ell )\leq C_\alpha \left(1+\frac{\ell +1}{T}\right), \qquad \mathbb E(w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)+1)^2\leq C_\alpha \quad (T\geq 1).  \] For $T\geq 2$, consider the event $E_ T=\{ |N_ T-T|\leq T/2\} $. On this event, the expansion of the Gamma ratio and the bounded derivative of $s\mapsto s^{1-\alpha }$ on $[1/2,3/2]$ give \[  |w_{\alpha ,T}(N_ T)-1| \leq C_\alpha \left(\frac{|N_ T-T|}{T}+\frac1T\right).  \] By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, its expectation is at most $C_\alpha T^{-1/2}$. On the complement, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\mathbb P(E_ T^ c)\leq 4/T$, and the preceding second-moment bound together with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives the same estimate for the contribution of $E_ T^ c$. Enlarging the constant handles $1\leq T\leq 2$. $\square$ For integers $q\geq 0$ and $0\leq s<r$, put \[  L_ s(q)=\left\lceil \frac{q-s}{r}\right\rceil \geq 0.  \] If a monomial degree is written as $k=r\ell +s$, the condition $k\geq q$ becomes $\ell \geq L_ s(q)$. Proposition 18.41.6 . 79BA8CB51C0E There is a constant $C_ r>0$, depending only on $r$, such that for $m>0$, $z\ne 0$ and $T=m|z|^{2r}\geq 1$, 69B0FF116418 18.41.7 \begin{equation}  \left|\frac{\pi B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z)}{mr^2|z|^{2r-2}} -\frac1r\sum _{s=0}^{r-1}\mathbb P\{ N_ T\geq L_ s(q)\} \right| \leq C_ r T^{-1/2} \quad (q\geq 0). \end{equation} In particular, the error is uniform in the vanishing order $q$. Proof. Let $\rho =|z|>0$ and put $\alpha _ s=(s+1)/r$ for integers $0\leq s<r$. Grouping the positive series ( 18.41.2 ) by the residues $s$ and using $T=m\rho ^{2r}$, we obtain the exact identity \[  \begin{split}  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z) & =\frac r{\pi \rho ^2}\sum _{s=0}^{r-1} \mathrm{e}^{-T}\sum _{\ell \geq L_ s(q)} \frac{T^{\ell +\alpha _ s}}{\Gamma (\ell +\alpha _ s)}\\ & =\frac{rT}{\pi \rho ^2}\sum _{s=0}^{r-1} \mathbb E\bigl [w_{\alpha _ s,T}(N_ T) \mathbf1_{\{ N_ T\geq L_ s(q)\} }\bigr ]. \end{split}  \] Divide by $mr^2\rho ^{2r-2}/\pi =r^2T/(\pi \rho ^2)$ and apply lemma 18.41.5 to each of the finitely many residues. Since the indicators are bounded by one independently of their thresholds, the resulting error is uniform in $q$. $\square$

A vanishing order proportional to $m$ removes the kernel density inside a fixed circle. Inside that circle the limit of the potentials is logarithmic, and outside it agrees with the smooth weight. Throughout this subsection, $m$ tends to infinity through positive integers. For $\lambda >0$, set $q_ m=\lfloor m\lambda floor $ and $R_\lambda =(\lambda /r)^{1/(2r)}$. Define \[  V_\lambda (z)=  egin{cases}  |z|^{2r},& |z|\geq R_\lambda ,\  \lambda \log (|z|^2/R_\lambda ^2)+\lambda /r,& 0<|z|<R_\lambda ,\  -\infty ,& z=0. \end{cases}  \] In the following theorem, $\delta _0$ denotes the unit point mass at zero. Recall that in dimension one the non-pluripolar measure of a subharmonic function discards the mass carried by its polar set. text: Proposition 18.41.13 . 2E997A26D38A Fix a real $\tau $. Choose $z_ m\ne 0$ with \[  m|z_ m|^{2r}=\frac{q_ m}{r}+\tau \sqrt{\frac{q_ m}{r}},  \] which is positive for all sufficiently large $m$.
