title: 18.42 Localization on curves
text:
We now transfer the transition of proposition 18.41.13 to a compact curve. The selected sections concentrate on a shrinking disk around the distinguished point. When the remainder of the metric weight is negligible on that disk, the norm there can be compared directly with the model norm, and restriction to the disk gives an upper bound for the kernel. For the lower bound, positivity of the curvature away from the distinguished point permits a global $L^2$ correction of localized model sections that preserves the growing vanishing order. Let $C$ be a connected compact Riemann surface, let $x\in C$, and let $(L,h)$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $C$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Fix an integer $r\geq 1$. Suppose that in a holomorphic coordinate $z$ centered at $x$ and a holomorphic frame $e$, \[  |e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\phi },\qquad \phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1}).  \] Let $
u $ be a smooth positive volume form on $C$, written as $a(z)\, \mathrm{d}A$ in this coordinate, where $\mathrm{d}A$ is Euclidean area and $a(0)=1$. For positive integers $m$, choose nonnegative integers $q_ m$ such that \[  q_ m\longrightarrow \infty ,\qquad q_ m=o(m^{1/(2r+1)}).  \] Write $\mathfrak m_ x$ for the ideal sheaf of $x$, and equip \[  V_ m=H^0(C,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^{q_ m})  \] with the norm $\| s\| _ m^2=\int _ C|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm{d}
u $. Its density is $B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2$ for any orthonormal basis $(s_{m,j})$, and $B_ m=0$ if $V_ m=0$. As in section 18.41 , $\Phi $ denotes the standard Gaussian distribution function. Theorem 18.42.1 . F3F808FEE505 For a fixed real $	au $, let $x_ m$ lie in the coordinate neighborhood and satisfy \[  T_ m:=m|z(x_ m)|^{2r}=q_ m/r+	au \sqrt{q_ m/r}.  \] Then C94B49B08D68 18.42.2  egin{equation}  \limsup _{m	o \infty }  rac{\pi B_ m(x_ m)}{mr^2|z(x_ m)|^{2r-2}}\leq \Phi (	au ). \end{equation} If the curvature of $(L,h)$ is semipositive on $C$ and strictly positive on $C\setminus \{ x\} $, this ratio converges to $\Phi (	au )$. Proof. We compare $B_ m$ with the model kernels of section 18.41 on a shrinking disk, which gives the upper bound. For the lower bound, we cut off model polynomials concentrated near $x$ and correct them to global sections by an $L^2$ estimate. Put $z_ m=z(x_ m)$, $ho _ m=|z_ m|$, $R_ m=(q_ m/(rm))^{1/(2r)}$ and \[  S_ m= rac{mr^2ho _ m^{2r-2}}\pi .  \] Then $R_ m	o 0$ and $ho _ m/R_ m	o 1$, and $T_ m>0$ for all sufficiently large $m$. Positive constants denoted by $M$, with subscripts when needed, may change between estimates. They are independent of $m$ and of the argument of $z_ m$; they may depend on the fixed geometric data, $r$, $	au $, and fixed auxiliary cutoffs or radii. We write $q=q_ m$ when no confusion is possible. The model densities $B_{m,r}^{(q)}$ are those of section 18.41 . Step 1: the kernel on a shrinking disk. Fix a real $A>1$ and set $D_ m=\{ |z|<A R_ m\} $. On $D_ m$, \[  m|\phi (z)-|z|^{2r}|\leq M_ A mR_ m^{2r+1} =M_ A rac{q_ mR_ m}{r}=o(1),\qquad \sup _{D_ m}|a-1|=o(1).  \] The first limit follows from $q_ mR_ m=r^{-1/(2r)}(q_ m^{2r+1}/m)^{1/(2r)}	o 0$. Hence, on $D_ m$, the norm defined by $h^ m$ and $
u $ and the radial norm with weight $\mathrm{e}^{-m|z|^{2r}}\, \mathrm{d}A$ differ by a factor $1+o(1)$, uniformly over all holomorphic functions on $D_ m$. The same comparison holds for the corresponding pointwise weights at $z_ m$. For integers $k\geq 0$, let $I_{m,k}$ and $J_{m,k}$ be the squared norms of $z^ k$ on $D_ m$ and on the whole plane, respectively, with this radial weight. Polar integration gives \[   egin{aligned}  I_{m,k}& = rac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\gamma ((k+1)/r,U_ m), & U_ m& =m(A R_ m)^{2r},\  J_{m,k}& = rac\pi r m^{-(k+1)/r}\Gamma ((k+1)/r), & \gamma (b,U)& =\int _0^ U t^{b-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{aligned}  \] Here $b,U>0$. By Parseval's identity on circles and Tonelli's theorem, the normalized monomials form a complete orthonormal system in the space of holomorphic functions on $D_ m$ with finite radial norm: the squared norm of a Taylor series is the sum of the squared norms of its monomials, so its partial sums converge in that norm. Therefore the density of the subspace of functions vanishing to order at least $q$ is \[  B_ m^{D}(z_ m)=\mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}\sum _{k\geq q} rac{ho _ m^{2k}}{I_{m,k}}.  \] Point evaluation is continuous by the local submean inequality, so this sum is also the supremum of $\mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}|f(z_ m)|^2$ over the unit ball of that subspace. Choose fixed real numbers $1<c<d<A^{2r}$ and put $k_ m=\lfloor rcT_ mfloor $. For large $m$, $k_ m\geq q$ and $U_ m\geq dT_ m$. Uniformly for $0\leq k\leq k_ m+1$, FAC71C0D28AA 18.42.3  egin{equation}   rac{I_{m,k}}{J_{m,k}}=1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-\eta T_ m}) \end{equation} for some fixed $\eta >0$. Indeed, let $G_ b$ be a random variable with Gamma density $t^{b-1}\mathrm{e}^{-t}/\Gamma (b)$ on $(0,\infty )$. A change of variable gives $\mathbb E\mathrm{e}^{sG_ b}=(1-s)^{-b}$ for $0<s<1$. With $b=(k+1)/r\leq cT_ m+O_ r(1)$, Markov's inequality yields \[  1- rac{\gamma (b,U_ m)}{\Gamma (b)} \leq \mathrm{e}^{-sU_ m}(1-s)^{-b}.  \] Since $d>c$, choose $s>0$ small enough that $sd+c\log (1-s)>0$. The right side is at most $M\mathrm{e}^{-\eta T_ m}$, as required. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the positive radial measure gives $I_{m,k+1}^2\leq I_{m,k}I_{m,k+2}$, so $I_{m,k+1}/I_{m,k}$ increases with $k$. By ( 18.42.3 ) and the asymptotics of Gamma ratios, \[  ho _ m^2 rac{I_{m,k_ m}}{I_{m,k_ m+1}} =(1+o(1))T_ m^{1/r}  rac{\Gamma ((k_ m+1)/r)}{\Gamma ((k_ m+2)/r)} \longrightarrow c^{-1/r}<1.  \] Choose $\kappa \in (c^{-1/r},1)$. For all large $m$, the ratio of consecutive terms $ho _ m^{2k}/I_{m,k}$ is at most $\kappa $ for every $k\geq k_ m$. Consequently, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-T_ m}\sum _{k>k_ m} rac{ho _ m^{2k}}{I_{m,k}} \leq  rac{\kappa }{1-\kappa } \mathrm{e}^{-T_ m} rac{ho _ m^{2k_ m}}{I_{m,k_ m}} =o(S_ m).  \] For the last equality, replace $I_{m,k_ m}$ by $J_{m,k_ m}$ using ( 18.42.3 ). The resulting term is one of the terms of the series for $B_{m,r}^{(k_ m)}(z_ m)$. In ( 18.41.7 ) for this kernel, each residue threshold divided by $T_ m$ tends to $c>1$, so Chebyshev's inequality makes all the Poisson tails tend to zero, and the comparison error is $O(T_ m^{-1/2})$. Hence $B_{m,r}^{(k_ m)}(z_ m)=o(S_ m)$. For the terms with $q\leq k\leq k_ m$, we use ( 18.42.3 ). Since $I_{m,k}\leq J_{m,k}$ for every $k$, we obtain \[  B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z_ m)\leq B_ m^{D}(z_ m) \leq (1+o(1))B_{m,r}^{(q)}(z_ m)+o(S_ m).  \] By proposition 18.41.13 , 7549BC9C0F5C 18.42.4  egin{equation}  B_ m^{D}(z_ m)/S_ m\longrightarrow \Phi (	au ). \end{equation} The global norm of a selected section dominates its norm on $D_ m$. title: 18.42.9 Curvature quadrature domains
text: The disk comparison above requires the error of the metric weight to be small throughout the disk carrying the norm. A larger range of orders is obtained by absorbing the harmonic part of this error into the holomorphic sections. The transition then takes place on the boundary of the region where the remaining obstacle potential detaches from the weight with first-order contact, and a quadrature identity for the curvature determines that boundary. Keep $C,x,(L,h),r,z,e$ and $\nu =a(z)\, \mathrm{d}A$ from section 18.42 , and assume that the curvature of $(L,h)$ is semipositive on $C$ and strictly positive on $C\setminus \{ x\} $. We now allow integers $q=q_ m\to \infty $ with $q=o(m)$. Write $V_{m,q}=H^0(C,L^ m\otimes \mathfrak m_ x^ q)$, and let $B_{m,q}$ be its density for the norm of section 18.42 . Put \[  \rho =\phi _{z\bar z},\qquad t=q/m,\qquad R=(t/r)^{1/(2r)}.  \] Write $\mathbb D$ for the unit disk. Lemma 18.42.10 . 58D1933573E2 Let $b>1$, and let $Q(R,\zeta )$ be a real function, jointly smooth for small real $R$ and $|\zeta |<b$, with $Q(0,\zeta )=|\zeta |^{2r}$. Write $Q_ R=Q(R,\cdot )$, and suppose that every $Q_ R$ is subharmonic and that $Q_{R,\zeta \bar\zeta }>0$ on a fixed neighborhood of the unit circle. For small $R$, let $U_ R$ be the largest subharmonic function on $\{ |\zeta |<b\} $ such that $U_ R\leq Q_ R$ and $U_ R\leq 2r\log |\zeta |+O(1)$ near zero. Then the noncontact set $\Omega _ R=\{ U_ R<Q_ R\} $ is connected, and its boundary is a radial graph near the unit circle. Let $F_ R:\mathbb D\to \Omega _ R$ be the conformal map with $F_ R(0)=0$ and $F_ R'(0)>0$. For every fixed $k$ and all sufficiently small $R$, depending on $k$, the map $F_ R$ and the harmonic function $(U_ R-2r\log |\zeta |)\circ F_ R$ depend smoothly on $R$ in the Hölder spaces $C^{k,\alpha }(\overline{\mathbb D})$, and they differ from their values at $R=0$ by $O(R)$. The arguments below use only finitely many of these norms, so the dependence of the range of $R$ on $k$ is harmless. Proof. Fix $k\geq 3$ and $0<\alpha <1$. Let $A^{k,\alpha }$ be the real Banach space of functions that are holomorphic on $\mathbb D$, of class $C^{k,\alpha }$ on its closure, and real at zero. For $h\in A^{k,\alpha }$ near zero set $f(u)=u(1+h(u))$. For small $h$, the map $f$ is univalent, with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)>0$. The Cauchy projections are bounded on these Hölder spaces. This follows from the Hilbert kernel on the circle: subtract the value at the evaluation point, split the integral at twice the length of the increment, and use the Hölder bound for differences on the inner part and the bound for the differentiated kernel on the outer part. This gives the $C^{0,\alpha }$ bound, and commuting angular derivatives with the projections gives the $C^{k,\alpha }$ bound. The superposition operator $h\mapsto (Q_ R)_\zeta \circ f$ involves no derivatives of $h$ and is smooth. Thus $T$ is a smooth map into the product of the space of negative-mode functions with $\mathbb R$. At $(R,h)=(0,0)$ we have $T=0$ and \[  D_ hK(0,0)v=r^2(v+\bar v),\qquad D_ hT(0,0)v=(r^2\overline{v-v(0)},\, 2r^2v(0)).  \] This is a bounded real-linear isomorphism, so the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces gives a unique normalized branch $f_ R$ of solutions of $T(R,h)=0$, depending smoothly on $R$ in the fixed space, with $\| f_ R-\mathrm{id}\| =O(R)$. The branches obtained for larger $k$ agree with this one by uniqueness in the smaller space. For each fixed order, this gives the spatial estimates and the expansions in $R$ needed below, on a parameter interval that depends on the order. The equation $T=0$ prescribes only the real part of $[K]_0$; we show that the imaginary part vanishes as well. Since $P_-K=0$, the function $K$ extends holomorphically to $\mathbb D$, and $K(0)=[K]_0$ is purely imaginary. On the other hand, Stokes' formula gives \[  \frac1{2\pi \mathrm{i}}\int _{|u|=1}(Q_ R)_\zeta (f_ R(u))f_ R'(u)\, \mathrm{d}u =\frac1\pi \int _{f_ R(\mathbb D)}(Q_ R)_{\zeta \bar\zeta }\, \mathrm{d}A\in \mathbb R.  \] On the circle the integrand equals $(r+K)f_ R'/f_ R$, whose residue at zero is $r+K(0)$. Hence $K(0)$ is real as well, and therefore zero. Consequently \[  S_ R(\zeta )=\frac{r+K(f_ R^{-1}(\zeta ))}{\zeta } =r/\zeta +H_ R(\zeta )  \] with $H_ R$ holomorphic on $\Omega _ R=f_ R(\mathbb D)$, and $S_ R=(Q_ R)_\zeta $ on the boundary of $\Omega _ R$. Let \[  U_ R=2r\log |\zeta |+2\operatorname {Re}\int _0^\zeta H_ R(w)\, \mathrm{d}w+C_ R.  \] Its complex gradient agrees with that of $Q_ R$ on the boundary, so the difference $Q_ R-U_ R$ is constant there; choose the constant $C_ R$ to make it zero. Then the difference and its gradient vanish on the boundary. Since the tangential second derivative of the difference also vanishes there, its inward normal second derivative equals $\Delta Q_ R>0$. Hence $Q_ R-U_ R>0$ in an inner collar of uniform width. At $R=0$, \[  U_0=1+2r\log |\zeta |,\qquad |\zeta |^{2r}-1-2r\log |\zeta |>0\quad (0<|\zeta |<1).  \] By uniform convergence, this gap keeps a positive minimum on the remaining compact subsets of the interior for small $R$, and the logarithmic term controls a neighborhood of zero. Set $U_ R=Q_ R$ outside $\Omega _ R$. Since values and gradients match across the boundary, the Laplacian of the patched function carries no measure on the boundary. Its curvature is $r\delta _0$ inside $\Omega _ R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ R\geq 0$ outside, so it is an admissible minorant. If $v$ is any competitor, then $v-U_ R$ is subharmonic on $\Omega _ R\setminus \{ 0\} $, bounded above near zero and nonpositive on the boundary. Removability of the singularity at zero and the maximum principle give $v\leq U_ R$ in $\Omega _ R$, and outside $\Omega _ R$ this follows from $v\leq Q_ R$. This identifies the envelope and shows that there are no further noncontact components. The radial graph property and the estimates for the harmonic part follow from the normalized map and its dependence on the parameter. We henceforth write $F_ R=f_ R$. $\square$ We apply the lemma to the given weight. By Taylor's formula with integral remainder, for small real $R$, \[  Q_ R(\zeta )=R^{-2r}\phi (R\zeta ) =|\zeta |^{2r}+R E(R,\zeta )  \] with a jointly smooth function $E$. Choose the holomorphic primitive with $G_ R(0)$ real, and write the envelope in $\Omega _ R$ as \[  U_ R=2r\log |\zeta |+2\operatorname {Re} G_ R(\zeta ),\qquad G_ R=1/2+O(R).  \] Set $D_ t=R\Omega _ R$. In the original coordinate $z$, the obstacle potential is $\phi _ t(z)=R^{2r}U_ R(z/R)$ inside $D_ t$ and $\phi $ outside. Replacing $\phi $ by $\phi _ t$ in this chart and keeping $h$ elsewhere defines a global singular metric on $L$. Its local potential is $C^1$ across the boundary, bounded above by $\phi $, and has the pole $2t\log |z|+O(1)$. On the boundary, $\phi _ z=t/z+g_ t'$ for a holomorphic function $g_ t$. Green's formula therefore gives the quadrature identity 8F00DDA42676 18.42.11 \begin{equation}  \int _{D_ t}\rho (z)f(z)\, \mathrm dA=\pi t f(0) \end{equation} for every function $f$ holomorphic near $\overline{D_ t}$. The curvature of the singular metric is $t\delta _ x$ inside $D_ t$ and the original curvature outside. Finally, we write the boundary as $\Gamma _ t=\{ R c_ R(\theta )\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }\} $ with a positive periodic function $c_ R$, where $c_ R-1=O(R)$ in each fixed norm used below.

To prove the transition at the boundary $\Gamma _ t$, we again correct localized sections by an $L^2$ estimate. The singular metric of subsection 18.42.9 , whose curvature at $x$ is the point mass $t\delta _ x$, enforces the growing vanishing order of the correction. Its curvature vanishes on the rest of $D_ t$, so a bounded function varying on the scale $R$ must first restore strict positivity there. Lemma 18.42.13 . u }^2, \end{equation} where both sides are the $L^2$ norms defined by $h^ m$ and $

This function is uniformly bounded and its Hessian is $O(R^{-2})$. On the support of its negative curvature, the curvature $mho $ is comparable to $q/R^2$; since $q	o \infty $, it absorbs the negative part. Inside $D_ t$, the function $b_ R$ contributes the curvature $c/R^2$. Elsewhere in a fixed coordinate disk, the original curvature is bounded below by a fixed multiple of $m|z|^{2r-2}$, and off that disk it is at least $cm$. Since $mR^2	o \infty $, all these bounds dominate $c/R^2$ and the bounded Ricci term of $
u $. We use the $L^2$ estimate for $ ar\partial $ with a pointwise lower bound for the curvature of a singular metric, in the form described in section 25.16 . As in the proof of theorem 18.42.1 , we regard $L^ m$-valued $(0,1)$-forms as $(1,1)$-forms with values in $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ and sections of $L^ m$ as $(1,0)$-forms with values in the same bundle; this identification preserves the pointwise norms and brings in the Ricci term of $
u $. The estimate then reads as follows: if $H$ is a singular metric on $L^ m$ and the curvature of $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$ is at least $\lambda 
u $ for a continuous function $\lambda >0$, then \[  \int _ C|v|_ H^2\, \mathrm{d}
u \leq \int _ C\lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |_{H,
u }^2\, \mathrm{d}
u .  \] On the support of $\alpha $ we have $\lambda ^{-1}=O(R^2/q)$, $\phi _ t=\phi $, and $b_ R$ is bounded. Elsewhere $\phi _ t\leq \phi $ gives $\mathrm{e}^{-m\phi }\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-\psi _ m}$. title: 18.42.26 Growth ranges and compact examples
text: In the coordinate $z$, the quadrature boundary $\Gamma _ t$ differs from the model circle $|z|=R$ by $O(R^2)$. Comparing this displacement with the transition width $R/\sqrt q$ gives the range of orders in which the uncorrected law holds for every metric. A holomorphic change of coordinate produces a compact example in which the displacement has exactly this size. Theorem 18.42.27 . 5C5A28D66191 Keep the setting of subsection 18.42.9 , fix the integer $r\geq 1$ and a real $\tau $, and consider observation points with coordinates $z_ m$ and the law 4AA63CACA524 18.42.28 \begin{equation}  \frac{\pi B_{m,q}(z_ m)}{mr^2|z_ m|^{2r-2}} \longrightarrow \Phi (\tau ),\qquad m|z_ m|^{2r}=q/r+\tau \sqrt{q/r}, \end{equation} where the second relation prescribes the radii of the observation points. If $q=o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, this law holds for every choice of the geometric data and every sequence of arguments of $z_ m$. This range is optimal: for every sequence $q\to \infty $ with $q=o(m)$ that is not $o(m^{1/(r+1)})$, there is a compact example satisfying the same hypotheses in which the law fails along a subsequence. For fixed geometric data, write $\Gamma _ t$ as $\{ |z|=R c_ R(\theta )\} $. Then ( 18.42.28 ) holds for every fixed $\tau $ and every sequence of arguments if and only if 168E8A4B3B56 18.42.29 \begin{equation}  \sqrt q\, \| c_ R-1\| _\infty \longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Proof. By lemma 18.42.10 , $c_ R-1=O(R)$ in every fixed norm required here. The observation points in ( 18.42.28 ) satisfy \[  |z_ m|/R=1+\tau /(2\sqrt{rq})+O(q^{-1}).  \] Since the slope of the boundary graph tends to zero, the argument of $\Phi $ in theorem 18.42.15 is $\tau +o(1)$ whenever $\sqrt q R\to 0$, and this condition is equivalent to $q=o(m^{1/(r+1)})$. Moreover, $a(z)=1+o(1)$ and $\rho (z)=r^2|z|^{2r-2}(1+o(1))$ at these points, so the two normalizations agree. Thus theorem 18.42.15 proves the law for all data in this range. The same reasoning shows that ( 18.42.29 ) is sufficient. For necessity, suppose that ( 18.42.29 ) fails. On a subsequence, choose an angle realizing the maximal boundary displacement and observe at $|z|=R$ with $\tau =0$. A nonzero finite subsequential limit of the scaled displacement gives a nonzero Gaussian argument, and an infinite one gives saturation to zero or one. Radial and normal distances have relative error tending to zero, because the graph has vanishing slope. In either case the limit differs from $1/2$. It remains to construct the compact examples. On $\mathbb P^1$ choose a radial metric on $\mathcal O(d)$ whose local potential $f(u)$, $u=|w|^2$, equals $u^ r$ near zero, such that $g(u)=uf'(u)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty )$ and tends to $d$, and such that $g(u)=d-\epsilon /u$ for large $u$, with a constant $\epsilon >0$. Then $f=d\log u+\mathrm{constant}+\epsilon /u$ near infinity, so the potential in the frame at infinity is smooth with strictly positive curvature. For sufficiently small $t$, the hole $D_ t$ lies in the region where $f(u)=u^ r$ and equals the disk $|w|<R$: rotational invariance and uniqueness make it a disk, and its curvature mass is $rR^{2r}=t$. Hence the transition and saturation statements of theorem 18.42.15 apply to this compact example. Now use instead the coordinate $z$ defined by $w=z+cz^2$, with a constant $c>0$. In this coordinate the same compact metric satisfies $\phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+O(|z|^{2r+1})$, the volume form still has $a(0)=1$, and vanishing orders are unchanged. Theorem 18.42.15 , together with its saturation statement when the argument diverges, then gives a limit strictly larger than $1/2$. This proves that the range is sharp. $\square$

title: 18.42.30 Corrections from the smooth weight
text: The boundary $\Gamma _ t$ can be expanded in powers of $R$, and the leading terms of this expansion give explicit corrections to the uncorrected law. Write \[  \phi (z)=|z|^{2r}+P_{2r+1}(z,\bar z)+O(|z|^{2r+2}),\qquad P(\theta )=P_{2r+1}(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta },\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta }),  \] where $P_{2r+1}$ is a real homogeneous polynomial of degree $2r+1$ in $(z,\bar z)$. Let $\Lambda $ be the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator of the unit circle, $\Lambda \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} n\theta }=|n|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} n\theta }$. The first boundary coefficient is given by 49C316E4C1B2 18.42.31 \begin{equation}  c_ R=1+Rb_1+O(R^2),\qquad b_1=-\frac{((2r+1)-\Lambda )P}{4r^2}. \end{equation} To derive this, write the interior obstacle, to first order in $R$ and in polar coordinates $(s,\theta )$ for $\zeta $, as $1+2r\log s+R H$ with $H$ harmonic. Matching values on the boundary $s=1+Rb_1$ gives $H|_{s=1}=P$; the terms involving $b_1$ cancel there, since the radial model already matches first derivatives. Matching radial derivatives then gives $4r^2b_1+(2r+1)P-\Lambda P=0$. If $P_{2r+1}$ is harmonic, then $\Lambda P=(2r+1)P$ and $b_1=0$, as it must be, since such a term can be removed by a change of frame. For $q=O(m^{1/(r+1)})$, the argument of $\Phi $ at the uncorrected observation point of ( 18.42.28 ) is FBDC714894A5 18.42.32 \begin{equation}  \tau +\frac{\sqrt q R}{2r^{3/2}}((2r+1)-\Lambda )P(\theta )+o(1), \end{equation} uniformly in $\theta $, and the normalized kernel differs from $\Phi $ of this argument by $o(1)$. The remainder is small because $\sqrt q R^2\to 0$ in this range. For $w=z+cz^2$ we have $P=2r\operatorname {Re}(c\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$, and the shift is $2\sqrt{rq}R\operatorname {Re}(c\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$, in agreement with the compact example above. For every fixed integer $J\geq 1$, the parameter construction of lemma 18.42.10 gives \[  c_ R=1+\sum _{j=1}^ J R^ j b_ j+O(R^{J+1})  \] in every fixed norm needed. The coefficients satisfy an explicit recursion, obtained by expanding the interior harmonic obstacle in powers of $R$. At order $j$, matching values determines the boundary data of the new harmonic term from the Taylor term of degree $2r+j$ of $\phi $ and all preceding coefficients, and harmonic extension determines the term itself. Matching derivatives then gives an equation $4r^2b_ j+\text{(known terms)}=0$; the new coefficient $b_ j$ does not enter the value equation of order $j$. For $j\geq 2$, nonlinear contributions of lower-order terms also appear. Replacing $\Gamma _ t$ by the curve given by the truncated expansion moves the center of the transition by $O(R^{J+2})$. This curve can therefore be used in place of $\Gamma _ t$ whenever \[  \sqrt q R^{J+1}\to 0, \quad \hbox{equivalently}\quad q=o(m^{(J+1)/(r+J+1)}).  \] If $b_1=\cdots =b_{j-1}=0$ but $b_ j\not\equiv 0$, the criterion ( 18.42.29 ) shows that, for this fixed weight, the uncorrected law holds exactly in the range $q=o(m^{j/(r+j)})$, and this range is sharp when all directions of observation are allowed. Indeed, the higher terms are relatively $O(R)$ at an angle where $b_ j\ne 0$. In the radial case $\phi =f(u)$ with $u=|z|^2$, the hole is a disk by uniqueness and rotational invariance. By ( 18.42.11 ), its boundary circle $\{ u=u_*\} $ is determined by \[  m u_*f'(u_*)=q.  \] With $\rho (u)=f'(u)+uf''(u)$, the asymptotic variance of the dominant monomial degree is $m u\rho (u)$, and the corresponding Gaussian argument is 065262EB036B 18.42.33 \begin{equation}  \frac{m u f'(u)-q}{\sqrt{m u\rho (u)}}. \end{equation} For bounded arguments, Taylor expansion at $u_*$ identifies it with $2\sqrt{m\rho (u_*)}(\sqrt u-\sqrt{u_*})+o(1)$. Hence theorem 18.42.15 proves this radial formula for all sublinear orders. For $f=u^ r+c u^{r+1}+\cdots $, the first shift at the uncorrected observation point is $c(r+1)r^{-3/2}\sqrt q R^2$, so the critical growth is $m^{2/(r+2)}$. This larger radial threshold does not apply in arbitrary coordinates. No fixed finite Taylor jet of the weight determines the correction for every $q=o(m)$. For example, near zero take \[  f(u)=u^ r+c u^ r \mathrm{e}^{-1/\sqrt u},\qquad c>0,  \] with the second term extended by zero at $u=0$, and interpolated globally as above. It has the same Taylor jet as $u^ r$ at zero to every finite order, but at $u=R^2$ its relative contribution to $uf'(u)$ is $c \mathrm{e}^{-1/R}(1+1/(2rR))$. For $q=\lfloor m/\log m\rfloor $, we have $\sqrt q \mathrm{e}^{-1/R}/R\to \infty $. Hence the uncorrected observation point with $\tau =0$ lies outside the true boundary circle by many transition widths, and the normalized kernel tends to one. The quadrature-domain correction includes this flat contribution.

section: 18.43 A logarithmic kernel scale in two dimensions
text:
In the curve models above, the metric weight has a single homogeneous leading term. In two dimensions, a mixed monomial in the weight can compete with the pure monomials and introduce a logarithm into the scale of the kernel. For an explicit metric on $\mathbb P^2$, the relevant global section norm can be computed directly. Write $\mathrm dA$ for Euclidean area on $\mathbb C$. We first isolate the integral responsible for the logarithm. Lemma 18.43.1 . 99A4F9F834BF Set $W(a,b)=ab+a^3+b^3$ on $[0,\infty )^2$. As $t	o \infty $, \[   egin{gathered} J(t):=\int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)}\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db = rac{\log t}{3t}+O(t^{-1}), \ \int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty (a+b)\mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)} \, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db=O(t^{-4/3}). \end{gathered}  \] Proof. Put $A=t^{-2/3}$ and $B=t^{-1/3}$; the logarithm comes from the interval $A\leq a\leq B$. For $a>0$, the substitution $u=tab$ gives \[  H_ t(a):=\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-t(ab+b^3)}\, \mathrm db = rac1{ta}\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-u-u^3/(t^2a^3)}\, \mathrm du.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm e^{-v}\leq v$ for $v\geq 0$, \[  0\leq  rac1{ta}-H_ t(a)\leq  rac6{t^3a^4}.  \] Over $A\leq a\leq B$, the integral of this error is $O(t^{-1})$. Replacing $\mathrm e^{-ta^3}$ by one in $\int _ A^ B\mathrm e^{-ta^3}/(ta)\, \mathrm da$ costs at most $\int _ A^ B a^2\, \mathrm da=O(t^{-1})$ as well. Thus the middle interval contributes \[  \int _ A^ B\mathrm e^{-ta^3}H_ t(a)\, \mathrm da = rac1t\log  rac BA+O(t^{-1}) = rac{\log t}{3t}+O(t^{-1}).  \] For $a<A$, the bound $H_ t(a)\leq \int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-tb^3}\, \mathrm db=O(t^{-1/3})$ gives a contribution $O(t^{-1})$. For $a>B$, use $H_ t(a)\leq 1/(ta)$ and substitute $v=ta^3$ to obtain the bound \[  \int _ B^\infty  rac{\mathrm e^{-ta^3}}{ta}\, \mathrm da = rac1{3t}\int _1^\infty  rac{\mathrm e^{-v}}v\, \mathrm dv =O(t^{-1}).  \] Finally, $aH_ t(a)\leq 1/t$ gives \[  \int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty a\mathrm e^{-tW(a,b)} \, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db \leq  rac1t\int _0^\infty \mathrm e^{-ta^3}\, \mathrm da =O(t^{-4/3}).  \] Symmetry proves the same bound for $b$. $\square$ On $L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)$, define a Hermitian metric by \[  |S|_ h^2([Z])=  rac{|S(Z)|^2}{ igl (|Z_0|^6+3|Z_0Z_1Z_2|^2+3|Z_1|^6+3|Z_2|^6 igr )^{1/3}} \qquad (S	ext{ a linear form}).  \] The denominator is positive away from zero and homogeneous of degree two in $|Z|$, so the metric is well defined and smooth. Its local weight is one third of the logarithm of a sum of squared absolute values of holomorphic cubic functions, so its curvature is semipositive. In the chart $Z_0
e 0$, put $z_ j=Z_ j/Z_0$ and $p=[1:0:0]$. The frame $e=Z_0$ has AAC0258C6A86 18.43.2  egin{equation}  |e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\phi },\qquad \phi (z)=	frac 13\log  igl (1+3W(|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2) igr ). \end{equation} In particular the curvature vanishes at $p$. Proposition 18.43.3 . BDAF8AE299D2 Let $
u $ be a smooth positive probability volume form on $\mathbb P^2$, invariant under the rotations of $z_1$ and of $z_2$, and write \[  
u =ho (z)\, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2),\qquad ho _0=ho (0)>0  \] in the chart above. Give $H^0(\mathbb P^2,L^ m)$ the norm $\int _{\mathbb P^2}|s|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm d
u $, and let $B_ m$ be its kernel density. Then \[  B_ m(p)= rac{3}{\pi ^2ho _0} rac m{\log m} \left(1+O((\log m)^{-1})ight).  \] For the Fubini–Study probability volume, the leading constant is $3/2$. Proof. The homogeneous monomials form an orthogonal basis, because the metric and the volume are invariant under the two independent rotations and distinct monomials transform by distinct characters. At $p$, only $Z_0^ m$ has a nonzero value, equal to one in the frame $e^{\otimes m}$. Consequently $B_ m(p)=I_ m^{-1}$, where \[  I_ m=\int _{\mathbb P^2}|Z_0^ m|_{h^ m}^2\, \mathrm d
u =\int _{\mathbb C^2}(1+3W(|z_1|^2,|z_2|^2))^{-m/3} ho (z)\, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2).  \] Here the omitted projective line $\{ Z_0=0\} $ has zero volume. By rotational invariance, the first derivatives of $ho $ vanish at zero, so $ho (z)=ho _0+O(|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)$ near zero. In the variables $a=|z_1|^2$ and $b=|z_2|^2$, polar integration has Jacobian $\pi ^2\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db$. Choose a fixed small $\delta >0$. On $W\leq \delta $, set $\ell (W)=	frac 13\log (1+3W)$. For constants $c,C>0$ independent of $m$, \[  cW\leq \ell (W)\leq W,\qquad 0\leq \mathrm e^{-m\ell (W)}-\mathrm e^{-mW} \leq CmW^2\mathrm e^{-cmW} \leq  rac Cm\mathrm e^{-cmW/2}.  \] The first estimate of lemma 18.43.1 bounds the integral of this error in the weight by $O(m^{-2}\log m)$, and the second bounds the error from replacing $ho $ by $ho _0$ by $O(m^{-4/3})$. On the complement $W>\delta $, the contribution to $I_ m$ is at most $(1+3\delta )^{-m/3}$, because $
u $ has mass one, and the corresponding tail of the exponential model is at most $\mathrm e^{-m\delta /2}J(m/2)$. Therefore \[  I_ m=\pi ^2ho _0J(m)+O(m^{-4/3})+O(m^{-2}\log m) = rac{\pi ^2ho _0}{3m}\log m+O(m^{-1}).  \] Inverting proves the first assertion. The Fubini–Study probability volume has the local expression \[  
u = rac2{\pi ^2}(1+|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2)^{-3} \, \mathrm dA(z_1)\, \mathrm dA(z_2).  \] It has mass one, since $2\int _0^\infty \int _0^\infty (1+a+b)^{-3}\, \mathrm da\, \mathrm db=1$, and its density at zero is $2/\pi ^2$. The leading constant is therefore $3/2$. $\square$ Thus the full kernel, without any selection, already has a logarithmic factor at this fixed curvature zero, and its coefficient depends on the volume density at $p$. The calculation does not give a transition for growing vanishing ideals; that would require control of the norms of the selected monomials on the moving scale, as in the curve case.

title: 18.44.6 Corrected and homogeneous centers
section: 18.44 Anisotropic point jets and isolated poles on fibrations
text: The transition in theorem 18.44.2 is centered at the radii determined by the functions $H_ j$. Replacing them by the radii of the homogeneous leading terms of the weight introduces a shift, which is negligible exactly in a range of orders determined by the largest exponent $r_ j$. Fix positive numbers $\alpha _ j$ with sum one and a real $\tau $, and set 452067A980A7 18.44.7 \begin{equation}  R=\sum _ j\alpha _ jr_ j,\qquad T_ m=k_ m+\tau \sqrt{Rk_ m},\qquad t_ j=H_ j^{-1}(\alpha _ jT_ m/m). \end{equation} Then $\sum _ j\mu _ j=T_ m$ and $V\sim Rk_ m$, so ( 18.44.3 ) holds for every sublinear growing order. The radii $|z_ j|=\sqrt{t_ j}$ are asymptotic to $(\alpha _ jk_ m/(r_ jm))^{1/(2r_ j)}$. Proposition 18.44.8 . 443408C4E29A Keep $\alpha _ j,\tau ,R,T_ m$ as above, but use instead the homogeneous radii given by $t_ j=(\alpha _ jT_ m/(r_ jm))^{1/r_ j}$, and put $r_*:=\max _ jr_ j$. For the metrics of this section, the law \[  \frac{\pi ^ qB_ m(z)}{m^ q\prod _ jr_ j^2|z_ j|^{2r_ j-2}}\longrightarrow \Phi (\tau )  \] holds for every fixed $\tau $ if and only if $k_ m=o(m^{2/(r_*+2)})$. If $k_ m/m^{2/(r_*+2)}\to c\in (0,\infty )$, the left side instead tends to \[  \Phi \bigl (\tau +C_\alpha c^{(r_*+2)/(2r_*)}\bigr ),\qquad C_\alpha =\frac1{\sqrt R}\sum _{j:r_ j=r_*} (r_*+1)\varepsilon _ j(\alpha _ j/r_*)^{1+1/r_*}.  \] If that ratio tends to infinity while $k_ m=o(m)$, the limit is $1$. Proof. By ( 18.44.1 ), $\sum _ j\mu _ j=T_ m+\Delta _ m$ with \[  \Delta _ m=\sum _ j(r_ j+1)\varepsilon _ jmt_ j^{r_ j+1} +O\left(\sum _ jmt_ j^{2r_ j}\right),\qquad V\sim Rk_ m.  \] Since $r_ j\geq 2$, each error term is negligible compared with the corresponding positive correction. Consequently \[  \frac{\Delta _ m}{\sqrt{Rk_ m}}=(1+o(1))\sum _ j \frac{(r_ j+1)\varepsilon _ j(\alpha _ j/r_ j)^{1+1/r_ j}}{\sqrt R} k_ m^{1/2+1/r_ j}m^{-1/r_ j}.  \] At the critical scale only the indices with $r_ j=r_*$ contribute in the limit. Below it every term tends to zero, and above it a positive term diverges. The Gaussian limit of the normalized sum proved above applies in all three cases; in the last case its tightness gives probability one. Moreover, $a(t)\to 1$ and $g_ j(t_ j)/(r_ j^2t_ j^{r_ j-1})\to 1$, so the two normalizations agree. If $k_ m/m^{2/(r_*+2)}$ does not tend to zero, a subsequence has a positive finite or infinite limit, and the law fails at $\tau =0$. This proves both directions of the equivalence for these metrics. $\square$

title: 18.45 Newton selection and moment-shell limits
text:
On a product of projective lines, selecting the monomials whose exponents lie in the dilates of a fixed polytope gives a graded family of section spaces for which the lower bound for the potentials can be proved directly, without a general approximation theorem. The limit of the kernel measures depends on the dimension of the polytope. When this dimension is smaller than that of the manifold, the limit is carried by a family of real tori and differs from the mixed curvature measures of the envelope. Let $X=(\mathbb P^1)^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, and let $L=\mathcal O(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n)$, where each $k_ j$ is a positive integer. Equip $L$ with its product Fubini–Study metric $h$. On the torus $T=(\mathbb C^*)^ n$, in the standard frame $e$, write \[  r_ j=\log |z_ j|^2,\qquad \varphi _0(r)=\sum _ jk_ j\log (1+\mathrm e^{r_ j}),\qquad 	heta =c_1(L,h)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _0.  \] Put $P=\prod _ j[0,k_ j]$. Fix a nonempty rational polytope $Q$ contained in the interior of $P$ whose affine span has the form \[  \operatorname {aff}Q=b+W,\qquad b\in \mathbb Z^ n,  \] with $W\subseteq \mathbb R^ n$ a rational linear subspace. Set $d=\dim Q$ and $\Lambda =W\cap \mathbb Z^ n$. Let $\mathrm dq_\Lambda $ be the Lebesgue measure on $b+W$ normalized so that a fundamental domain of the lattice $\Lambda $ has volume one; when $d=0$, it is the unit point mass at $b$. Write $\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)$ for the volume of $Q$ with respect to $\mathrm dq_\Lambda $. In this section the selected spaces are defined directly by monomials, without a selecting potential: we select exactly the monomials with exponents in $mQ$, 4515165DA915 18.45.1  egin{equation}  V_ m=\operatorname {span}\{ z^\alpha e^ m: \alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n\} . \end{equation} Each of these monomials is a global section of $L^ m$, since $0\leq \alpha _ j\leq mk_ j$. Since $Q$ is convex, products of selected sections are selected, so these spaces form a graded family. Choose a smooth real torus-invariant function $w$ on $X$ such that the function $F=\varphi _0+w$ of $r$ has positive definite Hessian $D^2F(r)$ for every $r\in \mathbb R^ n$. Choose a smooth strictly positive torus-invariant probability measure $
u $ on $X$. On $T$ we then have $\mathrm d
u =a(r)\, \mathrm dr\, \mathrm d	au $, where $a>0$, $\int a\, \mathrm dr=1$, and $\mathrm d	au $ is the Haar probability measure on $(S^1)^ n$ in the angular variables. Give $V_ m$ the Hilbert norm $\int _ X|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm e^{-mw}\, \mathrm d
u $, and for an orthonormal basis put \[  \mathcal B_ m=\sum _ j|s_{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2,\qquad B_ m=\mathrm e^{-mw}\mathcal B_ m,\qquad U_ m=m^{-1}\log \mathcal B_ m.  \] As in section 18.30 , the density $B_ m$ includes the continuous weight.

title: 18.45.2 The growth constraint and its envelope

text:
Let $H_ Q(r)=\max _{q\in Q}q\cdot r$ be the support function of $Q$, and define  egin{align*}  \mathcal C_ Q& =\{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ): v+\varphi _0\leq H_ Q+C_ v	ext{ on }T	ext{ for some constant }C_ v\} ,\  E_ Q& =\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathcal C_ Q: v\leq w	ext{ quasi-everywhere on }X\} ight)^*. \end{align*} This growth condition replaces the multiplier-ideal condition of section 18.32 ; we do not identify $E_ Q$ with an ideal envelope. Lemma 18.45.3 . F0A638931204 The gradient $
abla F:\mathbb R^ n	o \operatorname {int}P$ is a smooth diffeomorphism. With $r(q)=(
abla F)^{-1}(q)$ and $F^*(q)=q\cdot r(q)-F(r(q))$, set \[  G_ Q(r)=\max _{q\in Q}\{ q\cdot r-F^*(q)\} .  \] Then $E_ Q=G_ Q-\varphi _0$ on $T$, and $E_ Q=-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Moreover, a global section $s$ of $L^ m$ belongs to $V_ m$ exactly when 1887637715F3 18.45.4  egin{equation}  |s/e^ m|^2\leq C_ s\mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}\quad 	ext{on }T \quad 	ext{for some finite }C_ s. \end{equation} Proof. In the charts at infinity one sees that every global section of $L^ m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $mk_ j$ in each variable $z_ j$. If $s\in V_ m$, the growth bound follows from the triangle inequality, since $|z^\alpha |^2=\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r}\leq \mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}$ for $\alpha \in mQ$. Conversely, averaging the growth bound over the angles gives $\sum _\alpha |c_\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r} \leq C_ s\mathrm e^{mH_ Q(r)}$ for the coefficients $c_\alpha $ of $s$. If some $c_\alpha 
eq 0$ had $\alpha 
otin mQ$, a vector $u$ with $\alpha \cdot u>mH_ Q(u)$, which exists by separation, would contradict this bound along the ray $r=tu$, $t	o \infty $. Thus the growth condition controls each monomial separately, even though the monomials of $s$ may cancel pointwise. For $p\in \operatorname {int}P$, put $\delta _ p=\min _ j(p_ j,k_ j-p_ j)>0$. Since $w$ is bounded, 25029B67571A 18.45.5  egin{equation}  F(r)-p\cdot r\geq \delta _ p\sum _ j|r_ j|-\| w\| _\infty . \end{equation} By strict convexity, $F-p\cdot r$ therefore has a unique minimizer, at which $
abla F=p$. Conversely, every gradient of $F$ lies in $P$: compare the supporting hyperplanes of the convex function $F$ with the asymptotic slopes of $\varphi _0$. By the inverse function theorem the image of $
abla F$ is open, so it is contained in the interior of $P$. This proves that $
abla F$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\operatorname {int}P$. On a compact neighborhood of $Q$ in $\operatorname {int}P$, the inverse gradient and the first and second derivatives of $F^*$ are bounded, and the Hessian of $F^*$ is positive definite. We next show that $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ is a competitor. In a product chart in which some of the coordinates are inverted, the local potential of $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ is \[  \max _{q\in Q}\left\{ \sum _ j c_ j(q)\log |\zeta _ j|^2-F^*(q)ight\} , \qquad c_ j(q)=q_ j	ext{ or }k_ j-q_ j.  \] All $c_ j$ are bounded below by a fixed positive number. The expression is locally bounded above, tends uniformly to $-\infty $ at the coordinate hyperplanes when the other coordinates stay bounded, and is locally integrable by comparison with one fixed summand. At points where it is finite, a maximizing summand gives the submean inequality for plurisubharmonic functions; at points where it equals $-\infty $, this inequality is automatic. These local expressions glue. Boundedness of $F^*$ on $Q$ gives $G_ Q-H_ Q=O(1)$, and Fenchel's inequality gives $G_ Q\leq F$, that is, $G_ Q-\varphi _0\leq w$. Thus $G_ Q-\varphi _0$, extended by $-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$, belongs to $\mathcal C_ Q$ and satisfies the obstacle condition. Now let $v$ be any competitor. The obstacle condition holds everywhere: the exceptional pluripolar set has Lebesgue measure zero, and submean values over shrinking balls carry the inequality with the continuous obstacle to every point. Consider the maximum over the angles, $M(r)=\max _	au \{ v(\mathrm e^{r/2}	au )+\varphi _0(r)\} $, where $\mathrm e^{r/2}	au $ denotes the point with coordinates $\mathrm e^{r_ j/2}	au _ j$. By compactness, $M$ is upper semicontinuous. Rotating a point at which the maximum is attained gives the submean inequality for the invariant function $z\mapsto M(\log |z_1|^2,\ldots ,\log |z_ n|^2)$, which is therefore plurisubharmonic on $T$. It extends across the affine coordinate hyperplanes by the local upper bound. If $M(r)=-\infty $ for some $r$, successive one-variable maximum principles would force this function to be $-\infty $ on the corresponding polydisk, contradicting $v
ot\equiv -\infty $. Thus $M$ is finite. In logarithmic coordinates this invariant function depends only on the real parts, so its positive complex Hessian shows that $M$ is convex. We have $M\leq F$ and $M\leq H_ Q+C_ v$. Comparing along rays shows that every supporting slope of $M$ lies in $Q$. At any $r$, choose such a slope $p$. Since $M\leq F$ gives $M^*\geq F^*$, convex duality yields $M(r)=p\cdot r-M^*(p)\leq p\cdot r-F^*(p)\leq G_ Q(r)$. Hence $v\leq G_ Q-\varphi _0$ on $T$. Submean values over shrinking balls and the uniform decay of $G_ Q-\varphi _0$ near $X\setminus T$ show that $v=-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Since $G_ Q-\varphi _0$, extended by $-\infty $, is already upper semicontinuous, this proves the identity for the envelope after upper regularization. $\square$

title: 18.45.6 Norms, lattice growth and the lower bound
search_title: Norms, lattice growth and the lower bound
text: Theorem 18.45.7 . 2EC775894117 The norms are nondegenerate and satisfy the Bernstein–Markov inequality of section 18.31 for the weight $w$. Writing $N_ m=\dim V_ m$, we have \[  N_ m=m^ d\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)+O(m^{d-1})\quad (d\geq 1), \qquad N_ m=1\quad (d=0).  \] For all sufficiently large $m$, 2BD2A5FCA69D 18.45.8 \begin{equation}  |U_ m-E_ Q|\leq \frac{C}{m} \left(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|+\log m\right)\quad \text{on }T. \end{equation} Consequently $U_ m\to E_ Q$ locally uniformly on $T$ and in $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms on $X$, and the closed positive currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ m$ converge weakly to $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q$. Both $U_ m$ and $E_ Q$ equal $-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Proof. Since the volume form is smooth and positive, the norm is positive on every nonzero section. Orthogonality of the angular Fourier modes diagonalizes it: \begin{align*}  A_ m(\alpha )& =\| z^\alpha e^ m\| _ m^2 =\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)}a(r)\, \mathrm dr,\\  \mathcal B_ m(r)& =\sum _{\alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n} \frac{\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-m\varphi _0(r)}}{A_ m(\alpha )}. \end{align*} For $q=\alpha /m$, the function $F(r)-q\cdot r$ has the unique minimum value $-F^*(q)$, attained at $r(q)$. Taylor's formula on a ball of radius $m^{-1/2}$ about $r(q)$, with uniform bounds on a compact neighborhood of $r(Q)$, yields 2A24E3900F00 18.45.9 \begin{equation}  c m^{-n/2}\mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}\leq A_ m(\alpha ) \leq \mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}. \end{equation} The upper bound uses only the minimum and $\int a\, \mathrm dr=1$. Since $b\in \mathbb Z^ n$, we have $(m\operatorname {aff}Q)\cap \mathbb Z^ n=mb+\Lambda $. Counting fundamental cells of $\Lambda $ in $m(Q-b)$ gives the dimension estimate: the cells meeting the relative boundary of $m(Q-b)$ lie in a boundary layer of fixed width, and there are $O(m^{d-1})$ of them. The same cells give convergence of the lattice Riemann sums on $Q$. Every $q\in Q$ lies within $O(m^{-1})$ of $Q_ m=Q\cap (b+m^{-1}\Lambda )$: move $q$ by $O(m^{-1})$ towards a fixed relative interior point so that a ball larger than the covering radius of the lattice fits inside $Q$, and then round to a lattice point inside that ball. This works for all sufficiently large $m$, and for a singleton it is exact. Put $G_{Q,m}=\max _{q\in Q_ m}(q\cdot r-F^*(q))$. The approximation by the grid gives $0\leq G_ Q-G_{Q,m}\leq C(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|)/m$. The formula for $\mathcal B_ m$ and ( 18.45.9 ) give \[  G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0\leq U_ m\leq G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0+ \frac{(n/2)\log m+\log N_ m-\log c}{m}.  \] This proves ( 18.45.8 ). The selected monomials vanish on every component of $X\setminus T$. The functions $\log |z_ j|^2$ have finite $L^ p$ norms for each finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms, so ( 18.45.8 ) gives the global convergence, and differentiation in the sense of distributions gives the convergence of the currents. Fenchel's inequality $\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)\leq mF^*(\alpha /m)$ and ( 18.45.9 ) also give $\sup _ X B_ m\leq C N_ m m^{n/2}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the orthonormal basis, $\sup _ X|s|_{h^ m}\mathrm e^{-mw/2} \leq C m^{d/2+n/4}\| s\| _ m$ for $s\in V_ m$. The finitely many initial degrees can be absorbed in $C$, and a polynomial bound implies the Bernstein–Markov inequality with any positive exponential loss. $\square$

text: Theorem 18.45.7 . 2EC775894117 The norms are nondegenerate and satisfy the Bernstein–Markov inequality of section 18.31 for the weight $w$. Writing $N_ m=\dim V_ m$, we have \[  N_ m=m^ d\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda (Q)+O(m^{d-1})\quad (d\geq 1), \qquad N_ m=1\quad (d=0).  \] For all sufficiently large $m$, 2BD2A5FCA69D 18.45.8 \begin{equation}  |U_ m-E_ Q|\leq \frac{C}{m} \left(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|+\log m\right)\quad \text{on }T. \end{equation} Consequently $U_ m\to E_ Q$ locally uniformly on $T$ and in $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms on $X$, and the closed positive currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ m$ converge weakly to $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}E_ Q$. Both $U_ m$ and $E_ Q$ equal $-\infty $ on $X\setminus T$. Proof. Since the volume form is smooth and positive, the norm is positive on every nonzero section. Orthogonality of the angular Fourier modes diagonalizes it: \begin{align*}  A_ m(\alpha )& =\| z^\alpha e^ m\| _ m^2 =\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)}a(r)\, \mathrm dr,\\  \mathcal B_ m(r)& =\sum _{\alpha \in mQ\cap \mathbb Z^ n} \frac{\mathrm e^{\alpha \cdot r-m\varphi _0(r)}}{A_ m(\alpha )}. \end{align*} For $q=\alpha /m$, the function $F(r)-q\cdot r$ has the unique minimum value $-F^*(q)$, attained at $r(q)$. Taylor's formula on a ball of radius $m^{-1/2}$ about $r(q)$, with uniform bounds on a compact neighborhood of $r(Q)$, yields 2A24E3900F00 18.45.9 \begin{equation}  c m^{-n/2}\mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}\leq A_ m(\alpha ) \leq \mathrm e^{mF^*(q)}. \end{equation} The upper bound uses only the minimum and $\int a\, \mathrm dr=1$. Since $b\in \mathbb Z^ n$, we have $(m\operatorname {aff}Q)\cap \mathbb Z^ n=mb+\Lambda $. Counting fundamental cells of $\Lambda $ in $m(Q-b)$ gives the dimension estimate: the cells meeting the relative boundary of $m(Q-b)$ lie in a boundary layer of fixed width, and there are $O(m^{d-1})$ of them. The same cells give convergence of the lattice Riemann sums on $Q$. Every $q\in Q$ lies within $O(m^{-1})$ of $Q_ m=Q\cap (b+m^{-1}\Lambda )$: move $q$ by $O(m^{-1})$ towards a fixed relative interior point so that a ball larger than the covering radius of the lattice fits inside $Q$, and then round to a lattice point inside that ball. This works for all sufficiently large $m$, and for a singleton it is exact. Put $G_{Q,m}=\max _{q\in Q_ m}(q\cdot r-F^*(q))$. The approximation by the grid gives $0\leq G_ Q-G_{Q,m}\leq C(1+\sum _ j|r_ j|)/m$. The formula for $\mathcal B_ m$ and ( 18.45.9 ) give \[  G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0\leq U_ m\leq G_{Q,m}-\varphi _0+ \frac{(n/2)\log m+\log N_ m-\log c}{m}.  \] This proves ( 18.45.8 ). The selected monomials vanish on every component of $X\setminus T$. The functions $\log |z_ j|^2$ have finite $L^ p$ norms for each finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms, so ( 18.45.8 ) gives the global convergence, and differentiation in the sense of distributions gives the convergence of the currents. Fenchel's inequality $\alpha \cdot r-mF(r)\leq mF^*(\alpha /m)$ and ( 18.45.9 ) also give $\sup _ X B_ m\leq C N_ m m^{n/2}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the orthonormal basis, $\sup _ X|s|_{h^ m}\mathrm e^{-mw/2} \leq C m^{d/2+n/4}\| s\| _ m$ for $s\in V_ m$. The finitely many initial degrees can be absorbed in $C$, and a polynomial bound implies the Bernstein–Markov inequality with any positive exponential loss. $\square$

Example 18.45.14 . 9600E351F18B On $(\mathbb P^1)^2$ take $L=\mathcal O(4,4)$, $w=0$, and $Q=\{ (2+t,2-t):-1/2\leq t\leq 1/2\} $. Then $\Lambda =\mathbb Z(1,-1)$, $\mathrm dq_\Lambda =\mathrm dt$, and \[  V_ m=\operatorname {span}\{ z_1^{2m+j}z_2^{2m-j}e^ m: j\in \mathbb Z,\  |j|\leq m/2\} , \qquad N_ m=2\lfloor m/2floor +1.  \] The limit $\mu _ Q$ has mass one: it is the average, over $-1/2\leq t\leq 1/2$, of the Haar probability measures on the real tori $\{ |z_1|^2=(2+t)/(2-t),\  |z_2|^2=(2-t)/(2+t)\} $; indeed, these equations describe the inverse gradient map. The moment shell is a compact three-dimensional part of the hypersurface $|z_1z_2|=1$. Writing $c(p)=p\log (p/4)+(4-p)\log ((4-p)/4)$, we have $F^*(2+t,2-t)=2c(2+t)$, which gives the envelope explicitly. The quotient of two adjacent selected monomials is $z_1/z_2$. In homogeneous coordinates $z_ j=v_ j/u_ j$, the corresponding map $[v_1u_2:u_1v_2]$ to $\mathbb P^1$ is undefined at $(0,0)$ and $(\infty ,\infty )$. e 0$. Then $\omega =\mathrm e^ f\omega _0$ is a torus-invariant Hermitian form, and $\mathrm d\omega =\mathrm e^ f\mathrm df\wedge \omega _0
e 0$ wherever $\mathrm df
e 0$. Sampling with $
u =\omega ^2/\int _ X\omega ^2$ gives the same limit of mass one, while the curvature remains $	heta =4\omega _0$. The assumption $b\in \mathbb Z^ n$ excludes a parity obstruction: if $Q=\{ b\} $ with $b$ half-integral, then $mQ$ contains no lattice point for odd $m$. To identify the envelope, let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be a competitor, that is, $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}\psi $ in the multiplier-ideal order of section 5.33 and $v\leq 0$ quasi-everywhere. By theorem 5.37.3 , the Lelong numbers of $v$ at the points of $D_0$ and $D_\infty $ are at least $1/2$. Fix $y\in Y$ and restrict $v$ to the line $\mathbb P^1	imes \{ y\} $. The restriction is either identically $-\infty $ or $\sigma _0$-plurisubharmonic. By the identification of Lelong numbers with atoms in lemma 5.37.18 , the curvature measure of the restriction has atoms of mass at least $1/2$ at these two points. By Stokes' theorem its total mass is one, so these atoms exhaust the measure. The difference between the restriction and $\psi _0$ is therefore harmonic on the compact projective line, hence constant. It follows that $v(z,y)=\psi _0(z)+c(y)$ off $D_0\cup D_\infty $, where $c(y)=-\infty $ on lines along which $v$ is identically $-\infty $. Submean values over shrinking balls upgrade the obstacle condition to $v\leq 0$ everywhere. Since $\max \psi _0=-\log 2$, we get $c\leq \log 2$, and hence $v\leq E$. On $D_0\cup D_\infty $ both $v$ and $E$ equal $-\infty $. Conversely, $E\leq 0$ and $E$ differs from $\psi $ by a constant, so $E$ is itself a competitor. This proves ( 18.46.3 ). The full kernel on $X$ is $(m+1)^{q+1}$, so evaluation gives $\sup _ X|s|_{h^ m}\leq (m+1)^{(q+1)/2}\| s\| _ m$ for every selected section. Taking logarithms in ( 18.46.5 ) gives \[  |U_ m-E|\leq  rac{C_ q}{m}  igl (1+|\log |z|^2|+\log m igr ) \quad 	ext{off }D_0\cup D_\infty ,  \] because $|\psi _0|=\log (2\cosh (	frac 12\log |z|^2))$ is bounded by $\log 2+	frac 12|\log |z|^2|$. The function $\log |z|^2$ belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms. This proves the convergence of the potentials, and differentiating the $L^1$ limit proves the convergence of the currents. For every $m\geq 2$, both $U_ m$ and $E$ are $-\infty $ on $D_0\cup D_\infty $. Let $P_ k$ be the probability measure on the first factor with density $C_ k\mathrm e^{2k\psi _0}$ with respect to $\sigma _0$. Under $P_ k$ the angle of $z$ is uniformly distributed, and $x$ has the beta distribution with parameters $(k+1,k+1)$, whose mean is $1/2$ and whose variance is $1/[4(2k+3)]$. Chebyshev's inequality and continuity of the test functions in the angle therefore give $P_ kightharpoonup \varsigma $. The measure identities \[  \mathcal B_{2k}
u =(2k+1)^ q P_ k\otimes 
u _ Y, \qquad \mathcal B_{2k+1}
u =2(2k+2)^ q P_ k\otimes 
u _ Y  \] prove both limits along even and odd degrees and the limit after division by $N_ m$. Since the two limits have different total masses, the $q$-normalized family does not converge. For two odd degrees, the monomials of minimal order along $D_0$ are selected, but their product misses the condition in the even sum degree by one order. Since the envelope has zero non-pluripolar top mass, theorem 18.35.5 , whose hypotheses require positive mass, does not apply to this selecting potential.

section: 18.47 Three monomial bands from a multiplier-ideal selection
text:
For an isolated logarithmic pole of coefficient one on a complex surface, the multiplier ideal in degree $m$ requires vanishing of order $m-1$, whereas domination by the pole would require order $m$. At the two base points of the pencil below, the multiplier-ideal conditions select three neighboring bands of monomials. All three contribute to the limit of the kernel measures, even though the competitor classes defined by multiplier ideals and by domination coincide. Let $X=\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$, and let $L=\mathcal O(1,1)$ carry its product Fubini–Study metric $h$, with $	heta =c_1(L,h)$. Let $[T_ j:Z_ j]$ be homogeneous coordinates on the $j$th factor, write $z_ j=Z_ j/T_ j$, and set \[  \psi =\max \{ \log |T_1T_2|_ h^2,\log |Z_1Z_2|_ h^2\} , \qquad p_+=(0,\infty ),\quad p_-=(\infty ,0).  \] The two sections $T_1T_2$ and $Z_1Z_2$ of $L$ vanish simultaneously only at $p_\pm $, so these are the only poles of $\psi $. In local frames the potentials of $\psi $ are maxima of logarithms of squared moduli of holomorphic functions, so $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. On the torus $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ put \[  x_ j=\log |z_ j|^2,\qquad s=x_1+x_2,\qquad \varphi _ X=\log (1+\mathrm e^{x_1})+\log (1+\mathrm e^{x_2}).  \] Then $\psi =\max (0,s)-\varphi _ X$. In this model the norm is computed on the compact set $K=\{ x\in [-1,2]^2\} \subset (\mathbb C^*)^2$, which has nonempty interior. On $K$ let \[  w= rac{x_1^2+x_2^2}{2}-\varphi _ X, \qquad \mathrm d
u = rac19\, \mathrm dx_1\, \mathrm dx_2\, \mathrm d	au _1\, \mathrm d	au _2,  \] where $\mathrm d	au _ j$ is the Haar probability measure in the angle of $z_ j$. Thus $
u $ is a probability measure supported on $K$, not a smooth positive volume form on $X$. With $\psi $ as selecting potential, set \[   egin{aligned}  V_ m& =H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(m\psi )), & N_ m& =\dim V_ m,\  \| \sigma \| _ m^2& =\int _ K|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\mathrm e^{-mw}\, \mathrm d
u , & \mathcal B_ m& =\sum _ j|\sigma _{m,j}|_{h^ m}^2, \end{aligned}  \] where $(\sigma _{m,j})$ is an orthonormal basis. The norm is positive definite by the identity theorem on the interior of $K$. As in section 18.30 , we use $U_ m=m^{-1}\log \mathcal B_ m$ on $X$ and $B_ m=\mathrm e^{-mw}\mathcal B_ m$ on $K$. Only the values of $w$ on $K$ enter the norm and the envelope. Lemma 18.47.1 . 511A1D146037 For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, \[  v\preceq _{\mathcal I}\psi \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad v\leq \psi +C_ v \quad \hbox{for some finite }C_ v,  \] where $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ is the multiplier-ideal order of section 5.33 . Consequently, for every obstacle, the envelopes defined with these two conditions agree. At either pole, for every real $t>0$, \[  \mathcal I(t\psi )=\mathfrak m_{p_\pm }^{\max \{ \lfloor tfloor -1,0\} }.  \] Away from the poles, $\mathcal I(t\psi )$ is the full structure sheaf. Proof. Near $p_+$ use the coordinates $\zeta _1=z_1$, $\zeta _2=1/z_2$ and the frame $T_1Z_2$. In this frame the two pencil sections $T_1T_2$ and $Z_1Z_2$ have coefficients $\zeta _2$ and $\zeta _1$, so \[  \psi =\log \max (|\zeta _1|^2,|\zeta _2|^2) -\log (1+|\zeta _1|^2)-\log (1+|\zeta _2|^2) =\log |\zeta |^2+O(1).  \] The same calculation applies at $p_-$. The formula for the ideals is lemma 5.37.1 with normal dimension two and coefficient one, including the case of equality in the integrability condition. Now suppose that $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}\psi $. By theorem 5.37.3 , the Lelong numbers satisfy $
u (v,p_\pm )\geq 1$; here $
u (v,p)$ is the Lelong number of section 5.34 , not the measure $
u $. Let $\phi $ be the plurisubharmonic local potential of $v$ in a frame near $p_\pm $, and consider its radial maximum \[  M(a)=\sup _{|\zeta |\leq \mathrm e^{a/2}}\phi (\zeta )  \] inside a fixed coordinate ball. This function is finite and convex: by the three-circles theorem, the corresponding maximum on each complex line through the pole is convex, and $M$ is the supremum of these functions; lines on which $\phi $ is identically $-\infty $ do not affect the supremum. The limiting slope of $M$ as $a	o -\infty $ is the Lelong number. For $a<a_0$, convexity therefore gives \[  M(a)\leq M(a_0)+
u (v,p_\pm )(a-a_0)\leq a+C.  \] Consequently $v\leq \psi +C$ near both poles. After $C$ is increased, the same bound holds on the compact complement, because $v$ is bounded above and $\psi $ is finite and continuous there. Conversely, domination $v\leq \psi +C$ implies the inclusions of multiplier ideals at all weights, by the definition through integrability. Thus the two competitor classes coincide before any obstacle is imposed. $\square$ The pencil also describes the competitors that are not torus-invariant. Let $\omega _{m FS}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$, normalized to have integral one. Lemma 18.47.2 . 2BCFCC9C8808 On $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $ set \[  f=[T_1T_2:Z_1Z_2],\qquad \psi _{m FS}=\log (|T_1T_2|_ h^2+|Z_1Z_2|_ h^2).  \] Every $v$ in the class of lemma 18.47.1 has the form \[  v=\psi _{m FS}+u\circ f, \qquad u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\omega _{m FS}),  \] on $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $, and $v(p_\pm )=-\infty $. Conversely, for every such $u$, the function $\psi _{m FS}+u\circ f$, extended by $-\infty $ at the two poles, belongs to that class. Proof. For $\xi \in \mathbb C^*$, the curve of the pencil \[  C_\xi =\{ Z_1Z_2=\xi T_1T_2\}   \] is a smooth rational curve of bidegree $(1,1)$ through both poles, and its $	heta $-degree is two. The restriction of $v$ to this connected curve is either identically $-\infty $ or $	heta |_{C_\xi }$-plurisubharmonic. In the latter case, its curvature measure has total mass two by Stokes' theorem. The local upper bounds of lemma 18.47.1 give Lelong numbers at least one at the two poles, hence, by the identification of Lelong numbers with atoms in lemma 5.37.18 , atoms of mass at least one there. These atoms exhaust the measure. The curvature of $\psi |_{C_\xi }$ consists of the same two unit atoms. Thus $v-\psi $ is harmonic, in the sense of distributions, on the compact curve $C_\xi $, and therefore constant. On the torus use the holomorphic coordinates $(z_1,\xi =z_1z_2)$. Local integrability and Fubini's theorem show that, for almost every $\xi $, the restriction of $v$ to $C_\xi $ is not identically $-\infty $; by the preceding paragraph it is then finite off the poles. Hence the restriction of $v$ to the transverse curve $S=\{ z_1=1\} \simeq \mathbb P^1$ is not identically $-\infty $. Put $u=v|_ S+\log 2$. Since $	heta |_ S=\omega _{m FS}$ and $\psi _{m FS}|_ S=-\log 2$, the constants on the curves $C_\xi $ give the asserted identity almost everywhere on the torus. Both sides have plurisubharmonic local potentials, so they agree everywhere off the poles. The logarithmic upper bounds give the value $-\infty $ at the poles. Conversely, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _{m FS}+u\circ f)=f^*(\omega _{m FS}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\geq 0$ off the poles. In a chart at a pole, the local potential is bounded above by $\log (|\zeta _1|^2+|\zeta _2|^2)+C$, since $u$ is bounded above. It therefore extends across the pole as a plurisubharmonic function with value $-\infty $ there, which gives a global $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function dominated by $\psi +C$. $\square$ Theorem 18.47.3 . 1D58A228EF5A For these $K$ and $w$, the partial envelope ( 18.32.1 ) is \[   egin{aligned}  E_{	heta ,K}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(w)& =P=g(s)-\varphi _ X,\  g(s)& =\sup _{0\leq t\leq 1}(ts-t^2) = egin{cases}  0,& s\leq 0,\  s^2/4,& 0\leq s\leq 2,\  s-1,& s\geq 2. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] Here $P$ is given by this formula on the torus and extends to a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ with $P(p_\pm )=-\infty $ and $\psi -1\leq P\leq \psi $. Proof. For an arbitrary competitor $v$, lemma 18.47.2 gives, in terms of the affine coordinate $\xi $ of $\mathbb P^1$, \[  \chi (\xi )=\log (1+|\xi |^2)+u(\xi ), \qquad v=\chi (z_1z_2)-\varphi _ X.  \] On the interior of $K$, the obstacle condition, which holds quasi-everywhere, becomes an inequality everywhere, by the submean inequality and the continuity of $w+\varphi _ X$. Evaluating at $x_1=x_2=s/2$, with $s=\log |\xi |^2$, gives \[  \chi (\xi )\leq s^2/4\quad (-2<s<4)  \] for every argument of $\xi $. At $s=0$ this bounds $\chi $ by zero on $|\xi |=1$, and the maximum principle for the subharmonic function $\chi $ bounds it by zero on the whole disk $|\xi |\leq 1$. At infinity use the local potential \[  \chi _\infty (\eta )=\chi (1/\eta )+\log |\eta |^2.  \] The obstacle at $s=2$ bounds it by $-1$ on $|\eta |=\mathrm e^{-1}$, and the same maximum principle gives $\chi (\xi )\leq s-1$ for $s\geq 2$. Together with the obstacle for $0\leq s\leq 2$, this proves $\chi \leq g$, without any invariance assumption on the competitor. Conversely, $g$ is convex with slopes in $[0,1]$, so $g(\log |\xi |^2)-\log (1+|\xi |^2)$ is an $\omega _{m FS}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^1$. By lemma 18.47.2 , it defines the global function $P$. Directly, \[  \max (0,s)-1\leq g(s)\leq \max (0,s),\qquad g(s)\leq s^2/4\leq (x_1^2+x_2^2)/2.  \] Thus $P$ belongs to the competitor class of lemma 18.47.1 and satisfies the obstacle condition everywhere on $K$. Since it dominates every competitor, it is the envelope, including its values $-\infty $ at the poles. $\square$ Proposition 18.47.4 . AD8335312F45 For every $m\geq 1$ the selected space is \[  V_ m=\operatorname {span}\{ Z_1^ aT_1^{m-a}Z_2^ bT_2^{m-b}: 0\leq a,b\leq m,\  |a-b|\leq 1\} , \qquad N_ m=3m+1.  \] In particular, $N_ m$ grows linearly in $m$. These spaces are not multiplicative. If the sections were instead required to satisfy $|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\leq C\mathrm e^{m\psi }$, only the monomials with $a=b$ would remain. The measure $
u $ is Bernstein–Markov for $(K,w)$. Proof. At $p_+$ the monomial with exponents $(a,b)$ has local exponents $(a,m-b)$, and at $p_-$ it has local exponents $(m-a,b)$. By lemma 18.47.1 , both total orders must be at least $m-1$. Distinct exponent pairs cannot cancel, so these conditions select exactly the monomials with $|a-b|\leq 1$. The three bands $a=b$, $a=b+1$ and $a=b-1$ have $m+1$, $m$ and $m$ elements. The bound $|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\leq C\mathrm e^{m\psi }$ would require total order $m$ at both poles and leave only the diagonal. The product of two sections with offset $a-b=1$ has offset two and lies outside the selected space of the sum degree; such products fail for every pair of positive degrees. Thus the linear growth of $N_ m$ is not the growth of a graded section ring. Integration over the angles makes all global monomials orthogonal, including those outside the selected space. For $t\in [0,1]$ set \[  I_ m(t)=\int _{-1}^2\mathrm e^{m(tx-x^2/2)}\, \mathrm dx =\mathrm e^{mt^2/2}J_ m(t),\qquad J_ m(t)=\int _{-1}^2\mathrm e^{-m(x-t)^2/2}\, \mathrm dx.  \] The squared norm of the monomial with exponents $(a,b)$ is CA62D9FD1FF2 18.47.5  egin{equation}  A_ m(a,b)= rac19 I_ m(a/m)I_ m(b/m). \end{equation} With $c=\int _{-1}^1\mathrm e^{-y^2/2}\, \mathrm dy$, uniformly in $t\in [0,1]$, \[   rac c{\sqrt m}\leq J_ m(t)\leq \sqrt{ rac{2\pi }m},\qquad J_ m(t)=\sqrt{ rac{2\pi }m}  igl (1+O(m^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{-m/2}) igr ).  \] For the lower bound, integrate over the interval of radius $m^{-1/2}$ centered at $t$; for the last assertion, note that each of the two omitted Gaussian tails is at most $\mathrm e^{-m/2}/m$. Hence 8DAD90BE35BE 18.47.6  egin{equation}   rac{c^2}{9m}\mathrm e^{(a^2+b^2)/(2m)} \leq A_ m(a,b)\leq  rac{2\pi }{9m}\mathrm e^{(a^2+b^2)/(2m)}. \end{equation} For $x\in [-1,2]^2$, completing squares bounds the weighted contribution of each normalized monomial by $9m/c^2$. Summing over all $(m+1)^2$ global monomials and using the evaluation inequality gives \[  \sup _ K|\sigma |_{h^ m}\mathrm e^{-mw/2} \leq C m^{3/2}\| \sigma \| _ m \quad (\sigma \in H^0(X,L^ m)).  \] This polynomial bound proves the Bernstein–Markov property. On the selected space the same argument gives the factor $Cm$. $\square$ Theorem 18.47.7 . A0E408FAE124 With values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$ at the poles, the potentials satisfy FCE7FB3D2455 18.47.8  egin{equation}  U_ m\geq P+ rac{\log (9m/(2\pi ))}{m}- rac1{4m^2}. \end{equation} They converge to $P$ locally uniformly on $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $, in $L^ p$ with respect to a smooth volume form on $X$ for every finite $p$, at the rate $O(\log m/m)$, and pointwise on $X$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. The currents $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ m$ converge weakly to $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P$. Moreover, $\mathrm e^{U_ m}	o \mathrm e^ P$ uniformly on $X$, although for each fixed $m\geq 2$ the difference $U_ m-P$ is unbounded above near either pole. Define a probability measure $\mu $ by \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int _0^1\int f(\mathrm e^{t/2}	au _1,\mathrm e^{t/2}	au _2) \, \mathrm d	au _1\, \mathrm d	au _2\, \mathrm dt.  \] Then, against every continuous test function on $X$, \[  N_ m^{-1}B_ m
u ightharpoonup \mu ,\qquad m^{-1}B_ m
u ightharpoonup 3\mu .  \] The measures $2m^{-2}B_ m
u $, normalized by the ambient dimension, tend to zero in total variation. The envelope satisfies $\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P)^2angle =0$. Proof. The diagonal monomials belong to $V_ m$. The upper bound for their norms in ( 18.47.6 ) gives \[  \mathcal B_ m\geq  rac{9m}{2\pi }\mathrm e^{-m\varphi _ X} \max _{0\leq j\leq m}\mathrm e^{js-j^2/m}.  \] For $0\leq s\leq 2$, the grid point $j/m$ nearest to $s/2$ loses at most $1/(4m^2)$ compared with $g(s)$; outside this interval the maximizing endpoint lies on the grid. This proves ( 18.47.8 ) on the torus. For a monomial with offset one, $(a,b)=(j+1,j)$, the lower bound in ( 18.47.6 ) shows that the exponent of its normalized contribution, apart from $-m\varphi _ X$ and constants, is at most both \[  js-j^2/m+x_1,\qquad (j+1)s-(j+1)^2/m+1-x_2.  \] The band with $(a,b)=(j,j+1)$ is obtained by interchanging the indices. Put \[  R(x)=1+\min (\mathrm e^{x_1},\mathrm e^{1-x_2}) +\min (\mathrm e^{x_2},\mathrm e^{1-x_1}).  \] The lower bound for the norms and the count of monomials give 39BC26BE8655 18.47.9  egin{equation}  U_ m\leq P+ rac{C+2\log (m+1)+\log R(x)}m. \end{equation} The function $R$ extends continuously across the coordinate divisors away from the poles. In a chart at $p_+$, put $A=|\zeta _1|^2$ and $B=|\zeta _2|^2$. The possibly large term of $R$ satisfies \[  \min (1/B,\mathrm e/A)\leq (\mathrm e+1)/(A+B),  \] and the other term is bounded; the same holds at $p_-$. Thus $R\leq C(1+r^{-2})$ near either pole, where $r=|\zeta |$ is the local radius, and $\log R$ belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$ with respect to smooth volume forms. For $m\geq 2$, all selected sections vanish at the poles. The two diagonal sections $T_1^ mT_2^ m$ and $Z_1^ mZ_2^ m$ have no other common zeros, so $\mathcal B_ m>0$ off the poles. Away from the poles, $P$ and $U_ m$ are continuous, so both inequalities extend from the torus to $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $. They give the asserted local uniform convergence and convergence in $L^ p$, and differentiation of the $L^1$ limit in the sense of distributions gives the weak convergence of the currents. At the poles both $U_ m$ and $P$ equal $-\infty $ for $m\geq 2$, which also proves the pointwise statement on $X$. For a fixed $m\geq 2$, the lowest-order terms of the selected sections at a pole include every binary monomial of degree $m-1$, and the sum of their squared moduli is comparable to $r^{2(m-1)}$ in all directions. Hence \[  U_ m=(1-1/m)\log r^2+O_ m(1),\qquad P=\log r^2+O(1),  \] so the difference $U_ m-P$ tends to $+\infty $ near each pole. Nevertheless, ( 18.47.9 ) gives, uniformly in $m\geq 2$ and $r<1$, \[  \mathrm e^{U_ m}\leq Cr^{2-2/m}\leq Cr,\qquad \mathrm e^ P\leq Cr^2.  \] Combined with uniform convergence on compact subsets away from the poles, these bounds give uniform convergence of $\mathrm e^{U_ m}$. The contribution of each normalized monomial to $B_ m
u $ is exactly the product of two truncated Gaussian probability measures in $x_1,x_2$, centered at $(a/m,b/m)$, with the Haar probability measures in the angles. Completing squares in ( 18.47.5 ) and using its uniform bounds proves concentration at these centers, uniformly over all three bands; for example, the probability of $|x_1-a/m|\geq \eta $ is at most $C_\eta \sqrt m\, \mathrm e^{-m\eta ^2/2}$. Uniform continuity of a test function then reduces the sum to three lattice Riemann sums. Each band contains asymptotically one third of the $N_ m$ monomials, and in each band the centers $(a/m,b/m)$ approach the diagonal point $(t,t)$, $t\in [0,1]$. This proves both positive limits. The total mass of $2m^{-2}B_ m
u $ is $2(3m+1)/m^2	o 0$, which proves the convergence to zero in total variation. Off the poles, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P$ is the pullback by $f$ of the current on $\mathbb P^1$ defined by $g$. The function $g$ is $C^{1,1}$, and the local complex Hessian of $g(s)$ has rank at most one. Smooth convex approximations and the product of locally bounded potentials show that its square vanishes, as in the Hessian argument of section 18.45 . The non-pluripolar product assigns no mass to the two poles, so the global square is zero. In particular, the positive-mass hypothesis of theorem 18.35.5 fails in this model. $\square$ Parametrize the real three-dimensional shell $S$ carrying $\mu $ by $\Psi (t,	au _1,	au _2)=(\mathrm e^{t/2}	au _1,\mathrm e^{t/2}	au _2)$, $0<t<1$. For a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, which need be neither closed nor torus-invariant, write $\Psi ^*\mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_{\omega ,S}=\mathcal J_\omega \, \mathrm dt\, \mathrm d	au _1\, \mathrm d	au _2$, as in section 18.45 . Since the boundary of $S$ has zero mass, the densities of $\mu $ and $3\mu $ with respect to $\mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_{\omega ,S}$ are $1/(\mathcal J_\omega \circ \Psi ^{-1})$ and $3/(\mathcal J_\omega \circ \Psi ^{-1})$. The mixed measure $\langle 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Pangle \wedge \omega $ has a locally bounded density off the poles and gives $S$ zero mass, so it cannot reproduce the positive limit of the kernel measures.

text: Lemma 18.47.2 . 2BCFCC9C8808 On $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $ set \[  f=[T_1T_2:Z_1Z_2],\qquad \psi _{\rm FS}=\log (|T_1T_2|_ h^2+|Z_1Z_2|_ h^2).  \] Every $v$ in the class of lemma 18.47.1 has the form \[  v=\psi _{\rm FS}+u\circ f, \qquad u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\omega _{\rm FS}),  \] on $X\setminus \{ p_+,p_-\} $, and $v(p_\pm )=-\infty $. Conversely, for every such $u$, the function $\psi _{\rm FS}+u\circ f$, extended by $-\infty $ at the two poles, belongs to that class. Proof. For $\xi \in \mathbb C^*$, the curve of the pencil \[  C_\xi =\{ Z_1Z_2=\xi T_1T_2\}   \] is a smooth rational curve of bidegree $(1,1)$ through both poles, and its $\theta $-degree is two. The restriction of $v$ to this connected curve is either identically $-\infty $ or $\theta |_{C_\xi }$-plurisubharmonic. In the latter case, its curvature measure has total mass two by Stokes' theorem. The local upper bounds of lemma 18.47.1 give Lelong numbers at least one at the two poles, hence, by the identification of Lelong numbers with atoms in lemma 5.37.18 , atoms of mass at least one there. These atoms exhaust the measure. The curvature of $\psi |_{C_\xi }$ consists of the same two unit atoms. Thus $v-\psi $ is harmonic, in the sense of distributions, on the compact curve $C_\xi $, and therefore constant. On the torus use the holomorphic coordinates $(z_1,\xi =z_1z_2)$. Local integrability and Fubini's theorem show that, for almost every $\xi $, the restriction of $v$ to $C_\xi $ is not identically $-\infty $; by the preceding paragraph it is then finite off the poles. Hence the restriction of $v$ to the transverse curve $S=\{ z_1=1\} \simeq \mathbb P^1$ is not identically $-\infty $. Put $u=v|_ S+\log 2$. Since $\theta |_ S=\omega _{\rm FS}$ and $\psi _{\rm FS}|_ S=-\log 2$, the constants on the curves $C_\xi $ give the asserted identity almost everywhere on the torus. Both sides have plurisubharmonic local potentials, so they agree everywhere off the poles. The logarithmic upper bounds give the value $-\infty $ at the poles. Conversely, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _{\rm FS}+u\circ f)=f^*(\omega _{\rm FS}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\geq 0$ off the poles. In a chart at a pole, the local potential is bounded above by $\log (|\zeta _1|^2+|\zeta _2|^2)+C$, since $u$ is bounded above. It therefore extends across the pole as a plurisubharmonic function with value $-\infty $ there, which gives a global $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function dominated by $\psi +C$. $\square$

title: Theorem 18.47.3
section: 18.47 Three monomial bands from a multiplier-ideal selection
text: Theorem 18.47.3 . 1D58A228EF5A For these $K$ and $w$, the partial envelope ( 18.32.1 ) is \[  \begin{aligned}  E_{\theta ,K}[\psi ]_{\mathcal I}(w)& =P=g(s)-\varphi _ X,\\  g(s)& =\sup _{0\leq t\leq 1}(ts-t^2) =\begin{cases}  0,& s\leq 0,\\  s^2/4,& 0\leq s\leq 2,\\  s-1,& s\geq 2. \end{cases}\end{aligned}  \] Here $P$ is given by this formula on the torus and extends to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ with $P(p_\pm )=-\infty $ and $\psi -1\leq P\leq \psi $. Proof. For an arbitrary competitor $v$, lemma 18.47.2 gives, in terms of the affine coordinate $\xi $ of $\mathbb P^1$, \[  \chi (\xi )=\log (1+|\xi |^2)+u(\xi ), \qquad v=\chi (z_1z_2)-\varphi _ X.  \] On the interior of $K$, the obstacle condition, which holds quasi-everywhere, becomes an inequality everywhere, by the submean inequality and the continuity of $w+\varphi _ X$. Evaluating at $x_1=x_2=s/2$, with $s=\log |\xi |^2$, gives \[  \chi (\xi )\leq s^2/4\quad (-2<s<4)  \] for every argument of $\xi $. At $s=0$ this bounds $\chi $ by zero on $|\xi |=1$, and the maximum principle for the subharmonic function $\chi $ bounds it by zero on the whole disk $|\xi |\leq 1$. At infinity use the local potential \[  \chi _\infty (\eta )=\chi (1/\eta )+\log |\eta |^2.  \] The obstacle at $s=2$ bounds it by $-1$ on $|\eta |=\mathrm e^{-1}$, and the same maximum principle gives $\chi (\xi )\leq s-1$ for $s\geq 2$. Together with the obstacle for $0\leq s\leq 2$, this proves $\chi \leq g$, without any invariance assumption on the competitor. Conversely, $g$ is convex with slopes in $[0,1]$, so $g(\log |\xi |^2)-\log (1+|\xi |^2)$ is an $\omega _{\rm FS}$-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^1$. By lemma 18.47.2 , it defines the global function $P$. Directly, \[  \max (0,s)-1\leq g(s)\leq \max (0,s),\qquad g(s)\leq s^2/4\leq (x_1^2+x_2^2)/2.  \] Thus $P$ belongs to the competitor class of lemma 18.47.1 and satisfies the obstacle condition everywhere on $K$. Since it dominates every competitor, it is the envelope, including its values $-\infty $ at the poles. $\square$

AD8335312F45 For every $m\geq 1$ the selected space is \[  V_ m=\operatorname {span}\{ Z_1^ aT_1^{m-a}Z_2^ bT_2^{m-b}: 0\leq a,b\leq m,\  |a-b|\leq 1\} , \qquad N_ m=3m+1.  \] In particular, $N_ m$ grows linearly in $m$. These spaces are not multiplicative. If the sections were instead required to satisfy $|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\leq C\mathrm e^{m\psi }$, only the monomials with $a=b$ would remain. The measure $\nu $ is Bernstein–Markov for $(K,w)$. Proof. At $p_+$ the monomial with exponents $(a,b)$ has local exponents $(a,m-b)$, and at $p_-$ it has local exponents $(m-a,b)$. By lemma 18.47.1 , both total orders must be at least $m-1$. Distinct exponent pairs cannot cancel, so these conditions select exactly the monomials with $|a-b|\leq 1$. The three bands $a=b$, $a=b+1$ and $a=b-1$ have $m+1$, $m$ and $m$ elements. The bound $|\sigma |_{h^ m}^2\leq C\mathrm e^{m\psi }$ would require total order $m$ at both poles and leave only the diagonal. The product of two sections with offset $a-b=1$ has offset two and lies outside the selected space of the sum degree; such products fail for every pair of positive degrees. Thus the linear growth of $N_ m$ is not the growth of a graded section ring. Integration over the angles makes all global monomials orthogonal, including those outside the selected space. For $t\in [0,1]$ set \[  I_ m(t)=\int _{-1}^2\mathrm e^{m(tx-x^2/2)}\, \mathrm dx =\mathrm e^{mt^2/2}J_ m(t),\qquad J_ m(t)=\int _{-1}^2\mathrm e^{-m(x-t)^2/2}\, \mathrm dx.  \] The squared norm of the monomial with exponents $(a,b)$ is CA62D9FD1FF2 18.47.5 \begin{equation}  A_ m(a,b)=\frac19 I_ m(a/m)I_ m(b/m). \end{equation} With $c=\int _{-1}^1\mathrm e^{-y^2/2}\, \mathrm dy$, uniformly in $t\in [0,1]$, \[  \frac c{\sqrt m}\leq J_ m(t)\leq \sqrt{\frac{2\pi }m},\qquad J_ m(t)=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi }m} \bigl (1+O(m^{-1/2}\mathrm e^{-m/2})\bigr ).  \] For the lower bound, integrate over the interval of radius $m^{-1/2}$ centered at $t$; for the last assertion, note that each of the two omitted Gaussian tails is at most $\mathrm e^{-m/2}/m$. Hence 8DAD90BE35BE 18.47.6 \begin{equation}  \frac{c^2}{9m}\mathrm e^{(a^2+b^2)/(2m)} \leq A_ m(a,b)\leq \frac{2\pi }{9m}\mathrm e^{(a^2+b^2)/(2m)}. \end{equation} For $x\in [-1,2]^2$, completing squares bounds the weighted contribution of each normalized monomial by $9m/c^2$. Summing over all $(m+1)^2$ global monomials and using the evaluation inequality gives \[  \sup _ K|\sigma |_{h^ m}\mathrm e^{-mw/2} \leq C m^{3/2}\| \sigma \| _ m \quad (\sigma \in H^0(X,L^ m)).  \] This polynomial bound proves the Bernstein–Markov property. On the selected space the same argument gives the factor $Cm$. $\square$
