title: Example 10.18.3
text: Example 10.18.3 . 0C57A6C5BFEC The weak closure $\mathscr C_\omega $ of the smooth strictly positive normalized Gauduchon forms can be smaller than $\mathscr G_\omega $, even on a Kähler surface. Let $X$ be the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at one point and $C$ its exceptional curve. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ and a smooth closed representative $\beta _ C$ of the class of $[C]$. Then \[  T_ C=\frac{[C]}{\int _ C\omega }\in \mathscr G_\omega , \qquad \int _ X\beta _ C\wedge T_ C=\frac{-1}{\int _ C\omega }<0,  \] whereas every smooth strictly positive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ satisfies $\int _ X\beta _ C\wedge T=\int _ C T>0$. In particular $T_ C\notin \mathscr C_\omega $. Proof. The integration current $[C]$ is positive and closed, so its normalization belongs to $\mathscr G_\omega $. Its pairing with the smooth form $\beta _ C$ is the self-intersection $C^2=-1$, computed in example 12.6.3 . For smooth $T$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ give the second identity. Since the pairing with the fixed smooth form $\beta _ C$ is continuous under weak convergence of currents, it is nonnegative on the weak closure of the smooth tests, and this closure does not contain $T_ C$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.18.4
text: Corollary 10.18.4 . 852EFF5927B9 Assume $b>0$ and that $D_ p$ has a smooth maximizing sequence $(T_ j)$ with uniformly integrable densities $p k_{T_ j}$. Let $E$ be an effective real divisor whose class has a smooth semipositive representative $\beta _ E$. If \[  \int _{\{ \beta _ E=0\} }f\, \mathrm{d}V=0,  \] then no threshold subsolution $u$ for $f$ satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq [E]$. Proof. Suppose such a subsolution exists. By proposition 10.18.1 , there is a maximizing current $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ with $\int _ X\beta _ E\wedge T=0$. We use the matrix-density notation of section 12.7 : $\sigma _ T=\omega \wedge T$ is the trace measure of $T$, $P_ T$ is its matrix density and $B$ is the coefficient matrix of $\beta _ E$. Since both matrices are positive semidefinite, the vanishing pairing gives $\operatorname {tr}(BP_ T)=0$ at $\sigma _ T$-almost every point. Wherever $B\ne 0$, this forces $P_ T$ to be singular: a positive definite $P_ T$ would have strictly positive trace against the nonzero positive semidefinite matrix $B$. The determinant measure $\Gamma _0(T)$ vanishes where $P_ T$ is singular, so it is concentrated on $\{ \beta _ E=0\} $. By theorem 12.9.1 , $\Gamma _0(T)=k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$, and the hypothesis on $f$ gives $p k_ T=0$ almost everywhere. This contradicts $D_ p(T)=\rho _\omega (p)>0$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.18.5
text: Corollary 10.18.5 . A786309EB514 Assume $b>0$ and that $D_ p$ has a smooth maximizing sequence $(T_ j)$ with uniformly integrable densities $p k_{T_ j}$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be a threshold subsolution for $f$, and suppose that $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq [E]$ for an effective real divisor $E$ whose Bott–Chern class is nef. Let $\beta _ E$ be any smooth closed representative of that class. Then for every smooth strictly positive probability measure $\mu $, the Gauduchon root volume of definition 12.2.1 satisfies \[  \lambda _\mu (\beta _ E)=0.  \] Proof. By proposition 10.18.1 , there is a maximizing current $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ with $\int _ X\beta _ E\wedge T=0$. If $\lambda _\mu (\beta _ E)>0$, then proposition 12.34.2 gives $\Gamma _0(T)=0$, hence $D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=0$, contradicting the positivity of its maximal value. Since the nef class of $\beta _ E$ has $\lambda _\mu (\beta _ E)\geq 0$, the conclusion follows for each $\mu $. $\square$

title: 10.19 Currents on the elliptic threefold
text: On the elliptic threefold of section 12.19 , closed classes can be described completely. The product of the two horizontal forms is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact, so every positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(1,1)$-current has zero vertical component, and the fiberwise descent of lemma 11.22.4 identifies it with a current on the base. Closedness descends as well. The closed positive cones, the singularity envelopes and the spaces of sections selected by multiplier ideals are therefore all computed on the base surface. Let $X$ be the compact threefold of section 12.19 , and let \[  \pi :X\longrightarrow B=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1  \] be its elliptic fibration. Write $\sigma _1,\sigma _2$ for the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, each of integral one, and put $\alpha =\pi ^*\sigma _1$ and $\beta =\pi ^*\sigma _2$. The product coordinates of that construction show that $\pi $ is locally a holomorphic product with fiber the elliptic curve $E$. The logarithmic ratio $t$ of that construction is defined only on the covering space, but its differentials descend to $X$. We take for $\omega $ the balanced metric $\omega =\alpha +\beta +D$, where $D=\mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$. By proposition 12.19.18 , it satisfies \[  \alpha \wedge \beta =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega .  \] The arguments below use this identity, not the vanishing of the lower Monge–Ampère mass. Lemma 10.19.1 . 464DA68EB4DA Every positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ has the form \[  T=\pi ^*S  \] for a unique positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(1,1)$-current $S$ on $B$. Moreover, $T$ is closed if and only if $S$ is closed. Here $\pi ^*S$ is the pullback of currents under the holomorphic submersion $\pi $. Proof. The measure $T\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta $ is positive. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, Stokes' theorem for currents gives \[  \int _ XT\wedge \alpha \wedge \beta =\tfrac 12\int _ X\omega \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0,  \] so this measure vanishes. All products in this identity pair a current with smooth forms. Now apply lemma 11.22.4 to $\pi $, with the base Hermitian form $\eta =\sigma _1+\sigma _2$. Since $\eta ^2=2\sigma _1\wedge \sigma _2$, we have $T\wedge \pi ^*\eta ^2=0$, and since the fiber is a compact connected elliptic curve, the lemma gives the unique positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed current $S$. The same lemma shows that $S$ is closed when $T$ is; conversely, pullback commutes with $\mathrm{d}$. $\square$ This description concerns $(1,1)$-currents. It does not conflict with the Gauduchon forms of lemma 12.19.13 : those have bidegree $(2,2)$ and satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma _ j=0$, with bounded degree and divergent volume of their positive roots, and they belong to a different cone of currents. Proposition 10.19.2 . 24BCA82D5034 Pullback \[  \pi ^*:H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(B,\mathbb R) \longrightarrow H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)  \] is injective. The pseudoeffective and nef cones on $X$ coincide and are \[  \operatorname {Psef}(X)=\operatorname {Nef}(X) =\{ a\{ \alpha \} _{\mathrm{BC}}+b\{ \beta \} _{\mathrm{BC}}: a,b\geq 0\} .  \] For the trace functional of the Gauduchon metric $\omega $, the slice of this cone at trace one is the segment $a+b=(8\pi )^{-1}$. Every class in the cone has a smooth semipositive representative, and none is big. The real form $\beta -\alpha $ is de Rham exact but represents a nonzero Bott–Chern class. Proof. Suppose a smooth closed real form $\tau $ on $B$ satisfies $\pi ^*\tau =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ smooth on $X$. The restriction of $u$ to each compact connected elliptic fiber is harmonic, hence constant, and local holomorphic sections show that $u=v\circ \pi $ for a smooth function $v$ on $B$. Thus $\pi ^*(\tau -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=0$, which implies $\tau =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ because $\pi $ is a submersion. This proves injectivity. The usual cohomology computation for $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, together with the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma on this Kähler surface, gives \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(B,\mathbb R) =\mathbb R\{ \sigma _1\} \oplus \mathbb R\{ \sigma _2\} , \qquad \int _ B\sigma _1\wedge \sigma _2=1, \qquad \sigma _1^2=\sigma _2^2=0.  \] If $S$ is a positive closed current on $B$, the two coefficients of its class are \[  a=\int _ BS\wedge \sigma _2\geq 0, \qquad b=\int _ BS\wedge \sigma _1\geq 0.  \] By lemma 20.4.10 and lemma 10.19.1 , every pseudoeffective class on $X$ is the pullback of the class of such a current, and it therefore lies in the cone of the statement. Conversely, every class in that cone has the smooth semipositive representative $a\alpha +b\beta $ and is therefore nef. A nef class is pseudoeffective by the compactness argument following proposition 10.11.2 . This proves the equality of the cones; the whole Bott–Chern group of $X$ is not needed. Since $\omega ^2=2\alpha \wedge \beta +2(\alpha +\beta )\wedge D$ and $\int _ E D=4\pi $ on each fiber, integration along the fibers gives \[  \int _ X(a\alpha +b\beta )\wedge \omega ^2=8\pi (a+b).  \] This proves the assertion about the slice. By proposition 12.19.22 , $X$ carries no closed Kähler current, so none of these classes is big. Finally, the one-form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$ is globally defined on $X$ and satisfies \[  \mathrm{d}(\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t)=\beta -\alpha .  \] The class of $\sigma _2-\sigma _1$ on $B$ is nonzero, and injectivity makes its pullback nonzero in Bott–Chern cohomology. Thus de Rham exactness does not imply $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exactness in this example. $\square$ Consequently, every pseudoeffective class on this threefold is nef and has empty non-nef locus, whereas its non-Kähler locus is all of $X$, since no class is big. All its closed positive representatives come from the two-dimensional base; in particular $(a\alpha +b\beta )^3=0$.

title: 10.19.3 Potentials and envelopes from the base
search_title: Potentials and envelopes from the base
text: Descent also applies to potentials and preserves both ordinary singularity types and multiplier ideals, so the singularity envelopes in these backgrounds are computed on the base. The three-dimensional Monge–Ampère measures of these potentials nevertheless vanish, because their currents have only two horizontal directions. We use the ordinary singularity order $\preceq $ and equivalence $\sim $ of definition 16.7.1 , the ideal order $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ and equivalence $\sim _{\mathcal I}$, which compare the multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(ku)$ at all weights $k>0$, and the ordinary and multiplier-ideal envelopes $P_\theta [u]$ and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ of definition 5.40.4 , definition 18.4.1 . Proposition 10.19.4 . 2555699F5657 Let $a,b\geq 0$, put $\theta _ B=a\sigma _1+b\sigma _2$ and $\theta =\pi ^*\theta _ B$. Pullback is a bijection \[  \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta _ B)\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\qquad v\longmapsto v\circ \pi .  \] It preserves the ordinary singularity order and equivalence, as well as the ideal order and equivalence. For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\theta _ B)$, \[  P_\theta [v\circ \pi ]=P_{\theta _ B}[v]\circ \pi , \qquad P_\theta [v\circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta _ B}[v]_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi .  \] Nevertheless, every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=0.  \] Proof. The form $\theta _ B$ is closed, and $\pi $ is a proper holomorphic submersion with connected fibers, so proposition 5.43.5 gives the asserted bijection. Since $\pi $ is surjective, an ordinary singularity inequality holds upstairs exactly when it holds downstairs, with the same constant. By lemma 5.37.7 , multiplier ideals of potentials on $B$ pull back to those of the composed potentials on $X$, at every positive weight. Restriction to local holomorphic sections shows conversely that an inclusion of multiplier ideals on $X$ implies the corresponding inclusion on $B$. Hence the ideal orders and equivalences correspond as well. The competitors defining both envelopes correspond under the bijection, including the bound by zero and the required ordinary or ideal condition, and their pointwise suprema commute with pullback. Upper semicontinuous regularization also commutes with pullback: in a product chart, the supremum of a pulled-back function over a sufficiently small product neighborhood equals its supremum over the corresponding base neighborhood. This proves the two envelope identities. Finally, write $u=v\circ \pi $ and, for positive integers $j$, set $u_ j=\max \{ u,-j\} $, which descends to $v_ j=\max \{ v,-j\} $. Since $\theta _ B$ is semipositive, these are bounded admissible potentials. By lemma 5.28.4 , $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^3=0$ because the base has dimension two. The definition of the extended non-pluripolar measure by increasing truncations now proves the last assertion. $\square$ Thus the ordinary and ideal envelopes coincide in these backgrounds exactly when they coincide on the base, while every three-dimensional Monge–Ampère measure vanishes. Criteria from the closed theory that require positive volume do not apply to these classes, which are not big. The Hermitian background $\omega $ behaves differently: its Monge–Ampère equations with smooth positive densities are solvable, even though the infimum of its masses is zero.

10.19.7 The boundary volume and section growth
search_title: The boundary volume and section growth
text: Although no class $a\{ \alpha \} +b\{ \beta \} $ is big, its small Hermitian perturbations have positive Gauduchon variational volume $\mathcal V_\mu $ (definition 12.2.1 ). For the volume form of the balanced metric, the zero potential solves the normalized Monge–Ampère equation for every positive combination of $\alpha $, $\beta $ and $D$, so the volume is an explicit cubic polynomial in the perturbation parameter. Its order of vanishing at the nef boundary records how many of the two horizontal coefficients vanish. Proposition 10.19.8 . 141C0ACF5576 On the elliptic threefold, let $a,b\geq 0$, put $\theta =a\alpha +b\beta $, and let $\mu _0=\omega ^3/(24\pi )$. Then for every $\epsilon >0$, E7BC529546A7 10.19.9 \begin{equation}  \mathcal V_{\mu _0}(\theta +\epsilon \omega ) =24\pi \epsilon (a+\epsilon )(b+\epsilon ). \end{equation} In particular, $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=0$ for every smooth positive probability measure $\mu $. Let $q$ be the number of positive coefficients among $a,b$. Then the degeneration orders of proposition 12.20.1 are \[  \underline a(\theta )=\overline a(\theta )=3-q,  \] for every smooth positive probability measure and every Hermitian perturbation direction. Proof. The forms $\alpha ,\beta ,D$ are semipositive of rank one, so their squares vanish, and their sum $\omega $ is strictly positive. Thus \[  \Omega _\epsilon =\theta +\epsilon \omega =(a+\epsilon )\alpha +(b+\epsilon )\beta +\epsilon D>0.  \] Since $\omega ^3=6\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D$ and $\int _ X\omega ^3=24\pi $, the wedge expansion gives \[  \Omega _\epsilon ^3 =6\epsilon (a+\epsilon )(b+\epsilon )\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D =24\pi \epsilon (a+\epsilon )(b+\epsilon )\mu _0.  \] Hence the zero potential solves the smooth normalized equation for $\Omega _\epsilon $ and $\mu _0$. By theorem 12.2.3 , the scalar of this equation is $\mathcal V_{\mu _0}(\Omega _\epsilon )$, which proves ( 10.19.9 ). The continuity of the volume at nef classes in theorem 12.11.1 and comparison of smooth densities then give $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=0$. As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, the leading term of ( 10.19.9 ) is $24\pi ab\epsilon $ if $a$ and $b$ are both positive, $24\pi (a+b)\epsilon ^2$ if exactly one of them is positive, and $24\pi \epsilon ^3$ if both vanish. The logarithmic quotients defining the orders therefore have limits $1,2,3$, respectively. Their independence of the density and of the perturbing metric is part of proposition 12.20.1 . $\square$ The same number $q$ governs the growth of sections. For nonnegative integers $a,b$, the line bundle $L=\pi ^*\mathcal O_ B(a,b)$ satisfies \[  h^0(X,L^ m)=(am+1)(bm+1),  \] since the descent along compact fibers and the monomial count in the proof of proposition 10.19.6 also apply when one or both integers vanish. The growth degree of these spaces is exactly $q$, whereas the boundary order of the smooth curvature form $a\alpha +b\beta $ of $L$ is $3-q$. In this explicit family, the boundary order thus records the loss of algebraic growth dimension, even though the three-dimensional Monge–Ampère measures in the unperturbed background vanish. Formula ( 10.19.9 ) concerns one fixed smooth density; it does not assert that a total mass is conserved over all potentials. Indeed, by theorem 12.19.1 every Hermitian form on $X$, in particular each $\Omega _\epsilon $, has zero lower mass, while its upper mass is finite because $X$ has the bounded mass property (definition 13.14.14 , proposition 12.19.18 ). Whether comparable identifications hold beyond such explicit families is part of 12.33.4 .

title: 10.19.10 Limits of the minimizing Gauduchon forms
search_title: Limits of the minimizing Gauduchon forms
text: The Gauduchon metrics that minimize the quotient defining the volume in ( 10.19.9 ) can be identified explicitly: they are the equation metrics themselves. Their normalized squares converge smoothly at the nef boundary, although the normalized metrics may diverge. Recall from definition 12.2.1 that the root volume $\lambda _{\mu _0}$, with $\lambda _{\mu _0}^3=\mathcal V_{\mu _0}$, is the infimum over Gauduchon metrics $\gamma $ of $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^2$ divided by the denominator $D_{\mu _0}(\gamma )=\int _ X(\mu _0/\gamma ^3)^{1/3}\gamma ^3$. For positive functions of $\epsilon $, we write $f\asymp g$ if $f/g$ is bounded above and below by positive constants as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Proposition 10.19.11 . 983D2EEDBE68 Let $a,b\geq 0$, $\theta =a\alpha +b\beta $ and $\Omega _\epsilon =\theta +\epsilon \omega $. For every $\epsilon >0$, the metric $\Omega _\epsilon $ is Gauduchon, and it minimizes the quotient defining $\lambda _{\mu _0}(\Omega _\epsilon )$. Put \[  I_\epsilon =8\pi \bigl (ab+2(a+b)\epsilon +3\epsilon ^2\bigr ), \qquad T_\epsilon =\frac{\Omega _\epsilon ^2}{I_\epsilon }, \qquad \gamma _\epsilon =\frac{\Omega _\epsilon }{\sqrt{I_\epsilon }}.  \] Then $\int _ X\omega \wedge T_\epsilon =1$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_\epsilon =0$ and $T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^2$. As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, the forms $T_\epsilon $ converge smoothly to \[  T_0=\begin{cases}  (4\pi )^{-1}\alpha \wedge \beta ,& a,b>0,\\  (8\pi )^{-1}\alpha \wedge (\beta +D),& a>0,\  b=0,\\  (8\pi )^{-1}\beta \wedge (\alpha +D),& a=0,\  b>0,\\  (24\pi )^{-1}\omega ^2,& a=b=0. \end{cases}  \] In every case $\theta \wedge T_0=0$. If $q$ is the number of positive coefficients among $a,b$, the denominator of the normalized minimizing metric satisfies \[  D_{\mu _0}(\gamma _\epsilon ) =\frac{\bigl (24\pi \epsilon (a+\epsilon )(b+\epsilon )\bigr )^{2/3}}{I_\epsilon } \asymp \epsilon ^{q/3},  \] where the two comparison constants may depend on the fixed pair $(a,b)$. Proof. Write $x=a+\epsilon $, $y=b+\epsilon $ and $z=\epsilon $. Since $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=D^2=0$, \[  \Omega _\epsilon ^2 =2xy\alpha \wedge \beta +2xz\alpha \wedge D+2yz\beta \wedge D.  \] The forms $\alpha ,\beta $ are closed and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}D=2\alpha \wedge \beta $. Hence the first term is closed, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of each of the last two terms contains $\alpha ^2$ or $\beta ^2$ and therefore vanishes. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega _\epsilon ^2)=0$. Since the zero potential solves the normalized equation for $\Omega _\epsilon $ and $\mu _0$, the characterization of minimizing metrics in theorem 12.2.3 shows that $\Omega _\epsilon $ is a minimizer. Integration along the fibers gives $\int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta \wedge D=4\pi $. Hence \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \Omega _\epsilon ^2 =8\pi (xy+xz+yz)=I_\epsilon ,  \] which is the trace normalization. Dividing the three coefficients in the wedge expansion of $\Omega _\epsilon ^2$ by $I_\epsilon $ gives each of the stated limits; the convergence holds in every smooth norm, because the forms $\alpha \wedge \beta $, $\alpha \wedge D$ and $\beta \wedge D$ are fixed. The identities $\alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0$ then give $\theta \wedge T_0=0$ in all four cases. Set $c_\epsilon =24\pi \epsilon (a+\epsilon )(b+\epsilon )$. The equation for $\Omega _\epsilon $ gives \[  \gamma _\epsilon ^3 =\frac{c_\epsilon }{I_\epsilon ^{3/2}}\mu _0.  \] Substituting this in the definition of $D_{\mu _0}$ and using $\int _ X\mu _0=1$ yields $D_{\mu _0}(\gamma _\epsilon )=c_\epsilon ^{2/3}/I_\epsilon $. For fixed $(a,b)$ one has $c_\epsilon \asymp \epsilon ^{3-q}$ and $I_\epsilon \asymp \epsilon ^{2-q}$, so the quotient is of order $\epsilon ^{q/3}$. $\square$ In a coframe adapted to the three rank-one forms $\alpha $, $\beta $ and $D$, the three complementary products in the proof show that the limiting positive $(2,2)$-forms have coefficient matrices of rank $1$, $2$ and $3$ when $q=2$, $1$ and $0$, respectively. If $a,b>0$, the normalized metrics themselves converge smoothly to \[  \frac{a\alpha +b\beta }{\sqrt{8\pi ab}}.  \] If $a>0$ and $b=0$, however, the coefficient of $\alpha $ in $\gamma _\epsilon $ grows like a positive constant times $\epsilon ^{-1/2}$, while its other two coefficients tend to zero. Thus the metrics $\gamma _\epsilon $ are unbounded relative to the fixed metric $\omega $, although their squares converge smoothly; the same holds with $\alpha $ and $\beta $ interchanged. This divergence is unavoidable. In dimension three, a positive $(2,2)$-form of rank two is not the square of a semipositive $(1,1)$-form: the coefficients of such a square are the pairwise products of the eigenvalues of the $(1,1)$-form, and the number of nonzero products is three, one or zero. At the vertex $a=b=0$, the normalized metric instead stays equal to $\omega /\sqrt{24\pi }$. For a nonzero boundary class, the smooth limit $T_0$ annihilates $\theta $, and the denominators $D_{\mu _0}(\gamma _\epsilon )$ tend to zero; no concentration of the coefficient measures occurs in this family. This degeneration of the minimizing tests for a fixed density differs from the sequence of Gauduchon forms used in lemma 12.19.13 to prove that the lower mass vanishes. At the vertex, the denominator stays positive, and the order three comes entirely from the scaling $\Omega _\epsilon =\epsilon \omega $ of the background.

title: 10.20 Smooth equations on the ample locus

section: 10.20 Smooth equations on the ample locus
text: We now turn to the metric geometry of solutions of Monge–Ampère equations in big classes. In this section $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\alpha \in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is a big class with a smooth closed representative $\theta $. Its ample locus is $\operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )=X\setminus E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. The solution of the Monge–Ampère equation with a smooth positive density has minimal singularities, and a Kähler current with analytic singularities provides a barrier that is smooth on the ample locus. The interior estimate of corollary 15.18.50 then gives smoothness there. Let $\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$ be the volume of $\alpha $, the non-pluripolar mass of a current with minimal singularities in $\alpha $, and let $\mathcal E(X,\theta )$ be the class of potentials $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ of full mass , that is, with $\int _ X\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\rangle =\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. Theorem 10.20.1 . C4F23D785797 Let $\mu $ be a smooth positive volume form with $\mu (X)=\operatorname {vol}(\alpha )$. The normalized full-mass solution $\varphi \in \mathcal E(X,\theta )$ of 6DBC0A4AFE96 10.20.2 \begin{equation}  \bigl \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\bigr \rangle =\mu , \qquad \sup _ X\varphi =0, \end{equation} is smooth on $\operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )$, and the restriction of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ to this locus is a Kähler form. The existence and uniqueness of $\varphi $ are part of the classical theory of Monge–Ampère equations in big classes, discussed in section 25.21 ; only the regularity assertion needs proof. Proof. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ and put $f=\mu /\omega ^ n$. Since $X$ is compact and $\mu $ is smooth, $f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ for every finite $p>1$. The classical estimate for this equation, discussed in section 25.21 , shows that $\varphi $ has minimal singularities: there is a constant $C>0$ such that 658C9DBC52ED 10.20.3 \begin{equation}  V_\theta -C\leq \varphi \leq V_\theta . \end{equation} The upper bound follows from the normalization. Let $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ be a Kähler current with analytic singularities as in theorem 10.13.2 . Its potential $\rho $ has analytic singularities with smooth remainder, and for some constant $\varepsilon >0$, \[  T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega , \qquad \{ \rho =-\infty \} =E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ).  \] Thus $\rho $ is smooth on $\Omega =\operatorname {Amp}(\alpha )$. After subtracting a constant we may assume $\rho \leq 0$, hence $\rho \leq V_\theta $, and ( 10.20.3 ) gives \[  \rho -C\leq \varphi \leq 0.  \] In particular $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, and by locality its non-pluripolar equation there is the equation for bounded potentials. The density $f$ belongs to $L^ p$ on $X$ and is smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Hence all hypotheses of corollary 15.18.50 hold for the strict barrier $\rho $, so $\varphi $ is smooth and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ on $\Omega $. Since $\theta $ is closed, this form is Kähler. $\square$ The proof uses that the density is smooth and positive on the entire regular locus of the barrier. The theorem says nothing about the distance from the ample locus to its complement: the metric $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ may reach the omitted set along paths of finite length. To determine that length, one must compare the normal and tangential directions of the metric. The following sections first examine zeros of the density; singular radial densities then separate boundedness of the potential from completeness of the metric.

title: 10.21 Density zeros and metric degeneration
text: Where the density vanishes, the metric defined by a solution degenerates, and the rate of degeneration depends on how the zero arises. In complex dimension $n\geq 2$, a zero of the determinant can come from a ramified holomorphic map, from an exceptional fiber of a blowup, or from a singular Hessian. These mechanisms give different relations between the regularity of the potential and the distance to the zero set. Bounded Hölder solutions in a positive background exist by theorem 14.19.2 , theorem 15.5.1 , but their existence gives no pointwise estimate for the metric at such a zero. Proposition 10.21.1 . 8D773ECA9ED2 Let $F:X\to Y$ be a finite surjective holomorphic map between compact Kähler manifolds of dimension $n$, let $\omega _ Y$ be a Kähler form on $Y$, and suppose that the class $F^*[\omega _ Y]$ contains a Kähler form $\theta $. Then the full-mass solution in the background $\theta $ with measure $(F^*\omega _ Y)^ n$ has a smooth bounded potential with minimal singularities, and its current is the smooth semipositive form $F^*\omega _ Y$. Fix a smooth positive local volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. In a chart at a generic point of the ramification divisor, away from its other components, in which $F(z,w)=(z^ k,w)$ with $k\geq 2$, EA1615732A9D 10.21.2 \begin{equation}  (F^*\omega _ Y)^ n=|z|^{2(k-1)}G\, \mathrm{d} V, \qquad F^*\omega _ Y\asymp |z|^{2(k-1)}|\mathrm{d} z|^2+|\mathrm{d} w|^2, \end{equation} where $G$ is smooth and positive and $\asymp $ means that each side is bounded by a constant multiple of the other. The distance for $F^*\omega _ Y$ to the ramification divisor $\{ z=0\} $ is comparable to $|z|^ k$. Thus the metric on the complement of the ramification divisor is incomplete, although the current has no divisorial component. Finally, there is a strict barrier with logarithmic pole along the global ramification divisor. Proof. By the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma on the compact Kähler manifold $X$, the de Rham class $F^*[\omega _ Y]$ determines the Bott–Chern class, as in subsection 20.4.9 . Thus $F^*\omega _ Y=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a smooth function $u$ on $X$. Its mass is the full mass of the class, and uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 25.21 , identifies $u$ with the solution up to a constant. The Jacobian determinant of $(z,w)\mapsto (z^ k,w)$ is $kz^{k-1}$, and comparison of $\omega _ Y$ with the Euclidean form gives ( 10.21.2 ). Hence every path to $\{ z=0\} $ has length bounded below by the variation of a fixed multiple of $|z|^ k$ along it, and a radial path with fixed $w$ attains this order. The determinant of the differential $\mathrm{d}F$ defines the global ramification divisor $R$. Choose a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(R)$, with curvature form $\Theta _ R$ and canonical section $s_ R$. Since $\theta $ is Kähler, $\theta -\epsilon \Theta _ R>0$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon >0$, so by the Poincaré–Lelong formula $\epsilon \log |s_ R|^2-C$ is the potential of a strict positive $\theta $-current. The barrier is built from the global divisor $R$; no local branch coordinate is treated as a global line bundle. $\square$ Nonclosed backgrounds show the same behavior on manifolds that are not Kähler. On a Hopf manifold, the pullback of the standard invariant metric under a coordinate power map solves an equation in a nonclosed Hermitian background. Example 10.21.3 . 99FB104FBCD5 Let $n\geq 2$, $q>1$ and let $k\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $H_ q=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/(Z\sim qZ)$ be the Hopf manifold, and on the covering space put $R=\sum _ j|Z_ j|^2$, $S=\sum _ j|Z_ j|^{2k}$, \[  h_0=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\frac{\sum _ j\mathrm{d} Z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar Z_ j}{R}, \quad u_ k=\log S-k\log R,  \] \[  \theta _ k=k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log R+ \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \log S\wedge \bar\partial \log S.  \] These forms and functions are invariant under $Z\mapsto qZ$, so they descend to $H_ q$; the form $h_0$ descends to every Hopf manifold $H_{q'}$. The coordinate power map $F_ k([Z])=[(Z_1^ k,\ldots ,Z_ n^ k)]$ defines a finite surjective map $H_ q\to H_{q^ k}$: indeed $F_ k(qZ)=q^ kF_ k(Z)$, and the choices of roots are finite modulo scaling in the source. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log R$ is positive transverse to the complex Euler direction, while $\partial \log S$ is nonzero on that direction; hence $\theta _ k>0$. Direct differentiation gives 64F6BCAA5AB9 10.21.4 \begin{equation}  \theta _ k+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k=F_ k^*h_0 =\frac{\mathrm{i} k^2}{2\pi S}\sum _ j|Z_ j|^{2k-2}\mathrm{d} Z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar Z_ j. \end{equation} The background $\theta _ k$ is not closed, since $\mathrm{d}\theta _ k=F_ k^*(\mathrm{d} h_0)$ is not identically zero. Along a coordinate divisor $D=\{ Z_ j=0\} $, at a generic point and in local coordinates $(z,w)$ with $D=\{ z=0\} $, the determinant vanishes to order $2(k-1)$, the metric $F_ k^*h_0$ is comparable to $|z|^{2(k-1)}|\mathrm{d} z|^2+|\mathrm{d} w|^2$, and the distance to $D$ is of order $|z|^ k$, as in proposition 10.21.1 . A small logarithmic potential along $D$ gives a strict barrier. Choose a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(D)$ with curvature form $\Theta _ D$ and canonical section $s_ D$. For small $c>0$, set $h_ c=\theta _ k+c\Theta _ D$ and $U_ c=c\log |s_ D|^2+u_ k$. Then $h_ c>0$ and \[  h_ c+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ c=c[D]+F_ k^*h_0.  \] By theorem 13.14.3 , the extended Monge–Ampère measure of $U_ c$ in the background $h_ c$ is the singular measure $(F_ k^*h_0)^ n$. The ordinary singularity type of $U_ c$ is exactly that of $c\log |s_ D|^2$, which is not minimal, while its metric off $D$ is the same smooth metric $F_ k^*h_0$. Finally, $H_ q\cong S^{2n-1}\times S^1$ has $H^2(H_ q;\mathbb R)=0$. A Kähler form would therefore be exact, and Stokes' theorem would make its positive top-degree integral zero; thus $H_ q$ is not Kähler. In these constructions, the potential becomes bounded once its divisorial part is removed, and the zero set lies at finite distance. More generally, theorem 5.39.1 bounds the distance by the square root of a Hölder modulus of the potential wherever the current is a smooth positive metric. Continuity alone has no such consequence, as the radial examples of section 10.22 will show.

title: 10.21.5 Determinant and normal distance
text: The order of vanishing of the determinant alone does not determine the normal distance. An upper bound for the trace bounds all eigenvalues from above; combined with a lower bound for the determinant, it bounds the smallest eigenvalue from below, and hence the normal length. We use the local length distance $d_\eta ^ U$ of theorem 5.39.1 , the infimum of $\eta $-lengths of piecewise smooth paths in $U\setminus D$; the distance $d^ U_\eta (x,D)$ to $D$ is the infimum of the lengths of such paths starting at $x$ and tending to $D$. Proposition 10.21.6 . B9DD61C0FD5E Let $n\geq 2$, let $U\subset \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be a polydisk with coordinates $(z,w)$, and put $D=\{ z=0\} $. Let $\eta $ be a smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form on $U$, positive off $D$, whose Euclidean trace is bounded and whose determinant is comparable to $|z|^{2\ell }$ for an integer $\ell \geq 1$. Then on a smaller concentric polydisk, BC6A5A3DBD7A 10.21.7 \begin{equation}  c|z|^{\ell +1}\leq d_\eta ^ U((z,w),D)\leq C|z| \end{equation} for constants $c,C>0$. Both bounds are attained, up to constants, by smooth closed forms with the same determinant order. If the block of $\eta $ in the $w$-directions is uniformly positive, the distance is comparable to $|z|^{\ell +1}$. Proof. The least eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda _{\min }\geq \det \eta /(\operatorname {tr}\eta )^{n-1}\geq c|z|^{2\ell }$. Every path to $D$ therefore has length at least a constant times the integral of $|z|^\ell |\mathrm{d} z|$ along it, which gives the lower bound; a radial path and the trace bound give the upper bound. To see that both bounds occur, let $n=2$ first. For an integer $0\leq a\leq \ell $, take $\eta _ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|G_ a|^2$ with $G_ a(z,w)=(z^{a+1}/(a+1),z^{\ell -a}w)$; for $n>2$, append Euclidean coordinates. The Jacobian determinant of $G_ a$ is $z^\ell $, but at $(z,0)$ the first component of $G_ a$ forces a distance of order $|z|^{a+1}$, attained along a radial path. The cases $a=\ell $ and $a=0$ give the two endpoints. Finally, write the Hermitian coefficient matrix of $\eta $ in the normal and tangential directions as $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}h& b^*\\ b& B\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. When $B$ is uniformly positive, its Schur complement $h-b^*B^{-1}b=\det \eta /\det B$ is comparable to $|z|^{2\ell }$. Completing the square gives the lower bound of order $|z|^{\ell +1}$, and solving $\mathrm{d} w/\mathrm{d} s=-B^{-1}b\, \mathrm{d} z/\mathrm{d} s$ along a radial normal curve, on nested charts, gives a path of matching length. $\square$

title: 10.21.8 Smoothness of exceptional residuals
text: We return to the blowup $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_ Z Y\to Y$ of section 15.23 . Here $(Y,h)$ is a compact Hermitian $n$-fold, the smooth center $Z$ has codimension $r\geq 2$, $E$ is the exceptional divisor with canonical section $s_ E$, $\Theta _ E$ is the curvature form of a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(E)$, $L=\log |s_ E|^2$, and the background is $\theta =\pi ^*h+c\Theta _ E$ with $c>0$. By proposition 15.23.2 , every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has the form $u=cL+q\circ \pi +C$ with $q$ an $h$-plurisubharmonic function, and $u$ has minimal singularities exactly when $q$ is bounded; we then call $u$ a potential of minimal type . Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$, and use adapted coordinates in which $\pi (y,z,w)=(y,z,zw)$ and $E=\{ z=0\} $. Proposition 10.21.9 . 86DDC28E0989 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be of minimal type, and suppose that its residual current $S=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)-c[E]$ extends smoothly and semipositively across $E$. Then, on smaller adapted charts, $0\leq S^ n/\mathrm{d} V\leq C|z|^{2(r-1)}$. Consequently, if the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ has density $|z|^{2\ell }g$ with $g$ smooth and strictly positive, then $\ell \geq r-1$. This order condition is necessary but not sufficient for a smooth residual. In particular, in this background a smooth strictly positive density is incompatible with a smooth residual for a potential of minimal type. Proof. Write $u=cL+v$. Since $S=\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is smooth, the distributional Laplacian of $v$ is smooth, and local elliptic regularity makes $v$ smooth. On each fiber of $E\to Z$, a compact projective space, $\pi ^*h$ restricts to zero and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ restricts to the semipositive form $S$; the maximum principle therefore makes $v$ constant on the fiber. Hence every vertical diagonal entry of $S$ is a smooth nonnegative function vanishing at $z=0$, and is therefore $O(|z|^2)$. The other diagonal entries are bounded, so Hadamard's determinant inequality gives the stated bound. The pullback $\pi ^*h$ attains this order, while the examples below show that the order condition is not sufficient. The argument does not apply to prescribed nonminimal singularities, whose residuals can be positive on the exceptional fibers. $\square$ A singular Hessian, rather than a zero of the density, can also make a solution nonsmooth. The following local example has constant positive density and a potential that is not $C^1$, and it can be placed in a compact manifold. Example 10.21.10 . 9F3252D2DC77 On a polydisk with coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^{n-1}$, $n\geq 2$, set $P(z,w)=|z|^{2/n}(1+|w|^2)$. Off $z=0$, its Hessian block in the $w$-directions is $|z|^{2/n}I$ and its normal Schur complement is $n^{-2}|z|^{2/n-2}$, so its Hessian determinant is the positive constant $n^{-2}$. Since $P$ is bounded, it extends across $z=0$ as a plurisubharmonic function whose Monge–Ampère measure has no additional mass on the divisor. Yet $P$ is not $C^1$ along that divisor. This local example extends to a compact Kähler model on $\mathbb P^ n$. On an affine chart with coordinates $y=(z,w)$, the Fubini–Study form is $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|y|^2)$; for constants $\lambda >0$ and $B$, put $H=\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)$ and $Q=H-B$. Choose nested radii and the parameters so that $Q>P+2\epsilon $ on an outer collar of a ball and $Q<P-2\epsilon $ on an inner ball. A smooth convex regularized maximum $U=M_\epsilon (P,Q)$ then equals $P$ on the inner ball and $Q$ on the collar. Put $v=U-H$ on the ball and $v=-B$ outside it, so that $\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ on the ball and $\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ outside. This current is positive and smooth off $\{ z=0\} $; on the gluing annulus its density is at most $C|z|^{2/n-2}$, so it belongs globally to $L^ p$ for every $1<p<n/(n-1)$. On the inner ball the density is smooth and strictly positive, but the potential is not $C^1$. There the metric is comparable to $|z|^{2/n-2}|\mathrm{d} z|^2+|z|^{2/n}|\mathrm{d} w|^2$, and the distance to the divisor is of order $|z|^{1/n}$. The construction also works on a Hopf manifold. Choose a global Hermitian form equal to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\lambda |y|^2)$ on a coordinate ball and equal to a fixed nonclosed Hermitian form outside a slightly larger ball, using a convex interpolation of positive forms. Carry out the same regularized maximum with $H=\lambda |y|^2$ on the inner ball, and set $v=-B$ outside it. The background is still nonclosed on the outer region, and the local potential and density are unchanged. As in the projective case, the density is controlled globally only in $L^ p$. This example does not contradict corollary 15.18.50 . The density loses smoothness along the divisor $\{ z=0\} $ in the gluing region, so the polar set of an admissible barrier must contain that part of the divisor. Being analytic, it then also contains the continuation of the divisor into the inner ball. The corollary requires a smooth positive density on the entire regular locus of the barrier, and local smoothness of the density on the inner ball cannot replace this hypothesis. On a blowup, a radial potential of power type produces densities with exceptional zeros or poles of every order. These examples show that the order condition in proposition 10.21.9 is not sufficient. Example 10.21.11 . 554ACF84A13B Let $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_0\mathbb P^ n\to \mathbb P^ n$ be the blowup at the origin of an affine chart with coordinates $y$, let $E$ be its exceptional divisor, and write $s=|y|^2$. For every $\gamma ,c>0$, one can choose $\lambda >0$ so that the background $\theta =\pi ^*(\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}})+c\Theta _ E$ admits a potential $u=cL+q\circ \pi $ with bounded Hölder remainder $q$, hence of minimal type, whose total local potential $\lambda \log (1+s)+q$ equals $As^\gamma +B$ near the origin, for constants $A>0$ and $B\in \mathbb R$. To construct $q$, choose a smooth function $m$ with $m(s)>0$ and $m'(s)>0$, equal to $A\gamma s^\gamma $ near $s=0$ and to $\lambda s/(1+s)$ outside a slightly larger interval; taking $A$ small puts the values at the two ends in the right order. Match the positive derivative germs on narrow collars, fill the remaining positive deficit of the integral with a positive interior derivative and a bump, and integrate $U'=m/s$, choosing the constant so that $U(s)=\lambda \log (1+s)$ for large $s$. Set $q(y)=U(|y|^2)-\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)$ on the affine chart and extend it by zero outside. Since $m$ and $m'$ are positive, positivity holds throughout the compact interpolation region. On the blowup, in coordinates with $y=(z,zw)$, the total local potential of $u$ is $A|z|^{2\gamma }(1+|w|^2)^\gamma +B$. The density of $u$ is $|z|^{2\ell }G$ with $G$ smooth and positive and $\ell =n\gamma -1>-1$, since the Hessian determinant of $A|y|^{2\gamma }$ is $A^ n\gamma ^{n+1}s^{n(\gamma -1)}$ and the squared Jacobian of the blowup is $|z|^{2(n-1)}$. The metric off $E$ is comparable to D97EEB42728A 10.21.12 \begin{equation}  |z|^{2\gamma -2}|\mathrm{d} z|^2+|z|^{2\gamma }|\mathrm{d} w|^2, \end{equation} the distance to $E$ is of order $|z|^\gamma $, and the metric completion collapses $E$ to a point. If $\ell $ is a nonnegative integer, the density is smooth. At $\ell =0$ the density is smooth and strictly positive, but the remainder has exact normal Hölder exponent $2/n$ for $n>2$, is Lipschitz but not $C^1$ for $n=2$, and the normal coefficient of the metric is unbounded. For $-1<\ell <0$, the density belongs to $L^ p$ exactly when $p\ell >-1$. Taking $\ell =n$ gives a smooth density with a zero of order $2n\geq 2(n-1)$, while the residual Hessian remains nonsmooth; this proves the insufficiency asserted in proposition 10.21.9 . A small nonclosed perturbation of the background supported away from the origin leaves these local calculations unchanged, and gives the same examples in a nonclosed background, with the Monge–Ampère measure of the perturbed potential as prescribed measure.

title: 10.22 Radial densities and metric completeness
text: For a radially symmetric equation, the mass of the density inside a ball determines the radial derivative of the potential and hence both eigenvalues of its Hessian. Boundedness of the potential and finiteness of the distance to the center are then expressed by two different integrals of this derivative, and suitable singular densities separate the two properties. Throughout this section $n\geq 2$, the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$ is normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$, and on the standard affine chart with coordinates $y\in \mathbb C^ n$ we put $\omega _{\mathrm E}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|y|^2$, so that $\int _{\{ |y|^2<S\} }\omega _{\mathrm E}^ n=S^ n$ for $S>0$. We write $s=|y|^2$. Theorem 10.22.1 . A86593744D2D Fix $\lambda >0$ and a smooth positive function $D:(0,\infty )\to (0,\infty )$ such that $D(s)=\lambda ^ n/(1+s)^{n+1}$ for all sufficiently large $s$, and E811914EE11D 10.22.2 \begin{equation}  n\int _0^\infty s^{n-1}D(s)\, \mathrm{d} s=\lambda ^ n. \end{equation} Let $\mu _ D$ be the measure on $\mathbb P^ n$ equal to $D(|y|^2)\omega _{\mathrm E}^ n$ on the affine chart and to zero on the hyperplane at infinity; near that hyperplane it agrees with $(\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}})^ n$. Then the equation $\langle (\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n\rangle =\mu _ D$ has a unique normalized full-mass solution $q$. It is smooth off $y=0$, and on the affine chart its total local potential $\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)+q(y)$ is a radial function $U(s)$ satisfying F205E7AE4ECC 10.22.3 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  m(s)^ n& =n\int _0^ s t^{n-1}D(t)\, \mathrm{d} t,\qquad m(s)=sU'(s),\\  m'(s)& =\frac{s^{n-1}D(s)}{m(s)^{n-1}}>0. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The tangential and radial eigenvalues of its Hessian are $m/s$ and $m'$. For any sufficiently small $s_0>0$, the solution is bounded, equivalently has minimal singularities, precisely when B8FF1DABE923 10.22.4 \begin{equation}  \int _0^{s_0}\frac{m(s)}s\, \mathrm{d} s<\infty . \end{equation} The distance from the origin for the metric $\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$ on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ is finite precisely when 585DD6478F46 10.22.5 \begin{equation}  \int _0^{s_0}\frac{\sqrt{m'(s)}}{2\sqrt{s}}\, \mathrm{d} s<\infty . \end{equation} If this integral diverges, the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ is complete. Let $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_0\mathbb P^ n\to \mathbb P^ n$ be the blowup at the origin, with exceptional divisor $E$, and let $s_ E$ and $\Theta _ E$ be as in section 15.23 . For $\theta =\pi ^*(\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}})+c\Theta _ E$ with $c>0$, the full-mass solution on $X$ whose measure is the pullback of $\mu _ D$ has potential $c\log |s_ E|^2+q\circ \pi +C$, generic Lelong number exactly $c$ along $E$, and mass $\lambda ^ n$. In a blowup chart $\pi (z,w)=(z,zw)$, its density relative to the Euclidean volume form of the coordinates $(z,w)$, normalized as above, is C19D1AD0E901 10.22.6 \begin{equation}  |z|^{2(n-1)}D\bigl (|z|^2(1+|w|^2)\bigr ). \end{equation} Its ordinary singularity type is minimal precisely under ( 10.22.4 ). In the unbounded cases, the residual $q\circ \pi $ grows sublogarithmically and has zero generic Lelong number, but the type is not minimal. The metric off $E$ satisfies the same completeness criterion ( 10.22.5 ). Proof. Define $m$ by the first equation in ( 10.22.3 ). It is positive for $s>0$ and tends to zero at the origin. By ( 10.22.2 ) and the prescribed outer density, $m(s)=\lambda s/(1+s)$ for large $s$: the two expressions for $m^ n$ have the same limit at infinity and the same derivative for large $s$. Integrate $U'=m/s$, choosing the additive constant so that $U(s)=\lambda \log (1+s)$ for large $s$. The Hessian of $U(|y|^2)$ has eigenvalues $m/s$ and $m'$, and its determinant is $(m/s)^{n-1}m'=D$. Thus $q=U(|y|^2)-\lambda \log (1+|y|^2)$ extends by zero outside the affine chart and defines a positive current that is smooth off the origin. Subtracting its supremum gives the normalization. Since $U$ is increasing, it is bounded above near zero, so lemma 5.24.7 gives a plurisubharmonic extension across the origin, possibly with the value $-\infty $ there. If $U$ is unbounded, then $m(s)\to 0$ implies $U(s)=o(|\log s|)$: for each $\epsilon >0$, bound $m$ by $\epsilon $ on a small interval and integrate $m/s$. The closed non-pluripolar product equals $\mu _ D$ off the origin and puts no mass at the origin; the measure $\mu _ D$ has no atom there and has mass $\lambda ^ n$ by ( 10.22.2 ). Hence $q$ is a full-mass solution, and it is unique by the uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 25.21 . Integrating $U'=m/s$ shows that $U$ is bounded near the origin precisely under ( 10.22.4 ). Write $R=|y|$. For a path approaching the origin, the metric norm of its velocity is at least a fixed multiple of $\sqrt{m'(R^2)}|\dot R|$, and radial paths attain this bound up to a fixed constant. Since $\mathrm{d} R=\mathrm{d} s/(2\sqrt{s})$, this gives ( 10.22.5 ). The metric is smooth and positive on compact subsets away from the origin, so divergence of the integral is equivalent to completeness of the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $. On the blowup, apply proposition 15.23.2 and use the squared Jacobian $|z|^{2(n-1)}$. The closed non-pluripolar product is the extension by zero of the pullback density, has mass $\lambda ^ n=\operatorname {vol}([\theta ])$, and is unique in its full-mass class. By theorem 13.14.3 , the extended operator agrees with it on potentials that are continuous off $E$, even when the residual tends to $-\infty $ along $E$. Sublogarithmic growth gives the residual zero Lelong number, so the coefficient along $E$ is exactly $c$, but it does not give a bounded difference from $c\log |s_ E|^2$. The metric off $E$ is isometric to the metric on $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, which proves the same distance criterion. The inner asymptotics considered below can be glued to the prescribed outer density while keeping ( 10.22.2 ): take a small inner amplitude or radius, join through a smooth positive annulus, and add a nonnegative smooth annular bump to supply the remaining mass. Thus each of these asymptotic behaviors occurs for a density satisfying the hypotheses of the theorem. The assertions below concern the total local potential $U$; subtracting a smooth background potential can change a leading smooth term. $\square$ In the next theorem, $f\sim g$ means that $f/g\to 1$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Theorem 10.22.7 . FF884313C070 For the normalized family in theorem 10.22.1 , put $L=\log (1/s)$ for $0<s<1$. If $D(s)\sim Cs^{\ell -n+1}L^{-b}$ with $C>0$, $\ell >-1$ and $b\in \mathbb R$, put $\gamma =(\ell +1)/n$ and $K=(C/\gamma )^{1/n}$. Then 940248BAAEE2 10.22.8 \begin{equation}  m\sim Ks^\gamma L^{-b/n},\qquad U(s)-U(0)\sim \frac K\gamma s^\gamma L^{-b/n},\qquad m'\sim \gamma K s^{\gamma -1}L^{-b/n}. \end{equation} The residual is bounded and Hölder continuous. If $U$ is unbounded, then $m(s)\to 0$ implies $U(s)=o(|\log s|)$: for each $\epsilon >0$, bound $m$ by $\epsilon $ on a small interval and integrate $m/s$. The closed non-pluripolar product equals $\mu _ D$ off the origin and puts no mass at the origin; the measure $\mu _ D$ has no atom there and has mass $\lambda ^ n$ by ( 10.22.2 ). Hence $q$ is a full-mass solution, and it is unique by the uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 25.21 . title: 10.23 Equations on products with a curve

section: 10.23 Equations on products with a curve
text: On the product of a curve with a Hermitian manifold, a density depending only on the curve variable reduces the Monge–Ampère equation to a Poisson equation on the curve, even when the second factor is not Kähler. Explicit primitives then allow a comparison with the radial families. For a single logarithmic factor, boundedness of the potential and finiteness of the distance have the same threshold, whereas the iterated logarithmic family of theorem 10.22.7 separates them. Theorem 10.23.1 . 3BB4C60DE3DF Let $C$ be a compact Riemann surface with a positive $(1,1)$-form $\omega _ C$, let $(N,\omega _ N)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $n-1$, and put $h=\omega _ C+\omega _ N$ on $C\times N$, the two forms being pulled back by the projections. Let $p_0\in C$, and let $F\geq 0$ be an integrable function on $C$, smooth and positive away from $p_0$, with $\int _ CF\omega _ C=\int _ C\omega _ C$. Then there is a function $v$ on $C$ such that $v\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C$ solves the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)=(F\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)h^ n$, and the current of this solution has no divisorial component along $\{ p_0\} \times N$. Let $z$ be a coordinate centered at $p_0$, write $r=|z|$ and $\omega _ C=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )g(z)\, \mathrm{d} z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$, and call a local potential of $\omega _ C+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ near $p_0$ a total normal potential . If $Fg=C_0r^{2\tau }$ near $p_0$, with $C_0>0$ and $\tau >-1$, then up to a smooth harmonic term the total normal potential is $C_0r^{2(\tau +1)}/(\tau +1)^2$. The solution is bounded and Hölder continuous, hence has minimal singularities, and the normal distance to $\{ p_0\} \times N$ is of order $r^{\tau +1}$. If $\tau =-a$ with $0<a<1$, the density is locally $L^ p$ exactly when $pa<1$. If $\tau $ is a nonnegative integer, the potential is smooth. If $Fg=C_0r^{-2}t^{-b}$ near $p_0$, with $t=\log (1/r)$, the mass is finite exactly for $b>1$. The total normal potential, which has no atom at $p_0$, is 464F29927E86 10.23.2 \begin{equation}  P_ b(t)=\begin{cases}  \displaystyle \frac{4C_0t^{2-b}}{(b-1)(b-2)},& b\ne 2,\\[4pt] -4C_0\log t,& b=2, \end{cases} \end{equation} up to constants and smooth harmonic terms. It is bounded and continuous, equivalently the solution has minimal singularities, precisely when $b>2$, and it is then not Hölder continuous. The normal end has finite distance precisely when $b>2$. For $1<b\leq 2$ the end is complete, and the potential is unbounded and does not have minimal singularities, but it has zero Lelong number and trivial multiplier ideals. No density in this logarithmic family belongs to $L^ p$ for $p>1$. If $\omega _ C$ and $\omega _ N$ are Kähler, the unbounded solutions have full mass, and uniqueness in the closed theory excludes a different bounded solution for the same measure. A small strict logarithmic barrier along $\{ p_0\} \times N$ exists also when the solutions are bounded and have minimal singularities. Proof. On the curve, the real current $F\omega _ C-\omega _ C$ has integral zero and is therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ for a global distribution $v$, unique up to a constant. Its quasi-subharmonic representative is smooth off $p_0$ by the local Poisson equation. Since $F\omega _ C$ has no atom at $p_0$, neither does the current $\omega _ C+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Pull $v$ back to $C\times N$. Since every wedge product containing two factors from the curve vanishes, on the regular locus 1DB31DDE4B07 10.23.3 \begin{equation}  (h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=n(F\omega _ C)\wedge \omega _ N^{n-1} =(F\circ \operatorname {pr}_ C)h^ n. \end{equation} By theorem 13.14.3 , the extended product agrees with this smooth product off $\{ p_0\} \times N$ and gives that analytic set zero mass. The right side has the same property and finite mass. This proves the global equation, including the case in which the curve potential has a finite value at $p_0$ but is discontinuous there. For the power density, put $P_\tau (r)=C_0r^{2(\tau +1)}/(\tau +1)^2$. Direct differentiation gives $\partial _ z\bar\partial _ zP_\tau =C_0r^{2\tau }$, and the radial flux of $P_\tau $ through small circles vanishes as $r\downarrow 0$ when $\tau >-1$, so no Dirac term appears. The difference between the total potential and $P_\tau $ is therefore harmonic on the whole disk and smooth. To realize the model globally, cut off the local potential and solve the remaining smooth mean-zero equation on the curve. The normal line element of the metric is comparable to $r^\tau |\mathrm{d} r|$, which gives a distance of order $r^{\tau +1}$: a lower bound for all paths and an upper bound along a radial path. The $L^ p$ assertion is the convergence of $\int _0^\epsilon r^{1-2pa}\, \mathrm{d} r$. For the logarithmic density, $P_ b''(t)=4C_0t^{-b}$ and $\partial _ z\bar\partial _ zP_ b=P_ b''/(4r^2)=C_0r^{-2}t^{-b}$. The flux tends to zero for $b>1$, which excludes a logarithmic Dirac mass, and the same cutoff and smooth correction give a compact model. The mass of the density near $p_0$ is a constant multiple of $\int ^\infty t^{-b}\, \mathrm{d} t$, finite exactly for $b>1$, while the integral of its $p$th power, for $p>1$, diverges after the logarithmic change of variables. The primitive has a finite limit exactly for $b>2$, with tail of order $t^{2-b}$, which tends to zero more slowly than every power $r^\alpha $. The normal length is a constant multiple of $\int ^\infty t^{-b/2}\, \mathrm{d} t$, which has the same threshold. The projection to the curve bounds the length of every path from below by this normal integral, and a radial path with fixed point of $N$ attains it. For $1<b\leq 2$, $|P_ b(t)|/t\to 0$, so the Lelong number is zero. For every weight $k>0$, the integrand $\mathrm{e}^{-kP_ b}$ in polar coordinates is bounded by $\exp (-2t+o(t))$ with respect to $\mathrm{d}t$, which is integrable; hence all multiplier ideals are trivial. These properties do not imply bounded ordinary type. In a Kähler product, the normalized curve integral gives full non-pluripolar mass, and uniqueness of full-mass solutions in the closed theory, discussed in section 25.21 , excludes another bounded solution. A bounded competitor for the extended operator coincides globally with its deep truncations, so the same exclusion applies there. Finally, for $D=\{ p_0\} \times N$, a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(D)$ with curvature form $\Theta _ D$ and canonical section $s_ D$, and sufficiently small $\delta >0$, we have $h-\delta \Theta _ D>0$, so $\delta \log |s_ D|^2-C$ is a strict barrier. $\square$

We now consider exponential Monge–Ampère equations whose reference measure has a nonintegrable pole along a divisor, and ask whether the solution defines a complete metric on the locus where its current is smooth and positive. A divisorial part of a solution with minimal singularities can cancel the pole and leave the deleted divisor at finite distance. On the blowup of the projective plane at a point, the resulting metric away from the exceptional divisor is the pullback of the Fubini–Study metric. The class is big but not nef, and the equation has a unique solution of finite energy. Finite energy refers to the classical closed theory of Definition 16.5.10 . For a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ with big class on a compact Kähler surface $Y$, and for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ with minimal singularities, the Monge–Ampère energy relative to the envelope $V_	heta $ is \[  E_	heta (u)= rac13\sum _{j=0}^2 \int _ Y(u-V_	heta ) \left\langle (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ j\wedge (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V_	heta )^{2-j}ightangle .  \] For general $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$, $E_	heta (u)$ is the decreasing limit of $E_	heta (\max (u,V_	heta -k))$ as $k	o \infty $, and $\mathcal E^1(Y,	heta )$ is the set of potentials with $E_	heta (u)>-\infty $; they have full mass. otin W\}   \] is positive, and $c([0,t_0))\subset W$. The path has finite Fubini–Study length. For $t_ k
earrow t_0$, the lengths of its tails show that $c(t_ k)$ is a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric of $W$. It has no limit in $W$: intrinsic convergence implies ambient convergence, and the ambient limit is $c(t_0)
otin W$. Thus $U$ is incomplete. In the next construction, the pole of the measure along a divisor $D$ does produce a complete cusp, but a disjoint curve $E$, on which the class has degree zero, lies at finite distance. Theorem 10.24.7 . 8D207AFD99F5 There are a smooth projective surface $Y$, disjoint smooth divisors $E,D$, a smooth closed semipositive form $\theta $ with nef and big class, a smooth Hermitian norm on $\mathcal O_ Y(D)$, its defining section $\sigma $, and a smooth strictly positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, such that the equation D648DC7F97C0 10.24.8 \begin{equation}  \left\langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\right\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has zero Lelong numbers and is smooth on $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$, where its current $\Omega =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ is strictly positive. The curve $E$ lies in the null locus of $\{ \theta \} $. Every dense Zariski open set on which $\Omega $ is smooth and strictly positive is incomplete, although every path in $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$ approaching $D$ has infinite length. The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole along $D$ with smooth strictly positive coefficient. The solution is unbounded near $D$ and therefore does not have minimal singularities: since $\theta $ is semipositive, the envelope $V_\theta $ is zero. The theorem concerns nefness and bigness only; the additional compatibility identities of the geometric smoothing problem in subsection 10.24.13 are a separate question. The solution will be a radial function on $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, identified with $Y\setminus (E\cup D)$. Its current is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(\log |z|^2)$ for a convex function $F$ whose derivative increases from $0$ at $E$ to $1$ at $D$, and the volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ is defined from $F$. The following lemma constructs the profile $F$; its two end identities make the volume form smooth and positive across $E$ and $D$. Lemma 10.24.9 . 0A057E71255D There is $F\in C^\infty (\mathbb R)$ with $0<p:=F'<1$ and $p'>0$ such that, for $c=1/100$, some $B\in \mathbb R$ and $K=(9c^2/8)\mathrm{e}^{-B}>0$, 49DD99303236 10.24.10 \begin{align}  F(t)& =B-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}),&  pp'& =K\mathrm{e}^{F+t} & & (t\leq -2),\\  F(t)& =t+\log H(p(t)),&  pp'& =\mathrm{e}^{F-t} & & (t\geq 2),\tag{10.24.11} \end{align} where $H(p)=(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6$. At the two ends, \begin{align*}  F(t)& =B+3c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}+O(\mathrm{e}^ t),&  p'(t)& \sim (3c/4)\mathrm{e}^{t/2} & & (t\to -\infty ),\\  1-p(t)& \sim 2/t,& p'(t)& \sim 2/t^2 & & (t\to +\infty ), \end{align*} and $F(t)-t=-2\log t+\log 2+o(1)$ as $t\to +\infty $. Since $H'(p)=(p-1)p$, the increasing function \[  \mathcal T(p)=2+\int _{3/4}^{p}\frac{q}{H(q)}\, \mathrm{d}q  \] tends to $+\infty $ as $p\to 1$, because its integrand is asymptotic to $2/(1-p)^2$ there. Hence it has an inverse $p_ R(t)$, defined for $t\geq 2$ and on a neighborhood of $2$, with $p_ R(2)=3/4$ and $p_ R'=H(p_ R)/p_ R$. The function $F_ R=t+\log H(p_ R)$ has derivative $p_ R$ and satisfies the right identity. For $q=1-p_ R$, \[  (1/q)'=\frac{3-2q}{6(1-q)}\longrightarrow \frac12.  \] Hence $q\sim 2/t$ and $H(p_ R)\sim 2/t^2$, and the asymptotics at the right end follow. It remains to interpolate the derivatives. Set $d=p_ R(2)-p_ L(-2)>0$. Choose disjoint short collars in $[-2,2]$ at the two endpoints, and cutoffs $\alpha _ L,\alpha _ R$ equal to one on smaller collars. For small $\varepsilon >0$, the function \[  Q_0=\alpha _ Lp_ L'+\alpha _ Rp_ R' +\varepsilon (1-\alpha _ L-\alpha _ R)  \] is positive and agrees with the derivative germs at the endpoints. The background and the pole. Use the incidence surface of theorem 10.24.1 , with blowup map $\pi :Y\to \mathbb P^2$ and exceptional curve $E$ over $[1:0:0]$, and let $\beta ,\gamma $ be the pulled-back Fubini–Study forms as there. Put $D=\pi ^{-1}(Z_0=0)$ and $A=\pi ^*c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. Then $E\cap D=\varnothing $, $A^2=1$ and $A\cdot E=0$. The class $A$ is nef, since it has the smooth semipositive representative $\beta $. Moreover $\{ \gamma \} =A-[E]$, and $\beta +\varepsilon \gamma $ is Kähler for $\varepsilon >0$. Thus \[  \frac{\beta +\varepsilon \gamma }{1+\varepsilon } +\frac{\varepsilon }{1+\varepsilon }[E]  \] is a Kähler current in $A$, which proves bigness. Choose an even nonnegative smooth function $\zeta $, supported in $[-1,1]$, positive on its interior and of integral one. The smooth convex function \[  U(t)=\int _\mathbb R\max (0,t-x)\zeta (x)\, \mathrm{d}x  \] satisfies $U=0$ for $t\leq -1$, $U=t$ for $t\geq 1$, and $U',U''\geq 0$. On $Z_0\ne 0$, write $z=(Z_1/Z_0,Z_2/Z_0)$, $s=|z|^2$ and $t=\log s$, and give the section $Z_0$ of $\mathcal O(1)$ the squared norm $\mathrm{e}^{-U(t)}$; this norm is constant near the affine origin. Its curvature form $\theta $ and the norm of $\sigma $ are \[  \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U(t),\quad |\sigma |^2=\mathrm{e}^{-U(t)},\qquad \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h,\quad |\sigma |^2=|w|^2/h\quad \hbox{near }D.  \] The radial Hessian shows that $\theta $ is semipositive. It vanishes near $E$ and has rank one near $D$. In particular $V_\theta =0$, and the nef class has volume $A^2=1$. Extension of the potential. On $Y\setminus (E\cup D)\simeq \mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, set \[  \rho =F(t)-U(t),\qquad \Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(t),  \] so that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =\Omega $. The eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix of $\Omega $ are $p/s$ and $p'/s$, which are positive. Extend $\rho $ to $E$ by $B$ and to $D$ by $-\infty $. Near the affine origin, the smooth functions $F(\log (|z|^2+\varepsilon ))$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to the continuous extension of $F(\log |z|^2)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Indeed, their two Hessian eigenvalues are $p/(s+\varepsilon )$ and $(s p'+\varepsilon p)/(s+\varepsilon )^2$, with $p,p'$ evaluated at $\log (s+\varepsilon )$. Since $\theta =0$ there, pulling back to $Y$ proves positivity near $E$. Near $D$ put $t_\varepsilon =\log h-\log (|w|^2+\varepsilon )$ and $g(t)=F(t)-t$. The local potentials $g(t_\varepsilon )+\log h$ decrease to $\rho +\log h$, and their Hessians are \[  p(t_\varepsilon )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h +(1-p(t_\varepsilon ))\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|w|^2+\varepsilon ) +p'(t_\varepsilon )\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi } \partial t_\varepsilon \wedge \bar\partial t_\varepsilon \geq 0.  \] Thus $\rho $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $Y$. Since $\rho $ is bounded near $E$ and grows like a double logarithm near $D$, all its Lelong numbers vanish. The volume form and full mass. With Euclidean area $\mathrm{d}A$ in each complex variable, the radial determinant is 26865AC0337F 10.24.12 \begin{equation}  \Omega ^2=\frac{2}{\pi ^2}\frac{pp'}{s^2} \mathrm{d}A_{z_1}\mathrm{d}A_{z_2}. \end{equation} Define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\mathrm{e}^{-F}\Omega ^2$ off the two divisors. In an exceptional chart $z=(u,uv)$, the real Jacobian is $|u|^2$ and $s=|u|^2h$, so the left profile identity gives \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{2K}{\pi ^2h}\, \mathrm{d}A_ u\mathrm{d}A_ v.  \] At infinity, the map $z=(1/w,v/w)$ has real Jacobian $|w|^{-6}$, and the right profile identity gives \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{2}{\pi ^2h^3}\, \mathrm{d}A_ w\mathrm{d}A_ v, \qquad |\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\frac{2}{\pi ^2|w|^2h^2}\, \mathrm{d}A_ w\mathrm{d}A_ v.  \] The analogous second charts cover each divisor. The extensions are smooth and strictly positive, and they agree on overlaps because they agree on the punctured overlaps. The last expression exhibits the nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient. On the complement of the two divisors, $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\Omega ^2$; we extend this density by zero on $D$. Both measures give zero mass to the two divisors. In polar coordinates on $\mathbb C^2$, the Euclidean volume is $\pi ^2s\, \mathrm{d}s$ times the normalized angular measure, so \[  \int _ Y\langle \Omega ^2\rangle =\int _{-\infty }^{\infty }2pp'\, \mathrm{d}t =p(+\infty )^2-p(-\infty )^2=1.  \] This proves the global equation and shows that $\rho $ has full mass. Bounded truncations and energy. Near $D$ write $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log h$ and $\beta _ t=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\partial t\wedge \bar\partial t$. These forms have rank one, and \[  \theta =\alpha ,\quad \Omega =p\alpha +p'\beta _ t,\quad \Omega ^2=2pp'\alpha \wedge \beta _ t,\quad \Omega \wedge \theta =p'\alpha \wedge \beta _ t,\quad \theta ^2=0.  \] Integration of $\alpha \wedge \beta _ t$ over the angular and projective variables gives $\mathrm{d}t$. Since $|\rho |=O(\log t)$ and $p'=O(t^{-2})$, the integrals of $|\rho |$ against $\Omega ^2$ and $\Omega \wedge \theta $ near $D$ are finite. Near $E$ the potential is bounded and $\theta =0$, and the remaining region is compact with smooth data. Choose $M$ so that $\phi =\rho -M\leq 0$, and set $\phi _ k=\max (\phi ,-k)$. For large $k$ the truncation changes $\phi $ only in the cusp near $D$, where $\phi =\log H(p(t))-M$ is strictly decreasing. If $\phi (T_ k)=-k$, then $k=2\log T_ k+O(1)$. On $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, the radial local potential of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k$ is \[  G_ k(t)=\max (F(t)-M,t-k).  \] Near $D$, in the frame used above, the local potential of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ k$ is $G_ k(t)+\log |w|^2$, which equals the smooth function $\log h-k$; the term $\log |w|^2$ cancels the divisorial part of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ k(t)$. The corresponding bounded local potentials converge uniformly on compact sets, so their Bedford–Taylor products converge. Its total mass is infinite, but each exponential density $\mathrm{e}^{\rho }\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ and $\mathrm{e}^{u}\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ is a finite measure of mass $1$. Comparison on the two strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and lemma 5.24.3 gives equality of the potentials everywhere. The two metric ends. Fix $v=v_0$ in an exceptional chart and write $h_0=1+|v_0|^2$. Its complement $Y\setminus W$ is a proper analytic set containing $E$, and by local finiteness of irreducible components and compactness it has finitely many components, which are curves or points. Each curve other than $E$ meets $E$ in finitely many points. Choose a point of $E$ that avoids all these intersections and all point components. In a sufficiently small chart around it, the complement of $W$ is exactly $E$, so a tail of the radial path above lies in $W$. Its points approaching $E$ form a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric with no limit in $W$: the smooth positive metric induces the manifold topology of $W$, and the only ambient limit is the removed point. Hence $W$ is incomplete. Finally, on the cusp $\Omega =p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t+p'\, \mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, both terms are nonnegative, and $p'\geq c_0/t^2$ for large $t$ and some $c_0>0$. The length of any path with $t\to \infty $ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $\int |\mathrm{d}t|/t$, which diverges. Thus the end at finite distance is the null curve $E$, disjoint from the pole. $\square$

In a sufficiently small chart around it, the complement of $W$ is exactly $E$, so a tail of the radial path above lies in $W$. Its points approaching $E$ form a Cauchy sequence for the intrinsic metric with no limit in $W$: the smooth positive metric induces the manifold topology of $W$, and the only ambient limit is the removed point. Hence $W$ is incomplete. Finally, on the cusp $\Omega =p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t+p'\, \mathrm{d}t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}t$, both terms are nonnegative, and $p'\geq c_0/t^2$ for large $t$ and some $c_0>0$. The length of any path with $t\to \infty $ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $\int |\mathrm{d}t|/t$, which diverges. Thus the end at finite distance is the null curve $E$, disjoint from the pole. $\square$

text: Lemma 10.24.9 . 0A057E71255D There is $F\in C^\infty (\mathbb R)$ with $0<p:=F'<1$ and $p'>0$ such that, for $c=1/100$, some $B\in \mathbb R$ and $K=(9c^2/8)\mathrm{e}^{-B}>0$, 49DD99303236 10.24.10 \begin{align}  F(t)& =B-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}),&  pp'& =K\mathrm{e}^{F+t} & & (t\leq -2),\\  F(t)& =t+\log H(p(t)),&  pp'& =\mathrm{e}^{F-t} & & (t\geq 2),\tag{10.24.11} \end{align} where $H(p)=(1-p)^2(1+2p)/6$. At the two ends, \begin{align*}  F(t)& =B+3c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}+O(\mathrm{e}^ t),&  p'(t)& \sim (3c/4)\mathrm{e}^{t/2} & & (t\to -\infty ),\\  1-p(t)& \sim 2/t,& p'(t)& \sim 2/t^2 & & (t\to +\infty ), \end{align*} and $F(t)-t=-2\log t+\log 2+o(1)$ as $t\to +\infty $. Proof. For $t\leq -2$ put $L(t)=-3\log (1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})$. With $q=c\mathrm{e}^{t/2}$, \[  p_ L=L'=\frac{3q}{2(1-q)},\qquad p_ L'=\frac{3q}{4(1-q)^2},\qquad p_ Lp_ L'=\frac{9c^2}{8}\mathrm{e}^{t}(1-c\mathrm{e}^{t/2})^{-3}.  \] This proves the left identity for every additive constant $B$. Since $H'(p)=(p-1)p$, the increasing function \[  \mathcal T(p)=2+\int _{3/4}^{p}\frac{q}{H(q)}\, \mathrm{d}q  \] tends to $+\infty $ as $p\to 1$, because its integrand is asymptotic to $2/(1-p)^2$ there. Hence it has an inverse $p_ R(t)$, defined for $t\geq 2$ and on a neighborhood of $2$, with $p_ R(2)=3/4$ and $p_ R'=H(p_ R)/p_ R$. The function $F_ R=t+\log H(p_ R)$ has derivative $p_ R$ and satisfies the right identity. For $q=1-p_ R$, \[  (1/q)'=\frac{3-2q}{6(1-q)}\longrightarrow \frac12.  \] Hence $q\sim 2/t$ and $H(p_ R)\sim 2/t^2$, and the asymptotics at the right end follow. It remains to interpolate the derivatives. Set $d=p_ R(2)-p_ L(-2)>0$. Choose disjoint short collars in $[-2,2]$ at the two endpoints, and cutoffs $\alpha _ L,\alpha _ R$ equal to one on smaller collars. For small $\varepsilon >0$, the function \[  Q_0=\alpha _ Lp_ L'+\alpha _ Rp_ R' +\varepsilon (1-\alpha _ L-\alpha _ R)  \] is positive and agrees with the derivative germs at the endpoints. The collars and $\varepsilon $ can be chosen so that $\int _{-2}^2Q_0<d$. Adding a nonnegative smooth bump in the interior, with integral $d-\int _{-2}^2Q_0$, gives a positive function $Q$, and we put \[  p(t)=p_ L(-2)+\int _{-2}^ tQ(x)\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] This function matches both endpoint germs, is increasing and takes values in $(0,1)$. Integrating $F'=p$ with $F(2)=F_ R(2)$ gives the required $F$ and fixes the constant $B$ at the left end. The left expansion follows directly. $\square$
