text: Exponential equations of this kind arise as auxiliary elliptic equations in the smoothing of singular initial data by geometric flows; the completeness question for them is discussed in section 25.19 . In that setting the class, the divisor and the volume form are not arbitrary: they are determined by the initial potential through a log resolution. The following example shows that incompleteness persists under these compatibility conditions. Let $(X,\omega )$ be a compact Kähler manifold and $\phi _0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ an initial potential with analytic singularities. Compatible data on a log resolution $\pi :Y\to X$ satisfy 349718BCBE33 10.24.14 \begin{gather}  \pi ^*\phi _0=\sum _ jm_ j\log |\sigma _ j|^2+\ell _0,\qquad \pi ^*(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _0)=\sum _ jm_ j[D_ j]+R_0, \\  K_ Y=\pi ^*K_ X+\sum _ jb_ jD_ j,\qquad \pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ X=\prod _ j|\sigma _ j|^{2b_ j}\mathrm{d}V_ Y. \tag{10.24.15} \end{gather} Here $D=\sum _ jD_ j$ is a divisor with simple normal crossings, $\sigma _ j$ is a defining section of $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)$ with a smooth Hermitian metric, the numbers $m_ j$ and $b_ j$ are the coefficients of the pulled-back singularity and of the relative canonical divisor, $\ell _0$ is smooth, $R_0$ is a smooth closed semipositive form, and $\mathrm{d}V_ X$, $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ are smooth positive volume forms. If $\Theta _ j$ denotes the curvature form of the metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(D_ j)$, put \[  \lambda =\max _ j\frac{m_ j}{1+b_ j},\qquad \Theta =\sum _ j(1+b_ j)\Theta _ j,\qquad \theta =\lambda \Theta +R_0,\qquad |\sigma |^2=\prod _ j|\sigma _ j|^2.  \] The number $\lambda $ is the inverse of the exponential integrability index of $\phi _0$: by ( 10.24.14 ) and ( 10.24.15 ), $\mathrm{e}^{-q\phi _0}$ is integrable exactly when $q\lambda <1$. The metric in the next theorem is the solution of the auxiliary elliptic equation ( 10.24.17 ) in this background. Theorem 10.24.16 . 0AE1F943A249 There are compatible data ( 10.24.14 )–( 10.24.15 ) on smooth projective surfaces, with $\mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2$, $R_0$ Kähler and $D$ a disjoint union of two smooth curves, such that the equation 6ABCE921A6F5 10.24.17 \begin{equation}  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution in $\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has the Lelong numbers of a potential with minimal singularities, but every dense Zariski open set on which its current is smooth and strictly positive is incomplete. The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth strictly positive coefficient along both components of $D$. The class $\{ \theta \} $ in this example is not nef. Thus this theorem and theorem 10.24.7 show separately that neither the compatibility identities nor nefness of the class implies completeness. We do not know whether completeness holds when the class is nef and the compatibility identities hold. In neither example is the auxiliary metric identified with the metric of the maximal flow. The cusp in the example comes from a rotation-invariant solution of an exponential equation on $\mathbb P^1$ whose measure has a simple pole. Lemma 10.24.18 . F2C09635072E On $\mathbb P^1$, let $z=Z_1/Z_0$, $r=|z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $h=r/(1+r)$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\alpha =1$. For every $c>2$ there is a $c\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, depending only on $|z|$ and smooth off $0$, such that 6251B9B58B26 10.24.19 \begin{equation}  g_1:=c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{u}h^{-1}c\alpha . \end{equation} It has zero Lelong number at $0$, mass $\int g_1=c$, and \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|\alpha +\int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|g_1<\infty .  \] Moreover, with $t=\log r$ and $s=-\log r$, there is $A\in \mathbb R$ such that, as $s\to \infty $, \[  \begin{aligned}  u& =\log (2/c)-2\log (s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\\  u_ t& =\frac{2}{s+A}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\qquad u_{tt}=\frac{2}{(s+A)^2}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. Barriers and the radial inverse. Set $L=1-\log h=1+\log (1+1/r)$ and $w=-2\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=\left(-\frac2L+\frac2{rL^2}\right)\alpha ,\qquad Q(r):=\frac{c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\mathrm{e}^{w}h^{-1}c\alpha } =\frac{crL^2-2rL+2}{c(1+r)}.  \] The function $Q$ is positive, since $L\geq 1$ and $c>2$. Its limits are $2/c$ at $0$ and $1-2/c$ at infinity, so $0<q_-\leq Q\leq q_+<\infty $ for some constants $q_\pm $. Choose $a_0\leq \min (0,\log q_-)$ and $b_0\geq \max (0,\log q_+)$. Then $l=w+a_0$ and $H=w+b_0$ satisfy \[  c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}l\geq \mathrm{e}^{l}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\leq \mathrm{e}^{H}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad l\leq w\leq H.  \] Exhaust $\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the disks $|\zeta |<R$ in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, and solve the equation on them with boundary value $w$. For $q=|\zeta |^2$, the equation becomes \[  \Delta u=f(q)\mathrm{e}^{u}-g(q),\qquad f(q)=\frac{4c}{1+q},\qquad g(q)=\frac{4c}{(1+q)^2},  \] where $\Delta $ is the Euclidean real Laplacian. For $k>0$, the regular radial solution $v=V(q)$ of $(-\Delta +k)v=F(q)$ satisfies 6AD6B6EC392C 10.24.20 \begin{equation}  V(q)=A_0+\frac14\int _0^ q\log (q/t)\bigl (kV(t)-F(t)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation} The $j$-fold iterate of the integral kernel applied to the constant $1$ is $q^ j/(4^ j(j!)^2)$, so successive approximation converges uniformly on every finite interval. The coefficient of $A_0$ in the solution is $\sum _{j\geq 0}(kq/4)^ j/(j!)^2>0$, so exactly one value of $A_0$ gives any prescribed value at $q=R^2$. Moreover, \[  V'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (kV(qt)-F(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and this formula gives smoothness at $q=0$ by induction. The maximum principle for $-\Delta +k$ shows that this radial inverse is unique and preserves order. Choose $k\geq \sup f\mathrm{e}^{H}$ on the fixed disk, and let $T(v)$ be the radial solution of $(-\Delta +k)T(v)=kv-f\mathrm{e}^{v}+g$ with boundary value $w$; the right side is nondecreasing in $v$ on $[l,H]$. The barrier inequalities give $l\leq T(l)$ and $T(H)\leq H$, so the iterates of $T$ starting from $l$ increase and stay below $H$. The derivative formula gives a uniform bound for their first derivatives on the fixed interval. Compactness and monotonicity give uniform convergence; passing to the limit in ( 10.24.20 ) proves the equation, and the averaged derivative formula bootstraps the limit to smoothness. The same barriers bound the solutions on every fixed disk in $\zeta $ as $R\to \infty $. For an exact solution $U(q)$ of the nonlinear equation, \[  U'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (f(qt)\mathrm{e}^{U(qt)}-g(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and induction gives bounds for all derivatives on compact intervals. A diagonal limit is therefore smooth on the $\zeta $-plane, including the point $z=\infty $, and satisfies $u=-2\log (-\log r)+O(1)$ at $0$. The asymptotics, mass and energy. In the variable $t=\log r$, the equation reads \[  u_{tt}=\frac{c\mathrm{e}^{u}}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t} -\frac{c\mathrm{e}^ t}{(1+\mathrm{e}^ t)^2}.  \] Put $v(t)=u(t)+c\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(s)=v(-s)$. Then \[  V''=k_0(s)\mathrm{e}^{V},\qquad k_0(s)=c(1+\mathrm{e}^{-s})^{-(c+1)},\qquad V=-2\log s+O(1).  \] Convexity and this sublinear decay imply $V'<0$ and $V'\to 0$ at infinity. The function $J=(V')^2-2k_0\mathrm{e}^{V}$ satisfies $J'=-2k_0'\mathrm{e}^{V}$ and tends to zero. Since $k_0'=O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$ and $\mathrm{e}^{V}\asymp s^{-2}$, \[  J(s)=2\int _ s^\infty k_0'(\tau )\mathrm{e}^{V(\tau )}\, \mathrm{d}\tau =O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}s^{-2}).  \] Thus $(\mathrm{e}^{-V/2})'=\sqrt{c/2}(1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}))$, and integration gives $\mathrm{e}^{-V/2}=\sqrt{c/2}(s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$. This identity and the differential equation give all three asymptotic formulas. The local potential $u+c\log (1+r)$ extends subharmonically across $0$ by lemma 5.24.7 . Its radial slope tends to zero at the puncture, so the extension adds no point mass. The density of $g_1$ is asymptotic to \[  \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\frac{2}{r s^2} \, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z.  \] Stokes' theorem for currents gives mass $c$. The energy integral at the cusp is bounded by $C\int ^\infty (\log s)/s^2\, \mathrm{d}s$, and the integral against the smooth form $\alpha $ is finite as well. $\square$ Proof of theorem 10.24.16 . The initial data and the resolution. Take $X=\mathbb P^1_ Z\times \mathbb P^1_ W$, with the pulled-back normalized Fubini–Study forms $\alpha ,\beta $ of the two factors, and put \[  \omega =6(\alpha +\beta ),\qquad \mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2=72\alpha \wedge \beta .  \] Let $H=(Z_1=0)$ and $p=([0:1],[1:0])=(\infty ,0)$. Define \[  \begin{gathered} h_ H=\frac{|Z_1|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad \eta =\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2} +\frac{|W_1|^2}{|W_0|^2+|W_1|^2},\\ \phi _0=2\log h_ H+2\log \eta . \end{gathered}  \] The zero sets of $h_ H$ and $\eta $ are $H$ and $\{ p\} $, which are disjoint. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be the blowup at $p$, write $E$ for the exceptional curve, and set $H_ Y=\pi ^{-1}H$ and $D=H_ Y+E$. The surface $Y$ is smooth, compact, connected and projective, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $p$. Use $|\sigma _ H|^2=\pi ^*h_ H$ and $|\sigma _ E|^2=\pi ^*\eta $. Near $p$, put $x=Z_0/Z_1$ and $y=W_1/W_0$. In the blowup chart $x=a$, $y=ab$, \[  \pi ^*\eta =|a|^2A(a,b),\qquad A(a,b)=\frac1{1+|a|^2}+\frac{|b|^2}{1+|ab|^2}>0.  \] Thus $\pi ^*\eta $ defines a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$ across $E$. The second chart is obtained by interchanging $x$ and $y$, and the metric factors satisfy the transition rule. The sections $Z_0W_0$, $\sqrt2Z_0W_1$, $Z_1W_1$ of $\mathcal O(1,1)$ have summed squared Fubini–Study norm $\eta $, and near $p$ they generate the ideal $(x,\sqrt2xy,y)=(x,y)$. Dividing their pullbacks by $\sigma _ E$ gives a morphism $F:Y\to \mathbb P^2$ with 0053482330EE 10.24.21 \begin{equation}  F^*\gamma =\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )-\Theta _ E,\qquad \Theta _ H=\pi ^*\alpha , \end{equation} where $\gamma $ is the normalized Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$. In the first chart $F=[1:\sqrt2ab:b]$, so $F|_ E$ is an isomorphism onto a line. Near $p$, \[  \eta =\frac{|x|^2+|y|^2+2|xy|^2}{(1+|x|^2)(1+|y|^2)}.  \] Thus $\phi _0$ has analytic singularities. In the convention $\frac1{2m}\log \sum |f_ j|^2$, the coefficient $2$ is obtained by raising the numerator to the fourth power and expanding it as a sum of squared holomorphic monomials. The resolved identities are 82395B883364 10.24.22 \begin{align}  \pi ^*\phi _0& =2\log |\sigma _ H|^2+2\log |\sigma _ E|^2,\\  R_0& =\pi ^*\omega -2\Theta _ H-2\Theta _ E =2\pi ^*\alpha +4\pi ^*\beta +2F^*\gamma .\notag \end{align} The first two terms of $R_0$ are positive away from $E$, and along $E$ their kernel is $TE$, on which $F^*\gamma $ is positive. Hence $R_0$ is Kähler. The resolved current is $2[H_ Y]+2[E]+R_0$, which shows that $\phi _0$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic away from $p$; since it is bounded above, it extends across $p$. In the notation of ( 10.24.14 ), $m_ H=m_ E=2$ and $\ell _0=0$. The Jacobian determinant of the blowup in the chart is $a$, so $b_ E=1$ and $b_ H=0$. Directly, $\mathrm{e}^{-q\phi _0}$ is integrable near $H$ exactly when $q<1/2$ and near $p$ exactly when $q<1$. Consequently $\lambda =\max \{ 2,1\} =2$, and 8B89C7F09EDA 10.24.23 \begin{equation}  \Theta =\Theta _ H+2\Theta _ E,\qquad \theta =2\Theta +R_0=\pi ^*\omega +2\Theta _ E. \end{equation} Since $\Theta _ E|_ E=-\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, the class $\{ \theta \} $ has degree $-2$ on $E$, so it is not nef. It is big, since the potential $3\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ gives the current \[  (\pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E)+3[E],\qquad \pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E=5\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )+F^*\gamma >0.  \] The prescribed volume. Define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\pi ^*\omega ^2/|\sigma _ E|^2$ off $E$. In the chart above, \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{72\, \mathrm{d}A_ a\mathrm{d}A_ b}{\pi ^2A(a,b)(1+|a|^2)^2(1+|ab|^2)^2},  \] since the factor $|a|^2$ from the Jacobian cancels exactly. The second chart gives the extension on the rest of $E$, and the extensions agree on overlaps. Thus $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ is a smooth strictly positive volume form with $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ X=|\sigma _ E|^2\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, as required in ( 10.24.15 ). Since $H_ Y$ and $E$ are disjoint, the measure $|\sigma _ H\sigma _ E|^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient along each component. The solution and the minimal reference. Take $u$ from lemma 10.24.18 with $c=6$, pulled back to $X$ from the first factor, and put $g_ X=(6\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+6\beta $. This form is smooth and strictly positive near $p$, and \[  g_ X^2=\mathrm{e}^{u}h_ H^{-1}\omega ^2.  \] Set $P=2\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ and $\rho =P+\pi ^*u$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P=2[E]+\pi ^*\omega ,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =2[E]+\pi ^*g_ X.  \] Off $D$, the equation follows from the identity \[  \mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma _ H\sigma _ E|^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\mathrm{e}^{\pi ^*u}|\sigma _ H|^{-2}|\sigma _ E|^2\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\pi ^*g_ X^2.  \] Both measures extend by zero on $D$, which proves the global non-pluripolar equation. Let $\psi $ be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Off $E$, the function $\psi -P$ descends to an $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function on $X\setminus \{ p\} $, which by lemma 5.24.8 extends across $p$ and is bounded above on $X$. Thus $\psi \leq P+C_\psi $ off $E$, and lemma 5.24.3 gives the inequality everywhere. Since $P$ itself is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it has minimal singularities. The current of $P$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ X\omega ^2=72$, which is therefore the volume of the class, whereas the cup-product square of the class is $72+4E^2=68$. The cusp has mass $6$ and no atom, so the current of $\rho $ also has mass $\int _ Xg_ X^2=72$, and $\rho $ has full mass. Near $E$, $\pi ^*u$ is smooth, so $\rho $ has the Lelong numbers of $P$; along $H_ Y$ the cusp has zero Lelong number. The solution $\rho $ does not itself have minimal singularities, because $u$ is unbounded below near $H$. Relative energy and uniqueness. Choose $M$ with $u-M\leq 0$ and use the potential $P+M$, which has minimal singularities, as reference. The canonical approximants of $\rho $ are \[  \rho _ k=\max (\rho ,P+M-k)=P+M+\pi ^*u_ k,\qquad u_ k=\max (u-M,-k),  \] and their difference from the reference off $E$ is $\pi ^*u_ k$. On the curve let $b(t)=6\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(t)=b(t)+u(t)$. For large $k$ there is a unique level $t=T_ k$ in the cusp with $u(T_ k)-M=-k$. If $S_ k=-T_ k$, the asymptotics of lemma 10.24.18 give $S_ k\asymp \mathrm{e}^{k/2}$. The local potential of the truncated curve current is $b+u_ k=\max (V-M,b-k)$. On $\{ t<T_ k\} $ its mass is $b'(T_ k)$, and at $t=T_ k$ its derivative jumps upward by $u_ t(T_ k)$. Smooth convex approximation and continuity of Bedford–Taylor products of bounded potentials therefore give total mass $V'(T_ k)=O(S_ k^{-1})$ on the cutoff region $\{ t\leq T_ k\} $. There $u_ k=-k$, so the absolute energy contribution of this region is \[  kV'(T_ k)=O(k\mathrm{e}^{-k/2})\longrightarrow 0.  \] Outside it the density and the potential are unchanged, and $\int |u|g_1$ is finite. Consequently $\int |u_ k|g_{1,k}$ has a finite limit, where $g_{1,k}=6\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k$, and $\int |u_ k|\alpha $ converges by dominated convergence. The mixed measures of the product current and of its reference are \[  \omega ^2=72\alpha \wedge \beta ,\quad (g_{1,k}+6\beta )\wedge \omega =6g_{1,k}\wedge \beta +36\alpha \wedge \beta ,\quad (g_{1,k}+6\beta )^2=12g_{1,k}\wedge \beta .  \] Their pullbacks are exactly the mixed non-pluripolar measures on $Y$, which do not charge $E$. All three relative energy integrals of the canonical approximants therefore have finite limits. This proves $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$; replacing $P+M$ by the normalized envelope $V_\theta $ changes the reference by a bounded amount and does not affect this conclusion. Uniqueness follows from the full-mass comparison argument in the proof of theorem 10.24.1 . The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has infinite mass, but the two exponential densities being compared have mass $72$. Comparison on the strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and hence equality of the quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials everywhere. The missing metric boundary. The set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive is $Y\setminus (H_ Y\cup E)$: the cusp coefficient diverges at $H_ Y$, and the nonzero current $2[E]$ excludes smoothness along $E$. The smooth part $\pi ^*g_ X$ also degenerates along $TE$. Let $U$ be a dense Zariski open set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive. As in the proof of theorem 10.24.7 , choose a point of $E$ avoiding every other component of the analytic set $Y\setminus U$; in a small chart around it the complement of $U$ is exactly $E$. A transverse path $a=\xi >0$, $b=b_0$ lies in $U$ for small $\xi $ and approaches that point. Since $g_ X$ is smooth near $p$ and $\pi $ is smooth, the coefficients of $\pi ^*g_ X$ are bounded in the chart, so the path has bounded speed and finite remaining length. Its tails give an intrinsic Cauchy sequence with no limit in $U$, since its only ambient limit is the removed point and a smooth positive Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology. Hence every such $U$ is incomplete. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.24.16
section: 10.24 An incomplete metric in a big class
text: Theorem 10.24.16 . 0AE1F943A249 There are compatible data ( 10.24.14 )–( 10.24.15 ) on smooth projective surfaces, with $\mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2$, $R_0$ Kähler and $D$ a disjoint union of two smooth curves, such that the equation 6ABCE921A6F5 10.24.17 \begin{equation}  \langle (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^2\rangle =\mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma |^{-2}\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \end{equation} has a unique solution in $\mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$. The solution has the Lelong numbers of a potential with minimal singularities, but every dense Zariski open set on which its current is smooth and strictly positive is incomplete. The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth strictly positive coefficient along both components of $D$. Proof of theorem 10.24.16 . The initial data and the resolution. Take $X=\mathbb P^1_ Z\times \mathbb P^1_ W$, with the pulled-back normalized Fubini–Study forms $\alpha ,\beta $ of the two factors, and put \[  \omega =6(\alpha +\beta ),\qquad \mathrm{d}V_ X=\omega ^2=72\alpha \wedge \beta .  \] Let $H=(Z_1=0)$ and $p=([0:1],[1:0])=(\infty ,0)$. Define \[  \begin{gathered} h_ H=\frac{|Z_1|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad \eta =\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2} +\frac{|W_1|^2}{|W_0|^2+|W_1|^2},\\ \phi _0=2\log h_ H+2\log \eta . \end{gathered}  \] The zero sets of $h_ H$ and $\eta $ are $H$ and $\{ p\} $, which are disjoint. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be the blowup at $p$, write $E$ for the exceptional curve, and set $H_ Y=\pi ^{-1}H$ and $D=H_ Y+E$. The surface $Y$ is smooth, compact, connected and projective, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $p$. Use $|\sigma _ H|^2=\pi ^*h_ H$ and $|\sigma _ E|^2=\pi ^*\eta $. Near $p$, put $x=Z_0/Z_1$ and $y=W_1/W_0$. In the blowup chart $x=a$, $y=ab$, \[  \pi ^*\eta =|a|^2A(a,b),\qquad A(a,b)=\frac1{1+|a|^2}+\frac{|b|^2}{1+|ab|^2}>0.  \] Thus $\pi ^*\eta $ defines a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O_ Y(E)$ across $E$. The second chart is obtained by interchanging $x$ and $y$, and the metric factors satisfy the transition rule. The sections $Z_0W_0$, $\sqrt2Z_0W_1$, $Z_1W_1$ of $\mathcal O(1,1)$ have summed squared Fubini–Study norm $\eta $, and near $p$ they generate the ideal $(x,\sqrt2xy,y)=(x,y)$. Dividing their pullbacks by $\sigma _ E$ gives a morphism $F:Y\to \mathbb P^2$ with 0053482330EE 10.24.21 \begin{equation}  F^*\gamma =\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )-\Theta _ E,\qquad \Theta _ H=\pi ^*\alpha , \end{equation} where $\gamma $ is the normalized Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$. In the first chart $F=[1:\sqrt2ab:b]$, so $F|_ E$ is an isomorphism onto a line. Near $p$, \[  \eta =\frac{|x|^2+|y|^2+2|xy|^2}{(1+|x|^2)(1+|y|^2)}.  \] Thus $\phi _0$ has analytic singularities. In the convention $\frac1{2m}\log \sum |f_ j|^2$, the coefficient $2$ is obtained by raising the numerator to the fourth power and expanding it as a sum of squared holomorphic monomials. The resolved identities are 82395B883364 10.24.22 \begin{align}  \pi ^*\phi _0& =2\log |\sigma _ H|^2+2\log |\sigma _ E|^2,\\  R_0& =\pi ^*\omega -2\Theta _ H-2\Theta _ E =2\pi ^*\alpha +4\pi ^*\beta +2F^*\gamma .\notag \end{align} The first two terms of $R_0$ are positive away from $E$, and along $E$ their kernel is $TE$, on which $F^*\gamma $ is positive. Hence $R_0$ is Kähler. The resolved current is $2[H_ Y]+2[E]+R_0$, which shows that $\phi _0$ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic away from $p$; since it is bounded above, it extends across $p$. In the notation of ( 10.24.14 ), $m_ H=m_ E=2$ and $\ell _0=0$. The Jacobian determinant of the blowup in the chart is $a$, so $b_ E=1$ and $b_ H=0$. Directly, $\mathrm{e}^{-q\phi _0}$ is integrable near $H$ exactly when $q<1/2$ and near $p$ exactly when $q<1$. Consequently $\lambda =\max \{ 2,1\} =2$, and 8B89C7F09EDA 10.24.23 \begin{equation}  \Theta =\Theta _ H+2\Theta _ E,\qquad \theta =2\Theta +R_0=\pi ^*\omega +2\Theta _ E. \end{equation} Since $\Theta _ E|_ E=-\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, the class $\{ \theta \} $ has degree $-2$ on $E$, so it is not nef. It is big, since the potential $3\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ gives the current \[  (\pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E)+3[E],\qquad \pi ^*\omega -\Theta _ E=5\pi ^*(\alpha +\beta )+F^*\gamma >0.  \] The prescribed volume. Define $\mathrm{d}V_ Y=\pi ^*\omega ^2/|\sigma _ E|^2$ off $E$. In the chart above, \[  \mathrm{d}V_ Y=\frac{72\, \mathrm{d}A_ a\mathrm{d}A_ b}{\pi ^2A(a,b)(1+|a|^2)^2(1+|ab|^2)^2},  \] since the factor $|a|^2$ from the Jacobian cancels exactly. The second chart gives the extension on the rest of $E$, and the extensions agree on overlaps. Thus $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ is a smooth strictly positive volume form with $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V_ X=|\sigma _ E|^2\mathrm{d}V_ Y$, as required in ( 10.24.15 ). Since $H_ Y$ and $E$ are disjoint, the measure $|\sigma _ H\sigma _ E|^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has a nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient along each component. The solution and the minimal reference. Take $u$ from lemma 10.24.18 with $c=6$, pulled back to $X$ from the first factor, and put $g_ X=(6\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+6\beta $. This form is smooth and strictly positive near $p$, and \[  g_ X^2=\mathrm{e}^{u}h_ H^{-1}\omega ^2.  \] Set $P=2\log |\sigma _ E|^2$ and $\rho =P+\pi ^*u$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P=2[E]+\pi ^*\omega ,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =2[E]+\pi ^*g_ X.  \] Off $D$, the equation follows from the identity \[  \mathrm{e}^{\rho }|\sigma _ H\sigma _ E|^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\mathrm{e}^{\pi ^*u}|\sigma _ H|^{-2}|\sigma _ E|^2\mathrm{d}V_ Y =\pi ^*g_ X^2.  \] Both measures extend by zero on $D$, which proves the global non-pluripolar equation. Let $\psi $ be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Off $E$, the function $\psi -P$ descends to an $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function on $X\setminus \{ p\} $, which by lemma 5.24.8 extends across $p$ and is bounded above on $X$. Thus $\psi \leq P+C_\psi $ off $E$, and lemma 5.24.3 gives the inequality everywhere. Since $P$ itself is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it has minimal singularities. The current of $P$ has non-pluripolar mass $\int _ X\omega ^2=72$, which is therefore the volume of the class, whereas the cup-product square of the class is $72+4E^2=68$. The cusp has mass $6$ and no atom, so the current of $\rho $ also has mass $\int _ Xg_ X^2=72$, and $\rho $ has full mass. Near $E$, $\pi ^*u$ is smooth, so $\rho $ has the Lelong numbers of $P$; along $H_ Y$ the cusp has zero Lelong number. The solution $\rho $ does not itself have minimal singularities, because $u$ is unbounded below near $H$. Relative energy and uniqueness. Choose $M$ with $u-M\leq 0$ and use the potential $P+M$, which has minimal singularities, as reference. The canonical approximants of $\rho $ are \[  \rho _ k=\max (\rho ,P+M-k)=P+M+\pi ^*u_ k,\qquad u_ k=\max (u-M,-k),  \] and their difference from the reference off $E$ is $\pi ^*u_ k$. On the curve let $b(t)=6\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(t)=b(t)+u(t)$. For large $k$ there is a unique level $t=T_ k$ in the cusp with $u(T_ k)-M=-k$. If $S_ k=-T_ k$, the asymptotics of lemma 10.24.18 give $S_ k\asymp \mathrm{e}^{k/2}$. The local potential of the truncated curve current is $b+u_ k=\max (V-M,b-k)$. On $\{ t<T_ k\} $ its mass is $b'(T_ k)$, and at $t=T_ k$ its derivative jumps upward by $u_ t(T_ k)$. Smooth convex approximation and continuity of Bedford–Taylor products of bounded potentials therefore give total mass $V'(T_ k)=O(S_ k^{-1})$ on the cutoff region $\{ t\leq T_ k\} $. There $u_ k=-k$, so the absolute energy contribution of this region is \[  kV'(T_ k)=O(k\mathrm{e}^{-k/2})\longrightarrow 0.  \] Outside it the density and the potential are unchanged, and $\int |u|g_1$ is finite. Consequently $\int |u_ k|g_{1,k}$ has a finite limit, where $g_{1,k}=6\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k$, and $\int |u_ k|\alpha $ converges by dominated convergence. The mixed measures of the product current and of its reference are \[  \omega ^2=72\alpha \wedge \beta ,\quad (g_{1,k}+6\beta )\wedge \omega =6g_{1,k}\wedge \beta +36\alpha \wedge \beta ,\quad (g_{1,k}+6\beta )^2=12g_{1,k}\wedge \beta .  \] Their pullbacks are exactly the mixed non-pluripolar measures on $Y$, which do not charge $E$. All three relative energy integrals of the canonical approximants therefore have finite limits. This proves $\rho \in \mathcal E^1(Y,\theta )$; replacing $P+M$ by the normalized envelope $V_\theta $ changes the reference by a bounded amount and does not affect this conclusion. Uniqueness follows from the full-mass comparison argument in the proof of theorem 10.24.1 . The measure $|\sigma |^{-2}\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ has infinite mass, but the two exponential densities being compared have mass $72$. Comparison on the strict sublevel sets forces equality almost everywhere, and hence equality of the quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials everywhere. The missing metric boundary. The set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive is $Y\setminus (H_ Y\cup E)$: the cusp coefficient diverges at $H_ Y$, and the nonzero current $2[E]$ excludes smoothness along $E$. The smooth part $\pi ^*g_ X$ also degenerates along $TE$. Let $U$ be a dense Zariski open set on which the current is smooth and strictly positive. As in the proof of theorem 10.24.7 , choose a point of $E$ avoiding every other component of the analytic set $Y\setminus U$; in a small chart around it the complement of $U$ is exactly $E$. A transverse path $a=\xi >0$, $b=b_0$ lies in $U$ for small $\xi $ and approaches that point. Since $g_ X$ is smooth near $p$ and $\pi $ is smooth, the coefficients of $\pi ^*g_ X$ are bounded in the chart, so the path has bounded speed and finite remaining length. Its tails give an intrinsic Cauchy sequence with no limit in $U$, since its only ambient limit is the removed point and a smooth positive Riemannian metric induces the manifold topology. Hence every such $U$ is incomplete. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.24.18
section: 10.24 An incomplete metric in a big class
text: Lemma 10.24.18 . F2C09635072E On $\mathbb P^1$, let $z=Z_1/Z_0$, $r=|z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $h=r/(1+r)$, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\alpha =1$. For every $c>2$ there is a $c\alpha $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, depending only on $|z|$ and smooth off $0$, such that 6251B9B58B26 10.24.19 \begin{equation}  g_1:=c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{e}^{u}h^{-1}c\alpha . \end{equation} It has zero Lelong number at $0$, mass $\int g_1=c$, and \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|\alpha +\int _{\mathbb P^1}|u|g_1<\infty .  \] Moreover, with $t=\log r$ and $s=-\log r$, there is $A\in \mathbb R$ such that, as $s\to \infty $, \[  \begin{aligned}  u& =\log (2/c)-2\log (s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\\  u_ t& =\frac{2}{s+A}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}),\qquad u_{tt}=\frac{2}{(s+A)^2}+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}). \end{aligned}  \] Proof. Barriers and the radial inverse. Set $L=1-\log h=1+\log (1+1/r)$ and $w=-2\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=\left(-\frac2L+\frac2{rL^2}\right)\alpha ,\qquad Q(r):=\frac{c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w}{\mathrm{e}^{w}h^{-1}c\alpha } =\frac{crL^2-2rL+2}{c(1+r)}.  \] The function $Q$ is positive, since $L\geq 1$ and $c>2$. Its limits are $2/c$ at $0$ and $1-2/c$ at infinity, so $0<q_-\leq Q\leq q_+<\infty $ for some constants $q_\pm $. Choose $a_0\leq \min (0,\log q_-)$ and $b_0\geq \max (0,\log q_+)$. Then $l=w+a_0$ and $H=w+b_0$ satisfy \[  c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}l\geq \mathrm{e}^{l}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad c\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\leq \mathrm{e}^{H}h^{-1}c\alpha ,\qquad l\leq w\leq H.  \] Exhaust $\mathbb P^1\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the disks $|\zeta |<R$ in the coordinate $\zeta =1/z$, and solve the equation on them with boundary value $w$. For $q=|\zeta |^2$, the equation becomes \[  \Delta u=f(q)\mathrm{e}^{u}-g(q),\qquad f(q)=\frac{4c}{1+q},\qquad g(q)=\frac{4c}{(1+q)^2},  \] where $\Delta $ is the Euclidean real Laplacian. For $k>0$, the regular radial solution $v=V(q)$ of $(-\Delta +k)v=F(q)$ satisfies 6AD6B6EC392C 10.24.20 \begin{equation}  V(q)=A_0+\frac14\int _0^ q\log (q/t)\bigl (kV(t)-F(t)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t. \end{equation} The $j$-fold iterate of the integral kernel applied to the constant $1$ is $q^ j/(4^ j(j!)^2)$, so successive approximation converges uniformly on every finite interval. The coefficient of $A_0$ in the solution is $\sum _{j\geq 0}(kq/4)^ j/(j!)^2>0$, so exactly one value of $A_0$ gives any prescribed value at $q=R^2$. Moreover, \[  V'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (kV(qt)-F(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and this formula gives smoothness at $q=0$ by induction. The maximum principle for $-\Delta +k$ shows that this radial inverse is unique and preserves order. Choose $k\geq \sup f\mathrm{e}^{H}$ on the fixed disk, and let $T(v)$ be the radial solution of $(-\Delta +k)T(v)=kv-f\mathrm{e}^{v}+g$ with boundary value $w$; the right side is nondecreasing in $v$ on $[l,H]$. The barrier inequalities give $l\leq T(l)$ and $T(H)\leq H$, so the iterates of $T$ starting from $l$ increase and stay below $H$. The derivative formula gives a uniform bound for their first derivatives on the fixed interval. Compactness and monotonicity give uniform convergence; passing to the limit in ( 10.24.20 ) proves the equation, and the averaged derivative formula bootstraps the limit to smoothness. The same barriers bound the solutions on every fixed disk in $\zeta $ as $R\to \infty $. For an exact solution $U(q)$ of the nonlinear equation, \[  U'(q)=\frac14\int _0^1\bigl (f(qt)\mathrm{e}^{U(qt)}-g(qt)\bigr )\, \mathrm{d}t,  \] and induction gives bounds for all derivatives on compact intervals. A diagonal limit is therefore smooth on the $\zeta $-plane, including the point $z=\infty $, and satisfies $u=-2\log (-\log r)+O(1)$ at $0$. The asymptotics, mass and energy. In the variable $t=\log r$, the equation reads \[  u_{tt}=\frac{c\mathrm{e}^{u}}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t} -\frac{c\mathrm{e}^ t}{(1+\mathrm{e}^ t)^2}.  \] Put $v(t)=u(t)+c\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ t)$ and $V(s)=v(-s)$. Then \[  V''=k_0(s)\mathrm{e}^{V},\qquad k_0(s)=c(1+\mathrm{e}^{-s})^{-(c+1)},\qquad V=-2\log s+O(1).  \] Convexity and this sublinear decay imply $V'<0$ and $V'\to 0$ at infinity. The function $J=(V')^2-2k_0\mathrm{e}^{V}$ satisfies $J'=-2k_0'\mathrm{e}^{V}$ and tends to zero. Since $k_0'=O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$ and $\mathrm{e}^{V}\asymp s^{-2}$, \[  J(s)=2\int _ s^\infty k_0'(\tau )\mathrm{e}^{V(\tau )}\, \mathrm{d}\tau =O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}s^{-2}).  \] Thus $(\mathrm{e}^{-V/2})'=\sqrt{c/2}(1+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s}))$, and integration gives $\mathrm{e}^{-V/2}=\sqrt{c/2}(s+A)+O(\mathrm{e}^{-s})$. This identity and the differential equation give all three asymptotic formulas. The local potential $u+c\log (1+r)$ extends subharmonically across $0$ by lemma 5.24.7 . Its radial slope tends to zero at the puncture, so the extension adds no point mass. The density of $g_1$ is asymptotic to \[  \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\frac{2}{r s^2} \, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z.  \] Stokes' theorem for currents gives mass $c$. The energy integral at the cusp is bounded by $C\int ^\infty (\log s)/s^2\, \mathrm{d}s$, and the integral against the smooth form $\alpha $ is finite as well. $\square$

title: 10.25 Normal length near a divisor
text:
To prove completeness near a divisor, one needs a lower bound for the metric in the normal direction. A lower bound for the determinant alone does not give it, because the tangential eigenvalues may absorb the volume. Dividing the determinant by the determinant of the tangential block gives the normal Schur complement. A lower bound for it by the inverse square of a defining function of the divisor, weakened by at most the square of the logarithm of that function, forces completeness. For solutions of exponential equations, this bound follows from bounds on the density, the potential and the tangential determinant, and an example on a torus shows that the logarithmic exponent $2$ is sharp. In this section $X$ is again a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $. Let $D\subset X$ be a nonempty smooth effective divisor, and put $M=X\setminus D$. Let $s_ D$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ X(D)$, equipped with a smooth Hermitian norm, and set \[  R=|s_ D|,\qquad \tau =-\log R^2.  \] Rescale the norm so that $\tau \geq 1$ on $M$. Write $J$ for the complex structure. For a smooth positive real $(1,1)$-form $T$ on $M$, we use the Riemannian metric $g_ T(v,v)=\pi T(v,Jv)$ on real tangent vectors $v$. Thus, if $T=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\sum H_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, then $g_ T(v,v)=\sum H_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j(v)\overline{\mathrm{d}z_ k(v)}$, and Hermitian norms below use this normalization of coefficients. Near $D$, the form $\partial \tau $ does not vanish (see ( 10.25.3 ) below), and we define the tangential hyperplane field, the tangential block and the determinant \[  E_\tau =\ker \partial \tau ,\qquad B_\tau =T|_{E_\tau },\qquad \det _\omega T=\frac{T^ n}{\omega ^ n}.  \] Similarly, $\det _\omega B_\tau $ denotes the determinant of $B_\tau $ relative to the restriction of $\omega $ to the complex hyperplane $E_\tau $; when $n=1$, it is $1$. Proposition 10.25.1 . D05A6736BCFF Suppose that there are constants $c>0$, $\tau _0\geq 1$ and $p\leq 2$ such that, on $\{ \tau >\tau _0\} $, C974FBD89E14 10.25.2 \begin{equation}  \frac{\det _\omega T}{\det _\omega B_\tau } \geq cR^{-2}\tau ^{-p}. \end{equation} Then $(M,g_ T)$ is complete. Proof. In a coordinate neighborhood meeting $D$, write $s_ D=z_1 e$, where $e$ is a local holomorphic frame with $|e|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\psi }$ and $\psi $ is smooth. Then \[  \tau =-\log |z_1|^2+\psi ,\qquad \partial \tau =-\frac{\mathrm{d}z_1}{z_1}+\partial \psi .  \] Covering the compact divisor by finitely many such neighborhoods and comparing with the smooth background, we obtain, after increasing $\tau _0$, 13887090B60F 10.25.3 \begin{equation}  c_1R^{-2}\leq |\partial \tau |_\omega ^2\leq C_1R^{-2} \quad \hbox{on }\{ \tau >\tau _0\}  \end{equation} for positive constants $c_1,C_1$. In particular, $E_\tau $ is a hyperplane there. At a point of this set, choose an $\omega $-unitary frame whose last $n-1$ vectors span $E_\tau $. Let $H$ be the Hermitian matrix that represents $g_ T$ as the quadratic form $w^*Hw$ in the complex components $w$, and write \[  H=\begin{pmatrix} h

& a^*

\\ a

& B

\end{pmatrix},\qquad S=h-a^*B^{-1}a=\frac{\det H}{\det B},  \] where $a$ is a column vector and $a^*$ its conjugate transpose. Completing the square gives, for a vector with components $(\xi ,\eta )$, \[  \begin{pmatrix} \bar\xi 

& \eta ^*

\end{pmatrix} H\begin{pmatrix} \xi 

\\ \eta 

\end{pmatrix} =S|\xi |^2+(\eta +B^{-1}a\xi )^*B(\eta +B^{-1}a\xi ) \geq S|\xi |^2.  \] For $n=1$ the same identity holds without the second term. For the complex components of a real vector $v$ we have $|\xi |=|\partial \tau (v)|/|\partial \tau |_\omega $, so ( 10.25.2 ) and ( 10.25.3 ) imply EA79C36F0DB1 10.25.4 \begin{equation}  g_ T(v,v)\geq c_2\tau ^{-p}|\partial \tau (v)|^2 \geq \frac{c_2}{4}\tau ^{-p}|\mathrm{d}\tau (v)|^2, \end{equation} where $c_2>0$ is uniform. The last inequality uses $\mathrm{d}\tau (v)=2\operatorname {Re}\partial \tau (v)$. Define a continuous function $\Phi _ p$ on $[1,\infty )$ by \[  \Phi _ p(t)= \begin{cases}  0,& t\leq \tau _0,\\  \displaystyle \int _{\tau _0}^ t x^{-p/2}\, \mathrm{d}x,& t>\tau _0. \end{cases}  \] Integrating ( 10.25.4 ) along piecewise smooth curves shows that $\Phi _ p\circ \tau $ is Lipschitz for the length distance of $g_ T$; this also holds for curves crossing $\{ \tau =\tau _0\} $, since $\Phi _ p$ is locally Lipschitz and constant below that level. Since $p\leq 2$, $\Phi _ p(t)$ tends to infinity with $t$, so $\Phi _ p\circ \tau $ is a proper function on $M$. A Cauchy sequence for the length distance has bounded values of this Lipschitz function and hence lies in a compact subset of $M$. It therefore has a subsequence converging in the manifold topology. On a coordinate ball about the limit, the smooth positive form $T$ is comparable to the Euclidean metric, so this subsequence also converges for the length distance. The Cauchy property then gives convergence of the whole sequence, which proves completeness. $\square$ Corollary 10.25.5 . A12B874B6590 In the preceding setting, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be smooth on $M$, with $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ there. Suppose that, for some $\lambda >0$ and some positive $f\in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\omega ^ n)$, \[  T^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\omega ^ n\quad \hbox{on }M.  \] Assume that, near $D$, there are constants $c,C>0$, $q>1$, $a\geq 0$ and $b\in \mathbb R$ such that 086B8F769EBF 10.25.6 \begin{equation}  f\geq cR^{-2}\tau ^{-q},\qquad u\geq -\frac{a}{\lambda }\log \tau -C,\qquad \det _\omega B_\tau \leq C\tau ^ b. \end{equation} If $q+a+b\leq 2$, then $(M,g_ T)$ is complete. Proof. The equation and the first two inequalities give $\det _\omega T\geq c\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda C}R^{-2}\tau ^{-(q+a)}$. Dividing by the third bound gives ( 10.25.2 ) with $p=q+a+b$, and proposition 10.25.1 applies. $\square$ Since $u$ is bounded above on the compact manifold $X$, integrability of $f$ also makes the measure $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\omega ^ n$ finite. The relevant tangential determinant is that of the intrinsic hyperplane field $E_\tau $, not that of an arbitrary block of coordinate directions.

title: Proposition 10.25.1
text:
Proposition 10.25.1 . D05A6736BCFF Suppose that there are constants $c>0$, $\tau _0\geq 1$ and $p\leq 2$ such that, on $\{ \tau >\tau _0\} $, C974FBD89E14 10.25.2 \begin{equation}  \frac{\det _\omega T}{\det _\omega B_\tau } \geq cR^{-2}\tau ^{-p}. \end{equation} Then $(M,g_ T)$ is complete. Proof. In a coordinate neighborhood meeting $D$, write $s_ D=z_1 e$, where $e$ is a local holomorphic frame with $|e|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\psi }$ and $\psi $ is smooth. title: 10.25.7 The critical exponent on a compact torus
search_title: The critical exponent on a compact torus
text: The exponent $2$ in corollary 10.25.5 is sharp. On a product torus, two explicit logarithmic profiles give a complete metric with $q+a+b=2$ and incomplete metrics with $q+a+b=2+\beta $ for every $\beta >0$. Both profiles have full mass, and the second one is bounded. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, let $\omega _ E=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$, and put $X=E^ n$, $D=\{ 0\} \times E^{n-1}$ and $M=X\setminus D$. Write $\pi _ j:X\to E$ for the coordinate projections and $\omega _0=\sum _{j=1}^ n\pi _ j^*\omega _ E$. Choose radii $0<r_1<r_2<\mathrm{e}^{-1}$ and a smooth radial cutoff $\chi $ on the coordinate disk $\{ |z|<r_2\} \subset E$, equal to $1$ on $\{ |z|\leq r_1\} $ and to $0$ near its outer boundary, with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. For fixed numbers $A,\eta ,\beta >0$, set $L=-\log |z|^2$ and define on $E$ E3D518CD1255 10.25.8 \begin{equation}  v_{\mathrm c}=-A\chi \log L,\qquad v_\beta =\eta \chi L^{-\beta }. \end{equation} Both functions are extended by zero outside the disk, and at its center we set $v_{\mathrm c}(0)=-\infty $ and $v_\beta (0)=0$. The bounded profile also occurs in example 15.21.4 . We write $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 13.14.3 . Lemma 10.25.9 . BCA9F26FE4F4 For $C>0$ sufficiently large, put $\theta =C\omega _0$. For either profile $v$ in ( 10.25.8 ), the function $u=\pi _1^*v$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the form $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is smooth and positive on $X\setminus D$, and \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\int _ X\theta ^ n.  \] The same $C$ may be used for the two fixed profiles. The bounded profile has minimal ordinary singularities; the profile $v_{\mathrm c}$ does not. Proof. For a twice differentiable function $G$ of $L=-\log |z|^2$, differentiation away from zero gives \[  \frac{\partial ^2G(L)}{\partial z\partial \bar z} =\frac{G''(L)}{|z|^2}.  \] On the inner disk this yields F60812366089 10.25.10 \begin{equation}  (v_{\mathrm c})_{z\bar z}=\frac{A}{|z|^2L^2},\qquad (v_\beta )_{z\bar z}=\frac{\eta \beta (\beta +1)}{|z|^2L^{\beta +2}}. \end{equation} Both densities are integrable at zero. Both profiles are locally integrable, and their distributional Hessians have no additional atom at zero. To see this, integrate twice by parts outside $\{ |z|=\varepsilon \} $: the boundary terms against a smooth test function are bounded by constant multiples of $\varepsilon |G(-\log \varepsilon ^2)|$ and $|G'(-\log \varepsilon ^2)|$, and both tend to zero for the two profiles. Thus ( 10.25.10 ) holds in the sense of distributions across the center. On the cutoff annulus all derivatives are bounded. Hence, for a sufficiently large common $C$, \[  \alpha _ v=C\omega _ E+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v  \] is a positive measure, smooth and strictly positive away from zero, with no atom at zero. Pairing $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with the constant test function gives $\int _ E\alpha _ v=C\int _ E\omega _ E$. Let $Y=E^{n-1}$, let $\pi _ Y:X\to Y$ be the projection onto the remaining factors, and let $\theta _ Y$ be $C$ times the sum of the $n-1$ flat forms of $Y$. On $X\setminus D$ the smooth wedge product is \[  T^ n=n\, \pi _1^*\alpha _ v\wedge \pi _ Y^*\theta _ Y^{n-1};  \] for $n=1$ this means just $\alpha _ v$, with $Y$ a point. The right side defines a finite product measure on $X$ that gives $D$ zero mass. By theorem 13.14.3 , the non-pluripolar measure agrees with this product off $D$ and gives the pluripolar set $D$ zero mass, so the two global measures are equal. Integrating the product proves the full-mass identity. Since $\theta >0$, its envelope is $V_\theta =0$ (section 5.40 ). The bounded profile therefore has minimal ordinary singularities, whereas $v_{\mathrm c}$ is not bounded below by $0$ minus a constant. $\square$ We apply the preceding results with $\omega =\theta $. Choose a smooth norm on $\mathcal O_ E(0)$, the line bundle of the point $0\in E$, for which its canonical section has squared norm $|z|^2$ near zero; such a norm is obtained from any smooth norm by multiplying by a smooth positive function prescribed on a smaller disk. Pull it back to $X$ and rescale it by a constant. For some fixed $K>0$ we may then arrange \[  R^2=\mathrm{e}^{-K}|z_1|^2,\qquad \tau =L+K  \] near $D$, and $\tau \geq 1$ on $M$. For both profiles, $E_\tau $ is exactly the tangent space of the remaining torus factors near $D$, so $\det _\theta B_\tau =1$. Example 10.25.11 . 36258B2EA152 Fix $\lambda >0$ and $0<A<1/\lambda $, and take $u_{\mathrm c}=\pi _1^*v_{\mathrm c}$ with the background of lemma 10.25.9 . This gives a complete metric on $M$ solving \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_{\mathrm c}) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_{\mathrm c}}f_{\mathrm c}\theta ^ n, \qquad f_{\mathrm c}\in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\theta ^ n),\quad f_{\mathrm c}>0,  \] where the right side is extended by zero on $D$. The three exponents in ( 10.25.6 ) can be taken to be \[  q=2-\lambda A>1,\qquad a=\lambda A,\qquad b=0,  \] so their sum equals the critical exponent $2$. Indeed, define $f_{\mathrm c}=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u_{\mathrm c}}\det _\theta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{\mathrm c})$ on $M$. On the inner disk the product structure gives \[  f_{\mathrm c}=L^{\lambda A} +\frac{A}{C|z_1|^2L^{2-\lambda A}}.  \] The substitution $L=-\log r^2$ in the radial integral shows that the second term is integrable precisely when $\lambda A<1$. The first term is integrable as well, and the density is smooth elsewhere. The identity of measures across $D$ follows from the preceding lemma. Since $\tau =L+K$, all three bounds hold with the stated exponents, and completeness follows from corollary 10.25.5 . Along a radial normal segment the divergence of the length at the critical exponent is also visible directly: \[  \int _0^{r_1}\frac{\sqrt A}{r(-\log r^2)}\, \mathrm{d}r=\infty .  \] For arbitrary paths, however, completeness requires the corollary, not just this family of radial paths. Example 10.25.12 . 2D0F50D560BC Fix $\lambda ,\eta ,\beta >0$ and take $u_\beta =\pi _1^*v_\beta $ with the background of lemma 10.25.9 . This is a continuous bounded solution of full mass with minimal ordinary singularities, and its metric on $M$ is incomplete, although \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_\beta )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\beta }f_\beta \theta ^ n, \qquad f_\beta \in C^\infty (M)\cap L^1(X,\theta ^ n),\quad f_\beta >0.  \] To see this, put $K_\beta =\eta \beta (\beta +1)$ and define the density by the equation on $M$. Near $D$ it is \[  f_\beta =\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \eta L^{-\beta }} \left(1+\frac{K_\beta }{C|z_1|^2L^{\beta +2}}\right).  \] It is integrable, and the global identity follows as before. Fix the other coordinates and let $z_1=r\downarrow 0$ along a radial segment starting at $r_0$, with $0<r_0<r_1$. The length of this segment is at most \[  \sqrt C\, r_0+\sqrt{K_\beta } \int _0^{r_0}\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{r(-\log r^2)^{1+\beta /2}} =\sqrt C\, r_0+\frac{\sqrt{K_\beta }}{\beta } (-\log r_0^2)^{-\beta /2}<\infty .  \] Points along this segment approaching $D$ form a Cauchy sequence with no limit in $M$. Here the smallest admissible exponents in ( 10.25.6 ) are $q=\beta +2$, $a=0$ and $b=0$: the density is asymptotic to a positive constant times $R^{-2}\tau ^{-(\beta +2)}$, the potential is bounded, and the tangential determinant is $1$. Their sum is $2+\beta $. Since $\beta >0$ is arbitrary, the threshold $2$ in the criterion cannot be replaced by any larger universal number, even in a Kähler class with a bounded full-mass solution. In these examples one may write $f=F/R^2$ with $F=R^2f$ smooth and positive on $M$, but $F$ does not extend smoothly and positively across $D$: the logarithmic factors make it tend to zero there. Thus the examples concern integrable divisorial poles weakened by logarithmic factors. They do not decide completeness for a nonintegrable pole with smooth positive coefficient across the divisor, nor the question of compatibility with the flow discussed in section 25.19 .

title: 10.26 Rigid boundary classes on a torus
search_title: Rigid boundary classes on a torus
section: 10.26 Rigid boundary classes on a torus
text:
We now turn to the boundary of the nef cone. A nef class with zero top intersection number may have a smooth semipositive representative and yet leave little freedom to vary it. On a complex torus, the kernel of a constant semipositive form controls this freedom: when the leaves of the kernel are dense, the form is the only closed positive current in its class. The same condition decides whether adding a small fixed Kähler form produces metrics whose diameters tend to zero. For Kähler forms converging to the boundary in other ways, the diameters can tend to zero even at a class with many semipositive representatives. Let $X=V/\Lambda $ be a complex torus, where $V\simeq \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Lambda $ is a full lattice. Let $	heta $ be a translation-invariant semipositive real $(1,1)$-form of rank $r$ with $1\leq r<n$, and fix a translation-invariant Kähler form $\kappa $. The class $\alpha =\{ 	heta \} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ is nef and has $\int _ X	heta ^ n=0$. It lies on the boundary of the nef cone: a Kähler form in $\alpha $ would have positive top intersection number, whereas Stokes' theorem gives every representative the top intersection number $\int _ X	heta ^ n=0$. We call $\alpha $ rigid if it contains exactly one closed positive current. Let $K=\ker 	heta \subset V$, a complex subspace of dimension $n-r$, and let $H\subset X$ be the closure of its image in $X$. This is a connected real subtorus, which need not be complex. Diameters are computed for the Riemannian metric $g_\eta (v,w)=\eta (v,Jw)$ associated with a positive form $\eta $, where $J$ is the complex structure. Theorem 10.26.1 . 9A07C571BD3F The following are equivalent: $\alpha $ is rigid; $H=X$; $\operatorname {diam}(X,	heta +t\kappa )	o 0$ as $t\downarrow 0$. In the first case the unique current is $	heta $. The third condition is independent of the chosen translation-invariant Kähler form $\kappa $. Proof. Rigidity when $H=X$. Suppose first that $H=X$. By lemma 20.4.10 , a positive current in $\alpha $ can be written $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ quasi-plurisubharmonic, in particular $u\in L^1(X)$. For a constant real vector $v\in K$, the coefficient $T(v,Jv)$ is a positive Radon measure. Its total integral against Haar measure is zero, because $	heta (v,Jv)=0$ and the remaining part of the coefficient is a combination of constant-coefficient derivatives of $u$. Hence this coefficient vanishes. Writing $D_ v$ for differentiation along $v$ and using that $K$ is complex, we obtain \[  (D_ v^2+D_{Jv}^2)u=0 \quad 	ext{as a distribution for every }v\in K.  \] For a real linear functional $\ell $ with $\ell (\Lambda )\subset \mathbb Z$, let $\widehat u(\ell )$ be the Fourier coefficient of $u$ at the character $\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\ell )$. The identity above gives \[   igl (\ell (v)^2+\ell (Jv)^2 igr )\widehat u(\ell )=0.  \] Since the image of $K$ is dense, a nonzero character cannot vanish identically on $K$. Thus every nonconstant Fourier coefficient of $u$ is zero, and convolution with a smooth approximate identity shows that $u$ is constant. Hence $T=	heta $. Nonrigidity when $H
e X$. If $H
e X$, a nontrivial character of the real torus $X/H$ gives a nonzero $\ell $ that vanishes on $K$. Put $\phi =\cos (2\pi \ell )$. Since $K$ is complex, the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ vanishes whenever one of its arguments lies in $K$. On a fixed complement of $K$, $	heta $ is positive definite and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ is uniformly bounded. Consequently, the forms $	heta \pm \varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ are semipositive for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. They represent the same class, and they are distinct because a nonconstant smooth function on a compact torus cannot have zero $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Hence $\alpha $ is not rigid. Collapse when $H=X$. Suppose again that $H=X$, and fix $\delta >0$. By density and compactness, there are finitely many vectors $k_1,\ldots ,k_ N\in K$ whose images form a $\delta $-net in the flat metric of $\kappa $. Put $R=\max _ j|k_ j|_\kappa $. Since $	heta (k_ j,Jk_ j)=0$, the straight path from $0$ to the image of $k_ j$ has $(	heta +t\kappa )$-length $\sqrt t\, |k_ j|_\kappa $. For $0<t\leq 1$ these metrics are bounded above by a fixed multiple of $\kappa $. Joining this path to a point within $\delta $ therefore gives \[  \operatorname {diam}(X,	heta +t\kappa ) \leq \sqrt t\, R+C\delta ,  \] since by translation invariance the diameter equals the supremum of the distances from $0$. Letting first $t\downarrow 0$ for this fixed net and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the third condition. No collapse when $H
e X$. If $H
e X$, choose $\ell $ as above. Its differential vanishes on $K$, so $|\mathrm d\ell (v)|\leq L|v|_	heta $ for some $L>0$, where $|v|_	heta $ is the seminorm defined by $	heta $. Since $	heta +t\kappa \geq 	heta $, the surjective map $\ell  mod \mathbb Z$ onto the circle of length one is $L$-Lipschitz for every $t>0$. Two points mapping to opposite points of the circle therefore have distance at least $1/(2L)$, and the diameters cannot tend to zero. This completes the proof of the equivalences. Since the second condition does not involve $\kappa $, neither does the third. $\square$ On a two-dimensional square torus, the slope of the kernel line decides rigidity. Example 10.26.2 . 5B00F62ACA6B On $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^2$, for $a\in \mathbb R$ set \[  	heta _ a= rac{\mathrm i}{2} (\mathrm dz_2-a\, \mathrm dz_1) \wedge (\mathrm d ar z_2-a\, \mathrm d ar z_1).  \] Its class is rigid exactly when $a$ is irrational. In that case its ray is irrational, that is, no nonzero real multiple of its de Rham class is rational, and every family $	heta _ a+t\kappa $ as above collapses to a point in diameter. For rational $a$ the class is not rigid, and these diameters have a positive lower bound. Proof. The kernel is the complex line $z_2=a z_1$. Write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$. An integral character has the form \[  \ell =m_1x_1+m_2x_2+n_1y_1+n_2y_2, \qquad m_ j,n_ j\in \mathbb Z,  \] and it vanishes on the kernel exactly when $m_1+a m_2=n_1+a n_2=0$. For irrational $a$, only the zero character does so, hence the image of the kernel is dense. For rational $a$, a nonzero such character exists. Now apply theorem 10.26.1 . section: 10.27 Nonrigid classes on a quotient resolution
text:
In contrast with example 10.26.2 , an irrational nef boundary ray can admit many smooth semipositive representatives. On a suitable two-dimensional torus, such representatives come from semipositive forms depending on a single real coordinate, with an irrational lattice direction making the ray irrational. If these forms vanish near the fixed points of the involution $z\mapsto -z$, they pass smoothly to the resolution of the quotient, a Kummer surface. Let $A=\mathbb C^2/\Lambda $ be a complex two-torus, let $Y=A/\{ \pm 1\} $, and let $r:X	o Y$ be the minimal resolution. The fixed points of the involution are the sixteen points of $A[2]=( rac12\Lambda )/\Lambda $, and their images are the sixteen singular points of $Y$. Lemma 10.27.1 . 22EA1C593ACD The surface $X$ is compact Kähler. Its exceptional set consists of sixteen disjoint projective lines with self-intersection $-2$. Proof. Blow up the sixteen fixed points on $A$ and take the quotient by the lifted involution. Near one exceptional line, a blowup chart has coordinates $(u,v)$ with $z_1=u$ and $z_2=uv$, and the involution is $(u,v)\mapsto (-u,v)$. The quotient chart has smooth coordinates $(s,v)=(u^2,v)$. On the other chart, $v'=1/v$ and $s'=v^2s$. These charts describe the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)$ near its zero section. The quotient is therefore smooth and resolves the double point, with the stated exceptional curve. Doing this at all fixed points gives the compact surface $X$. Choose a flat Kähler form on $A$ that equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho $, where $ho =|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$, on disjoint balls centered at the fixed points. Away from those points it descends to $Y$. On the resolution chart, \[  ho =|s|(1+|v|^2),\qquad ho ^2=|s|^2(1+|v|^2)^2.  \] Choose a smooth function $F$ on $[0,+\infty )$ with $F(ho )=cho ^2$ near zero, where $c>0$, with $F'>0$ on $(0,+\infty )$ and $F''\geq 0$, and with $F(ho )=ho -C$ for $ho \geq \delta $, for a sufficiently small $\delta >0$. Such a function is obtained by choosing $F'$ nondecreasing, linear near zero and equal to one beyond $\delta $. Replace the flat form in each ball by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F(ho )$. This agrees with the flat form near the boundary of the ball and extends smoothly across the exceptional line. The resulting closed form $\eta $ is positive off the exceptional set, while along it $\eta $ is positive in the normal direction and zero in the tangent direction. To restore positivity in the tangent direction, choose a smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one for $ho \leq \delta $ and zero for $ho \geq 2\delta $. For $s
e 0$, set \[  q_ v=\chi (ho )\log ho -\log |s|.  \] Near $s=0$ this equals $\log (1+|v|^2)$, so it extends smoothly. On the overlap of the two charts, $q_{v'}-q_ v=-2\log |v|$ is pluriharmonic, so their $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ forms agree. They define a smooth closed form $R$ supported in the resolved ball, positive in the tangent direction along the exceptional line and semipositive where $\chi =1$. Hence $\eta +\varepsilon R$ is positive where $\chi =1$, including along the line. On the compact transition annulus $\eta $ is already positive, so $\eta +\varepsilon R$ remains positive there for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, and outside the ball $R=0$. Adding these corrections in all the disjoint balls produces a Kähler form on $X$. $\square$ Fix now $a\in \mathbb R\setminus \mathbb Q$ and take for $\Lambda $ the lattice generated by \[  \lambda _1=(1,0),\quad \lambda _2=(a,1),\quad \lambda _3=(\mathrm i,0),\quad \lambda _4=(0,\mathrm i).  \] Write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$. Since $y_1$ takes integer values on $\Lambda $, the coordinate $y_1 mod \mathbb Z$ defines a map from $A$ to the circle $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. Call a smooth even function $h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z	o [0,+\infty )$ admissible if it has integral one and vanishes near $ rac12\mathbb Z$; such functions are obtained from even pairs of nonnegative bumps supported away from that set. For an admissible $h$, put \[  	heta _ h=h(y_1)\, \mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1.  \] Proposition 10.27.2 . 6055AD1EB4F6 The forms $	heta _ h$ descend and extend by zero to smooth semipositive closed forms $T_ h$ on $X$. They all represent one nonzero nef Bott–Chern class $\alpha $ with $\alpha ^2=0$. This class is not rigid, that is, it contains more than one closed positive current, and its image in real de Rham cohomology spans an irrational ray. Each $T_ h$ vanishes on a neighborhood of the exceptional set. Proof. The form $	heta _ h$ is closed, because $\mathrm dh(y_1)$ is proportional to $\mathrm dy_1$, and it is semipositive. Since $h$ is even, $	heta _ h$ is invariant under the involution. At every fixed point, $y_1$ belongs to $ rac12\mathbb Z$ modulo $\mathbb Z$, so the form vanishes on a neighborhood of that point. Its descent to the complement of the singular points of $Y$ therefore extends by zero across their resolved neighborhoods. This proves smoothness and the asserted vanishing. Let $h_1,h_2$ be admissible and put $k=h_1-h_2$. This function is even, has mean zero and vanishes near $ rac12\mathbb Z$. Choose $f$ with \[  f'(y)=4\pi \int _0^ y k(s)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad f''=4\pi k.  \] The derivative $f'$ is periodic and odd, so its mean is zero, and $f$ can be chosen periodic and even. Evenness and the zero mean of $k$ give $\int _0^{1/2}k=0$, hence $f'=0$ near $ rac12\mathbb Z$. Therefore $f(y_1)$ descends, and it extends by constants near each exceptional curve to a smooth function $G$ on $X$. Since \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y_1)= rac{f''(y_1)}{4\pi } \, \mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1 \quad 	ext{on }A, \qquad 	ext{we have}\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=T_{h_1}-T_{h_2}.  \] Thus all the forms $T_ h$ have the same Bott–Chern class $\alpha $. Distinct admissible functions give distinct forms, so $\alpha $ is not rigid. The forms are semipositive and have square zero, so $\alpha ^2=0$. By lemma 10.27.1 , adding any positive multiple of a Kähler form gives a Kähler representative of a nearby class; therefore $\alpha $ is nef. By the mean-one condition, the periods of $	heta _ h$ on the real two-tori generated by $(\lambda _1,\lambda _3)$ and by $(\lambda _2,\lambda _3)$ are $1$ and $a$, respectively. Translate both cycles by $(0,\mathrm i/4)$. The translated cycles lie in $\{ y_2=1/4\} $ modulo $\mathbb Z$ and avoid the sixteen fixed points, and their periods are unchanged because the form is closed. Their images in $X$ lie in the complement of the exceptional curves, which is doubly covered without ramification by $A\setminus A[2]$. The first period shows that $\alpha 
e 0$. If a nonzero multiple $b\alpha $ had a rational de Rham class, then evaluating it on these cycles would make both $b$ and $ba$ rational, contradicting $a
otin \mathbb Q$. Finally, since $\alpha ^2=0$, Stokes' theorem shows that $\alpha $ itself has no Kähler representative, so it lies on the boundary of the nef cone. $\square$

text:
The preceding constructions keep the manifold fixed. For a family of compact manifolds and a line bundle on the total space, one may ask whether a semipositive singular metric on the restriction of the bundle to a special fiber is the restriction of a semipositive metric over a neighborhood of that fiber. In a family of blowups of the projective plane at four points, the answer is negative. The obstruction comes from compact curves on the nearby fibers on which the bundle has degree zero: the curvature of a semipositive metric vanishes on such a curve, and this persists on a component of the limiting curve in the central fiber. It forces the restricted metric to have a logarithmic singularity of coefficient one at a point of that component, whereas the prescribed metric has coefficient one half there. Varying these curves also identifies exactly which central metrics extend. Let $\Delta $ be a disk with coordinate $t$, and let $[x:y:z]$ be homogeneous coordinates on $\mathbb P^2$. Blow up $\mathbb P^2	imes \Delta $ along the four disjoint sections \[   egin{aligned}  p_1(t)& =[1:0:0],& \qquad p_2(t)& =[0:1:0],\  p_3(t)& =[1:1:t],& \qquad p_4(t)& =[0:0:1], \end{aligned}  \] write $\pi :\mathcal X	o \Delta $ for the resulting family and $X_ t=\pi ^{-1}(t)$ for its fibers. Let $H$ be the pullback of the hyperplane line bundle, let $E_ i$ be the exceptional divisor over $p_ i$, and put \[  L=2H-E_1-E_2-E_3-E_4,\qquad L_ t=L|_{X_ t}.  \] We use additive notation for tensor products of line bundles and also for their divisor classes, and we write $K_{X_ t}$ for the canonical line bundle. A singular Hermitian metric $h$ has squared norm $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\varphi }$ in a local holomorphic frame $e$; the function $\varphi $ is its local weight , and its curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. The metric is semipositive if its local weights are plurisubharmonic. For an effective divisor with local equation $w$, the divisor metric on the associated line bundle is the singular metric for which the canonical section has norm one; its weight is $\log |w|^2$ and its curvature is the integration current along the divisor. Lemma 10.28.1 . 1959B582751F The family is smooth and projective with rational surface fibers, and $L$ is effective on $\mathcal X$. For every $t
e 0$, $L_ t$ is generated by global sections, has square zero and is nef. For every integer $m\geq 1$, \[  H^0(X_ t,K_{X_ t}+mL_ t)=0\qquad (t
e 0).  \] Proof. Near one of the sections, coordinates centered on it identify the blowup with $\operatorname {Bl}_0(\mathbb C^2)	imes \Delta $. Since the four centers are disjoint, these charts prove smoothness and the submersion property. The blowup of the projective morphism $\mathbb P^2	imes \Delta 	o \Delta $ is projective and proper, and each fiber $X_ t$ is the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at the four points $p_ i(t)$. The quadratic forms \[  F_1=x(z-ty),\qquad F_2=y(z-tx)  \] vanish along all four sections and therefore lift to sections of $L$. They are nonzero, which proves that $L$ is effective. For $t
e 0$, their common zeros in $\mathbb P^2$ are exactly the four points. In suitable affine coordinates $(u,v)$ centered at $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, their linear initial terms are \[  (v-tu,-tu),\quad (-tu,v-tu),\quad (v-tu,v),\quad (u,v).  \] Each pair is linearly independent. Hence, after the exceptional divisors are subtracted, the transformed sections have no common zero on an exceptional curve. The two transformed sections therefore generate $L_ t$, and $L_ t$ has nonnegative degree on every irreducible curve. On a fiber, $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E_ i=0$, and $E_ i\cdot E_ j=-\delta _{ij}$. Hence $L_ t^2=0$, and $K_{X_ t}=-3H+\sum _ iE_ i$ gives $K_{X_ t}\cdot L_ t=-2$. A nonzero section of $K_{X_ t}+mL_ t$ would have an effective zero divisor whose intersection with the nef line bundle $L_ t$ is $-2<0$, a contradiction. This argument also excludes a nowhere-vanishing section, whose zero divisor would have intersection zero. $\square$ On $X_0$, let $\ell $ be the strict transform of the line $\{ z=0\} $, which passes through $p_1(0)$, $p_2(0)$ and $p_3(0)$. In additive notation, \[  \ell =H-E_1-E_2-E_3,\qquad A=2L_0-\ell =3H-E_1-E_2-E_3-2E_4.  \] Lemma 10.28.2 . 510B6B95F8B4 The line bundle $A$ is generated by global sections. There is a semipositive metric $h_0$ on $L_0$ whose weight along $\ell $ is \[  \varphi _0=	frac 12\log |w|^2+	ext{a smooth function},  \] where $w$ is a local equation of $\ell $. It is smooth off $\ell $ and has analytic singularities. Proof. Consider the cubic forms \[  x^2z,\qquad xyz,\qquad y^2z,\qquad xy(x-y).  \] Their common zero set in $\mathbb P^2$ consists of the four central points. In affine coordinates at $p_1$, $p_2$ and $p_3$, their linear initial terms include $(z,y)$, $(z,x)$ and $(z,x-y)$, respectively, while at $p_4$ their quadratic initial terms include $x^2,xy,y^2$. These have no common zero on the corresponding exceptional projective lines. After the simple exceptional factors at $p_1,p_2,p_3$ and the double factor at $p_4$ are removed, the transformed cubics therefore generate $A$. Their Fubini–Study metric $h_ A$ is smooth and semipositive. Let $h_\ell $ be the divisor metric on $\mathcal O(\ell )$. Since $2L_0=A+\ell $, the square root of $h_ A\otimes h_\ell $ defines a metric $h_0$ on $L_0$, with \[  \Theta _{h_0}=	frac 12\Theta _{h_ A}+	frac 12[\ell ]\geq 0.  \] The stated form of the weight and of its singularities follows directly. $\square$ Lemma 10.28.3 . DFE3E0889355 The strict transforms of the conics \[  F_1-2F_2=z(x-2y)+txy=0  \] form a surface $\Gamma \subset \mathcal X$. For $t
e 0$, its fiber $C_ t$ is a smooth compact rational curve with $L_ t\cdot C_ t=0$. The central fiber of $\Gamma $ is $\ell +q$, where $q$ is the strict transform of the line $\{ x=2y\} $. The curves $\ell $ and $q$ meet transversely at one point $p$, and $L_0\cdot q=1$. Near every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, $\Gamma $ is smooth and $\pi |_\Gamma $ is a submersion. Proof. The symmetric matrix of the quadratic form has determinant $-t/2$, so the conic is smooth for $t
e 0$. It passes simply through all four centers, so its strict transform is a smooth rational curve of class $L_ t$, and its degree against $L_ t$ is $L_ t^2=0$. At $t=0$ the conic is the union of the lines $\{ z=0\} $ and $\{ x=2y\} $. The second line avoids $p_1,p_2,p_3$ and passes through $p_4$. Each component has multiplicity one at every center it contains, so the central fiber of $\Gamma $ contains no additional exceptional component. The two lines meet at $[2:1:0]$, transversely and away from every center. Since $q=H-E_4$, we have $L_0\cdot q=1$. Away from the centers, the defining equation at $t=0$ has nonzero derivative in the directions of $\mathbb P^2$ at every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, which proves the assertion there. Near $p_4$, use the blowup chart $z=1$, $x=r$, $y=rs$. After the exceptional factor is removed, the equation becomes \[  1-2s+trs=0.  \] At the central point of $q\cap E_4$ we have $r=0$ and $s=1/2$, and the derivative in $s$ is $-2$. Thus $(r,t)$ are local coordinates on $\Gamma $ there. These two cases cover $q\setminus \{ p\} $. $\square$ Theorem 10.28.4 . 195B9613F5AA There is no semipositive metric on $L$ over an open neighborhood of $X_0$ whose local weights, restricted to $X_0$, satisfy \[  \psi \geq \varphi _0-C  \] in compatible local frames, for a constant $C$. In particular, $h_0$ is neither the restriction of a semipositive metric on such a neighborhood nor of the same singularity type as such a restriction. Proof. Suppose that such a metric exists. Since $\pi $ is proper, we may shrink $\Delta $ so that the whole family lies in its domain: otherwise points outside the neighborhood over $t_ j	o 0$ would have a limit point on $X_0$ outside it. The lower bound makes the restricted weight finite at every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, because $\varphi _0$ is smooth there. Hence the restrictions of the weight to $\Gamma $ and to $q$ are not identically $-\infty $. Near a point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $, choose a product chart $(\zeta ,t)$ on $\Gamma $, as given by lemma 10.28.3 , and a holomorphic frame of $L$. The restricted weight $u(\zeta ,t)$ is plurisubharmonic and locally integrable. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every small $t
e 0$ its restriction to $C_ t$ is not identically $-\infty $, so the metric restricts to $C_ t$. The curvature of this restriction is a positive measure on the compact curve $C_ t$ of total mass $L_ t\cdot C_ t=0$, so it vanishes. Thus $u(\cdot ,t)$ is harmonic for almost every $t$. By lemma 10.28.6 below, whose proof does not use this theorem, the central slice $u(\cdot ,0)$ is harmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is finite. Hence the restricted weight is harmonic near every point of $q\setminus \{ p\} $. The restricted metric on $L_0|_ q$ therefore has curvature supported at $p$. This curvature is a positive measure of total mass $L_0\cdot q=1$, so it is the Dirac measure $[p]$. In a coordinate $w$ on $q$ centered at $p$, the restricted weight is therefore $\log |w|^2$ plus a harmonic function, because their difference has zero distributional Laplacian. Since $\ell $ and $q$ meet transversely, $\varphi _0|_ q=	frac 12\log |w|^2+O(1)$. The difference $\psi |_ q-\varphi _0|_ q$ thus tends to $-\infty $ at $p$, contradicting the assumed lower bound. $\square$ The obstruction concerns the prescribed singularity type. Since $L$ is effective on the total space, the divisor metric of the zero divisor of a nonzero section of $L$ is a semipositive metric on $\mathcal X$, with a different restriction to $X_0$.

title: Lemma 10.28.1
section: 10.28 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family

Lemma 10.28.1 . 1959B582751F The family is smooth and projective with rational surface fibers, and $L$ is effective on $\mathcal X$. For every $t
e 0$, $L_ t$ is generated by global sections, has square zero and is nef. For every integer $m\geq 1$, \[  H^0(X_ t,K_{X_ t}+mL_ t)=0\qquad (t
e 0).  \] Proof. Near one of the sections, coordinates centered on it identify the blowup with $\operatorname {Bl}_0(\mathbb C^2)	imes \Delta $. Since the four centers are disjoint, these charts prove smoothness and the submersion property. The blowup of the projective morphism $\mathbb P^2	imes \Delta 	o \Delta $ is projective and proper, and each fiber $X_ t$ is the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at the four points $p_ i(t)$. The quadratic forms \[  F_1=x(z-ty),\qquad F_2=y(z-tx)  \] vanish along all four sections and therefore lift to sections of $L$. They are nonzero, which proves that $L$ is effective. For $t
e 0$, their common zeros in $\mathbb P^2$ are exactly the four points. In suitable affine coordinates $(u,v)$ centered at $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, their linear initial terms are \[  (v-tu,-tu),\quad (-tu,v-tu),\quad (v-tu,v),\quad (u,v).  \] Each pair is linearly independent. Hence, after the exceptional divisors are subtracted, the transformed sections have no common zero on an exceptional curve. The two transformed sections therefore generate $L_ t$, and $L_ t$ has nonnegative degree on every irreducible curve. On a fiber, $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E_ i=0$, and $E_ i\cdot E_ j=-\delta _{ij}$. Hence $L_ t^2=0$, and $K_{X_ t}=-3H+\sum _ iE_ i$ gives $K_{X_ t}\cdot L_ t=-2$. A nonzero section of $K_{X_ t}+mL_ t$ would have an effective zero divisor whose intersection with the nef line bundle $L_ t$ is $-2<0$, a contradiction. This argument also excludes a nowhere-vanishing section, whose zero divisor would have intersection zero. $\square$
