title: 10.28.5 The image of metric restriction
section: 10.28 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
text:
The degree-zero conics also determine exactly which central metrics extend. We say that a semipositive metric $h$ on $L_0$ extends if there is a semipositive metric on $L$ over a neighborhood of $X_0$ whose local weights restrict to local weights of $h$; in particular, these restrictions are not identically $-\infty $. The following lemma is the slice argument used in the proof of theorem 10.28.4 . Lemma 10.28.6 . 66D32D3D118D Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a product of disks $D_\zeta 	imes D_ t$ with $0\in D_ t$, and suppose that $u$ is not identically $-\infty $. Suppose that $u(\cdot ,t)$ is harmonic for almost every $t$. Then $u(\cdot ,0)$ is harmonic or identically $-\infty $. Proof. Since $u$ is locally integrable, Fubini's theorem gives $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }u=0$ in the sense of distributions. On smaller product disks, form the averages \[  u_\varepsilon (\zeta )= rac1{\pi \varepsilon ^2} \int _{|t|<\varepsilon }u(\zeta ,t)\, \mathrm{d}A(t),  \] where $\mathrm{d}A$ is planar area. Local upper bounds for $u$ and the reverse Fatou lemma give upper semicontinuity, and Fubini's theorem gives the submean inequality in $\zeta $. The averages are locally integrable, since $u$ is integrable on compact product disks. Thus each $u_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic with zero distributional Laplacian, hence harmonic. Since $u$ is subharmonic in $t$, the disk averages decrease to $u(\zeta ,0)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. A decreasing limit of harmonic functions is harmonic or identically $-\infty $: if the values are bounded below at one point, Harnack's inequality, applied to the differences from the first function, bounds the differences on compact subdisks, and compactness of harmonic functions gives a harmonic limit. This proves the alternative on every smaller disk, and hence on $D_\zeta $. $\square$ Let $f:X_0	o \mathbb P^1$ be the morphism defined by the pencil of lines through $p_4=p_4(0)$, that is, by $[x:y:z]\mapsto [x:y]$, let $a=x/y$ be the affine coordinate on $\mathbb P^1$, and put $P=f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Lemma 10.28.7 . A52A7B9951F1 The pencil $f$ is a holomorphic map with connected fibers, $P=H-E_4$, and $L_0=\mathcal O(\ell )+P$. Let $h_\ell $ be the divisor metric on $\mathcal O(\ell )$, for which the canonical section $s_\ell $ satisfies $|s_\ell |_{h_\ell }=1$ away from $\ell $, and let $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study metric on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, with curvature $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. Then the metric \[  h_*=h_\ell \otimes f^*h_{\mathrm{FS}}  \] on $L_0$ extends to a semipositive metric on $L$ over the whole family. Its curvature is $[\ell ]+f^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. Proof. First blow up $p_4$ in $\mathbb P^2$. The map $[x:y]$ then becomes holomorphic: in the chart $x=r$, $y=rs$ with $z=1$, it is $[1:s]$, and the other chart covers the remaining direction. Its fibers are the strict transforms of the lines through $p_4$, and the pullback of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$ is $H-E_4$. Next blow up the other three central points, which lie in the directions $a=\infty ,0,1$, respectively. Each affected fiber becomes the union of its strict transform and one exceptional line meeting it, while every other fiber remains a projective line. This proves connectedness of the fibers and the formula for $P$. The equality $L_0=\mathcal O(\ell )+P$ follows from the divisor classes. In this identification, the restrictions of $F_1,F_2$ to $X_0$ are $s_\ell \otimes f^*x$ and $s_\ell \otimes f^*y$, where $x$ and $y$ are regarded as sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Indeed, at $t=0$ the forms are $xz$ and $yz$; the pullback of $\{ z=0\} $ is $\ell +E_1+E_2+E_3$, and removing the four exceptional factors from the transforms of $xz$ and $yz$ leaves exactly these sections. In a local frame of $L$, the weight $\log (|F_1|^2+|F_2|^2)$ defines a semipositive metric, since a change of frame multiplies both coefficients by the same nonvanishing holomorphic function. On every fiber $X_ t$ with $t
e 0$ the two sections have no common zero, so the weight is not identically $-\infty $ there. On the central fiber the weight is the sum of the divisor weight of $\ell $ and the pullback of the Fubini–Study weight, which proves the claim and the curvature formula. $\square$ Lemma 10.28.8 . 49F835066112 For $a\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0,1\} $, the strict transforms of the conics \[  F_1-aF_2=z(x-ay)+t(a-1)xy=0  \] have smooth rational fibers of $L_ t$-degree zero for $t
e 0$. Their central fiber is $\ell +q_ a$, where $q_ a=f^{-1}(a)$ is a smooth projective line of $L_0$-degree one. The two components meet transversely at $p_ a=[a:1:0]$, away from the blowup centers. Along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $, the surface formed by these conics is smooth and its projection to the disk is a submersion. Proof. The symmetric matrix of the quadratic form has determinant $-a(a-1)t/4$, so the conic is smooth for $t
e 0$; it passes simply through the four centers. Its strict transform has class $L_ t$, so its degree is $L_ t^2=0$. At $t=0$ the conic splits into the two lines $\{ z=0\} $ and $\{ x=ay\} $. Since $a$ is finite and $a
otin \{ 0,1\} $, the line $\{ x=ay\} $ does not pass through the other three central points, so no additional exceptional component occurs, and $q_ a=H-E_4$ has degree one against $L_0$. The two lines meet transversely at $p_ a$, away from all centers. Away from the centers, the central equation has nonzero derivative in the directions of $\mathbb P^2$ along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $. At the point of $q_ a$ on $E_4$, the chart $z=1$, $x=r$, $y=rs$ gives, after the exceptional factor is removed, \[  1-as+t(a-1)rs=0.  \] At $r=t=0$ and $s=1/a$, the derivative in $s$ is $-a
e 0$. These charts prove the final assertion. $\square$ Theorem 10.28.9 . 58E2ED8FCEB9 The semipositive metrics on $L_0$ that extend to semipositive metrics on $L$ over a neighborhood of $X_0$ are exactly the metrics \[  h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B,  \] where $h_ B$ ranges over all semipositive singular Hermitian metrics on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Every such central metric extends over the whole family. Proof. Necessity. Let $h$ be a semipositive metric on $L_0$ that extends. By properness we may shrink the disk so that the extending metric is defined on the whole family. On the locus where $f$ is smooth, local integrability and Fubini's theorem show that for almost every $a\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0,1\} $ the restriction of the weights of $h$ to $q_ a$ is not identically $-\infty $. Fix such an $a$. On each local product chart of the conic surface of lemma 10.28.8 along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $, the weight of the extending metric is not identically $-\infty $, since its central slice is not. By Fubini's theorem, the metric restricts to almost every nearby compact conic, and on such a conic its curvature is a positive measure of degree zero, hence zero. Lemma 10.28.6 therefore makes the central slice of the weight harmonic on each chart; the alternative $-\infty $ is excluded by the choice of $a$. Consequently, the curvature of $h|_{q_ a}$ is supported at $p_ a$. It is a positive measure of degree one, so it equals $[p_ a]$, which is also the curvature of $h_*|_{q_ a}$. The difference of the two weights is a globally defined harmonic function on the projective line $q_ a$: near $p_ a$, subtracting $\log |w|^2$ from either weight leaves a harmonic function, so the difference extends across $p_ a$. It is therefore constant. Thus the weight difference $u$ between $h$ and $h_*$ is constant along almost every fiber of $f$, away from $\ell $. Over every point of the base there are local holomorphic sections of $f$ avoiding $\ell $ and the exceptional curves: over the finite chart use $[a:1:1]$, and near infinity use $[1:b:1]$ with $b=1/a$. If $e_ B$ is a local frame of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, then $s_\ell \otimes f^*e_ B$ is a nonvanishing holomorphic frame of $L_0$ along these sections. Composing the weight of $h$ in this frame with a section defines a subharmonic weight on the base. It is not identically $-\infty $, because on almost every fiber the weight is harmonic away from $p_ a$. Two choices of section give the same function at almost every base point, because $u$ is constant on those fibers, and hence everywhere, since subharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. Changes of the base frame give the transition law of a metric. These weights therefore define a semipositive metric $h_ B$ on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Fubini's theorem on local product charts, together with the fact that $\ell $ and the exceptional fibers have zero volume, shows that $h$ and $h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B$ agree almost everywhere on $X_0$. By lemma 5.24.3 , their local plurisubharmonic weights agree everywhere, including on the three exceptional fibers. This proves necessity. Sufficiency. Let $h_ B$ be a semipositive metric on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, and represent it by a homogeneous weight $V$ on $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, with coordinates $(\xi _1,\xi _2)$ and $a=\xi _1/\xi _2$. In the chart $\xi _2
e 0$, if $\phi _ B$ is the weight of $h_ B$ in the frame given by the section $\xi _2$, set \[  V(\xi _1,\xi _2)=\phi _ B(\xi _1/\xi _2)+\log |\xi _2|^2.  \] The other chart gives the same function, by the transition law of the metric. The function $V$ is plurisubharmonic and satisfies $V(\lambda \xi _1,\lambda \xi _2)=V(\xi _1,\xi _2)+\log |\lambda |^2$ for $\lambda 
e 0$. The weight difference between $h_ B$ and $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ is bounded above on the compact base, so \[  V(\xi _1,\xi _2)\leq \log (|\xi _1|^2+|\xi _2|^2)+C.  \] Hence $V$ extends plurisubharmonically across the origin, with value $-\infty $ there, by lemma 5.24.7 . In each local frame of $L$, the function $V(F_1,F_2)$ is plurisubharmonic, and by homogeneity it transforms as the weight of a metric. Its restriction to each fiber $X_ t$ with $t
e 0$ is not identically $-\infty $: there the two generating sections define a nonconstant map onto $\mathbb P^1$, and the weight of $h_ B$ is not identically $-\infty $. On the central fiber, the factorization in lemma 10.28.7 and homogeneity give exactly the divisor weight of $\ell $ plus the pullback of the weight of $h_ B$. This is the required extension over $\mathcal X$. $\square$ Corollary 10.28.10 . 15454CA8E897 Among all semipositive metrics on $L_0$ that extend, $h_*$ has the least singular weights: every such metric has weights $\psi $ satisfying $\psi \leq \psi _*+C$ in compatible local frames, where $\psi _*$ is the weight of $h_*$; and $h_*$ itself extends. The assertion concerns metrics that extend, not all semipositive metrics on $L_0$. Proof. By theorem 10.28.9 , such a metric has the form $h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B$. Its weight difference from $h_*$ is the pullback of the global quasi-plurisubharmonic difference between the weights of $h_ B$ and $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$, which is bounded above on $\mathbb P^1$. This proves the inequality. That $h_*$ extends is lemma 10.28.7 . $\square$

In this identification, the restrictions of $F_1,F_2$ to $X_0$ are $s_\ell \otimes f^*x$ and $s_\ell \otimes f^*y$, where $x$ and $y$ are regarded as sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Indeed, at $t=0$ the forms are $xz$ and $yz$; the pullback of $\{ z=0\} $ is $\ell +E_1+E_2+E_3$, and removing the four exceptional factors from the transforms of $xz$ and $yz$ leaves exactly these sections. In a local frame of $L$, the weight $\log (|F_1|^2+|F_2|^2)$ defines a semipositive metric, since a change of frame multiplies both coefficients by the same nonvanishing holomorphic function. On every fiber $X_ t$ with $t\ne 0$ the two sections have no common zero, so the weight is not identically $-\infty $ there. On the central fiber the weight is the sum of the divisor weight of $\ell $ and the pullback of the Fubini–Study weight, which proves the claim and the curvature formula. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.28.8
section: 10.28 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
text:
Lemma 10.28.8 . 49F835066112 For $a\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0,1\} $, the strict transforms of the conics \[  F_1-aF_2=z(x-ay)+t(a-1)xy=0  \] have smooth rational fibers of $L_ t$-degree zero for $t
e 0$. Their central fiber is $\ell +q_ a$, where $q_ a=f^{-1}(a)$ is a smooth projective line of $L_0$-degree one. The two components meet transversely at $p_ a=[a:1:0]$, away from the blowup centers. Along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $, the surface formed by these conics is smooth and its projection to the disk is a submersion. Proof. The symmetric matrix of the quadratic form has determinant $-a(a-1)t/4$, so the conic is smooth for $t
e 0$; it passes simply through the four centers. Its strict transform has class $L_ t$, so its degree is $L_ t^2=0$. At $t=0$ the conic splits into the two lines $\{ z=0\} $ and $\{ x=ay\} $. Since $a$ is finite and $a
otin \{ 0,1\} $, the line $\{ x=ay\} $ does not pass through the other three central points, so no additional exceptional component occurs, and $q_ a=H-E_4$ has degree one against $L_0$. The two lines meet transversely at $p_ a$, away from all centers. Away from the centers, the central equation has nonzero derivative in the directions of $\mathbb P^2$ along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $. At the point of $q_ a$ on $E_4$, the chart $z=1$, $x=r$, $y=rs$ gives, after the exceptional factor is removed, \[  1-as+t(a-1)rs=0.  \] At $r=t=0$ and $s=1/a$, the derivative in $s$ is $-a
e 0$. These charts prove the final assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.28.9
section: 10.28 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
text:
Theorem 10.28.9 . 58E2ED8FCEB9 The semipositive metrics on $L_0$ that extend to semipositive metrics on $L$ over a neighborhood of $X_0$ are exactly the metrics \[  h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B,  \] where $h_ B$ ranges over all semipositive singular Hermitian metrics on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Every such central metric extends over the whole family. Proof. Necessity. Let $h$ be a semipositive metric on $L_0$ that extends. By properness we may shrink the disk so that the extending metric is defined on the whole family. On the locus where $f$ is smooth, local integrability and Fubini's theorem show that for almost every $a\in \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0,1\} $ the restriction of the weights of $h$ to $q_ a$ is not identically $-\infty $. Fix such an $a$. On each local product chart of the conic surface of lemma 10.28.8 along $q_ a\setminus \{ p_ a\} $, the weight of the extending metric is not identically $-\infty $, since its central slice is not. By Fubini's theorem, the metric restricts to almost every nearby compact conic, and on such a conic its curvature is a positive measure of degree zero, hence zero. Lemma 10.28.6 therefore makes the central slice of the weight harmonic on each chart; the alternative $-\infty $ is excluded by the choice of $a$. Consequently, the curvature of $h|_{q_ a}$ is supported at $p_ a$. It is a positive measure of degree one, so it equals $[p_ a]$, which is also the curvature of $h_*|_{q_ a}$. The difference of the two weights is a globally defined harmonic function on the projective line $q_ a$: near $p_ a$, subtracting $\log |w|^2$ from either weight leaves a harmonic function, so the difference extends across $p_ a$. It is therefore constant. Thus the weight difference $u$ between $h$ and $h_*$ is constant along almost every fiber of $f$, away from $\ell $. Over every point of the base there are local holomorphic sections of $f$ avoiding $\ell $ and the exceptional curves: over the finite chart use $[a:1:1]$, and near infinity use $[1:b:1]$ with $b=1/a$. If $e_ B$ is a local frame of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, then $s_\ell \otimes f^*e_ B$ is a nonvanishing holomorphic frame of $L_0$ along these sections. Composing the weight of $h$ in this frame with a section defines a subharmonic weight on the base. It is not identically $-\infty $, because on almost every fiber the weight is harmonic away from $p_ a$. Two choices of section give the same function at almost every base point, because $u$ is constant on those fibers, and hence everywhere, since subharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. Changes of the base frame give the transition law of a metric. These weights therefore define a semipositive metric $h_ B$ on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$. Fubini's theorem on local product charts, together with the fact that $\ell $ and the exceptional fibers have zero volume, shows that $h$ and $h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B$ agree almost everywhere on $X_0$. By lemma 5.24.3 , their local plurisubharmonic weights agree everywhere, including on the three exceptional fibers. This proves necessity. Sufficiency. Let $h_ B$ be a semipositive metric on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, and represent it by a homogeneous weight $V$ on $\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} $, with coordinates $(\xi _1,\xi _2)$ and $a=\xi _1/\xi _2$. In the chart $\xi _2
e 0$, if $\phi _ B$ is the weight of $h_ B$ in the frame given by the section $\xi _2$, set \[  V(\xi _1,\xi _2)=\phi _ B(\xi _1/\xi _2)+\log |\xi _2|^2.  \] The other chart gives the same function, by the transition law of the metric. The function $V$ is plurisubharmonic and satisfies $V(\lambda \xi _1,\lambda \xi _2)=V(\xi _1,\xi _2)+\log |\lambda |^2$ for $\lambda 
e 0$. The weight difference between $h_ B$ and $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ is bounded above on the compact base, so \[  V(\xi _1,\xi _2)\leq \log (|\xi _1|^2+|\xi _2|^2)+C.  \] Hence $V$ extends plurisubharmonically across the origin, with value $-\infty $ there, by lemma 5.24.7 . In each local frame of $L$, the function $V(F_1,F_2)$ is plurisubharmonic, and by homogeneity it transforms as the weight of a metric. Its restriction to each fiber $X_ t$ with $t
e 0$ is not identically $-\infty $: there the two generating sections define a nonconstant map onto $\mathbb P^1$, and the weight of $h_ B$ is not identically $-\infty $. On the central fiber, the factorization in lemma 10.28.7 and homogeneity give exactly the divisor weight of $\ell $ plus the pullback of the weight of $h_ B$. This is the required extension over $\mathcal X$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.28.10
section: 10.28 Semipositive metrics in a four-point blowup family
text: Corollary 10.28.10 . 15454CA8E897 Among all semipositive metrics on $L_0$ that extend, $h_*$ has the least singular weights: every such metric has weights $\psi $ satisfying $\psi \leq \psi _*+C$ in compatible local frames, where $\psi _*$ is the weight of $h_*$; and $h_*$ itself extends. The assertion concerns metrics that extend, not all semipositive metrics on $L_0$. Proof. By theorem 10.28.9 , such a metric has the form $h_\ell \otimes f^*h_ B$. Its weight difference from $h_*$ is the pullback of the global quasi-plurisubharmonic difference between the weights of $h_ B$ and $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$, which is bounded above on $\mathbb P^1$. This proves the inequality. That $h_*$ extends is lemma 10.28.7 . $\square$

title: 10.29 Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds
text: The compact manifolds studied so far in this chapter carry many closed positive currents, coming from divisors, fibrations or blowups. Inoue surfaces and their higher-dimensional analogues, the Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds, behave very differently. They are built from number fields, contain few or no complex subvarieties, and carry a natural closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form whose kernel is a holomorphic foliation by complex affine spaces. These leaves are Liouville and fill out real tori. As a result, every potential in this class is, up to a fixed logarithmic term, a continuous convex function of the transverse coordinates, so the class has no singular potentials at all, even though it contains positive currents supported on real hypersurfaces. In dimension three, a natural Gauduchon metric has an exactly quadratic mass functional of indefinite sign. Its masses lie on both sides of the background mass. These threefolds carry no Hermitian metric whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign, so the known curvature criteria for bounded masses do not apply, and whether the masses remain bounded is an open question ( 24.4.33 ).

title: 10.29.1 The construction
text: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $s+2t$, with $s\geq 1$ real embeddings $\sigma _1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s$ and $t\geq 1$ pairs of complex conjugate embeddings $\sigma _{s+k},\overline{\sigma }_{s+k}$, $1\leq k\leq t$. Write $\mathcal O_ K$ for its ring of integers and $\mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ for the group of totally positive units, that is, of units $\varepsilon $ with $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )>0$ for $1\leq j\leq s$. Let $\mathbb H\subset \mathbb C$ be the upper half-plane. Write points of $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ as $(w,z)$, with $w_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$, and put \[  \sigma _{\mathbb R}(a)=(\sigma _1(a),\ldots ,\sigma _ s(a)),\qquad \sigma _{\mathbb C}(a)=(\sigma _{s+1}(a),\ldots ,\sigma _{s+t}(a)).  \] An element $a\in \mathcal O_ K$ acts by the translation $(w,z)\mapsto (w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a),z+\sigma _{\mathbb C}(a))$, and $\varepsilon \in \mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ acts by \[  (w,z)\longmapsto \bigl (\sigma _1(\varepsilon )w_1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s(\varepsilon )w_ s,\,  \sigma _{s+1}(\varepsilon )z_1,\ldots ,\sigma _{s+t}(\varepsilon )z_ t\bigr ).  \] A subgroup $U\subset \mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ is admissible if its image \[  \Lambda _ U=\{ (\log \sigma _1(\varepsilon ),\ldots ,\log \sigma _ s(\varepsilon )):\varepsilon \in U\}   \] is a lattice in $\mathbb R^ s$. By Dirichlet's unit theorem, when $t=1$ every subgroup of finite index in $\mathcal O_ K^{*,+}$ is admissible. For admissible $U$, Oeljeklaus and Toma showed that the semidirect product $\Gamma =\mathcal O_ K\rtimes U$ acts freely and properly discontinuously on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ with compact quotient. The compact complex manifold \[  X=X(K,U)=(\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t)/\Gamma , \qquad n=\dim X=s+t,  \] is the Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold of type $(s,t)$. The same construction works if $\mathcal O_ K$ is replaced by any lattice $L\subset K$ of rank $s+2t$ that is stable under multiplication by $U$; for $s=t=1$ this produces the Inoue surfaces $S_ M$. The action is still free and cocompact: a point fixed by $(a,\varepsilon )$ with $\varepsilon \neq 1$ would have real coordinates $w_ j$, since $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )\neq 1$ by injectivity of $\sigma _ j$, and $(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(L)$ is again a lattice in $\mathbb R^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. All results of this section other than corollary 10.29.7 hold, with the same proofs, in this generality, with $L$ in place of $\mathcal O_ K$; the only property of $\mathcal O_ K$ they use is that it spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$. Corollary 10.29.7 also holds for every Inoue surface $S_ M$, since these contain no curves. The sources are discussed in section 25.18 . The functions $y_ j=\operatorname {Im}w_ j$ are invariant under the translations and are multiplied by $\sigma _ j(\varepsilon )$ under the unit $\varepsilon $. Hence the closed real $(1,1)$-form \[  \theta =-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _{j=1}^ s\log y_ j =\sum _{j=1}^ s\frac{\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_ j}{8\pi y_ j^2}  \] on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$ is $\Gamma $-invariant and descends to a closed semipositive form on $X$, still denoted $\theta $. It has rank $s$ everywhere, and its kernel is spanned by the vectors $\partial /\partial z_ k$. The potential $-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ itself is not invariant, since a unit adds $-\sum _ j\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon )$ to it.

title: 10.29.2 Potentials of the transverse form
text:
Two properties of the action force rigidity: the leaves $\{ w\} 	imes \mathbb C^ t$ are Liouville, and the real parts of the translations are dense. Lemma 10.29.3 . 72EDF5773FAC Since $t\geq 1$, the subgroup $\sigma _{\mathbb R}(\mathcal O_ K)$ is dense in $\mathbb R^ s$. Proof. A subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb R^ s$ is dense unless there is a nonzero linear form $\xi $ on $\mathbb R^ s$ with $\xi (G)\subseteq \mathbb Z$: the closure of $G$ is the sum of a linear subspace $V$ and a discrete subgroup of a complement of $V$, and if $V
eq \mathbb R^ s$ one can take $\xi $ vanishing on $V$ and integral on that discrete subgroup. Suppose $\xi (\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=\sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)\in \mathbb Z$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$. Since $\mathcal O_ K$ spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$, the map $a\mapsto \sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear map $K	o \mathbb Q$. The trace form of $K$ is nondegenerate, so there is $b\in K$ with \[  \sum _{j=1}^ s\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)=\operatorname {Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(ba) =\sum _{\sigma }\sigma (b)\sigma (a) \qquad (a\in K),  \] where $\sigma $ runs over all $s+2t$ embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb C$. Distinct field embeddings are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$, by Dedekind's lemma on characters. Comparing the coefficients of a complex embedding $\sigma _{s+1}$, which occurs only on the right, gives $\sigma _{s+1}(b)=0$. Hence $b=0$, and then $\xi _ j=\sigma _ j(b)=0$ for every $j$. $\square$ For $\varepsilon \in U$ and $y\in (0,\infty )^ s$, write $\sigma (\varepsilon )y=(\sigma _1(\varepsilon )y_1,\ldots ,\sigma _ s(\varepsilon )y_ s)$. Theorem 10.29.4 . 244BCBFB750A Let $\mathcal F_ U$ be the set of convex functions $f:(0,\infty )^ s	o \mathbb R$ such that 8DB42C059FB9 10.29.5  egin{equation}  f(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=f(y)-\sum _{j=1}^ s\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon ) \qquad (\varepsilon \in U). \end{equation} For $f\in \mathcal F_ U$, the function $u_ f(w,z)=f(y)+\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is $\Gamma $-invariant, and $f\mapsto u_ f$ is a bijection from $\mathcal F_ U$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. In particular, every $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is continuous and depends only on $y=\operatorname {Im}w$. Proof. We first note that a function $g$ on $\mathbb H^ s$ that depends only on $y$ is plurisubharmonic if and only if, as a function on $(0,\infty )^ s$, it is convex (with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$ and not identically $-\infty $). For smooth $g$ this follows from $\partial ^2g/\partial w_ j\partial \overline w_ k= rac14\partial ^2g/\partial y_ j\partial y_ k$. In general, convolution with a smooth radial kernel in $w$ produces smooth functions of $y$ alone; they decrease to $g$ if $g$ is plurisubharmonic, and they converge locally uniformly to $g$ if $g$ is convex, because a convex function that is not identically $-\infty $ on the open convex set $(0,\infty )^ s$ is finite and continuous there. Since decreasing limits of convex functions are convex and locally uniform limits of plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic, the claim follows. The identity ( 10.29.5 ) says exactly that $u_ f$ is invariant under $U$, and $u_ f$ is clearly invariant under the translations. On the universal cover, $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)\geq 0$. Hence $u_ f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and $f$ is recovered from $u_ f$, so the map is injective. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and let $	ilde u$ be its lift to $\mathbb H^ s	imes \mathbb C^ t$. Since $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	ilde u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(	ilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j)$ there, the function $q=	ilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s	imes \mathbb C^ t$. Step 1: constancy on the leaves. Fix $w^0\in \mathbb H^ s$. The restriction of $q$ to the slice $\{ w^0\} 	imes \mathbb C^ t$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is bounded above because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$. A plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb C^ t$ that is bounded above is constant, since its restriction to every complex line through two given points is a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ bounded above. Hence $	ilde u(w,z)=	ilde u(w,0)$ for all $(w,z)$. In particular, the function $F(w)=q(w,0)$ is not identically $-\infty $, because $	ilde u$ is not, and it is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s$. Step 2: invariance under real translations. The translations by $\mathcal O_ K$ and Step 1 give $F(w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=F(w)$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$, since $\log y_ j$ does not change under real translations. For $r>0$, the averages $F_ r$ of $F$ over the Euclidean balls of radius $r$ are defined on $\{ w:\min _ jy_ j>r\} $ and continuous there, because $F$ is locally integrable, and they are invariant under the same translations. By lemma 10.29.3 and continuity, each $F_ r$ is invariant under all translations by $\mathbb R^ s$. Since $F_ r$ decreases to $F$ as $r\downarrow 0$, the function $F$ is invariant under all real translations as well, so $F(w)=f(y)$ for a function $f$ on $(0,\infty )^ s$. Step 3: convexity and automorphy. Since $F=f(y)$ is plurisubharmonic, the first paragraph of the proof shows that $f$ is convex, finite and continuous. Finally, $u=u_ f$, and invariance of $u$ under $U$ is ( 10.29.5 ). $\square$ Corollary 10.29.6 . 98BD3A283B8E On every Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold, all functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ are continuous. Consequently, they all have the ordinary singularity type of $0$, all their Lelong numbers vanish, all their multiplier ideals are trivial, and $P_	heta [u]=V_	heta =0$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Moreover $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=0$ for every $u$, so $	heta $ is nef but not big. Proof. Continuous functions on a compact manifold are bounded, so any two of them are equivalent, and their Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals are those of a bounded function. Since $	heta \geq 0$, the constant $0$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, so $V_	heta =0$, and $P_	heta [u]=P_	heta [0]=V_	heta $. By theorem 10.29.4 , locally $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)$ with $f$ continuous and depending on the $s$ real variables $y_ j$; the Bedford–Taylor products of such a current vanish in degree $s+1\leq n$, because they are limits of the corresponding products for smooth convex approximants of $f$, whose complex Hessians have rank at most $s$. Thus $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The form $	heta $ is smooth and semipositive, hence nef. Suppose that $ho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfied $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. The function $ho $ is continuous, and on a small coordinate ball with coordinates $\zeta $ we may write $	heta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with $a$ smooth and $\delta \omega \geq \delta '\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2$ with $\delta '>0$. Then $a+ho -\delta '|\zeta |^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a+ho ))^ n$ as a sum of positive mixed Bedford–Taylor products gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (ho )\geq \delta '^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2)^ n
eq 0$ on the ball, a contradiction. Hence $	heta $ is not big. $\square$ Singular currents nevertheless occur in this class. Let $s=t=1$, so that $X$ is an Inoue surface and $U$ is generated by a unit $\varepsilon _0$ with $\lambda =\sigma _1(\varepsilon _0)>1$. Fix $y_0>0$, put $y_ k=\lambda ^ ky_0$ for $k\in \mathbb Z$, and let $f$ be the continuous function that is affine on each interval $[y_ k,y_{k+1}]$ with slope \[  a_ k=- rac{\log \lambda }{(\lambda -1)y_ k}, \qquad f(y_0)=0.  \] Then $a_ k(y_{k+1}-y_ k)=-\log \lambda $, so $f(\lambda y)=f(y)-\log \lambda $, and the slopes increase because $a_{k+1}=a_ k/\lambda $ and $a_ k<0$. Thus $f\in \mathcal F_ U$. On the universal cover, \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)= rac1{4\pi }\sum _{k\in \mathbb Z}(a_ k-a_{k-1})\,  \delta (y-y_ k)\, \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy,  \] with $a_ k-a_{k-1}>0$. The closed positive current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f$ therefore has a continuous potential but is supported on the compact real hypersurface of $X$ formed by the images of the hyperplanes $\{ y=y_ k\} $, a three-dimensional torus that is a union of leaves of the foliation $\{ w=	ext{const}\} $. On an Inoue surface, $	heta $ represents the canonical Bott–Chern class. Indeed, the Tricerri metric $\omega _ T=8\pi 	heta +y\, \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$ has $\omega _ T^2=(2/y)\, \mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$, so its normalized Chern–Ricci form $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (\omega _ T^2/\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z)$, which is $-\mathrm i\partial \overline\partial \log \det \omega _ T$ divided by $2\pi $ and represents $c_1^{BC}(X)$, equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log y=-	heta $. Hence theorem 10.29.4 describes all positive currents in $c_1^{BC}(K_ X)$, and none of them has a pole. Arbitrary backgrounds behave differently, since a Hermitian form has potentials with logarithmic poles. Nevertheless, when $t=1$ their singularities are confined to finite sets. By a theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky (section 25.18 ), an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$ contains no complex subvarieties of positive dimension. Corollary 10.29.7 . CBF3E42884D1 Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$, let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$. For every $c>0$, the set $\{ x:
u (u,x)\geq c\} $ is finite. Consequently, for every $k>0$ the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside a finite set, and $\mathcal I(ku)$ has finite colength. Proof. By Siu's theorem ( 5.34.2 ), the set $E_ c=\{ 
u (u,\cdot )\geq c\} $ is a compact analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset, because $
u (u,x)=0$ outside the pluripolar set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence $E_ c$ is finite by the theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky. By Skoda's integrability criterion, recalled in [ SGPT ] , $\mathcal I(ku)_ x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ whenever $k
u (u,x)<1$, so $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside the finite set $E_{1/k}$. A coherent ideal sheaf that is trivial outside a finite set has finite colength. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.29.3
text: Lemma 10.29.3 . 72EDF5773FAC Since $t\geq 1$, the subgroup $\sigma _{\mathbb R}(\mathcal O_ K)$ is dense in $\mathbb R^ s$. Proof. A subgroup $G$ of $\mathbb R^ s$ is dense unless there is a nonzero linear form $\xi $ on $\mathbb R^ s$ with $\xi (G)\subseteq \mathbb Z$: the closure of $G$ is the sum of a linear subspace $V$ and a discrete subgroup of a complement of $V$, and if $V\neq \mathbb R^ s$ one can take $\xi $ vanishing on $V$ and integral on that discrete subgroup. Suppose $\xi (\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=\sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)\in \mathbb Z$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$. Since $\mathcal O_ K$ spans $K$ over $\mathbb Q$, the map $a\mapsto \sum _ j\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-linear map $K\to \mathbb Q$. The trace form of $K$ is nondegenerate, so there is $b\in K$ with \[  \sum _{j=1}^ s\xi _ j\sigma _ j(a)=\operatorname {Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(ba) =\sum _{\sigma }\sigma (b)\sigma (a) \qquad (a\in K),  \] where $\sigma $ runs over all $s+2t$ embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb C$. Distinct field embeddings are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$, by Dedekind's lemma on characters. Comparing the coefficients of a complex embedding $\sigma _{s+1}$, which occurs only on the right, gives $\sigma _{s+1}(b)=0$. Hence $b=0$, and then $\xi _ j=\sigma _ j(b)=0$ for every $j$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.29.4
text: Theorem 10.29.4 . 244BCBFB750A Let $\mathcal F_ U$ be the set of convex functions $f:(0,\infty )^ s\to \mathbb R$ such that 8DB42C059FB9 10.29.5 \begin{equation}  f(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=f(y)-\sum _{j=1}^ s\log \sigma _ j(\varepsilon ) \qquad (\varepsilon \in U). \end{equation} For $f\in \mathcal F_ U$, the function $u_ f(w,z)=f(y)+\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is $\Gamma $-invariant, and $f\mapsto u_ f$ is a bijection from $\mathcal F_ U$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. In particular, every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is continuous and depends only on $y=\operatorname {Im}w$. Proof. We first note that a function $g$ on $\mathbb H^ s$ that depends only on $y$ is plurisubharmonic if and only if, as a function on $(0,\infty )^ s$, it is convex (with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$ and not identically $-\infty $). For smooth $g$ this follows from $\partial ^2g/\partial w_ j\partial \overline w_ k=\frac14\partial ^2g/\partial y_ j\partial y_ k$. In general, convolution with a smooth radial kernel in $w$ produces smooth functions of $y$ alone; they decrease to $g$ if $g$ is plurisubharmonic, and they converge locally uniformly to $g$ if $g$ is convex, because a convex function that is not identically $-\infty $ on the open convex set $(0,\infty )^ s$ is finite and continuous there. Since decreasing limits of convex functions are convex and locally uniform limits of plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic, the claim follows. The identity ( 10.29.5 ) says exactly that $u_ f$ is invariant under $U$, and $u_ f$ is clearly invariant under the translations. On the universal cover, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ f=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)\geq 0$. Hence $u_ f\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $f$ is recovered from $u_ f$, so the map is injective. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and let $\tilde u$ be its lift to $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. Since $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tilde u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\tilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j)$ there, the function $q=\tilde u-\sum _ j\log y_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s\times \mathbb C^ t$. Step 1: constancy on the leaves. Fix $w^0\in \mathbb H^ s$. The restriction of $q$ to the slice $\{ w^0\} \times \mathbb C^ t$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, and it is bounded above because $u$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$. A plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb C^ t$ that is bounded above is constant, since its restriction to every complex line through two given points is a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ bounded above. Hence $\tilde u(w,z)=\tilde u(w,0)$ for all $(w,z)$. In particular, the function $F(w)=q(w,0)$ is not identically $-\infty $, because $\tilde u$ is not, and it is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb H^ s$. Step 2: invariance under real translations. The translations by $\mathcal O_ K$ and Step 1 give $F(w+\sigma _{\mathbb R}(a))=F(w)$ for every $a\in \mathcal O_ K$, since $\log y_ j$ does not change under real translations. For $r>0$, the averages $F_ r$ of $F$ over the Euclidean balls of radius $r$ are defined on $\{ w:\min _ jy_ j>r\} $ and continuous there, because $F$ is locally integrable, and they are invariant under the same translations. By lemma 10.29.3 and continuity, each $F_ r$ is invariant under all translations by $\mathbb R^ s$. Since $F_ r$ decreases to $F$ as $r\downarrow 0$, the function $F$ is invariant under all real translations as well, so $F(w)=f(y)$ for a function $f$ on $(0,\infty )^ s$. Step 3: convexity and automorphy. Since $F=f(y)$ is plurisubharmonic, the first paragraph of the proof shows that $f$ is convex, finite and continuous. Finally, $u=u_ f$, and invariance of $u$ under $U$ is ( 10.29.5 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 10.29.6
text: Corollary 10.29.6 . 98BD3A283B8E On every Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold, all functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ are continuous. Consequently, they all have the ordinary singularity type of $0$, all their Lelong numbers vanish, all their multiplier ideals are trivial, and $P_\theta [u]=V_\theta =0$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Moreover $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=0$ for every $u$, so $\theta $ is nef but not big. Proof. Continuous functions on a compact manifold are bounded, so any two of them are equivalent, and their Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals are those of a bounded function. Since $\theta \geq 0$, the constant $0$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, so $V_\theta =0$, and $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [0]=V_\theta $. By theorem 10.29.4 , locally $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f(y)$ with $f$ continuous and depending on the $s$ real variables $y_ j$; the Bedford–Taylor products of such a current vanish in degree $s+1\leq n$, because they are limits of the corresponding products for smooth convex approximants of $f$, whose complex Hessians have rank at most $s$. Thus $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The form $\theta $ is smooth and semipositive, hence nef. Suppose that $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfied $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \omega $ with $\delta >0$. The function $\rho $ is continuous, and on a small coordinate ball with coordinates $\zeta $ we may write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ with $a$ smooth and $\delta \omega \geq \delta '\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2$ with $\delta '>0$. Then $a+\rho -\delta '|\zeta |^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a+\rho ))^ n$ as a sum of positive mixed Bedford–Taylor products gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\rho )\geq \delta '^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|\zeta |^2)^ n\neq 0$ on the ball, a contradiction. Hence $\theta $ is not big. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.29.7
text:
Corollary 10.29.7 . CBF3E42884D1 Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold with $t=1$, let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$. For every $c>0$, the set $\{ x:
u (u,x)\geq c\} $ is finite. Consequently, for every $k>0$ the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside a finite set, and $\mathcal I(ku)$ has finite colength. Proof. By Siu's theorem ( 5.34.2 ), the set $E_ c=\{ 
u (u,\cdot )\geq c\} $ is a compact analytic subset of $X$. It is a proper subset, because $
u (u,x)=0$ outside the pluripolar set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has Lebesgue measure zero. Hence $E_ c$ is finite by the theorem of Ornea and Verbitsky. By Skoda's integrability criterion, recalled in [ SGPT ] , $\mathcal I(ku)_ x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ whenever $k
u (u,x)<1$, so $\mathcal I(ku)$ is trivial outside the finite set $E_{1/k}$. A coherent ideal sheaf that is trivial outside a finite set has finite colength. $\square$

title: 10.29.8 Monge–Ampère masses on threefolds
text: Now let $s=2$ and $t=1$, so that $X$ is a threefold. A totally positive unit has norm $\sigma _1(\varepsilon )\sigma _2(\varepsilon )|\sigma _3(\varepsilon )|^2=1$, so the form $y_1y_2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ is $\Gamma $-invariant. The Hermitian form \[  \omega =\theta +\beta ,\qquad \beta =y_1y_2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2,  \] descends to $X$. Write $\mathrm dV_0=(\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1)\wedge (\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2)\wedge (\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z)$ on the universal cover, and $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3$. A unit that fixes $y_1$ satisfies $\sigma _1(\varepsilon )=1$, hence $\varepsilon =1$ because $\sigma _1$ is injective. Hence the map $X\to T_ U=\mathbb R^2/\Lambda _ U$, $[w,z]\mapsto (\log y_1,\log y_2)$, has as fibers the real tori $(\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$, and for every $\Lambda _ U$-periodic function $g$ of $\varsigma =(\log y_1,\log y_2)$ there is a constant $c_ X>0$, independent of $g$, with 3C8DE164722C 10.29.9 \begin{equation}  \int _ Xg(\varsigma )\, \frac{\mathrm dV_0}{y_1y_2} =c_ X\int _{T_ U}g\, \mathrm d\varsigma . \end{equation} We shall use an elementary property of lattices in the plane: every lattice $\Lambda \subset \mathbb R^2$ contains vectors in each of the four open quadrants. Indeed, let $\ell >0$ be the length of a shortest nonzero vector of $\Lambda $, and let $0<\delta <\ell $. By Minkowski's theorem, the symmetric convex set $\{ k:|k_1-k_2|<\delta ,\  |k_1+k_2|<N\} $ contains a nonzero lattice point once $N$ is large. Such a point satisfies $(k_1+k_2)^2=2|k|^2-(k_1-k_2)^2\geq 2\ell ^2-\delta ^2$, hence $4k_1k_2=(k_1+k_2)^2-(k_1-k_2)^2>0$; replacing $k$ by $-k$ if necessary gives a point in the open first quadrant, and the line $\mathbb R(1,-1)$ gives the other two quadrants in the same way. If $\lambda $ lies in the open first quadrant and $\mu \in \Lambda $ is independent of $\lambda $, then $N\lambda +\mu $ also lies there for large $N$, so the first quadrant contains two independent lattice vectors. Proposition 10.29.10 . E080ADB5BEF1 Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma threefold of type $(2,1)$ with the Hermitian form $\omega $ above. The form $\omega $ is Gauduchon, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ is neither semipositive nor seminegative. For every smooth real function $u$ on $X$, \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X\omega ^3+\frac{3}{16\pi ^3}\int _ X \operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0.  \] Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be bounded and depend only on $y$, and write $u=g(\varsigma )$ with $g$ periodic under $\Lambda _ U$. Then $g$ is Lipschitz, $P=1-\partial _1g$ and $Q=1-\partial _2g$ are nonnegative almost everywhere, and \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U}PQ\, \mathrm d\varsigma .  \] There is a constant $c_ U\geq 1$, depending only on $\Lambda _ U$, such that every such $u$ satisfies $c_ U^{-1}\int _ X\omega ^3\leq \mathrm M_\omega (u)\leq c_ U\int _ X\omega ^3$. There are smooth $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, depending only on $y$, with $\mathrm M_\omega (u)>\int _ X\omega ^3$, and others with $\mathrm M_\omega (u)<\int _ X\omega ^3$. Consequently $v_-(\omega )<\int _ X\omega ^3<v_+(\omega )$. Proof. (1) Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ has constant coefficients and $y_ j$ is pluriharmonic, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2,  \] where \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\bigl (\partial y_1\wedge \overline\partial y_2 +\partial y_2\wedge \overline\partial y_1\bigr ) =\frac{\mathrm i}{8\pi }\bigl (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2 +\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1\bigr ).  \] The Hermitian matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(y_1y_2)$ in the basis $\mathrm dw_1,\mathrm dw_2$ is a positive multiple of $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0& 1\\ 1& 0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which is indefinite. Accordingly, for $\eta _\pm =\mathrm dw_1\pm \mathrm dw_2$ the $(3,3)$-forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \mathrm i\eta _\pm \wedge \overline\eta _\pm $ are respectively negative and positive multiples of $\mathrm dV_0$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta $ is neither semipositive nor seminegative. Since $\theta $ is closed and $\beta ^2=0$, we have $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=2\theta \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta $, and this vanishes because every term of $\theta \wedge (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2+\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1)$ repeats a differential. (2) By theorem 11.1.5 with $n=3$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0$, $\mathrm M_\omega (u)-\int _ X\omega ^3=3\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ is closed, so Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\int _ X\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Now $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u=(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \partial u\wedge \overline\partial u$, and a direct computation in the coordinates $w_1,w_2,z$ gives \[  \mathrm i\, \partial u\wedge \overline\partial u\wedge \mathrm i\bigl (\mathrm dw_1\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_2+\mathrm dw_2\wedge \mathrm d\overline w_1\bigr ) \wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z =-2\operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial u}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0.  \] Collecting the constants $(1/2\pi )(1/8\pi )(1/2\pi )$ gives the formula. (3) Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has no components in the $z$-direction, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)+\beta $ splits into blocks, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ if and only if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 10.29.4 , $u=f(y)+\log (y_1y_2)$ with $f$ convex, so $g$ is locally Lipschitz, hence Lipschitz by periodicity. In the variables $\varsigma _ j=\log y_ j$, convexity of $f$ is equivalent to positivity of the symmetric matrix \[  H=I+D^2g-\operatorname {diag}(\partial _1g,\partial _2g),  \] as one checks from $y_ iy_ j\, \partial ^2f/\partial y_ i\partial y_ j=\partial ^2\Phi /\partial \varsigma _ i\partial \varsigma _ j-\delta _{ij}\, \partial \Phi /\partial \varsigma _ i$ for $\Phi (\varsigma )=f(\mathrm e^{\varsigma })=g(\varsigma )-\varsigma _1-\varsigma _2$. This condition is linear in $g$ with constant coefficients, so it is preserved by convolution with a smooth kernel on $\mathbb R^2$; the regularized functions are periodic, and they converge uniformly to $g$ with gradients converging almost everywhere. By the continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence and dominated convergence, it suffices to prove all assertions for smooth $g$ with $H\geq 0$. For such $g$, the function $u$ depends only on $y$, so $\partial u/\partial w_ j=-\frac{\mathrm i}2\partial u/\partial y_ j$ and the integrand in (2) is $\frac14\partial _{y_1}u\, \partial _{y_2}u=\partial _1g\, \partial _2g/(4y_1y_2)$. A direct computation gives $\omega ^3=3\theta ^2\wedge \beta =\frac{3}{64\pi ^3}\, \mathrm dV_0/(y_1y_2)$. By ( 10.29.9 ) and (2), \[  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U} \bigl (1+\partial _1g\, \partial _2g\bigr )\, \mathrm d\varsigma =\frac{\int _ X\omega ^3}{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U}PQ\, \mathrm d\varsigma ,  \] where the second equality uses $\int _{T_ U}\partial _ jg\, \mathrm d\varsigma =0$. The diagonal entry $H_{11}=P-\partial _1P\geq 0$ says that $\mathrm e^{-\varsigma _1}P$ is nonincreasing in $\varsigma _1$, that is, 62F4D45FFF73 10.29.11 \begin{equation}  P(\varsigma +\tau e_1)\leq \mathrm e^{\tau }P(\varsigma )\qquad (\tau \geq 0). \end{equation} If $P(\varsigma )<0$, the right side tends to $-\infty $ as $\tau \to \infty $, which is impossible for the bounded function $P$; hence $P\geq 0$, and likewise $Q\geq 0$. Thus $\partial _ jg\leq 1$. The lattice $\Lambda _ U$ contains two independent vectors $\lambda ,\lambda '$ with positive coordinates, and every point of $T_ U$ has the form $\varsigma +\tau \lambda +\tau '\lambda '$ with $\tau ,\tau '\in [0,1)$. Along $\tau \mapsto \varsigma +\tau \lambda $, the derivative of $g$ is at most $|\lambda |_1=\lambda _1+\lambda _2$, and its integral over $[0,1]$ vanishes by periodicity, so $|g(\varsigma +\tau \lambda )-g(\varsigma )|\leq |\lambda |_1$. Hence $\operatorname {osc}g\leq L$, with $L=|\lambda |_1+|\lambda '|_1$ depending only on $\Lambda _ U$. Averaging ( 10.29.11 ) in the form $P(\varsigma -\tau e_1)\geq \mathrm e^{-\tau }P(\varsigma )$ over $\tau \in [0,1]$ gives \[  (1-\mathrm e^{-1})P(\varsigma )\leq \int _0^1P(\varsigma -\tau e_1)\, \mathrm d\tau =1-g(\varsigma )+g(\varsigma -e_1)\leq 1+L.  \] On the other hand, averaging $P(\varsigma )\geq \mathrm e^{-\tau }P(\varsigma +\tau e_1)$ over $\tau \in [0,R]$ with $R=\max (2L,1)$ gives \[  P(\varsigma )\geq \frac{\mathrm e^{-R}}R\int _0^ RP(\varsigma +\tau e_1)\, \mathrm d\tau =\frac{\mathrm e^{-R}}R\bigl (R-g(\varsigma +Re_1)+g(\varsigma )\bigr ) \geq \frac{\mathrm e^{-R}}2.  \] The same bounds hold for $Q$. Therefore the average of $PQ$ over $T_ U$ lies between $\mathrm e^{-2R}/4$ and $\bigl ((1+L)/(1-\mathrm e^{-1})\bigr )^2$, which proves (3). (4) Let $k$ belong to the dual lattice $\Lambda _ U^*=\{ k\in \mathbb R^2:\langle k,\lambda \rangle \in \mathbb Z\text{ for all }\lambda \in \Lambda _ U\} $, and put $g_\epsilon (\varsigma )=\epsilon \cos (2\pi \langle k,\varsigma \rangle )$. For small $\epsilon >0$, the matrix $H$ of $g_\epsilon $ is positive definite, so $u_\epsilon =g_\epsilon (\varsigma )$ is a smooth function with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\epsilon >0$. By (3), \[  \frac{\mathrm M_\omega (u_\epsilon )}{\int _ X\omega ^3} =1+\frac1{|T_ U|}\int _{T_ U}\partial _1g_\epsilon \, \partial _2g_\epsilon \, \mathrm d\varsigma =1+2\pi ^2\epsilon ^2k_1k_2.  \] Since the lattice $\Lambda _ U^*$ has vectors in every open quadrant, we may choose $k$ with $k_1k_2>0$, respectively $k_1k_2<0$, which gives the two inequalities. $\square$ For a general smooth potential, averaging over the fibers separates the invariant part from the fluctuations. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ let $Au$ be the average of $u$ over the fibers of $X\to T_ U$, that is, over the translations $(w,z)\mapsto (w+r,z+\zeta )$ with $(r,\zeta )\in (\mathbb R^2\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$. These translations preserve $\omega $ on the universal cover. They do not descend to $X$ individually, but conjugation by a unit $\varepsilon $ carries the translation by $(r,\zeta )$ to the translation by $(\sigma _1(\varepsilon )r_1,\sigma _2(\varepsilon )r_2,\sigma _3(\varepsilon )\zeta )$, and this automorphism of the translation torus preserves its Haar measure because $\varepsilon $ has norm one. Hence $Au$ is a well-defined $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function depending only on $y$, and $c_ U^{-1}\int _ X\omega ^3\leq \mathrm M_\omega (Au)\leq c_ U\int _ X\omega ^3$ by proposition 10.29.10 . For smooth $u$, the integral of a $y$-derivative of $u-Au$ over a fiber vanishes, and so does the integral of an $x$-derivative. The cross terms between $Au$ and $u-Au$ in proposition 10.29.10 (2) therefore integrate to zero, and 61E93097052D 10.29.12 \begin{equation}  \mathrm M_\omega (u)=\mathrm M_\omega (Au)+\frac{3}{16\pi ^3}\int _ X \operatorname {Re}\Bigl (\frac{\partial v}{\partial w_1}\,  \overline{\frac{\partial v}{\partial w_2}}\Bigr )\mathrm dV_0, \qquad v=u-Au. \end{equation} Since the extrema of the masses of bounded potentials equal the extrema over smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials (proposition 13.14.15 , theorem 12.15.4 ), $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $ if and only if the fluctuation term in ( 10.29.12 ) is bounded above on smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions; likewise, $v_-(\omega )>0$ if and only if $\mathrm M_\omega (Au)$ plus the fluctuation term is bounded below by a positive constant on such functions.

text: Finally, we show that no Hermitian metric on these manifolds has a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of constant sign, so that curvature criteria based on such metrics cannot settle the boundedness of the masses. Proposition 10.29.14 . 48299489DE9D Let $X$ be an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold of type $(s,1)$ with $s\geq 2$. Then $X$ admits no Hermitian form $\widetilde\omega $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\omega $ is semipositive, or seminegative, on every complex $2$-plane. Proof. Suppose $\widetilde\omega $ is such a form, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde\omega \geq 0$ on every complex $2$-plane; the other case is analogous. Average the lift of $\widetilde\omega $ over the translations $(w,z)\mapsto (w+r,z+\zeta )$, $(r,\zeta )\in (\mathbb R^ s\times \mathbb C)/(\sigma _{\mathbb R},\sigma _{\mathbb C})(\mathcal O_ K)$, as in the definition of $Au$ above. The averaged form $\overline\omega $ is again $\Gamma $-invariant and Hermitian, its coefficients in the frame $\mathrm dw_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dw_ s,\mathrm dz$ depend only on $y$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega \geq 0$ on complex $2$-planes, because translations are holomorphic and positivity on $2$-planes is preserved by averaging. Let $h(y)>0$ be the coefficient of $\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$ in $\overline\omega $. Invariance under a unit $\varepsilon $ gives $h(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)|\sigma _{s+1}(\varepsilon )|^2=h(y)$, that is, $h(\sigma (\varepsilon )y)=\sigma _1(\varepsilon )\cdots \sigma _ s(\varepsilon )\, h(y)$, since $\varepsilon $ has norm one. Hence $h/(y_1\cdots y_ s)$ is invariant under $U$, and since $\Lambda _ U$ is a lattice it is bounded between two positive constants: 73E1BF5F8F36 10.29.15 \begin{equation}  c\, y_1\cdots y_ s\leq h(y)\leq C\, y_1\cdots y_ s. \end{equation} Let $v$ be a nonzero vector in the span of $\partial /\partial w_1,\ldots ,\partial /\partial w_ s$, and let $P$ be the complex $2$-plane spanned by $v$ and $\partial /\partial z$. Write $\overline\omega =\sum _{a,b}g_{ab}(y)\, \mathrm i\, \xi _ a\wedge \overline\xi _ b$ with $\xi =(\mathrm dw_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dw_ s,\mathrm dz)$. Since the forms $\xi _ a$ are closed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega =\sum _{a,b}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_{ab}\wedge \mathrm i\, \xi _ a\wedge \overline\xi _ b$, and each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_{ab}$ has only $w$-components. A term restricted to $P$ is nonzero only if it contains both $\mathrm dz$ and $\mathrm d\overline z$, which happens only for $\xi _ a=\xi _ b=\mathrm dz$. Hence the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\overline\omega $ to $P$ equals the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\overline z$, and its sign is that of the value of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $v$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq 0$ in the $w$-variables, and $h$ is convex in $y$. Let $R>1$ and put $A=(R,R^{-1},1,\ldots ,1)$, $B=(R^{-1},R,1,\ldots ,1)$ and $M=(A+B)/2$. By ( 10.29.15 ), $h(A),h(B)\leq C$, whereas $h(M)\geq c(R+R^{-1})^2/4$, which contradicts convexity for large $R$. In the seminegative case, $h$ is concave, so $t\mapsto h(t,\ldots ,t)$ grows at most linearly as $t\to \infty $; this contradicts the lower bound $h(t,\ldots ,t)\geq ct^ s$ with $s\geq 2$. $\square$ For $s=t=1$ the same averaging produces a coefficient $h$ comparable to $y$, which may be affine; indeed the Tricerri metric is pluriclosed. title: 23.2 Locally conformally Kähler geometry
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. A locally conformally Kähler (LCK) metric is a Hermitian metric that becomes Kähler after local conformal changes, and its Lee form measures the obstruction to making this change globally. On a covering on which the Lee form is exact, the Kähler metric and its admissible potentials change by the same character under deck transformations. Descending this potential calculus to $X$ gives a twisted complex Hessian with a zeroth-order term, so that even adding a constant to a potential changes the metric. The standard Vaisman metric on the Hopf manifold illustrates the difference between the two potential theories: although it is locally conformally Kähler, its ordinary potentials have unbounded Monge–Ampère masses. Prescribing the volume while keeping the Lee class and the Gauduchon gauge couples the determinant equation with an equation for the conformal factor. For a volume invariant under the Lee and anti-Lee flows of a Vaisman metric, uniqueness for the ordinary smooth equation gives a potential that is constant along these flows. Stokes' theorem in the transverse directions fixes the normalizing constant, and changing the Lee form reconstructs the required Vaisman metric. On scalar Hopf manifolds, radial symmetry reduces the coupled equations to a periodic ordinary differential equation. Its positive solutions are ordered by their Lee periods, so the metric is determined by its Lee period and its volume; for a nonconstant radial volume, this metric is not Vaisman. A different compatibility condition gives rigidity: when an LCK metric is both Gauduchon and Chern–Ricci flat, the Bianchi and Bochner identities force its harmonic Lee form to be parallel. The Lee form also produces a closed curvature class that can be nonzero in Bott–Chern cohomology while vanishing in de Rham cohomology. Pairing these classes with all Gauduchon metrics defines the Lee–Gauduchon cone, which detects their pseudoeffectivity and is invariant under bimeromorphic maps. Strongly Gauduchon metrics exclude all nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents and bound the linear mass of closed positive currents by their de Rham classes. The Calabi–Eckmann example separates this condition from the presence of zero in the Lee–Gauduchon cone, and a balanced elliptic fibration shows that it still allows zero lower Monge–Ampère mass.

title: 23.2.1 The Lee form and the Kähler covering
search_title: The Lee form and the Kähler covering
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
A Hermitian form is locally conformally Kähler when its exterior derivative is controlled by a closed one-form. Definition 23.2.2 . 48F6C713AFE3 A Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ is locally conformally Kähler , or LCK, if there is a smooth real one-form $\lambda $ on $X$ such that \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =\lambda \wedge \omega , \qquad \mathrm{d}\lambda =0.  \] The form $\lambda $ is called its Lee form . The metric is strictly LCK if $\lambda $ is not exact. A strictly LCK metric is Vaisman if its Lee form is parallel for the Levi–Civita connection of the associated Riemannian metric. Fix an LCK metric $\omega $ with Lee form $\lambda $. On a compact manifold a nonzero parallel one-form cannot be exact: the differential of a function vanishes at a maximum, whereas a parallel form has constant length. Thus a nonzero parallel Lee form is automatically nowhere zero and not exact. The Lee form is determined by $\omega $, because the map $a\mapsto a\wedge \omega $ is injective on one-forms: after wedging with $\omega ^{n-2}$, this follows from the bijectivity of the Lefschetz map $a\mapsto a\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ on one-forms. Locally write $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$. Then \[  \Omega =\mathrm{e}^{-f}\omega >0,\qquad \mathrm{d}\Omega =0,  \] so $\Omega $ is a Kähler form. Choose a connected regular covering $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ on which $\pi ^*\lambda =\mathrm{d}F$, for example the universal covering. The quotient of $\widetilde X$ by its deck group is $X$. The same construction gives a Kähler form 2E90E918DF55 23.2.3  egin{equation}  \widetilde\omega =\mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*\omega . \end{equation} For a deck transformation $\sigma $, the difference $\sigma ^*F-F=c_\sigma $ is constant, and \[  \sigma ^*\widetilde\omega =\chi (\sigma )\widetilde\omega , \qquad \chi (\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{-c_\sigma }.  \] Thus $\chi $ is a homomorphism from the deck group to the multiplicative group of positive real numbers, which records how the Kähler metric is rescaled. Forms on $\widetilde X$ transforming by $\chi $ may equivalently be viewed as forms on $X$ with values in the flat real line bundle defined by $\chi $, the weight bundle . In this sense an LCK form is closed as a form with values in the weight bundle, OV24LCK ]. Let $g$ be the Riemannian metric of $\omega $, let $J$ be the complex structure, and let $\lambda ^\sharp $ be the vector field dual to $\lambda $ with respect to $g$. On a chart where $\lambda =\mathrm df$, the metric $\widetilde g=\mathrm{e}^{-f}g$ is Kähler. For real vector fields $U,V$, the Levi–Civita connections $
abla $ of $g$ and $\widetilde
abla $ of $\widetilde g$ are related by \[  \widetilde
abla _ UV=
abla _ UV-	frac 12 igl (\lambda (U)V+\lambda (V)U-g(U,V)\lambda ^\sharp  igr ).  \] Substituting $JV$ for $V$ and using $\widetilde

abla _ UJ)V=	frac 12 igl (\lambda (JV)U-\lambda (V)JU+g(U,V)J\lambda ^\sharp +g(JU,V)\lambda ^\sharp  igr ). \end{equation} Both sides are global tensors, so this identity holds on all of $X$. For $a\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, the conformal change $\omega '=\mathrm{e}^ a\omega $ replaces the Lee form by $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$. In particular, the de Rham class $[\lambda ]$ depends only on the conformal class of $\omega $. If $\lambda $ is exact, the construction above gives a Kähler form on $X$ itself.

In the conformal class of an LCK metric, the Gauduchon representative is the one whose Lee form is harmonic. A closed $(1,1)$-form built from the Lee form pairs positively with this Gauduchon metric when the structure is strictly LCK, even though the form is de Rham exact. It therefore defines a nonzero Bott–Chern class, which obstructs Kähler modifications. Set \[  \lambda ^{\mathrm c} = rac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\lambda ^{0,1}-\lambda ^{1,0}),  \] so that $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ wherever $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$. The closed real $(1,1)$-form 29D45DC05342 23.2.6  egin{equation}  \kappa _\lambda :=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\lambda =-\mathrm{d}\lambda ^{\mathrm c} \end{equation} connects the Lee class with Bott–Chern cohomology. It is de Rham exact, but it need not be $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Proposition 23.2.7 . 11EBB7AD1165 An LCK metric is Gauduchon if and only if its Lee form is co-closed for that metric. Consequently, the Gauduchon representative in its conformal class has harmonic Lee form. Moreover, for every LCK metric, 35851308DD2B 23.2.8  egin{equation}  \int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =(n-1)\int _ X\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}. \end{equation} If $\lambda 
ot\equiv 0$, the right side is strictly positive. Proof. On a chart where $\omega $ is conformally Kähler, \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\omega ^{n-1}) =(n-1)\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}.  \] Let $*$ be the real Hodge star of the Riemannian metric associated with $\omega $, and let $\mathrm d^*$ be the formal adjoint of the exterior derivative. By the pointwise Hodge-star identities for Hermitian metrics, $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is a fixed nonzero constant multiple of $*\lambda $. Consequently, the Gauduchon condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{d}*\lambda =0$, that is, to $\mathrm{d}^*\lambda =0$. Since $\mathrm{d}\lambda =0$, co-closedness is equivalent to harmonicity. The Gauduchon representative exists by theorem 11.4.2 , and conformal changes preserve the LCK condition. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{d}(\omega ^{n-1})=(n-1)\lambda \wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ give \[   egin{split}  -\int _ X\mathrm{d}\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1} & =-\int _ X\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \mathrm{d}(\omega ^{n-1})\ & =(n-1)\int _ X\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \omega ^{n-1}. \end{split}  \] For a real one-form, $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =\mathrm i\lambda ^{1,0}\wedge \lambda ^{0,1}/(2\pi )$ is semipositive, and its trace with respect to $\omega $ is positive wherever $\lambda 
e 0$. This proves the last assertion. $\square$ The same construction applies to every closed real one-form and defines a linear map 624B1D55AC6E 23.2.9  egin{equation}  j_ X:H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R), \qquad [\lambda ]\longmapsto \{ \kappa _\lambda \} , \end{equation} which we call the Lee map . It is well defined, since replacing $\lambda $ by $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$ replaces $\kappa _\lambda $ by $\kappa _\lambda -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$. Consequently, the pairing of $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ with any Gauduchon form $\gamma ^{n-1}$ is well defined. For a strictly LCK structure, the Gauduchon representative in its conformal class gives a strictly positive pairing by ( 23.2.8 ). In particular $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} 
e 0$, although its image in de Rham cohomology is zero. Corollary 23.2.10 . F6950D5704C9 If $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric, then no class in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is big. In particular, $X$ does not belong to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$. Proof. If there were a big class, the modification criterion recalled in section 10.10 would give a modification $\pi :Y	o X$ with $Y$ compact Kähler. The form $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact, so the $\partial  ar\partial $-lemma on $Y$ gives a smooth real function $h$ on $Y$ with $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Since $\pi $ has degree one, pushing forward gives the current identity $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\pi _*h)$. By Stokes' theorem, the pairing of this current with a Gauduchon form is zero, which contradicts ( 23.2.8 ) for the Gauduchon representative of the LCK structure. $\square$ For the Hopf manifold considered below, $\kappa _\lambda =\alpha $ is a smooth semipositive form, so its class is nef. Its non-nef locus is empty, whereas its non-Kähler locus is all of $X$, by the convention for classes that are not big in section 10.10 . These statements concern the closed class $\{ \alpha \} $; the Monge–Ampère equations on the Hopf manifold use instead the strictly positive, nonclosed form $\omega $. Proposition 23.2.11 . 26993B1C8C74 Suppose that $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $ and that $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ is pseudoeffective. Then $X$ admits no balanced metric. Proof. Let $T=\kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ be a closed positive current representing the class. It is nonzero, since the class is nonzero, and it is de Rham exact. If a Hermitian metric $b$ were balanced, then $\mathrm{d}(b^{n-1})=0$, and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  \int _ XT\wedge b^{n-1}=0.  \] This is impossible, since the mass of a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current against a smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form is strictly positive. $\square$ The balanced obstruction motivates the following conjecture. Conjecture 23.2.12 . 4EA8A1D43A8C If $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $, then the Bott–Chern class $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ is pseudoeffective. The positivity in ( 23.2.8 ) tests the class only against the Gauduchon representative of the LCK metric. By theorem 11.6.1 , pseudoeffectivity requires a nonnegative pairing with every Gauduchon metric.

The form $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact, so the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma on $Y$ gives a smooth real function $h$ on $Y$ with $\pi ^*\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$. Since $\pi $ has degree one, pushing forward gives the current identity $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\pi _*h)$. By Stokes' theorem, the pairing of this current with a Gauduchon form is zero, which contradicts ( 23.2.8 ) for the Gauduchon representative of the LCK structure. $\square$

title: Proposition 23.2.11
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Proposition 23.2.11 . 26993B1C8C74 Suppose that $X$ carries a strictly LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $ and that $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ is pseudoeffective. Then $X$ admits no balanced metric. Proof. Let $T=\kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ be a closed positive current representing the class. It is nonzero, since the class is nonzero, and it is de Rham exact. If a Hermitian metric $b$ were balanced, then $\mathrm{d}(b^{n-1})=0$, and Stokes' theorem for currents would give \[  \int _ XT\wedge b^{n-1}=0.  \] This is impossible, since the mass of a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current against a smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form is strictly positive. $\square$

title: Conjecture 23.2.12
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry

title: 23.2.13 The least eigenvalue of Lee curvature
search_title: The least eigenvalue of Lee curvature
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Fix a strictly LCK metric $\omega $ with Lee form $\lambda $. The volume along $\omega +t\kappa _\lambda $ increases as long as this form is positive. If the least relative eigenvalue of $\kappa _\lambda $ is a negative constant, the first boundary form has a kernel everywhere and its total volume is zero. This contradiction gives a pointwise positivity criterion. Set $Q=\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\geq 0$. The form $Q$ is nonzero on an open set, since $\lambda $ is not exact and hence is not identically zero. Proposition 23.2.14 . E5F423FF7707 On the interval where $\eta _ t=\omega +t\kappa _\lambda >0$, the polynomial $V(t)=\int _ X\eta _ t^ n$ has degree at most $n-1$ and \[  V'(t)=n(n-1)\int _ XQ\wedge \omega \wedge \eta _ t^{n-2}>0.  \] Proof. Since $\mathrm d\eta _ t=\lambda \wedge \omega $ and $\mathrm d\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=-\kappa _\lambda $, Stokes' theorem gives \[  0=\int _ X\mathrm d(\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \eta _ t^{n-1}) =-\int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \eta _ t^{n-1} +(n-1)\int _ XQ\wedge \omega \wedge \eta _ t^{n-2}.  \] Differentiating the wedge polynomial proves the formula. The integrand on the right is positive wherever $\lambda \ne 0$, including when $n=2$. Its integral is therefore strictly positive. Finally, $\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact, so \[  \int _ X\kappa _\lambda ^ n =-\int _ X\mathrm d(\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge \kappa _\lambda ^{n-1})=0.  \] This removes the coefficient of degree $n$. $\square$ Theorem 23.2.15 . B8583A0E17A6 If the least eigenvalue of $\kappa _\lambda $ relative to $\omega $ is constant on $X$, then it is zero and $\kappa _\lambda $ is semipositive. Its ordinary Bott–Chern class is nonzero and pseudoeffective. If all relative eigenvalues are constant, the rank is constant and lies between $1$ and $n-1$. In particular, the conclusion holds on a compact quotient $\Gamma \backslash G$ with left-invariant complex structure and strictly LCK tensors. Proof. Let $r$ be the constant least relative eigenvalue. If $r<0$, put $t_0=-1/r$. Then $\eta _ t>0$ for $0\leq t<t_0$, whereas $\eta _{t_0}$ is semipositive with a kernel at every point. Thus $V(t_0)=0$. The preceding proposition and polynomial continuity instead give $V(t_0)\geq V(0)>0$. This proves $r\geq 0$ and semipositivity. The nonnegative smooth form $\kappa _\lambda ^ n$ has integral zero by the same proposition, hence vanishes everywhere. Thus the least eigenvalue is zero at every point. Applying the Lee degree ( 23.2.8 ) to a conformal Gauduchon representative, as above, proves that the class is nonzero. The form $\kappa _\lambda $ itself represents it positively. Constant spectrum gives constant rank. The positive pairing ( 23.2.8 ) excludes rank zero, and the vanishing top power excludes rank $n$. On the stated compact quotient, the relative matrix is constant in a left-invariant frame, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ The class is also nef: the same representative is bounded below by $-\epsilon h$ for every Hermitian form $h$ and every $\epsilon >0$. Thus proposition 23.2.11 excludes balanced metrics under the least-eigenvalue hypothesis. The hypothesis concerns the chosen LCK metric. The other eigenvalues may vary, as the following examples show. They also explain why first degeneration of a volume ray need not force its total volume to vanish without the constant-minimum condition. Example 23.2.16 . BBCE95D98A62 On the scalar Hopf manifold $H_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto z/2\rangle $, for every $n\geq 2$, there is a strictly LCK metric with indefinite Lee curvature and a smooth semipositive representative of its ordinary Bott–Chern class. The first boundary reached for increasing $t>0$ in $\omega +t\kappa _\lambda $ has positive total volume. Proof. Fix $0<\epsilon <1$ and put \[  \rho =\sum _ j|z_ j|^2,\qquad \Phi =\rho +\epsilon \operatorname {Re}(z_1^2),\qquad \omega =\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho }{\Phi },\qquad \lambda =-\mathrm d\log \Phi .  \] The bounds $(1-\epsilon )\rho \leq \Phi \leq (1+\epsilon )\rho $ give positivity. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ and both $\Phi $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ scale by $1/4$ under $z\mapsto z/2$, the metric and Lee form descend and satisfy the LCK equation. Polar coordinates identify the quotient with $S^{2n-1}\times (\mathbb R/(\log 2)\mathbb Z)$, so it is compact and connected. The Lee period from $z$ to $z/2$ is $2\log 2$, which proves strictness. Here $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \Phi $. With $F_ i=\bar z_ i+\epsilon z_1\delta _{i1}$, its complex Hessian is \[  (\log \Phi )_{i\bar j} =\frac{\delta _{ij}}{\Phi } -\frac{F_ i\overline{F_ j}}{\Phi ^2}.  \] Relative to $\omega $, the eigenvalues are $1$ with multiplicity $n-1$ and $h=1-|F|^2/\Phi $. Writing $z_1=x+\mathrm i y$ and $B=\sum _{j>1}|z_ j|^2$, one finds \[  h=\frac{\epsilon ((1-\epsilon )y^2-(1+\epsilon )x^2)}{(1+\epsilon )x^2+(1-\epsilon )y^2+B}, \qquad -\epsilon \leq h\leq \epsilon .  \] At $(1,0,\ldots ,0)$ the spectrum is $-\epsilon ,1,\ldots ,1$, hence is indefinite. The bounded smooth function $u=\log \rho -\log \Phi $ is deck invariant, and \[  \kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \rho \geq 0,  \] by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the Hessian of $\log \rho $. The correction also gives the standard Hopf conformal representative: $\mathrm e^{-u}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho /\rho $. The first boundary occurs at $t_0=1/\epsilon $. At that value, \[  1+h/\epsilon =\frac{2(1-\epsilon )y^2+B}{\Phi }.  \] It vanishes only on the real $z_1$ rays with the remaining coordinates zero. The other relative eigenvalues of $\omega +t_0\kappa _\lambda $ equal $1+1/\epsilon >0$. The boundary form is therefore semipositive and its top power is positive on a nonempty open set, proving positive total volume. $\square$ Example 23.2.17 . EB59EA55107F For every $n\geq 2$, the same $H_ n$ carries a family of strictly LCK metrics whose least Lee-curvature eigenvalue is identically zero and whose remaining relative spectrum is nonconstant. Thus constancy of the least eigenvalue is strictly weaker than constancy of the whole spectrum. Proof. Put $q=|z_1|^2$ and, for $0<\epsilon <1$, define \[  \Psi =\rho +\epsilon \frac{q^2}{\rho },\qquad \omega _\epsilon =\frac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi }{\rho },\qquad \lambda =-\mathrm d\log \rho .  \] For $a=q/\rho \in [0,1]$, direct differentiation gives \[  \left(\frac{q^2}{\rho }\right)_{i\bar j} =\frac{2}{\rho }(q_ i-a\rho _ i)(q_{\bar j}-a\rho _{\bar j}) +2a\delta _{i1}\delta _{j1}-a^2\delta _{ij}.  \] The first two terms are positive semidefinite and $a^2\leq 1$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq (1-\epsilon )\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho >0$. The potential is smooth on the punctured space and scales by $1/4$ under the deck map. Hence $\omega _\epsilon $ descends, satisfies the LCK equation and has Lee period $2\log 2$. Its Lee curvature is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \rho $, which is semipositive of rank $n-1$. The least relative eigenvalue is consequently zero everywhere. At $(1,0,\ldots ,0)$, the Hessian of $q^2/\rho $ is $\operatorname {diag}(1,-1,\ldots ,-1)$, giving the spectrum \[  0,(1-\epsilon )^{-1},\ldots ,(1-\epsilon )^{-1}.  \] At $(0,1,0,\ldots ,0)$ the term $q^2/\rho $ vanishes to fourth order, so its Hessian is zero and the spectrum is $0,1,\ldots ,1$. These spectra differ for every $\epsilon >0$. $\square$
