title: 23.2.18 Ordinary and twisted potentials
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Let $\omega $ be an LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda $. The Kähler covering provides a potential calculus compatible with the Lee equation. Conjugating the ordinary differential operators by the local conformal factor produces a twisted complex Hessian on $X$. For the fixed closed one-form $\lambda $, define \[  \mathrm{d}_\lambda =\mathrm{d}-\lambda \wedge , \qquad \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda =\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}-\lambda ^{\mathrm c}\wedge , \qquad D_\lambda =\mathrm{d}_\lambda \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda .  \] On a chart where $\lambda =\mathrm{d}f$, these operators satisfy A1632B661AC9 23.2.19 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}\mathrm{e}^{-f}, \qquad \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{e}^{-f}, \qquad D_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathrm{e}^{-f}. \end{equation} These identities show that $D_\lambda u$ is a real $(1,1)$-form for every smooth real function $u$, and that $\mathrm{d}_\lambda D_\lambda u=0$. Proposition 23.2.20 . B365A2A75E69 Let $u$ be a smooth real function. Then \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)-\lambda \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) =-\lambda \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,  \] whereas \[  \mathrm{d}(\omega +D_\lambda u) =\lambda \wedge (\omega +D_\lambda u).  \] Consequently, an ordinary potential preserves the LCK equation with the same Lee form precisely when $\lambda \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$. A twisted potential always preserves that equation, and it gives an LCK metric whenever $\omega +D_\lambda u>0$. Proof. The first identity follows from $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega =\lambda \wedge \omega $. The second follows from $\mathrm{d}_\lambda \omega =0$ and ( 23.2.19 ). $\square$ On the Kähler covering, a twisted potential becomes the automorphic function $\widetilde u=\mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*u$, and 48546D806E67 23.2.21 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{e}^{-F}\pi ^*(\omega +D_\lambda u) =\widetilde\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u. \end{equation} The top power $(\widetilde\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u)^ n$ transforms by $\chi ^ n$ under deck transformations, so its ratio to $\widetilde\omega ^ n$ is invariant and descends to $X$. A measure on $X$ is obtained from this ratio only after a metric in the conformal class has been fixed; the automorphic top-degree form cannot simply be integrated over the noncompact cover. The two kinds of potentials also differ in their normalization. Expanding the twisted Hessian gives F2EE69C448EB 23.2.22 \begin{equation}  D_\lambda u =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\mathrm{d}u\wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} -\lambda \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u +u\bigl (\kappa _\lambda +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}\bigr ). \end{equation} In particular, $D_\lambda 1=\kappa _\lambda +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ need not vanish, so adding a constant to $u$ can change the metric $\omega +D_\lambda u$. The usual normalization $\sup _ Xu=0$ is therefore not harmless for twisted equations. For a chosen Lee form $\lambda $ in its de Rham class, the real twisted Bott–Chern group in bidegree $(1,1)$ is \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC},\lambda }(X,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ \eta \in C^\infty (X,\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}): \mathrm{d}_\lambda \eta =0\} }{D_\lambda C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)}.  \] This is Bott–Chern cohomology with values in the weight bundle, OV24LCK ]. It differs both from ordinary Bott–Chern cohomology and from the quotient of all backgrounds by ordinary $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-terms considered in section 10.30 .

title: 23.2.23 The Vaisman metric on the Hopf manifold
search_title: The Vaisman metric on the Hopf manifold
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Return to the Hopf threefold and the forms $s$, $\alpha $, $\beta $ and $\omega =\alpha +\beta $ of section 23.1 ; recall that $s=\log |z|^2$ on the covering $\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} $. The radial description makes the Lee form explicit and shows that this Gauduchon metric is also Vaisman. Proposition 23.2.24 . 32084430C8AD The Gauduchon form $\omega =\alpha +\beta $ of section 23.1 is Vaisman, with Lee form $\lambda =-\mathrm{d}s$, and \[  \kappa _\lambda =\alpha , \qquad D_\lambda 1=\omega .  \] In particular, the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 fails for the ordinary potential theory of a background that is simultaneously Gauduchon and Vaisman. Proof. Using $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ and $\beta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, direct differentiation gives \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =-\mathrm{d}s\wedge \alpha =-\mathrm{d}s\wedge \omega , \qquad \mathrm{e}^ s\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{e}^ s)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2.  \] Although $s$ is not a function on the quotient, $\mathrm{d}s$ descends to it. Its integral along the loop induced by $z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z$ is $-2$, so the Lee form is not exact. Let $g_{S^5}$ be the round metric on the unit sphere. Up to a constant factor, the Riemannian metric associated with $\omega $ on the cover is \[  \frac{|\mathrm{d}z|^2}{|z|^2} =\mathrm{d}t^2+g_{S^5},\qquad t=\log |z|.  \] The one-form $\mathrm{d}t$ is parallel for this product metric, which proves the Vaisman condition. Finally, $\kappa _\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=\alpha $ and $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}=\beta $, so $D_\lambda 1=\omega $ by ( 23.2.22 ). The unbounded masses are given by theorem 23.1.1 . $\square$ The unbounded masses arise in the ordinary family $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, whose members need not satisfy the Lee equation. The volume problem within the class of Vaisman metrics imposes this additional geometric constraint.

title: 23.2.25 Volume equations in Gauduchon gauge
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Let $X$ again be a compact LCK manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. Prescribing the volume of an LCK metric in Gauduchon gauge couples two equations: one for the determinant and one for the conformal factor. To compare metrics with a fixed Lee class, we first identify the twisted groups for cohomologous Lee forms. For a closed real one-form $\lambda $, smooth real functions $a,u$ and a smooth differential form $\eta $, multiplication by $\mathrm{e}^{-a}$ gives \[  \mathrm{d}_\lambda (\mathrm{e}^{-a}\eta ) =\mathrm{e}^{-a}\mathrm{d}_{\lambda +\mathrm{d}a}\eta , \qquad D_\lambda (\mathrm{e}^{-a}u)=\mathrm{e}^{-a}D_{\lambda +\mathrm{d}a}u.  \] We use this identification when comparing classes; the additive constant in $a$ corresponds to a constant rescaling of the weight bundle. Let $\omega _1$ be an LCK Gauduchon metric with Lee form $\lambda $, and let $\omega _2$ be an LCK metric with Lee form $\lambda +\mathrm{d}a$. If their twisted classes agree under the chosen identification, then \[  \mathrm{e}^{-a}\omega _2=\omega _1+D_\lambda u=:A>0  \] for a smooth real function $u$. Substituting $\omega _2=\mathrm{e}^ aA$ shows that $\omega _2$ has the same volume form as $\omega _1$ and is Gauduchon exactly when C2B05F8B6DCA 23.2.26 \begin{equation}  \begin{cases}  A^ n=\mathrm{e}^{-na}\omega _1^ n,\\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)a}A^{n-1}\bigr )=0. \end{cases} \end{equation} The scalar Hermitian equation of section 14.1 does not impose the second equation, and it uses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in place of $D_\lambda u$. The prescribed-volume Gauduchon theorem, theorem 14.10.1 , does not assert that its solution is LCK or lies in the given twisted class. Problem 23.2.27 . 3B2DB14C0DFF Does a compact LCK manifold have at most one Gauduchon LCK metric with a given Lee class, a given twisted Bott–Chern class and a given smooth positive volume form? The identification of classes makes this uniqueness problem precise. The question concerns metrics: uniqueness of a scalar potential $u$ would additionally require control of the kernel of $D_\lambda $. The counterexamples with degenerate densities in section 14.20 concern ordinary potentials and do not decide this question.

title: 23.2.28 Invariant volumes on Vaisman manifolds
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
The flows of the Lee and anti-Lee vector fields preserve a Vaisman metric. For a prescribed volume invariant under these flows, uniqueness for the smooth Hermitian equation forces the potential to be constant along them. Stokes' theorem in the transverse directions then fixes the normalizing constant, and changing the Lee form by the differential of the potential produces a Vaisman metric with the prescribed volume. Theorem 23.2.29 . 19781C771E9D Let $\omega $ be a Vaisman metric on $X$ with Lee form $\lambda $, and let $\mu $ be a smooth positive volume form invariant under the flows of both the Lee field $\lambda ^\sharp $ and the anti-Lee field $J\lambda ^\sharp $. Assume \[  \int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n.  \] Then there is a unique Vaisman metric $\omega '$ with Lee class $[\lambda ]$ and $(\omega ')^ n=\mu $. We first describe the transverse geometry and the integration of transverse forms. Let $g$ be the Riemannian metric of $\omega $. Since $\lambda $ is parallel and not identically zero, it has constant squared norm $s=|\lambda |_ g^2>0$. Write \[  A=s^{-1}\lambda ^\sharp ,\qquad B=JA,\qquad 	au = rac{s}{4\pi },\qquad \eta =\kappa _\lambda .  \] Thus $\lambda (A)=1$ and $\lambda (B)=0$. Since $
abla \lambda =0$, the identity ( 23.2.4 ) gives 9A2166571118 23.2.30  egin{equation}   egin{split}  	au \omega & =\eta +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c},\  \eta (U,JV)& = rac1{4\pi } igl (sg(U,V)-\lambda (U)\lambda (V)-\lambda (JU)\lambda (JV) igr ). \end{split} \end{equation} To obtain these identities, use $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=-\lambda \circ J/(4\pi )$ and antisymmetrize $
abla \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$; the terms containing $
abla \lambda $ vanish. In particular, $\eta $ is a closed semipositive $(1,1)$-form whose kernel is the span $\mathcal F$ of $A$ and $B$. The field $A$ is parallel, and the same connection formula yields \[  
abla _ U B=	frac 12 igl (-JU+\lambda (U)B+\lambda (JU)A igr ), \qquad 
abla _ AJ=0.  \] The first identity shows that $B$ is a Killing field and that $[A,B]=0$. The second shows that $A$ is holomorphic, and integrability of $J$ then shows that $B=JA$ is holomorphic. Their flows preserve $g$, $J$, $\lambda $ and $\eta $. Consequently $\mathcal F$ is a holomorphic foliation by complex curves, and $\eta $ induces a Kähler form on each local transverse space. A form is called horizontal if its contractions with $A$ and $B$ vanish. A smooth function $v$ is basic for $\mathcal F$ if $Av=Bv=0$. For such a function, $\mathrm{d}v$, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ are horizontal and invariant under both flows; for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ this follows from Cartan's formula. Put $m=n-1$ and $\eta _ v=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Then E3B61067B040 23.2.31  egin{equation}  \int _ X\eta _ v^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =\int _ X\eta ^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}. \end{equation} Indeed, $\eta _ v^ m-\eta ^ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$, where $T=\sum _{j=0}^{m-1}\eta _ v^ j\wedge \eta ^{m-1-j}$ is closed and horizontal. Since $\mathrm{d}(\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c})=\lambda \wedge \eta $, the differential of $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge T\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ plus a term containing the horizontal form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge T\wedge \eta $ of degree $2m+1$, which vanishes because the transverse real dimension is $2m$. Stokes' theorem therefore proves ( 23.2.31 ). The following transverse maximum principle identifies the metric once its scale has been fixed. Proposition 23.2.32 . FCE8FB3BF729 Let $\mathcal F$ be a foliation of a connected compact manifold $M$ with a transverse holomorphic structure of complex dimension $m\geq 1$. Let $\eta _0,\eta _1$ be transverse Kähler forms, and let $v$ be a smooth real basic function, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ computed in transverse holomorphic coordinates. Suppose \[  \eta _1=\eta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v, \qquad \eta _1^ m=\eta _0^ m.  \] Then $v$ is constant and $\eta _1=\eta _0$. Proof. The function $v$ is constant on each local plaque. On every transverse coordinate chart it satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \sum _{j=0}^{m-1}\eta _1^ j\wedge \eta _0^{m-1-j}=0.  \] This is a linear elliptic equation without zeroth-order term. Let $c=\max _ Mv$. If $v=c$ at some point, the strong maximum principle on a connected transverse chart shows that $v=c$ throughout that chart, and since $v$ is basic, $v=c$ on the corresponding foliation chart. Hence $\{ v=c\} $ is nonempty, open and closed, and connectedness of $M$ proves the assertion. $\square$ of theorem 23.2.29 . Replacing $\omega $ by $	au \omega $ and $\mu $ by $	au ^ n\mu $ does not change the Lee form or the assertion, and it makes the new constant $	au $ equal to one. We may therefore assume $	au =1$, so that $\omega =\eta +\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$. Write $\mu =f\omega ^ n$; since $\mu $ and $\omega ^ n$ are invariant under both flows, the positive smooth function $f$ is basic. Existence. By theorem 14.2.1 , there are a unique smooth function $u$ and a unique constant $b$ such that \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mathrm{e}^ b f\omega ^ n, \qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0,\qquad \sup _ Xu=0.  \] Pullback by the flow of $A$ or of $B$ preserves the equation and the normalization, so uniqueness shows that $u$ is basic. Hence $\eta _ u=\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a transverse Kähler form, and \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}.  \] Integrating over $X$ and using ( 23.2.31 ) and $\int _ X\mu =\int _ X\omega ^ n$ gives $b=0$. Set $\lambda _ u=\lambda -\mathrm{d}u$ and 1958C8BBF316 23.2.33  egin{equation}  \omega _ u'=\eta _ u+\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}. \end{equation} Here $\eta _ u=\kappa _{\lambda _ u}$ has kernel $\mathcal F$, while $\lambda _ u(A)=1$ and $\lambda _ u(B)=0$; together these facts give $\omega _ u'>0$. Direct differentiation gives $\mathrm{d}\omega _ u'=\lambda _ u\wedge \omega _ u'$. Since $u$ is basic, $A$ is a holomorphic Killing field for the Riemannian metric $g_ u'$ of $\omega _ u'$, and ( 23.2.33 ) gives \[  g_ u'(A,\cdot )= rac1{4\pi }\lambda _ u.  \] Since $\lambda _ u$ is closed, $
abla ^{g_ u'}A$ is symmetric, whereas the Killing equation makes it skew-symmetric. Thus $A$ and $\lambda _ u$ are parallel, so $\omega _ u'$ is Vaisman with Lee class $[\lambda ]$. Finally, $\eta _ u^ m$ has top transverse degree, and every term of $\lambda _ u\wedge \lambda _ u^{\mathrm c}-\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ contains a horizontal one-form. Therefore \[  (\omega _ u')^ n =n\eta _ u^ m\wedge \lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c} =(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu .  \] Uniqueness. Let $\widehat\omega $ be another Vaisman solution, with Lee form $\widehat\lambda =\lambda +\mathrm{d}v$, and denote by $\widehat s,\widehat	au ,\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat\eta $ the corresponding objects for $\widehat\omega $. The form $\eta +\widehat\eta $ is de Rham exact and semipositive. Its top power is nonnegative and has zero integral, so it vanishes everywhere, and $\eta +\widehat\eta $ has a nonzero kernel at every point. The kernel of a sum of two semipositive Hermitian forms is the intersection of their kernels. Since both kernels are complex lines, they coincide, and both metrics define the same foliation $\mathcal F$. The nowhere vanishing holomorphic vector field $A-\mathrm iB$ trivializes the holomorphic tangent bundle of $\mathcal F$. The analogous field $\widehat A-\mathrm i\widehat B$ is a holomorphic multiple of it, and the multiple is constant because $X$ is compact. Write $\widehat A=aA+bB$ with $a,b\in \mathbb R$. Since $\widehat\lambda (\widehat A)=1$ and $\widehat\lambda (\widehat B)=0$, \[  \widehat A v=1-a,\qquad \widehat B v=b.  \] Both fields are complete and $v$ is bounded, so $v$ cannot grow linearly along their flows; hence these constants vanish, and $a=1$, $b=0$. Thus $\widehat A=A$, $\widehat B=B$, and $v$ is basic. From ( 23.2.30 ) we obtain the contraction formulas 8455EE64C6A0 23.2.34  egin{equation}  \iota _ B\iota _ A\widehat\omega ^ n = rac{n}{4\pi \widehat	au ^ n}\widehat\eta ^ m, \qquad \iota _ B\iota _ A(\omega _ u')^ n= rac{n}{4\pi }\eta _ u^ m. \end{equation} Since the two volume forms are equal, $\widehat\eta ^ m=\widehat	au ^ n\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta =\eta -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $v$ is basic, integrating against $\lambda \wedge \lambda ^{\mathrm c}$ and applying ( 23.2.31 ) twice gives $\widehat	au ^ n=1$. Thus $\widehat	au =1$ and $\widehat\eta ^ m=\eta _ u^ m$. Since $\widehat\eta -\eta _ u=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+u)$, proposition 23.2.32 shows that $v+u$ is constant. It follows that $\widehat\lambda =\lambda _ u$, $\widehat\eta =\eta _ u$ and $\widehat\omega =\omega _ u'$. $\square$

Since $\widehat\lambda (\widehat A)=1$ and $\widehat\lambda (\widehat B)=0$, \[  \widehat A v=1-a,\qquad \widehat B v=b.  \] Both fields are complete and $v$ is bounded, so $v$ cannot grow linearly along their flows; hence these constants vanish, and $a=1$, $b=0$. title: 23.2.35 Radial volumes on scalar Hopf manifolds
search_title: Radial volumes on scalar Hopf manifolds
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Let $n\geq 2$, put $m=n-1$, and consider the scalar Hopf manifold and its projection to $\mathbb P^ m$, \[  H_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm e z\rangle , \qquad q:H_ n\longrightarrow \mathbb P^ m.  \] Let $\omega _{\rm FS}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ m$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ m}\omega _{\rm FS}^ m=1$. The function $r=\log |z|^2$ is well defined modulo $2$ on $H_ n$, so its differential is a global one-form. Set \[  \alpha =q^*\omega _{\rm FS}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r,\qquad \beta =\mathrm dr\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r.  \] Both forms are defined on $H_ n$. The form $\alpha $ has rank $m$, and its kernel is the complex radial line; the form $\beta $ has rank one, and its kernel is the complementary horizontal subspace. Thus $\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta $ is a positive volume form. On each elliptic fiber of $q$, where $z$ moves along a complex line through the origin, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r=\mathrm d\arg z/(2\pi )$, so \[  \int _{q^{-1}(x)}\beta =2,\qquad \int _{H_ n}\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta =2.  \] We consider all metrics of the radial form 2622F07FBE04 23.2.36 \begin{equation}  \omega =C(r)\alpha +D(r)\beta ,\qquad C,D\in C^\infty (\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z),\quad C,D>0. \end{equation} The circle $\mathbb R/2\mathbb Z$ of values of $r$ is oriented by increasing $r$. The Lee period of such a metric is the integral of its Lee form over a radial loop along which $r$ increases from $0$ to $2$. Lemma 23.2.37 . AE38387ABD03 Every metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) is strictly LCK. Its Lee form and Lee period are \[  \lambda =l(r)\, \mathrm dr,\qquad l=\frac{C'-D}{C},\qquad L=-\int _0^2\frac{D}{C}\, \mathrm dr<0.  \] The metric is Gauduchon if and only if $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ for a constant $k$. In terms of the positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F=C^ mD$, this condition is equivalent to 0452243D80CF 23.2.38 \begin{equation}  C^ mC'=kC+F,\qquad D=\frac{F}{C^ m}. \end{equation} Every positive periodic solution has $k<0$, and 9A128F70476F 23.2.39 \begin{equation}  \begin{gathered} k\int _0^2C\, \mathrm dr+\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr=0, \\ l=kC^{-m},\qquad L(C)=-\int _0^2\frac{F}{C^{m+1}}\, \mathrm dr. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Proof. The differential identities are \[  \begin{gathered} \alpha ^{m+1}=\beta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm d\beta =-\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha ,\\ \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\beta =-\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =-\alpha ^2. \end{gathered}  \] They give $\mathrm d\omega =(C'-D)\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha =\lambda \wedge \omega $. The closed form $\lambda $ is the Lee form, since wedging one-forms with $\omega $ is injective. The integral of $C'/C$ over a period is zero, which proves the formula for $L$; since $L\neq 0$, the Lee form is not exact. Two radial Lee forms have the same de Rham class exactly when their periods agree: a difference with zero period has a periodic primitive, and the radial loop detects the converse. For a smooth function $G$ of $r$, the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=G'\alpha +G''\beta $. Also $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(G\beta )=-G\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$, so \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(G\beta )=-G'\alpha \wedge \beta -G\alpha ^2.  \] Expanding the powers of $\omega $ therefore gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \omega ^ m& =C^ m\alpha ^ m+mC^{m-1}D\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \beta ,\\  \omega ^ n& =nC^ mD\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta , \end{aligned}  \] and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ m)= \bigl [(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'\bigr ]\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Since $(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'=m\bigl (C^{m-1}(C'-D)\bigr )'$, this vanishes exactly when $C^{m-1}(C'-D)$ is constant. Multiplying the identity $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ by $C$ gives ( 23.2.38 ). Since $C^ mC'$ has zero integral over a period, integrating ( 23.2.38 ) gives the first identity in ( 23.2.39 ), which forces $k<0$. The formulas for $l$ and $L$ follow from the formula for the Lee form. $\square$ Lemma 23.2.40 . 1D02D96B9AF2 For fixed $F>0$ and each $k<0$, there is at most one positive $2$-periodic solution of ( 23.2.38 ). If $k_2>k_1$, the corresponding solutions satisfy $C_2>C_1$ everywhere and $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. Proof. Suppose $k_2>k_1$, and put $R=C_2-C_1$. At a zero of $R$, the equation gives $R'=(k_2-k_1)C_1^{1-m}>0$. Such zeros are isolated, so there are finitely many on the circle. A periodic differentiable function cannot cross zero only upwards, since returning around the circle would require a downward crossing. Hence $R$ has no zero and a constant strict sign. The identity $\int _0^2C_ i\, \mathrm dr=-\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr/k_ i$ shows that this sign is positive, and the formula for $L(C)$ in ( 23.2.39 ) then gives $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. For equal $k$, uniqueness for the smooth scalar equation $C'=kC^{1-m}+FC^{-m}$ on $C>0$ shows that two solutions which meet coincide. Two solutions which never meet are strictly ordered, which contradicts the equality of their integrals. This proves uniqueness for fixed $k$. $\square$ Theorem 23.2.41 . C4C3411B46C3 For every positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F$ and every $L_0<0$, there is exactly one metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) which is Gauduchon, has Lee period $L_0$, and satisfies \[  \omega ^ n=nF(r)\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Proof. Fix $k<0$, put $c=-k$, and let $f_0=\min F>0$ and $f_1=\max F$. The constant functions $f_0/c$ and $f_1/c$ are a subsolution and a supersolution, respectively, of $C'=C^{-m}(F-cC)$. By comparison, the forward flow of this equation preserves the compact interval $I_ k=[f_0/c,f_1/c]$ of positive numbers, and existence and uniqueness for smooth ordinary differential equations give a continuous time-two map $I_ k\to I_ k$. Its difference from the identity is nonnegative at the left endpoint and nonpositive at the right one, so the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point; if $f_0=f_1$, the constant $C=f_0/c$ is the solution. Since the equation is periodic, the solution through a fixed point extends to a smooth positive periodic solution. It is unique by lemma 23.2.40 and satisfies 07070AFDA51C 23.2.42 \begin{equation}  \frac{f_0}{-k}\leq C_ k(r)\leq \frac{f_1}{-k}. \end{equation} By lemma 23.2.40 , the period $L(k)=-\int _0^2F/C_ k^{m+1}\, \mathrm dr$ is strictly increasing in $k$. It is also continuous. Indeed, for $k$ in a compact neighborhood of any $k_0<0$, ( 23.2.42 ) gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds for $C_ k$, and the equation then bounds all derivatives. Any sequence $k\to k_0$ therefore has smoothly convergent subsequences, and the equation and uniqueness identify every limit with $C_{k_0}$. Thus $C_ k\to C_{k_0}$ uniformly, which gives continuity of the integral. The same bounds imply $L(k)\to 0$ as $k\uparrow 0$ and $L(k)\to -\infty $ as $k\to -\infty $. Hence exactly one $k$ has period $L_0$. For this $k$, set $D=F/C_ k^ m$. The identities of lemma 23.2.37 show that $C_ k\alpha +D\beta $ has the required properties. Conversely, every metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) with these properties gives a positive periodic solution of the same equation, so the ordering of the periods also proves uniqueness. $\square$ Proposition 23.2.43 . 503628CC8BE5 Let $\omega $ be a metric as in theorem 23.2.41 , with Lee form $\lambda $. There is a positive smooth function $U$ on $H_ n$ with $\omega =D_\lambda U$; in particular, the class of $\omega $ in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC},\lambda }(H_ n,\mathbb R)$ is zero. If $\omega _1,\omega _2$ are two such metrics, with positive potentials $U_1,U_2$ and cohomologous Lee forms $\lambda _1$ and $\lambda _2=\lambda _1+\mathrm da$, then for every choice of the additive constant in $a$, \[  \mathrm e^{-a}\omega _2-\omega _1=D_{\lambda _1}(\mathrm e^{-a}U_2-U_1).  \] In particular, among metrics of the form ( 23.2.36 ), a solution of ( 23.2.26 ) is determined by its volume form and Lee class, even if the potential $u$ in ( 23.2.26 ) is not assumed radial. Proof. Write $l=kC^{-m}<0$ and $f(r)=\int _0^ rl(s)\, \mathrm ds$ for real $r$. Then $f(r+2)=f(r)+L_0$. The solution of $U'-lU=C$ given by \[  \begin{aligned}  U(0)& =\frac{\mathrm e^{L_0}}{1-\mathrm e^{L_0}} \int _0^2\mathrm e^{-f(s)}C(s)\, \mathrm ds,\\  U(r)& =\mathrm e^{f(r)} \left(U(0)+\int _0^ r\mathrm e^{-f(s)}C(s)\, \mathrm ds\right) \end{aligned}  \] is positive on $[0,2]$ and satisfies $U(2)=U(0)$. Since the equation is periodic, all derivatives also match at the endpoints, so $U$ defines a positive smooth function on $H_ n$. By ( 23.2.19 ), its twisted Hessian is \[  \begin{split}  D_\lambda U & =(U'-lU)\alpha + \bigl [U''-2lU'+(l^2-l')U\bigr ]\beta \\ & =C\alpha +(C'-lC)\beta =\omega . \end{split}  \] This proves that the twisted class is zero. The identity $\mathrm e^{-a}D_{\lambda _2}U_2=D_{\lambda _1}(\mathrm e^{-a}U_2)$ of subsection 23.2.25 gives the formula for the difference. For two metrics of the form ( 23.2.36 ), equal volume forms give the same function $F$, and equal Lee classes give the same period, so theorem 23.2.41 applies. This uniqueness concerns the metric, not the potentials representing it. $\square$ Proposition 23.2.44 . A642AD47FF61 If $F$ is nonconstant, the metric of theorem 23.2.41 is not Vaisman. Proof. The radial complex line is orthogonal to $\ker \mathrm dr\cap \ker \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$. On a radial complex line, use a logarithmic coordinate $w=x+\mathrm i y$, so that $r=2x+\text{constant}$ and $\beta =\pi ^{-1}\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy$. The Riemannian metric of $\omega $ restricts there to $D\pi ^{-1}(\mathrm dx^2+\mathrm dy^2)$, whence \[  |\mathrm dr|_\omega ^2=\frac{4\pi }{D},\qquad |\lambda |_\omega ^2=4\pi k^2\frac{C^{-2m}}{D}.  \] A parallel Lee form has constant norm. Since $k\ne 0$, the Vaisman condition would therefore imply $D=Q C^{-2m}$ for a constant $Q>0$. At a maximum and at a minimum of $C$, where $C'=0$, the Gauduchon identity would then give $kC^{m+1}+Q=0$. This equation has only one positive root, so the maximum and the minimum of $C$ coincide. Thus $C$, $D$ and $F=C^ mD$ would all be constant, a contradiction. $\square$ Example 23.2.45 . FDF7812789EF For \[  \begin{gathered} 0<\varepsilon <\min \left\{ \frac12, \frac{(3/2)^{1-m}}{4\pi }\right\} , \\ C=1+\varepsilon \cos (\pi r),\qquad D=C'+C^{1-m}, \end{gathered}  \] the metric ( 23.2.36 ) is Gauduchon and non-Vaisman, with Lee form $\lambda =-C^{-m}\mathrm dr$ and density $F=C^ mC'+C$. The probability volume $\mathrm dV=\frac12\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta $ gives $\omega ^ n=2nF\, \mathrm dV$ and $\int _{H_ n}F\, \mathrm dV=1$. Proof. Since $1/2<C<3/2$ and $m\geq 1$, we have $D\geq (3/2)^{1-m}-\pi \varepsilon >\frac34(3/2)^{1-m}>0$. The Gauduchon identity holds with $k=-1$, giving the Lee form and the positive density $F=C^ mD$. Its values $F(0)=1+\varepsilon $ and $F(1)=1-\varepsilon $ differ, so proposition 23.2.44 applies. The integral of $C^ mC'$ over a period is zero and the average of $C$ is one, so integration along the fibers of $q$ gives $\int _{H_ n}F\, \mathrm dV=1$. $\square$ The volume form in this example is not invariant under the flow of the Lee field of the Vaisman metric $\alpha +\beta $, which translates $r$, so theorem 23.2.29 does not apply to it. For the new metric, the Gauduchon condition states that $lF/D=lC^ m=k$ is constant; up to a constant factor, this quantity is the flux of its Lee field through the level sets of $r$, and here it equals $-1$. The radial classification answers 23.2.27 within the family ( 23.2.36 ); uniqueness among arbitrary LCK metrics remains open.

title: Lemma 23.2.37
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 23.2.37 . AE38387ABD03 Every metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) is strictly LCK. Its Lee form and Lee period are \[  \lambda =l(r)\, \mathrm dr,\qquad l=\frac{C'-D}{C},\qquad L=-\int _0^2\frac{D}{C}\, \mathrm dr<0.  \] The metric is Gauduchon if and only if $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ for a constant $k$. In terms of the positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F=C^ mD$, this condition is equivalent to 0452243D80CF 23.2.38 \begin{equation}  C^ mC'=kC+F,\qquad D=\frac{F}{C^ m}. \end{equation} Every positive periodic solution has $k<0$, and 9A128F70476F 23.2.39 \begin{equation}  \begin{gathered} k\int _0^2C\, \mathrm dr+\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr=0, \\ l=kC^{-m},\qquad L(C)=-\int _0^2\frac{F}{C^{m+1}}\, \mathrm dr. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Proof. The differential identities are \[  \begin{gathered} \alpha ^{m+1}=\beta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm d\beta =-\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha ,\\ \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\beta =-\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =-\alpha ^2. \end{gathered}  \] They give $\mathrm d\omega =(C'-D)\mathrm dr\wedge \alpha =\lambda \wedge \omega $. The closed form $\lambda $ is the Lee form, since wedging one-forms with $\omega $ is injective. The integral of $C'/C$ over a period is zero, which proves the formula for $L$; since $L\neq 0$, the Lee form is not exact. Two radial Lee forms have the same de Rham class exactly when their periods agree: a difference with zero period has a periodic primitive, and the radial loop detects the converse. For a smooth function $G$ of $r$, the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=G'\alpha +G''\beta $. Also $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(G\beta )=-G\alpha \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$, so \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(G\beta )=-G'\alpha \wedge \beta -G\alpha ^2.  \] Expanding the powers of $\omega $ therefore gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \omega ^ m& =C^ m\alpha ^ m+mC^{m-1}D\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \beta ,\\  \omega ^ n& =nC^ mD\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta , \end{aligned}  \] and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ m)= \bigl [(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'\bigr ]\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Since $(C^ m)''-m(C^{m-1}D)'=m\bigl (C^{m-1}(C'-D)\bigr )'$, this vanishes exactly when $C^{m-1}(C'-D)$ is constant. Multiplying the identity $C^{m-1}(C'-D)=k$ by $C$ gives ( 23.2.38 ). Since $C^ mC'$ has zero integral over a period, integrating ( 23.2.38 ) gives the first identity in ( 23.2.39 ), which forces $k<0$. The formulas for $l$ and $L$ follow from the formula for the Lee form. $\square$

title: Lemma 23.2.40
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Lemma 23.2.40 . 1D02D96B9AF2 For fixed $F>0$ and each $k<0$, there is at most one positive $2$-periodic solution of ( 23.2.38 ). If $k_2>k_1$, the corresponding solutions satisfy $C_2>C_1$ everywhere and $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. Proof. Suppose $k_2>k_1$, and put $R=C_2-C_1$. At a zero of $R$, the equation gives $R'=(k_2-k_1)C_1^{1-m}>0$. Such zeros are isolated, so there are finitely many on the circle. A periodic differentiable function cannot cross zero only upwards, since returning around the circle would require a downward crossing. Hence $R$ has no zero and a constant strict sign. The identity $\int _0^2C_ i\, \mathrm dr=-\int _0^2F\, \mathrm dr/k_ i$ shows that this sign is positive, and the formula for $L(C)$ in ( 23.2.39 ) then gives $L(C_2)>L(C_1)$. For equal $k$, uniqueness for the smooth scalar equation $C'=kC^{1-m}+FC^{-m}$ on $C>0$ shows that two solutions which meet coincide. Two solutions which never meet are strictly ordered, which contradicts the equality of their integrals. This proves uniqueness for fixed $k$. $\square$

title: Theorem 23.2.41
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Theorem 23.2.41 . C4C3411B46C3 For every positive smooth $2$-periodic function $F$ and every $L_0<0$, there is exactly one metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) which is Gauduchon, has Lee period $L_0$, and satisfies \[  \omega ^ n=nF(r)\alpha ^ m\wedge \beta .  \] Proof. Fix $k<0$, put $c=-k$, and let $f_0=\min F>0$ and $f_1=\max F$. The constant functions $f_0/c$ and $f_1/c$ are a subsolution and a supersolution, respectively, of $C'=C^{-m}(F-cC)$. By comparison, the forward flow of this equation preserves the compact interval $I_ k=[f_0/c,f_1/c]$ of positive numbers, and existence and uniqueness for smooth ordinary differential equations give a continuous time-two map $I_ k\to I_ k$. Its difference from the identity is nonnegative at the left endpoint and nonpositive at the right one, so the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point; if $f_0=f_1$, the constant $C=f_0/c$ is the solution. Since the equation is periodic, the solution through a fixed point extends to a smooth positive periodic solution. It is unique by lemma 23.2.40 and satisfies 07070AFDA51C 23.2.42 \begin{equation}  \frac{f_0}{-k}\leq C_ k(r)\leq \frac{f_1}{-k}. \end{equation} By lemma 23.2.40 , the period $L(k)=-\int _0^2F/C_ k^{m+1}\, \mathrm dr$ is strictly increasing in $k$. It is also continuous. Indeed, for $k$ in a compact neighborhood of any $k_0<0$, ( 23.2.42 ) gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds for $C_ k$, and the equation then bounds all derivatives. Any sequence $k\to k_0$ therefore has smoothly convergent subsequences, and the equation and uniqueness identify every limit with $C_{k_0}$. Thus $C_ k\to C_{k_0}$ uniformly, which gives continuity of the integral. The same bounds imply $L(k)\to 0$ as $k\uparrow 0$ and $L(k)\to -\infty $ as $k\to -\infty $. Hence exactly one $k$ has period $L_0$. For this $k$, set $D=F/C_ k^ m$. The identities of lemma 23.2.37 show that $C_ k\alpha +D\beta $ has the required properties. Conversely, every metric of the form ( 23.2.36 ) with these properties gives a positive periodic solution of the same equation, so the ordering of the periods also proves uniqueness. $\square$

title: 23.2.46 Chern–Ricci flatness and Vaisman rigidity
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text:
Return to an LCK metric $\omega $ on $X$ with Lee form $\lambda $. Chern–Ricci flatness expresses the Riemannian Ricci tensor through $\lambda $ and its covariant derivative. The Bianchi and Bochner identities then relate the part of this derivative that is not $J$-invariant to the divergence of the Lee field. When the metric is Gauduchon, this divergence vanishes by proposition 23.2.7 , and the identities force the Lee form to be parallel. We write $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}=\operatorname {Ric}/(2\pi )$ for the normalized Chern–Ricci form, which represents the first Bott–Chern class $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)$, with $\operatorname {Ric}$ as in 12.34.3 . Theorem 23.2.47 . C4981F6B1F78 Let $\omega $ be a compact strictly LCK metric that is Chern–Ricci flat, and let $g$ be its associated Riemannian metric. Put $A=\lambda ^\sharp $, $q=\mathrm d_ g^*\lambda $ and \[  S^-(U,V)=	frac 12 igl ((
abla \lambda )(U,V)-(
abla \lambda )(JU,JV) igr ).  \] Then \[  \int _ X|S^-|_ g^2\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g = rac12\int _ X|q|^2\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] For this metric the following conditions are equivalent: $\omega $ is Gauduchon; $q=0$; $A$ is real holomorphic; and $\omega $ is Vaisman. Proof. We keep the divergence terms in the Ricci tensor and compare the Bianchi and Bochner identities before imposing the Gauduchon condition. All norms, traces and contractions use $g$. Put \[  B=JA,\qquad S=
abla \lambda ,\qquad S^+(U,V)=	frac 12 igl (S(U,V)+S(JU,JV) igr ),\qquad u=|\lambda |_ g^2.  \] Closedness of $\lambda $ makes $S$ symmetric, and $\operatorname {tr}_ gS=-q$. The tensors $S^+$ and $S^-=S-S^+$ are orthogonal. Write $J\lambda =-\lambda \circ J$, so that $\lambda ^{\mathrm c}=J\lambda /(4\pi )$. Step 1: the Ricci tensor. We first show that C15BADA6DBC4 23.2.48  egin{equation}  \operatorname {Ric}_ g =nS^+-(n-1)S+	frac {q-u}{2}g +	frac 12\lambda \otimes \lambda +	frac n2 J\lambda \otimes J\lambda . \end{equation} Locally write $\lambda =\mathrm df$ and put $\widetilde g=\mathrm e^{-f}g$. The real conformal Ricci formula in dimension $2n$ is \[  \operatorname {Ric}_{\widetilde g} =\operatorname {Ric}_ g+(n-1)S +	frac {n-1}{2}\lambda \otimes \lambda +	frac 12\{ -q-(n-1)u\} g.  \] The local metric $\widetilde g$ is Kähler. Since the Chern–Ricci form of $g$ vanishes, the Ricci form of $\widetilde g$ is $n\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial f=(n/2)\mathrm d(J\lambda )$. Applying ( 23.2.4 ) to $(
abla _ UJ\lambda )(V)=-S(U,JV)-\lambda ((
abla _ UJ)V)$ and antisymmetrizing gives \[  \mathrm d(J\lambda )(U,JV) =2S^+(U,V)-u g(U,V) +\lambda (U)\lambda (V)+J\lambda (U)J\lambda (V).  \] Evaluating the Kähler Ricci form on $(U,JV)$ and comparing with the conformal formula proves ( 23.2.48 ). Taking its trace gives the scalar curvature \[  s=(n-1)q-	frac {n-1}{2}u.  \] Step 2: the integral identity. Write $\| \cdot \| $ for the $L^2(g)$ norm and set \[  E_ A=\int _ X S(A,A)\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g, \qquad E_ B=\int _ X S(B,B)\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] Since $S(A,A)=A(u)/2$ and $\operatorname {div}A=-q$, integration by parts gives B65427234DA6 23.2.49  egin{equation}  \int _ Xu q\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g=2E_ A. \end{equation} Pair the contracted Bianchi identity $\delta \operatorname {Ric}_ g+\mathrm ds/2=0$ with $\lambda $ and integrate. Here $\delta $ is minus covariant contraction, the formal adjoint of the symmetric covariant derivative. Thus \[  0=\int _ X\langle \operatorname {Ric}_ g,Sangle \, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g +	frac 12\int _ Xs q\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] Substitution of equation 23.2.48 , equation 23.2.49 gives 900FA1D2D218 23.2.50  egin{equation}  0=n\| S^+\| ^2-(n-1)\| S\| ^2+	frac {n-2}{2}\| q\| ^2 +	frac {4-n}{2}E_ A+	frac n2E_ B. \end{equation} For the closed one-form $\lambda $, the integrated Bochner formula reads \[  \| q\| ^2=\| S\| ^2 +\int _ X\operatorname {Ric}_ g(A,A)\, \mathrm d\operatorname {vol}_ g.  \] The quartic terms in ( 23.2.48 ) cancel on $(A,A)$, and $J\lambda (A)=0$, so \[  \operatorname {Ric}_ g(A,A) =(1-	frac n2)S(A,A)+	frac n2 S(B,B)+	frac 12q u.  \] Using ( 23.2.49 ), we obtain 1F4612E67B59 23.2.51  egin{equation}  \| q\| ^2=\| S\| ^2+	frac {4-n}{2}E_ A+	frac n2E_ B. \end{equation} Eliminating $E_ A,E_ B$ between the two identities gives $n(\| S^+\| ^2-\| S\| ^2)+n\| q\| ^2/2=0$. Orthogonality proves the asserted identity for $S^-$. Step 3: rigidity. By proposition 23.2.7 , the Gauduchon condition is equivalent to $q=0$. In that case the integral identity forces $S=S^+$, hence $S(B,B)=S(A,A)$. Equation ( 23.2.49 ) gives $E_ A=E_ B=0$, and ( 23.2.51 ) implies $S=0$. Thus $\omega $ is Vaisman. Equation ( 23.2.4 ) gives $
abla _ AJ=0$. If $T$ is the symmetric endomorphism defined by $g(TU,V)=S(U,V)$, then \[  (\mathcal L_ AJ)V=JTV-TJV.  \] Consequently $A$ is real holomorphic exactly when $S=S^+$. The integral identity then gives $q=0$, hence $S=0$. Conversely, a parallel Lee form gives $q=0$ and $\mathcal L_ AJ=0$. Strictness ensures that the parallel Lee form is nonzero. $\square$ In the theorem, both conditions are imposed on the same metric. If $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)=0$, each conformal class of Hermitian metrics contains a Chern–Ricci-flat metric: if a smooth real function $h$ satisfies $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$, then \[  \operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\mathrm{e}^{h/n}\omega ) =\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega )-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0.  \] By Gauduchon's theorem, the same conformal class also contains a Gauduchon metric. The rigidity theorem applies when these two metrics coincide. The example below shows that changing the metric within its conformal class cannot always arrange this coincidence; the manifold existence question follows it.

title: 23.2.52 A flat conformal gauge that is not Gauduchon
search_title: A flat conformal gauge that is not Gauduchon
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: The two preferred conformal representatives need not coincide. The following example keeps the complex surface and the conformal class fixed; the obstruction is to imposing both conditions in that class. Example 23.2.53 . E37387C4675B There is a compact complex Kodaira surface with holomorphically trivial canonical bundle and a strictly LCK Chern–Ricci-flat metric $\omega $ that is not Gauduchon. No metric conformal to $\omega $ is both Gauduchon and Chern–Ricci flat, although the same conformal class contains a Vaisman metric. Proof. We construct the quotient and the two conformal metrics explicitly. On $G=\mathbb R^4$ use the multiplication \[  (x,y,z,t)(x',y',z',t') =(x+x',y+y',z+z'+xy',t+t').  \] The integer subgroup $\Gamma =\mathbb Z^4$ acts on the left by \[  (x,y,z,t)\longmapsto (x+a,y+b,z+c+ay,t+d).  \] Reducing $x,y,t$ and then $z$ to unit intervals gives a compact fundamental set, so $X=\Gamma \backslash G$ is connected and compact. The forms \[  e^1=\mathrm dx,\quad e^2=\mathrm dy,\quad e^3=\mathrm dz-x\, \mathrm dy,\quad e^4=\mathrm dt  \] descend to $X$, with $\mathrm de^3=-e^1\wedge e^2$ and the other derivatives zero. Declare $\phi ^1=e^1+\mathrm i e^2$ and $\phi ^2=e^3+\mathrm i e^4$ to be of type $(1,0)$. Since \[  \mathrm d\phi ^1=0,\qquad \mathrm d\phi ^2=-\tfrac {\mathrm i}{2}\phi ^1\wedge \overline{\phi ^1},  \] there is no $(0,2)$ component and the complex structure is integrable. The form $\Sigma =\phi ^1\wedge \phi ^2$ is closed and nowhere vanishing, hence is a holomorphic trivialization of the canonical bundle. In particular $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)=0$. Projection to $x+\mathrm i y$ exhibits this quotient as the Kodaira elliptic bundle over $\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$. Choose a smooth unit-periodic function $f(x)$ with $C=1-f''>0$, and put \[  \lambda _1=-e^4+f'e^1,\qquad \eta _1=J\lambda _1=e^3+f'e^2,\qquad \omega _1=\lambda _1\wedge \eta _1+C e^1\wedge e^2.  \] This is positive and Hermitian, with Riemannian metric \[  g_1=\lambda _1\otimes \lambda _1+\eta _1\otimes \eta _1 +C(e^1\otimes e^1+e^2\otimes e^2).  \] The identities $\mathrm d\lambda _1=0$ and $\mathrm d\eta _1=-C e^1\wedge e^2$ give $\mathrm d\omega _1=\lambda _1\wedge \omega _1$. The Lee period along the $t$-circle is $-1$, so this metric is strictly LCK. Its Lee dual is $-\partial _ t$, which is Killing because all coefficients are independent of $t$. Closedness of the Lee form and the Killing equation make $\nabla ^{g_1}\lambda _1$ both symmetric and skew-symmetric; thus $\omega _1$ is Vaisman. Write $e^{1234}=e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3\wedge e^4$. The volume is $\omega _1^2/2=C e^{1234}$, whereas $\Sigma \wedge \overline\Sigma $ has constant density in this coframe. For $h=C^{-1/2}$, the conformal metric $\omega =h\omega _1$ has volume $e^{1234}$ and therefore is Chern–Ricci flat. Its Lee form is \[  \lambda =-e^4+\mathrm d(f+\log h).  \] Let $E_ i$ be dual to $e^ i$. Solving $g(A,\cdot )=\lambda $ gives \[  A=h'E_1+(f'h'-h^{-1})E_4.  \] The metric volume is $\mathrm dx\, \mathrm dy\, \mathrm dz\, \mathrm dt$, and the fields $E_ i$ have zero divergence for this volume. Hence $\operatorname {div}A=h''$ and $q=-h''$. For the choice \[  f(x)=\frac{\cos (2\pi x)}{16\pi ^2},\qquad C(x)=1+\tfrac 14\cos (2\pi x)\geq \tfrac 34,  \] one has \[  q(0)=-\frac{4\sqrt5\pi ^2}{25},\qquad q(1/2)=\frac{4\sqrt3\pi ^2}{9}.  \] Thus $\omega $ is not Gauduchon, and theorem 23.2.47 also excludes the Vaisman condition for this flat metric. Finally, if $\mathrm e^ v\omega $ is also Chern–Ricci flat, then the conformal Ricci formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=0$. The real pluriharmonic function $v$ is constant on the connected compact complex manifold by the maximum principle. A constant multiple of $\omega $ still has nonzero divergence of its Lee field, so no flat metric in this conformal class is Gauduchon. The metric $\omega _1$ already constructed is a Vaisman representative of the class. $\square$ Conjecture 23.2.54 . 8DB45FD59BAD If $X$ satisfies $c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)=0$ and admits a strictly LCK metric, then $X$ admits a Vaisman metric. The analytic problem is to achieve Chern–Ricci flatness and the Gauduchon condition simultaneously within a family of LCK metrics. The conjecture asks for one Vaisman metric; it does not assert that the Lee form of every LCK metric on $X$ is parallel.

title: 23.2.55 The Lee–Gauduchon cone
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: For the rest of the chapter, $X$ is an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$, not necessarily LCK. By theorem 11.6.1 , a class in the image of the Lee map $j_ X$ of ( 23.2.9 ) is pseudoeffective exactly when it pairs nonnegatively with every Gauduchon metric. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})$ is closed, and these pairings depend only on its de Rham class. The classes obtained in this way lie in the annihilator of $\ker j_ X$, where they form an open convex cone, and strict positivity against this cone detects every nonzero pseudoeffective class in the image of $j_ X$. Set $V_ X=H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ and \[  K_ X=\ker j_ X,\qquad W_ X=K_ X^\perp \subset H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R),  \] where the annihilator is taken with respect to the Poincaré pairing \[  \langle [\lambda ],a\rangle =\int _ X\lambda \wedge a \qquad \bigl (a\in H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\bigr ).  \] Let \[  \mathcal C_ X =\{ [\lambda ]\in V_ X:j_ X([\lambda ])\text{ is pseudoeffective}\} .  \] This is a convex cone, since pseudoeffective classes form a convex cone. The image of $j_ X$ lies in the kernel of the natural map from Bott–Chern to de Rham cohomology, and it can be strictly smaller than this kernel, as example 23.2.72 will show. Lemma 23.2.56 . 70F067DD267F The space $K_ X$ consists of the de Rham classes of real parts of closed holomorphic one-forms. Moreover, \[  \mathcal C_ X\cap (-\mathcal C_ X)=K_ X.  \] Proof. If $j_ X([\lambda ])=0$, write $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\lambda =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\mathrm{d}=-\mathrm{d}\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$, the form $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Since the two equations separate the $\partial $- and $\bar\partial $-derivatives, its $(1,0)$-part is holomorphic and closed. Thus $\lambda +\mathrm{d}f$ is the real part of the closed holomorphic form $2(\lambda +\mathrm{d}f)^{1,0}$. Conversely, the real part of a closed holomorphic one-form is closed for both operators, so its image under $j_ X$ is zero. By proposition 10.11.2 , the pseudoeffective Bott–Chern cone contains no line. Thus $j_ X(\xi )$ and $-j_ X(\xi )$ are both pseudoeffective exactly when $j_ X(\xi )=0$, which is the identity $\mathcal C_ X\cap (-\mathcal C_ X)=K_ X$. $\square$ Definition 23.2.57 . FC269BC81E64 The Lee–Gauduchon cone is \[  \operatorname {LG}(X) =\bigl \{ [\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]: \gamma \text{ is a Gauduchon metric on }X\bigr \} .  \] For a closed real one-form $\lambda $ and any smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$, integration by parts gives FB0122E5265C 23.2.58 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\lambda \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma =\int _ X\kappa _\lambda \wedge \Gamma . \end{equation} The form $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma $ is closed, and both sides depend only on the cohomology classes involved. In particular, the class $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ]$ annihilates $K_ X$, so $\operatorname {LG}(X)\subseteq W_ X$. Proposition 23.2.59 . EBFA309383E5 The cone $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ is nonempty, convex and open in $W_ X$. Its linear span is $W_ X$. Proof. Let $\mathcal Z_ X$ be the real vector space of smooth $(n-1,n-1)$-forms $\Gamma $ satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Gamma =0$, and set \[  q_ X(\Gamma )=[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ].  \] We first show that $q_ X(\mathcal Z_ X)=W_ X$. The inclusion into $W_ X$ follows from ( 23.2.58 ). If $[\lambda ]$ annihilates the image of $q_ X$, then by ( 23.2.58 ) the class $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ has zero pairing with every Gauduchon form. The generalized Lamari criterion, theorem 11.6.1 , implies that both $\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ and $-\{ \kappa _\lambda \} $ are pseudoeffective, so $[\lambda ]\in K_ X$ by lemma 23.2.56 . Thus the image of $q_ X$ and $W_ X$ have the same annihilator in $V_ X$, and since the Poincaré pairing between $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}$ and $H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}$ is nondegenerate, they are equal. Let $\mathcal Z_ X^+$ be the set of strictly positive forms in $\mathcal Z_ X$. By the linear-algebra construction used in the proof of theorem 11.6.1 , every such form is the $(n-1)$st power of a unique Hermitian form, which is then Gauduchon. Hence \[  \operatorname {LG}(X)=q_ X(\mathcal Z_ X^+).  \] By Gauduchon's theorem, $\mathcal Z_ X^+$ is nonempty, and it is a convex cone; hence so is $\operatorname {LG}(X)$. For openness, choose forms $\Gamma _1,\ldots ,\Gamma _ r\in \mathcal Z_ X$ whose images form a basis of $W_ X$. If $\Gamma \in \mathcal Z_ X^+$, then $\Gamma +\sum _ i t_ i\Gamma _ i$ remains strictly positive for all sufficiently small real $t_ i$, and the images of these forms cover a neighborhood of $q_ X(\Gamma )$ in $W_ X$. This includes the case $W_ X=\{ 0\} $, with the empty basis. Since a nonempty open subset spans the ambient vector space, the assertion about the span follows. $\square$ Theorem 23.2.60 . DB27896B9A96 The cone $\mathcal C_ X$ is closed, and \[  \mathcal C_ X =\{ \xi \in V_ X:\langle \xi ,a\rangle \geq 0 \text{ for every }a\in \operatorname {LG}(X)\} .  \] Conversely, \[  \operatorname {LG}(X) =\{ a\in W_ X:\langle \xi ,a\rangle >0 \text{ for every }\xi \in \mathcal C_ X\setminus K_ X\} .  \] Proof. The first equality is theorem 11.6.1 applied to the smooth closed form $\kappa _\lambda $, together with ( 23.2.58 ). It expresses $\mathcal C_ X$ as an intersection of closed half-spaces, so this cone is closed. If $a=[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$ and $\xi =[\lambda ]\in \mathcal C_ X\setminus K_ X$, choose a closed positive current $T=\kappa _\lambda +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. It is nonzero because it represents the nonzero class $j_ X(\xi )$. Therefore \[  \langle \xi ,a\rangle =\int _ XT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0.  \] Conversely, suppose that $a\in W_ X\setminus \operatorname {LG}(X)$. Separating the point $a$ from the nonempty open convex cone $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ in the finite-dimensional space $W_ X$ gives a nonzero linear functional $\ell $ on $W_ X$ such that \[  \ell (a)\leq 0,\qquad \ell (b)\geq 0 \quad (b\in \operatorname {LG}(X)).  \] Indeed, in the usual separating inequalities the constant can be taken to be zero, by scaling the elements of the cone. By Poincaré duality, $\ell =\langle \xi ,\cdot \rangle $ for a class $\xi \in V_ X$ that is unique modulo $K_ X$, and $\xi \notin K_ X$ because $\ell \neq 0$. The first equality of the theorem gives $\xi \in \mathcal C_ X$, and then $\langle \xi ,a\rangle \leq 0$ shows that $a$ does not belong to the right side of the second equality. This proves the second equality; if $\operatorname {LG}(X)=W_ X$, there is nothing to prove. $\square$

title: 23.2.61 Bimeromorphic invariance
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: A modification induces an isomorphism on degree-one cohomology, and a class on the base is pseudoeffective exactly when its pullback is. These two facts identify the cones $\mathcal C_ X$, and duality then identifies the Lee–Gauduchon cones. Lemma 23.2.62 . D4DABE9DA177 Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification between connected compact complex manifolds, and let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Then \[  \{ \theta \} \text{ is pseudoeffective} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \{ \pi ^*\theta \} \text{ is pseudoeffective}.  \] The pullback on real Bott–Chern cohomology in bidegree $(1,1)$ is injective. Proof. By proposition 10.11.2 , both pullback and pushforward preserve pseudoeffectivity; the pullback of potentials is the one used in lemma 5.43.19 . Since $\pi $ has degree one, \[  \pi _*\pi ^*\{ \theta \} =\{ \theta \} .  \] Indeed, the identity of currents $\pi _*\pi ^*\theta =\theta $ follows by integration over the locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism, whose complement has volume zero. This left inverse proves injectivity and the reverse implication for pseudoeffectivity. $\square$ Degree-one cohomology is compared by moving cycles away from the image of the exceptional set. Lemma 23.2.63 . ED85C468C237 If $\pi :Y\to X$ is a modification between connected compact complex manifolds, then \[  \pi ^*:H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y,\mathbb R)  \] is an isomorphism. Its Poincaré dual is the isomorphism $\pi _*:H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(Y,\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Proof. For a proper analytic subset $A$ of a connected complex manifold $M$, the restriction map $H^1(M,\mathbb R)\to H^1(M\setminus A,\mathbb R)$ is injective, and it is an isomorphism if $A$ has complex codimension at least two. Indeed, choose a Whitney stratification of $A$. General position moves every one-cycle off the strata, which have real codimension at least two. If those codimensions are at least four, it also moves every two-chain with boundary in $M\setminus A$ off the strata, relative to its boundary. Thus the map $H_1(M\setminus A,\mathbb R)\to H_1(M,\mathbb R)$ is surjective in the first case and bijective in the second, and dualizing over $\mathbb R$ gives the assertions about restriction. Since $X$ is smooth, there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of complex codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $U=X\setminus A$. Restriction from $X$ to $U$ is therefore an isomorphism, whereas restriction from $Y$ to $\pi ^{-1}U$ is injective. Every class on $\pi ^{-1}U\simeq U$ extends to $X$ and hence pulls back to a class on $Y$. The commutative diagram of restriction maps now shows that $\pi ^*$ is an isomorphism, and Poincaré duality and the projection formula give the assertion for $\pi _*$. $\square$ Theorem 23.2.64 . 403FA017D33B Let $X$ and $Y$ be bimeromorphic connected compact complex manifolds. Under the natural identification of their first de Rham cohomology groups, and the Poincaré-dual identification of their de Rham cohomology groups of degree $2n-1$, the spaces $K_ X,W_ X$ and the cones $\mathcal C_ X,\operatorname {LG}(X)$ correspond to those of $Y$. Proof. First let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification. Holomorphic pullback commutes with $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$, so \[  j_ Y(\pi ^*\xi )=\pi ^*j_ X(\xi ).  \] By lemma 23.2.62 , a class $\xi $ lies in $\mathcal C_ X$ if and only if $\pi ^*\xi $ lies in $\mathcal C_ Y$, and likewise for $K_ X$ and $K_ Y$, since the pullback is injective on Bott–Chern classes. By lemma 23.2.63 , every degree-one class on $Y$ is of the form $\pi ^*\xi $. Thus the isomorphism $\pi ^*$ in degree one identifies the two cones and the two kernels. Its dual $\pi _*$ identifies $W_ Y$ with $W_ X$, and theorem 23.2.60 gives \[  \pi _*\operatorname {LG}(Y)=\operatorname {LG}(X).  \] For a bimeromorphic map between $X$ and $Y$, resolve its graph to obtain modifications $p:Z\to X$ and $q:Z\to Y$ from a compact complex manifold $Z$. The preceding argument applies to both maps and identifies the cones and kernels via $(q^*)^{-1}p^*$ and its Poincaré dual. These identifications do not depend on the resolution: they are compatible with restriction to a common open set on which the original map is an isomorphism, and by the injectivity of degree-one restriction proved above, this determines each class. The dual identifications are therefore canonical as well. $\square$

title: 23.2.65 Balanced metrics and the Hopf cone
search_title: Balanced metrics and the Hopf cone
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: If zero belongs to the Lee–Gauduchon cone, then the image of $j_ X$ contains no nonzero pseudoeffective class; this is the case when $X$ carries a balanced metric. On the Hopf threefold, by contrast, the Lee form spans a ray of classes with pseudoeffective image under $j_ X$, and the Lee–Gauduchon cone is an open half-line. Corollary 23.2.66 . BF1CE00DF8A7 The following conditions are equivalent: \[  0\in \operatorname {LG}(X),\qquad \operatorname {LG}(X)=W_ X,\qquad \mathcal C_ X=K_ X.  \] A balanced metric implies these conditions. On a manifold in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, one has $W_ X=\{ 0\} $ and $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $. Proof. An open cone in a finite-dimensional vector space that contains zero is the entire space, since scaling a neighborhood of zero reaches every point. The two dual descriptions in theorem 23.2.60 now prove the equivalences, including the case $W_ X=\{ 0\} $. If $b$ is a balanced metric, the form $b^{n-1}$ is closed and of pure type, hence also $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Thus $b$ is Gauduchon and gives the element $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(b^{n-1})]=0$ of $\operatorname {LG}(X)$. On a compact Kähler manifold the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma gives $j_ X=0$, since every $\kappa _\lambda $ is closed and de Rham exact. Thus $K_ X=V_ X$ and $W_ X=\{ 0\} $, and since $\operatorname {LG}(X)$ is nonempty, $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $. By theorem 23.2.64 , this conclusion extends to Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$. $\square$ Consequently, a nonzero pseudoeffective class in the image of $j_ X$ obstructs balanced metrics on every compact complex manifold bimeromorphic to $X$. For LCK manifolds, 23.2.12 would provide such a class. For the Hopf threefold of section 23.1 , with the Lee form $\lambda $ of proposition 23.2.24 , the covering description identifies the underlying manifold with $S^1\times S^5$, so $V_ X=\mathbb R[\lambda ]$. The class $j_ X([\lambda ])=\{ \alpha \} $ is nonzero by ( 23.2.8 ), and it is pseudoeffective because $\alpha \geq 0$. Its negative multiples are not pseudoeffective, since their pairing with the Gauduchon metric $\omega $ is negative. Thus \[  K_ X=0,\qquad \mathcal C_ X=\mathbb R_{\geq 0}[\lambda ],\qquad \operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ a\in H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R): \langle [\lambda ],a\rangle >0\} .  \] The same manifold has unbounded Monge–Ampère masses by theorem 23.1.1 . The positive ray detected here controls pairings with cohomology classes, which are linear and do not bound those nonlinear masses.

title: 23.2.67 Strongly Gauduchon metrics
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: As in subsection 23.2.55 , $X$ is an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. The closed form underlying a strongly Gauduchon metric pairs positively with every nonzero closed positive $(1,1)$-current, and this pairing depends only on the de Rham class of the current. It therefore bounds the mass of closed positive currents in terms of their de Rham classes and excludes nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents. The Lee–Gauduchon cone, by contrast, tests only the de Rham-exact Bott–Chern classes in the image of $j_ X$. On the Calabi–Eckmann threefold this image vanishes while a nonzero positive exact current exists, so the two conditions differ. Definition 23.2.68 . ADA9E5EAD64C A Hermitian metric $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon if $\gamma ^{n-1}$ is the $(n-1,n-1)$-component of a smooth closed real $(2n-2)$-form. Write the closed real form in the definition as \[  \Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}+\beta +\overline\beta , \qquad \beta \text{ of type }(n,n-2).  \] Then $\partial (\gamma ^{n-1})=-\bar\partial \beta $. Conversely, this equation and its conjugate give $\mathrm{d}\Theta =0$, because all other components of $\mathrm d\Theta $ have a type with an entry exceeding $n$. Thus $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon if and only if $\partial (\gamma ^{n-1})$ is $\bar\partial $-exact. Applying $\bar\partial $ shows that a strongly Gauduchon metric is Gauduchon. Every balanced metric is strongly Gauduchon, with $\Theta =\gamma ^{n-1}$. Proposition 23.2.69 . 4CCB765ECCA2 If $\gamma $ is a strongly Gauduchon metric, then $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\gamma ^{n-1})]=0$; in particular $0\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$. Moreover, $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if there is no nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$ that is de Rham exact. Proof. Put $\Gamma =\gamma ^{n-1}$ and use $\beta $ as above. Then \[  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma =\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\bar\partial \beta -\partial \overline\beta ) =\mathrm{d}\! \left(\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\beta -\overline\beta )\right).  \] Thus $[\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\Gamma ]=0$. Next, let $S$ be a real current of degree one such that $T=\mathrm{d}S$ is a nonzero positive $(1,1)$-current, and let $\Theta $ be a closed real form with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part $\Gamma $. By type considerations and Stokes' theorem for currents, \[  \int _ XT\wedge \Gamma =\int _ XT\wedge \Theta =0.  \] But the first integral is strictly positive because $T\ne 0$ and $\Gamma >0$, a contradiction. Thus a strongly Gauduchon metric excludes nonzero positive exact currents. Conversely, suppose that no strongly Gauduchon metric exists. In the real Fréchet space of smooth $(2n-2)$-forms, let $\mathcal Z$ be the closed subspace of closed forms, and let $\mathcal P$ be the open convex cone of forms with strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-part. This cone is nonempty, since it contains $h^{n-1}$ for any Hermitian metric $h$. The two sets are disjoint, because the positive $(n-1)$st root of the $(n-1,n-1)$-part of a form in their intersection would be a strongly Gauduchon metric. The Hahn–Banach separation theorem therefore gives a nonzero real current $T$ of degree two such that \[  T|_{\mathcal Z}=0,\qquad T(\Theta )\geq 0\quad (\Theta \in \mathcal P).  \] Fix $\Theta _0\in \mathcal P$. If a real form $\Psi $ has zero $(n-1,n-1)$-part, then $\Theta _0+t\Psi \in \mathcal P$ for every $t\in \mathbb R$, so $T(\Psi )=0$. Thus $T$ is of type $(1,1)$. For any semipositive $(n-1,n-1)$-form $\Gamma $, we have $\Gamma +\varepsilon \Theta _0\in \mathcal P$ for $\varepsilon >0$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $T(\Gamma )\geq 0$; thus $T$ is positive. Since $T$ annihilates every exact test form, it is closed. By the de Rham theorem for currents and Poincaré duality, its cohomology class is determined by its pairings with closed forms of complementary degree. All these pairings vanish, so $T=\mathrm{d}S$ for a real current $S$. Thus $T$ is a nonzero positive exact current, which proves the converse. $\square$ Equivalently, $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if every nonzero pseudoeffective Bott–Chern class has nonzero image in de Rham cohomology. Indeed, a closed positive current representing the zero Bott–Chern class has zero pairing with a Gauduchon metric and therefore vanishes, so the Bott–Chern classes of the nonzero positive de Rham-exact currents are exactly the nonzero pseudoeffective classes with zero de Rham image. The same criterion characterizes the manifolds on which de Rham classes control the masses of closed positive currents. Corollary 23.2.70 . 86E2247D209D Fix a Hermitian metric $h$ on $X$ and a norm on $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Then $X$ admits a strongly Gauduchon metric if and only if there is a constant $C>0$ such that every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ satisfies 24F2C25D4A8F 23.2.71 \begin{equation}  \int _ XT\wedge h^{n-1}\leq C\| [T]_{\mathrm{dR}}\| . \end{equation} Under this condition, the family of closed positive $(1,1)$-currents whose de Rham classes belong to a fixed compact set is weakly compact, and the image of the pseudoeffective Bott–Chern cone in $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$ is a closed convex cone containing no line. Proof. Suppose that $\gamma $ is strongly Gauduchon, and choose a smooth closed real form $\Theta $ whose $(n-1,n-1)$-part is $\gamma ^{n-1}$. By compactness, $h^{n-1}\leq A\gamma ^{n-1}$ for some $A>0$. Positivity and type considerations then give \[  \int _ XT\wedge h^{n-1} \leq A\int _ XT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =A\langle [T]_{\mathrm{dR}},[\Theta ]_{\mathrm{dR}}\rangle .  \] The last pairing is a fixed linear functional on the finite-dimensional de Rham group, which proves ( 23.2.71 ). Conversely, this bound forces every closed positive de Rham-exact current to vanish, and proposition 23.2.69 gives a strongly Gauduchon metric. For the compactness assertion, the bound gives uniformly bounded trace masses. A weak limit of such currents is positive and closed, and its de Rham class is the limit of their classes, as one sees by pairing with a finite basis of smooth closed forms of complementary degree and using Poincaré duality. Thus the family is weakly closed, and the usual weak compactness of positive currents with bounded mass proves the assertion. Let $c_ j$ be a convergent sequence in the image cone, and choose closed positive currents $T_ j$ with $[T_ j]_{\mathrm{dR}}=c_ j$. By the compactness assertion, a subsequence converges to a closed positive current representing the limit of the classes. Its Bott–Chern class is pseudoeffective, so the image cone is closed. Convexity follows from addition and nonnegative scaling. Finally, if both $c$ and $-c$ lie in the image, choose closed positive currents $T$ and $S$ representing them. Their sum is de Rham exact, so ( 23.2.71 ) gives $T+S=0$, and positivity gives $T=S=0$, hence $c=0$. $\square$ Example 23.2.72 . 1EE117A3B0B0 There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ with \[  \operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} ,\qquad V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0,  \] but with no strongly Gauduchon metric. Moreover, $X$ has a nonzero pseudoeffective Bott–Chern class whose de Rham image is zero; this class is not in the image of $j_ X$. Proof. Consider the holomorphic action of the additive group $\mathbb C$ on \[  \widetilde X=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )\times (\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} ), \qquad t\cdot (z,w)=(\mathrm{e}^ t z,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}w).  \] The action is free, since $\mathrm{e}^ t=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}=1$ forces $t=0$. It is also proper. Indeed, if both $(z,w)$ and $t\cdot (z,w)$ range in compact subsets of $\widetilde X$, then the norms of the four vectors $z$, $w$, $\mathrm e^ tz$ and $\mathrm e^{\mathrm it}w$ in $\mathbb C^2$ are bounded above and away from zero. Writing $t=a+\mathrm i b$, the ratios of these norms bound $\mathrm{e}^ a$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-b}$ above and away from zero, so $a$ and $b$ stay bounded. A free proper holomorphic action has local holomorphic slices, and its quotient $X$ is a Hausdorff complex manifold of dimension three. Every orbit meets $S^3\times S^3$ exactly once, at the image of $(z,w)$ under the group element with \[  a=-\log |z|,\qquad b=\log |w|.  \] These expressions depend smoothly on $(z,w)$, so the slice $S^3\times S^3$ identifies the quotient with $S^3\times S^3$ as a smooth manifold. In particular, $X$ is compact and connected, and \[  H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R) =H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0.  \] It follows that $V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0$ and $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $; the latter cone is nonempty by Gauduchon's theorem and lies in the zero group $H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto ([z],[w])$ is invariant under the action and descends to a holomorphic map \[  p:X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1.  \] It is a submersion, because the map on $\widetilde X$ is a submersion and the orbits of the action lie in its fibers. Let $\eta $ be the sum of the Fubini–Study forms on the two factors. The smooth form \[  \alpha =p^*\eta  \] is closed, semipositive and of rank two everywhere. It is nonzero and de Rham exact, since $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0$. By proposition 23.2.69 , $X$ admits no strongly Gauduchon metric. The Bott–Chern class of $\alpha $ is nonzero: otherwise $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$, and the integral of $\alpha $ against any Gauduchon form would vanish, contradicting $\alpha \geq 0$ and $\alpha \ne 0$. The class is pseudoeffective, since $\alpha $ is a positive representative. Finally, $j_ X$ has zero domain, so this class is not in its image. $\square$ Thus $0\in \operatorname {LG}(X)$ does not imply the existence of a strongly Gauduchon metric, and hence does not imply the existence of a balanced metric. On the threefold of proposition 12.19.18 , which carries a balanced and hence strongly Gauduchon metric, let $\alpha ,\beta $ be the two pulled-back Fubini–Study forms. The nonzero class $\{ \beta -\alpha \} $ has zero de Rham image, and neither it nor its negative is pseudoeffective, by proposition 10.19.2 . Every Hermitian form on this threefold has zero lower mass in the sense of definition 13.14.14 . Thus the existence of a strongly Gauduchon metric guarantees neither injectivity of the map from Bott–Chern to de Rham cohomology nor the positive lower mass needed for solvability with every finite non-pluripolar measure.

By the compactness assertion, a subsequence converges to a closed positive current representing the limit of the classes. Its Bott–Chern class is pseudoeffective, so the image cone is closed. Convexity follows from addition and nonnegative scaling. Finally, if both $c$ and $-c$ lie in the image, choose closed positive currents $T$ and $S$ representing them. Their sum is de Rham exact, so ( 23.2.71 ) gives $T+S=0$, and positivity gives $T=S=0$, hence $c=0$. $\square$
