title: Example 23.2.72
topic: Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: Example 23.2.72 . 1EE117A3B0B0 There is a connected compact complex threefold $X$ with \[  \operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} ,\qquad V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0,  \] but with no strongly Gauduchon metric. Moreover, $X$ has a nonzero pseudoeffective Bott–Chern class whose de Rham image is zero; this class is not in the image of $j_ X$. Proof. Consider the holomorphic action of the additive group $\mathbb C$ on \[  \widetilde X=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )\times (\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} ), \qquad t\cdot (z,w)=(\mathrm{e}^ t z,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}w).  \] The action is free, since $\mathrm{e}^ t=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}=1$ forces $t=0$. It is also proper. Indeed, if both $(z,w)$ and $t\cdot (z,w)$ range in compact subsets of $\widetilde X$, then the norms of the four vectors $z$, $w$, $\mathrm e^ tz$ and $\mathrm e^{\mathrm it}w$ in $\mathbb C^2$ are bounded above and away from zero. Writing $t=a+\mathrm i b$, the ratios of these norms bound $\mathrm{e}^ a$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-b}$ above and away from zero, so $a$ and $b$ stay bounded. A free proper holomorphic action has local holomorphic slices, and its quotient $X$ is a Hausdorff complex manifold of dimension three. Every orbit meets $S^3\times S^3$ exactly once, at the image of $(z,w)$ under the group element with \[  a=-\log |z|,\qquad b=\log |w|.  \] These expressions depend smoothly on $(z,w)$, so the slice $S^3\times S^3$ identifies the quotient with $S^3\times S^3$ as a smooth manifold. In particular, $X$ is compact and connected, and \[  H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R) =H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0.  \] It follows that $V_ X=K_ X=W_ X=0$ and $\operatorname {LG}(X)=\{ 0\} $; the latter cone is nonempty by Gauduchon's theorem and lies in the zero group $H^5_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto ([z],[w])$ is invariant under the action and descends to a holomorphic map \[  p:X\longrightarrow \mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1.  \] It is a submersion, because the map on $\widetilde X$ is a submersion and the orbits of the action lie in its fibers. Let $\eta $ be the sum of the Fubini–Study forms on the two factors. The smooth form \[  \alpha =p^*\eta  \] is closed, semipositive and of rank two everywhere. It is nonzero and de Rham exact, since $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb R)=0$. By proposition 23.2.69 , $X$ admits no strongly Gauduchon metric. The Bott–Chern class of $\alpha $ is nonzero: otherwise $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$, and the integral of $\alpha $ against any Gauduchon form would vanish, contradicting $\alpha \geq 0$ and $\alpha \ne 0$. The class is pseudoeffective, since $\alpha $ is a positive representative. Finally, $j_ X$ has zero domain, so this class is not in its image. $\square$

title: 13.16 Volumes under bounded mass
text: In a Hermitian background, Monge–Ampère masses need not be bounded above or away from zero. On the standard Hopf threefold the masses of smooth admissible potentials of a Gauduchon form are unbounded (theorem 23.1.1 ), while on the threefold of theorem 12.19.1 every Hermitian form $h$ admits smooth admissible potentials whose masses tend to zero. In this part such bounds are imposed explicitly. The upper bound is the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 : $v_+(\omega )<+\infty $ for one, and hence for every, Hermitian form $\omega $ (proposition 13.14.15 ), where $v_+(\omega )$ and $v_-(\omega )$ denote the supremum and the infimum of the masses of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions. A lower bound takes one of two forms. In section 15.37 , which does not assume bounded mass, it is positive lower mass $v_-(\theta )>0$ of a semipositive background $\theta $. In this chapter and in section 10.31 , which assume bounded mass, it is usually a positive lower singularity volume of the particular potentials involved, rather than a bound for all bounded potentials. In a closed background, the non-pluripolar mass of a potential depends only on its ordinary singularity type. In a nonclosed background, potentials of the same type can have different masses, so a singularity type carries two numbers, the infimum and the supremum of the masses of its members. These lower and upper singularity volumes keep the order information needed for comparison. Bounded mass makes the upper volume finite, and a positive lower volume prevents the auxiliary envelopes used below from collapsing. Together these bounds turn a small upper-volume deficit into a large admissible stretch, and this relates equality of volumes to the relative full-mass class and to ordinary envelopes. The upper volume of the maximum of two potentials measures how far apart their ordinary envelopes are. On models with a uniform positive lower-volume bound, the stretching estimate controls three-point comparisons, monotone limits and convergence in capacity. The comparison itself need not satisfy the triangle inequality, even on the projective plane, and at zero volume it can identify distinct models (example 13.22.3 ). Finite chains nevertheless give a complete metric once the reciprocal of the lower volume is included to prevent escape to zero volume. Analytic regularization identifies the multiplier-ideal models among the resulting limits, and strict barriers allow these comparisons to persist under small changes of background. On a curve, the polar part of the curvature current determines the ordinary model, and the volume comparison is the total variation of polar measures. This description extends to the zero-volume boundary. Taking the atomic part gives the nearest ideal model, while diffuse polar curvature measures the failure of analytic approximation. Area rescaling and smooth gauges then describe changes of background, including the collapse of all normalized potentials when the backgrounds converge uniformly to a form of zero area. Throughout the chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with the bounded mass property, and $\theta $ is a big smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, not necessarily closed; bigness means that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, some $\varepsilon >0$ and a Hermitian form $\omega $ (section 5.40 ). From section 13.28 on, we work instead on a compact Riemann surface with the backgrounds specified there. We recall the notation used from earlier chapters. For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, $u\preceq v$ means $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ means $u\preceq v\preceq u$; the classes of $\sim $ are the ordinary singularity types (definition 16.7.1 ). Similarly, $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ means $\mathcal I(tu)\subseteq \mathcal I(tv)$ for every $t>0$, and $u\sim _{\mathcal I}v$ means that these multiplier ideals are equal (section 5.33 ). For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ is the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 , which is finite under bounded mass by proposition 13.14.16 . The lower and upper singularity volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of definition 16.28.58 are the infimum and the supremum of $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ over all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\sim u$. A statement about $\operatorname {vol}_\theta $, without a bar, is asserted for both volumes. Given an obstacle $f$, we denote by $P_\theta (f)$ the regularized upper envelope of the $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions lying below $f$, and we write $P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min (u,v))$ for the rooftop envelope and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ (section 5.40 ). The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ is the regularized supremum of all $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $h\preceq u$ and $h\leq 0$ (definition 5.40.4 ), and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 18.4.1 , defined in the same way with $h\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ in place of $h\preceq u$. We call $u$ an ordinary model if $P_\theta [u]=u$, and an ideal model if $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$. Both kinds have supremum zero, and every ideal model is an ordinary model by corollary 18.4.4 . Finally, $\nu (u,x)$ denotes the Lelong number at $x$, and a potential is called analytic if it has analytic singularities in the rational-coefficient convention of section 5.34 .

title: 13.17 Comparison of singularity volumes
text: Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta $. By proposition 13.14.16 , theorem 13.14.3 , the mass of every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential is at most $v_+(\Omega )$. Hence, for $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  0\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)<+\infty .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, both volumes equal $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, because in the closed theory the non-pluripolar mass depends only on the singularity type Theorem 13.8.7 . For a nonclosed background the two volumes can differ even at $u=0$, as example 11.1.12 shows. Both volumes increase when the background increases or the singularities become milder. In the proof, a rooftop envelope for the lower volume and a maximum for the upper volume produce competitors of the required singularity types, and locality of non-pluripolar products confines the error to sets whose mass tends to zero. Theorem 13.17.1 . D7019DA65027 Let $\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. Suppose $\theta _1$ is big, $\theta _1\leq \theta _2$, and $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. Then \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2).  \] Proof. We first treat the lower volume. After adding a constant to $u_1$ we may assume $u_1\leq u_2$. Choose $v_2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ with $v_2\sim u_2$ and, for real $t>0$, consider the rooftop envelope \[  p_ t=P_{\theta _1}(u_1+t,v_2).  \] Since $u_1\leq u_2\leq v_2+C$ for a constant $C$, the function $u_1-C$ is a competitor; moreover $p_ t\leq u_1+t$. Hence $p_ t\sim u_1$. By the contact theorem (theorem 15.8.6 ), the measure $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t)$ is carried by the union of $\{ p_ t=u_1+t\} \subset \{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ and $\{ p_ t=v_2\} $. On the first set, ordered contact in background $\theta _1$ (proposition 13.14.6 ) bounds it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$. On the second set, $p_ t$ is also $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $v_2$; positivity of the mixed products (lemma 13.14.2 ) and ordered contact in background $\theta _2$ bound it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} }\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1) +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2).  \] As $t\to +\infty $, the first measure on the right has total mass tending to zero: the sets $\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ decrease to a subset of the pole set of $u_1$, and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$ is a finite measure that puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1)\leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$, and taking the infimum over $v_2$ proves the first inequality. For the upper volume, choose any $v_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ with $v_1\sim u_1$, and put $w_ t=\max (v_1,u_2-t)$ for $t>0$. This function is $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and satisfies $w_ t\sim u_2$. On the set $D_ t=\{ v_1>u_2-t\} $, locality and positivity of the mixed products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1) \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(w_ t).  \] The sets $D_ t$ exhaust the complement of the pole set of $v_1$, which carries no mass. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ therefore gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2)$, and taking the supremum over $v_1$ proves the second inequality. $\square$ Adding a positive current also increases both volumes. For the lower volume, the potential of the added current is subtracted inside an envelope, which produces a competitor in the original background. Proposition 13.17.2 . 1C00C4C5A656 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$ for a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $X$. Then, for either the lower or the upper volume, \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\theta +\eta }(u+v).  \] Proof. The form $\theta +\eta $ is big: adding the positive current $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ to a strictly positive current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ gives a strictly positive current $\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho +v)$. For the upper volume, add $v$ to each competitor $u'\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u'+v\sim u+v$, and positivity of the mixed products shows that $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(u'+v)\geq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u')$. For the lower volume, choose $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\eta )$ with $w\sim u+v$, and let $p=P_\theta (w-v)$. Since $w-v=u+O(1)$ outside the pole sets, a translate of $u$ is a competitor and $p\leq u+C$ for a constant $C$. Thus $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p\sim u$. By the contact theorem, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ is carried by $D=\{ p+v=w\} $. Furthermore $p+v\leq w$ everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact therefore give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(p+v) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\eta }(w).  \] Integrating and taking the infimum over $w$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.17.1
text: Theorem 13.17.1 . D7019DA65027 Let $\theta _1,\theta _2$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms on $X$. Suppose $\theta _1$ is big, $\theta _1\leq \theta _2$, and $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. Then \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2).  \] Proof. We first treat the lower volume. After adding a constant to $u_1$ we may assume $u_1\leq u_2$. Choose $v_2\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _2)$ with $v_2\sim u_2$ and, for real $t>0$, consider the rooftop envelope \[  p_ t=P_{\theta _1}(u_1+t,v_2).  \] Since $u_1\leq u_2\leq v_2+C$ for a constant $C$, the function $u_1-C$ is a competitor; moreover $p_ t\leq u_1+t$. Hence $p_ t\sim u_1$. On the first set, ordered contact in background $\theta _1$ (proposition 13.14.6 ) bounds it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$. On the second set, $p_ t$ is also $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $v_2$; positivity of the mixed products (lemma 13.14.2 ) and ordered contact in background $\theta _2$ bound it by $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(p_ t) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} }\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1) +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2).  \] As $t\to +\infty $, the first measure on the right has total mass tending to zero: the sets $\{ u_1\leq v_2-t\} $ decrease to a subset of the pole set of $u_1$, and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(u_1)$ is a finite measure that puts no mass on pluripolar sets. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _1}(u_1)\leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(v_2)$, and taking the infimum over $v_2$ proves the first inequality. For the upper volume, choose any $v_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _1)$ with $v_1\sim u_1$, and put $w_ t=\max (v_1,u_2-t)$ for $t>0$. This function is $\theta _2$-plurisubharmonic and satisfies $w_ t\sim u_2$. On the set $D_ t=\{ v_1>u_2-t\} $, locality and positivity of the mixed products imply \[  \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1) \leq \mathbf1_{D_ t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _2}(w_ t).  \] The sets $D_ t$ exhaust the complement of the pole set of $v_1$, which carries no mass. Integrating and letting $t\to +\infty $ therefore gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _1}(v_1)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _2}(u_2)$, and taking the supremum over $v_1$ proves the second inequality. $\square$

text: Proposition 13.17.2 . 1C00C4C5A656 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta )$ for a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ on $X$. Then, for either the lower or the upper volume, \[  \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\theta +\eta }(u+v).  \] Proof. For the lower volume, choose $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\eta )$ with $w\sim u+v$, and let $p=P_\theta (w-v)$. For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $b\geq 1$, the competitor family $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)$ consists of all $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$. Since $u\preceq v$, the difference of Lelong numbers is nonnegative, and it is at most $

This leads to a second description of the relative envelope class. Fix a reference potential $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Definition 13.18.4 . FC98C471363B The relative full-mass class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )\} .  \] Conversely, convex combinations turn the envelope condition into equality of volumes. Theorem 13.18.5 . D73DFBAE1EC1 Suppose $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )>0$. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,	heta ,\varphi ).  \] Every member $u$ of this class also satisfies $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (\varphi )$. Proof. First let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\varphi )$. title: Lemma 13.18.1
section: 13.18 Volume deficits and relative full mass
text: Lemma 13.18.1 . 92ABF533A916 Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u\preceq v$, and put \[  \delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)>0, \qquad D=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] If $b>1$ and $b^ nD<\delta $, then $\mathcal A_ b(u,v)\neq \varnothing $; that is, the stretching envelope $Q_ b(u,v)$ is defined. Proof. Adding constants to $u$ and $v$ only translates the competitors, so we may assume $v\leq 0$. Write $V=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)$. Since $D<b^{-n}\delta $, the definition of the upper volume gives $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim u$ and 8F79AE2F6948 13.18.2 \begin{equation}  V-\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)<b^{-n}\delta . \end{equation} After a translation of $w$ we may also assume $w\leq v$. For positive integers $j$, put \[  w_ j=\max (w,v-j),\qquad h_ j=Q_ b(w_ j,v).  \] The function $v-bj$ is a competitor for $h_ j$, and the defining convex inequality together with $w_ j\leq v$ gives $h_ j\leq v$. Thus $v-bj\leq h_ j\leq v$, so $w_ j\sim v$ and $h_ j\sim v$, and $h_ j$ decreases as $j$ increases. We claim that the decreasing limit $h$ of the $h_ j$ is not identically $-\infty $. If it were, theorem 5.25.2 would give $\sup _ Xh_ j\to -\infty $. By theorem 15.8.6 , the measure of $h_ j$ is carried by the contact set $C_ j=\{ b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v=w_ j\} $. Positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact for $b^{-1}h_ j+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w_ j$ give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h_ j) \leq b^ n\mathbf1_{C_ j}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j).  \] Fix a positive integer $k$. If $h\equiv -\infty $, then $h_ j\leq -bk$ everywhere for all large $j>k$. Since $v\leq 0$, every point of $C_ j$ then satisfies $w_ j\leq -k$, hence $w\leq -k$. Moreover $w_ j=w$ on $\{ w>-k\} \subset \{ w>v-j\} $, so locality gives \[  \begin{split}  \delta \leq \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h_ j) & \leq b^ n\int _{\{ w\leq -k\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)\\ & \leq b^ n\left(V-\int _{\{ w>-k\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\right). \end{split}  \] Here the first inequality uses $h_ j\sim v$, and the last uses $w_ j\sim v$. Letting $k\to \infty $ contradicts ( 13.18.2 ), since the finite non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)$ gives no mass to the pole set of $w$. This proves the claim. Consequently $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $b^{-1}h+(1-b^{-1})v\leq w$. If $w\leq u+C$, then $h-bC\in \mathcal A_ b(u,v)$, which proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Definition 13.18.4
section: 13.18 Volume deficits and relative full mass
text: Definition 13.18.4 . FC98C471363B The relative full-mass class of $\varphi $ is \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\preceq \varphi , \  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )\} .  \]

title: Theorem 13.18.5
section: 13.18 Volume deficits and relative full mass
text: Theorem 13.18.5 . D73DFBAE1EC1 Suppose $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Every member $u$ of this class also satisfies $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )$. Proof. First let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. For each $a\in (0,1)$, a member of $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )$ with $b=(1-a)^{-1}$ gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that $a\varphi +(1-a)h\leq u$. By theorem 13.17.1 , proposition 13.17.2 and homogeneity, for either volume, \[  a^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (\varphi ) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (a\varphi +(1-a)h) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] Letting $a\to 1$ proves that both volumes of $u$ equal those of $\varphi $; this direction does not use positive lower volume. Conversely, let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. Then $D=0$ in lemma 13.18.1 with $v=\varphi $, so $\mathcal A_ b(u,\varphi )\neq \varnothing $ for every $b>1$. For $b=1$ the family contains $u$. This is the defining condition of $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$

title: 13.19 Domination and ordinary envelopes
text: Since $u\preceq P_\theta [u]$, monotonicity gives one inequality between the volumes of a potential and those of its ordinary envelope. For the reverse inequality we identify a limit of obstacle envelopes by means of contact support and a domination principle. In the domination argument, positive lower volume guarantees that the stretching envelopes are defined. From now on we write $\mu _ w=\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)$ for $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Theorem 13.19.1 . B390F0847B3A Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have positive lower volume, let $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\preceq \varphi $, and let $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ u\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mu _ v,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Put $\ell =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\varphi )>0$ and $\mathcal E_\varphi =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. We may replace $v$ by $\max (u,v)$: by locality, the hypothesis is unchanged on $\{ u<v\} $, and by upward stability (proposition 16.28.62 ) the new $v$ lies in $\mathcal E_\varphi $. Thus we may assume $u\leq v$. Translate $u,v$ by the same constant so that $v\leq \varphi $, and then translate all three potentials so that $\varphi \leq 0$. The idea is to stretch $u$ away from $v$; the stretched potentials keep lower volume $\ell $, and this is incompatible with a strict inequality $u<v$ on a set of positive volume. Set \[  q_ b=Q_ b(u,v),\qquad D_ b=\{ b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v=u\} .  \] Lemma 16.28.63 gives $q_ b\in \mathcal E_\varphi $ and $q_ b\leq u$. Since $b^{-1}q_ b+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$ with contact set $D_ b$, contact support and positivity of the mixed products give \[  b^{-n}\mu _{q_ b}+(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ v \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mu _ u.  \] Here $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b$. Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. On $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ the hypothesis bounds the right-hand side by $c\mu _ v$, and subtracting finite measures shows that $\mu _{q_ b}$ vanishes there. Thus $\mu _{q_ b}$ is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u=v\} \subset \{ q_ b=u\} $. Since $q_ b\leq u$, ordered contact for this pair and theorem 13.18.5 , which gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ b)=\ell $, now yield 50B3C0245F90 13.19.2 \begin{equation}  \ell \leq \mu _{q_ b}(X)\leq \mu _ u(\{ q_ b=u\} ). \end{equation} Suppose now that $u<v$ somewhere. Then there is $\delta >0$ such that $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ has positive Lebesgue measure; otherwise $u\geq v$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . On this set the convex inequality gives $q_ b\leq u-(b-1)\delta $. The family $q_ b$ decreases in $b$ and is bounded above by $u$. Its limit is $-\infty $ on a set of positive measure, so it cannot be $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and is therefore identically $-\infty $. Hence theorem 5.25.2 gives $\sup _ Xq_ b\to -\infty $. The sets $\{ q_ b=u\} \subset \{ u\leq \sup _ Xq_ b\} $ then have $\mu _ u$-mass tending to zero, because $\mu _ u$ is finite and puts no mass on the pole set of $u$. This contradicts ( 13.19.2 ). $\square$ Corollary 13.19.3 . 85CE662E8010 For $u,v$ as in theorem 13.19.1 and $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mu _ v \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u\geq v.  \] If $\mu _ u\leq c\mu _ v$ on $X$ for a finite $c\geq 0$, then $c\geq 1$. Proof. Fix $\delta >0$. On $\{ u<v-\delta \} $ the weighted inequality gives $\mu _ u\leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _ v=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }\mu _{v-\delta }$. Theorem 13.19.1 , applied to $v-\delta $ with $c=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda \delta }<1$, gives $u\geq v-\delta $; now let $\delta \downarrow 0$. If the second assertion failed, the theorem would apply with the same $c<1$ to every translate $v+A$, $A\in \mathbb R$, and would give $u\geq v+A$ for all $A$. This is impossible at a point where $u$ and $v$ are both finite. $\square$ The next lemma concerns the envelope obtained by replacing the obstacle $0$ in definition 5.40.4 by a potential $w$. Lemma 13.19.4 . 50A87754E163 Let $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta (u,w)\not\equiv -\infty $, and define the relative obstacle envelope \[  P_\theta [u](w)=\left(\lim _{C\to \infty }P_\theta (u+C,w)\right)^*.  \] Then \[  \mu _{P_\theta [u](w)} \leq \mathbf1_{\{ P_\theta [u](w)=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] Proof. Set $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ for $C\geq 0$ and $p=P_\theta [u](w)$. The envelopes $p_ C$ increase with $C$, lie between $p_0$ and $w$, and converge to $p$ in capacity by lemma 5.29.19 . By the contact theorem, $\mu _{p_ C}$ is carried by $\{ p_ C=\min (u+C,w)\} $. Assigning the points where $u+C=w$ to the second term, ordered contact gives \[  \mu _{p_ C}\leq \mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=u+C<w\} }\mu _ u +\mathbf1_{\{ p_ C=w\} }\mu _ w.  \] The first measure has total mass at most \[  \varepsilon _ C=\mu _ u(\{ u\leq \sup _ Xw-C\} )\longrightarrow 0,  \] because $\mu _ u$ is finite and non-pluripolar. Testing against nonnegative continuous functions and applying the lower semicontinuity of lemma 13.14.8 gives $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$. The bounded quasi-continuous weight $\chi =\min (1,(w-p)_+)$, defined arbitrarily on the pluripolar set where $w-p$ is undefined, vanishes on $\{ p_ C=w\} $, since $p_ C\leq p\leq w$. Thus $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _{p_ C}\leq \varepsilon _ C$. Weighted lower semicontinuity gives $\int _ X\chi \, \mu _ p=0$, so $\mu _ p$ is carried by $\{ p=w\} $. Together with $\mu _ p\leq \mu _ w$, this proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 13.19.5 . CB29AE1DFDA3 For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $p=P_\theta [u]$, \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] If this volume is positive, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p),\qquad u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p),\qquad P_\theta [p]=p.  \] Proof. Since $u\preceq p$, monotonicity gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. In particular, the lower volumes agree if $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)=0$. Suppose henceforth that $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq p$, and choose any $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim p$. Fix $K\geq 0$ with $p-K\leq w\leq p+K$. The rooftop envelope $p_ C=P_\theta (u+C,w)$ satisfies $u-K\leq p_ C\leq u+C$ for each $C\geq 0$, so it is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and equivalent to $u$. Its regularized increasing limit $r=P_\theta [u](w)$ satisfies \[  P_\theta (u+C+K,0)-K\leq p_ C\leq w, \qquad p-K\leq r\leq w\leq p+K.  \] Indeed, the leftmost potential lies below $u+C$, and below $p-K\leq w$ because $P_\theta (u+C+K,0)\leq P_\theta [u]=p$; it is therefore a competitor for the rooftop. Letting $C\to \infty $ gives the lower bound for $r$. Thus $r\sim p$, and proposition 16.28.62 puts $r$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$. By lemma 13.19.4 , $\mu _ r$ vanishes on $\{ r<w\} $. Theorem 13.19.1 , with coefficient $c=0$ and reference $p$, gives $r\geq w$; hence $r=w$. Since $p_ C\to r$ in capacity, lower semicontinuity of the total mass (lemma 13.14.8 ) and $p_ C\sim u$ yield \[  \int _ X\mu _ w\leq \liminf _{C\to \infty }\int _ X\mu _{p_ C} \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Taking the supremum over $w\sim p$ gives $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)\leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$, and hence equality of the upper volumes. Theorem 13.18.5 then gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,p)$ and equality of the lower volumes. Finally, proposition 16.28.65 gives $P_\theta [p]=P_\theta [u]=p$. $\square$ The ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$ is in general less singular than $u$. When the pole set of $u$ is a compact set of Hausdorff dimension zero, however, the full local Monge–Ampère product of theorem 5.27.18 is defined, and the ordinary envelope preserves its restriction to the pole set. Bounded mass controls the local approximations in every degree, and the products of lower degree put no mass on the pole set. Theorem 13.19.6 . C0F29EF85157 Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, and let $S\subset X$ be a compact set of Hausdorff dimension zero. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus S$, has pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} =S$, and has positive lower singularity volume. Put $p=P_\omega [u]$ and $p_ m=P_\omega (u+m,0)$ for real $m>0$. For $v=u$, $v=p$ and $v=p_ m$, the weak limit \[  \Phi _ v=\lim _{k\to \infty } (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (v,-k))^ n  \] of the bounded truncations exists and is a finite positive measure, which we call the full Monge–Ampère measure of $v$. On each coordinate chart, its restriction $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$ equals $\mathbf1_ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+q))^ n_{\mathrm{full}}$ for every smooth function $q$ making $v+q$ plurisubharmonic there; in particular, it does not depend on $q$. Moreover, \[  \mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p=\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ u,  \] and $\Phi _{p_ m}\to \Phi _ p$ weakly as $m\to \infty $. Proof. Step 1: the rooftops. Adding a constant to $u$ changes neither $p$ nor the family $(p_ m)_{m>0}$, apart from a shift of the parameter $m$. We may therefore assume $u\leq 0$. Then \[  u\leq p_ m\leq \min (u+m,0),\qquad p_ m\uparrow p,  \] where the increasing limit is understood after upper semicontinuous regularization. Thus $p_ m\sim u$, and $p_ m$ and $p$ are locally bounded off $S$. By theorem 13.19.5 , $p$ is an ordinary model with the same volumes as $u$. By lemma 5.29.19 , $p_ m\to p$ in capacity. On compact subsets of $X\setminus S$ the potentials have a common bounded range, so all bounded local products converge there, by the bounded product theory of section 5.27 . Step 2: full measures. Let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ be locally bounded off $S$, and put $v_ k=\max (v,-k)$. On each chart choose a smooth $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \omega $, so that the functions $v_ k+q$ are plurisubharmonic and decrease to $v+q$. Theorem 5.27.18 then gives full weak limits in every degree, \[  W_ j(v)=\lim _{k\to \infty }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k)^ j, \qquad \Phi _ v=\lim _{k\to \infty }(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k)^ n.  \] Indeed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ k+q)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$, and the powers can be expanded in the closed positive powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ k+q)$ and smooth forms. The local limits patch together because the approximating bounded currents are global. The limits are currents of order zero with finite mass on the compact manifold $X$, and $\Phi _ v$ is positive. Stokes' theorem for the bounded potentials $v_ k$ gives $\int _ XW_ n(v)=0$. Consequently F93B2C2EE801 13.19.7 \begin{equation}  J(v):=\Phi _ v(X) =\int _ X\omega ^ n+ \sum _{j=1}^{n-1}\binom nj \int _ XW_ j(v)\wedge \omega ^{n-j}. \end{equation} The measure $\Phi _ v$ equals $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)$ off $S$. Every closed positive power of degree less than $n$ in this expansion has coefficient measures vanishing on $S$, by corollary 5.34.3 . Thus only the top closed power contributes to $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$. This identifies $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ v$ with $\mathbf1_ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+q))^ n_{\mathrm{full}}$ and proves independence of $q$. These assertions are local on each chart and do not require a single chart containing $S$. Finally, $J(v)\leq v_+(\omega )$, since every truncation $v_ k$ has mass at most $v_+(\omega )$. Step 3: convergence of the lower-degree powers. We need local trace bounds for the closed powers of $p_ m$ that are uniform in $m$. Fix a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood and write $\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$. Choose $B>0$ with $B\kappa \geq \omega $ there, and $A>1$ with $A\omega -B\kappa \geq \kappa $. For $p_{m,k}=\max (p_ m,-k)$, the closed current $T_{m,k}=B\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_{m,k}$ is positive and \[  Q_{m,k}:=A\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_{m,k}\geq T_{m,k}+\kappa .  \] Expanding $Q_{m,k}^ n$ with the smooth positive difference $Q_{m,k}-T_{m,k}\geq \kappa $ gives, for $1\leq j\leq n$, \[  \binom nj T_{m,k}^ j\wedge \kappa ^{n-j} \leq Q_{m,k}^ n, \qquad \int _ XQ_{m,k}^ n\leq A^ n v_+(\omega ).  \] The last bound holds because $Q_{m,k}=A(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_{m,k}/A))$ and $p_{m,k}/A$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives trace bounds, independent of $m$, for every full closed power of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_ m+B|z|^2)$. For $j<n$, every subsequential weak limit of these closed positive $(j,j)$-currents puts no mass on $S$, again by corollary 5.34.3 . Off $S$ the bounded capacity convergence identifies the limit with the corresponding full power of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p+B|z|^2)$, which also puts no mass on $S$. Hence the limit is unique. Expanding back in the smooth correction and using a finite coordinate cover yields \[  W_ j(p_ m)\longrightarrow W_ j(p),\qquad 1\leq j<n.  \] Hence ( 13.19.7 ) gives $J(p_ m)\to J(p)$. Step 4: the residual measures. Let $R=\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ u$. Since $p_ m-u$ is bounded, the equality case of lemma 5.27.19 , applied on each chart after a common smooth correction, gives $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _{p_ m}=R$ for every $m$. The total masses $J(p_ m)$ are bounded by $v_+(\omega )$, so along any sequence $m_ i\to \infty $ a subsequence of $\Phi _{p_{m_ i}}$ converges weakly to a measure $\eta $. Since $\Phi _{p_ m}-R$ is positive, so is $\eta -R$. Off $S$, $\eta $ equals $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (p)$, by the bounded convergence of Step 1, and its total mass is $\lim _ mJ(p_ m)=J(p)$ by Step 3. The measure $\Phi _ p$ has the same total mass and the same restriction to $X\setminus S$, so \[  \Phi _ p(S)=\eta (S)\geq R(S).  \] On the other hand, $u\leq p$, so the inequality in lemma 5.27.19 gives $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p\leq R$ on each chart. Together with the previous inequality, this forces $\Phi _ p(S)=R(S)$, hence $\mathbf1_ S\Phi _ p=R$, which is the asserted equality of residual measures. It also gives $\mathbf1_ S\eta =R$, since $\eta -R\geq 0$ and $\eta (S)=R(S)$. As $\eta $ and $\Phi _ p$ also agree off $S$, we conclude that $\eta =\Phi _ p$. Every weak subsequential limit of $\Phi _{p_ m}$ is therefore $\Phi _ p$, which proves the convergence $\Phi _{p_ m}\to \Phi _ p$. $\square$ Corollary 13.19.8 . B0CCD40EE4B7 If $\varphi $ is an ordinary model of positive lower volume, then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ) =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=\varphi \} .  \] Proof. The first equality is theorem 13.18.5 . Membership in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ implies $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ by proposition 16.28.65 . Conversely, if $P_\theta [u]=\varphi $, then theorem 13.19.5 puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$. $\square$
