title: 13.22 Cauchy convergence of model potentials
text: The maximum of two potentials is a common upper bound for both, and the sum of the two upper-volume deficits from this maximum measures how far apart their ordinary envelopes are. A uniform positive lower-volume bound controls how this quantity changes when a third potential is introduced, and this replaces the triangle inequality in the Cauchy argument below. From now on we write $U(u)=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $M=U(V_\theta )$; by monotonicity, $U\leq M$ on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We also fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ for $L^1$ norms. Definition 13.22.1 . A220D62C8412 For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, define \[  d_\theta (u,v)=2U(\max (u,v))-U(u)-U(v).  \] For $\delta >0$, put \[  \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )= \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [u]=u, \  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\geq \delta \} .  \] We call $d_\theta $ the volume comparison . A sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy if $d_\theta (u_ j,u_ k)\to 0$ as $j,k\to \infty $, and it converges to $u$ for $d_\theta $ if $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. The volume comparison is finite, nonnegative and symmetric. It need not satisfy the triangle inequality (example 13.27.1 ), which is why we do not call it a distance. It depends only on the ordinary singularity types, since replacing either input by an equivalent one changes the maximum by a bounded amount. Monotonicity also gives 451874D2170D 13.22.2 \begin{equation}  |U(u)-U(v)|\leq d_\theta (u,v),\qquad u\leq v\  \Longrightarrow \  d_\theta (u,v)=U(v)-U(u). \end{equation} In the separation result below, the restriction to positive lower volume is necessary, even for a closed positive background. Example 13.22.3 . 4B14FA731306 For every $n\geq 2$ there are a closed positive $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on the projective manifold $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$ and two ordinary models $a\not\sim b$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1},\theta )$ such that \[  P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}=b,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (a) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (b)=0,\qquad d_\theta (a,b)=0.  \] For every $n\geq 3$, the same assertions hold for a suitable nonclosed positive form $\theta $ on a projective manifold of dimension $n$ with the bounded mass property. Proof. Take the closed positive product background of example 18.15.4 on $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^{n-1}$. Its models satisfy $a\leq b$ and $U(a)=U(b)=0$. Thus $\max (a,b)=b$, and the defining formula gives \[  d_\theta (a,b)=2U(b)-U(a)-U(b)=0.  \] The other assertions are part of that example. For the nonclosed case use example 18.15.5 ; its models are again ordered and have zero upper volumes, so the same calculation applies. $\square$ Proposition 13.22.4 . 38359A611D4C For potentials $u,v$ of positive lower volume, \[  d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (P_\theta [u],P_\theta [v]),\qquad d_\theta (u,v)=0\  \Longleftrightarrow \  P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [v].  \] There is $C_\theta >0$, depending on $\theta $ and $\mathrm{d}V$, such that, for $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, \[  \| u-v\| _{L^1}\leq 2C_\theta \min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (u,v)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} .  \] Proof. Translate the inputs below zero, and put $p=P_\theta [u]$, $q=P_\theta [v]$, $m=\max (u,v)$ and $r=P_\theta [m]$. Since $u\leq p$, $v\leq q$ and the envelope is monotone, \[  m\leq \max (p,q)\leq r.  \] All these potentials have positive lower volume. Theorem 13.19.5 and monotonicity therefore give $U(m)=U(\max (p,q))=U(r)$, while $U(u)=U(p)$ and $U(v)=U(q)$. This proves the first identity. If $d_\theta (u,v)=0$, then $U(u)=U(v)=U(m)$, since both are at most $U(m)$. Thus $u,v\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,m)$, and theorem 13.18.5 , proposition 16.28.65 give $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [m]=P_\theta [v]$. Conversely, if $p=q$, the first identity gives $d_\theta (u,v)=d_\theta (p,p)=0$. Now let $u,v\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and set $s=d_\theta (u,v)$. By theorem 5.25.2 , there is $C_\theta $ bounding the $L^1$ norm of every $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential with supremum zero. Since ordinary models have supremum zero, the estimate holds if $s\geq \delta /2$. Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and put $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from $u$ to $m$ is at most $s$, and the lower volume of $m$ is at least $\delta $. Thus lemma 13.18.1 , with $b=t^{-1}$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  (1-t)m+th\leq u.  \] For each competitor $g$ for $P_\theta [h]$ (so $g\leq 0$ and $g\preceq h$), the potential $(1-t)m+tg$ lies below zero and is more singular than $u$. Since $u=P_\theta [u]$, it lies below $u$, and taking the envelope gives \[  (1-t)m+tP_\theta [h]\leq u.  \] Hence $0\leq m-u\leq t(m-P_\theta [h])\leq -tP_\theta [h]$, and $\int _ X(m-u)\, \mathrm{d}V\leq tC_\theta $ because $P_\theta [h]$ has supremum zero. The same argument applies to $v$, and adding the two estimates gives the assertion, since $|u-v|\leq (m-u)+(m-v)$. If $s=0$, the argument works for every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. $\square$ Although the triangle inequality fails, the volume comparison satisfies it up to an error that is controlled uniformly on $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. Proposition 13.22.5 . 412DBAD823B9 For $u,v,w\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, DBE56A98BF3E 13.22.6 \begin{equation}  d_\theta (u,w)\leq d_\theta (u,v)+d_\theta (v,w) +2nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (v,w)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} Consequently every $d_\theta $-convergent sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and its limit is unique. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (v,w)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the inequality follows from $d_\theta (u,w)\leq 2M$. If $0<s<\delta /2$, set $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. Lemma 13.18.1 , applied to $v\preceq \max (v,w)$, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)\max (v,w)+th\leq v.  \] This inequality also gives $h\leq v$. Set $r=\max (u,v)$ and $z=\max (u,v,w)$. Where $z=\max (v,w)$, the inequality above bounds $(1-t)z+th$ by $v\leq r$; where $z=u$, both $u$ and $h$ lie below $r$. Thus \[  (1-t)z+th\leq r.  \] Addition, homogeneity and volume monotonicity give \[  U(z)-U(r)\leq \bigl (1-(1-t)^ n\bigr )U(z)\leq nMt.  \] Since $\max (u,w)\leq z$, it follows that \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,w) & \leq 2U(r)+2nMt-U(u)-U(w)\\ & =d_\theta (u,v)+U(v)-U(w)+2nMt\\ & \leq d_\theta (u,v)+s+2nMt. \end{split}  \] Here the last step uses ( 13.22.2 ). For $s=0$, the same proof works with every $t\in (0,1)$; let $t\downarrow 0$. This proves ( 13.22.6 ). Applying it with the limit as the middle point shows that a convergent sequence is Cauchy. If a sequence converges to two limits, applying it with a member of the sequence as the middle point shows that the two limits have volume comparison zero; by proposition 13.22.4 , they are equal. $\square$ Theorem 13.22.7 . 62ECCE0A41E6 Every $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ converges for $d_\theta $ to a unique element of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. It also converges to that element in $L^1(X,\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. The plan is to dominate a fast subsequence by the ordinary envelopes of its tail suprema; these decrease to the limit, and the stretching lemma controls the volume they add. Choose a subsequence $a_ j$ of the given sequence such that \[  d_\theta (a_ j,a_{j+1})<\delta \, 2^{-(j+1)n} \qquad (j\geq 1).  \] For $k\geq 0$, set \[  v_ j^ k=\max (a_ j,\ldots ,a_{j+k}),\qquad v_ j=\left(\sup _{l\geq j}a_ l\right)^*.  \] For every $l\geq j$, lemma 13.18.1 with $b=2^ l$, applied to $a_ l\preceq \max (a_ l,a_{l+1})$, gives $h_ l\leq a_ l$ satisfying \[  (1-2^{-l})\max (a_ l,a_{l+1})+2^{-l}h_ l\leq a_ l.  \] The argument by cases in the proof of proposition 13.22.5 gives \[  (1-2^{-l})v_ j^{l+1-j}+2^{-l}h_ l\leq v_ j^{l-j}.  \] Consequently \[  U(v_ j^{l+1-j})-U(v_ j^{l-j})\leq nM2^{-l}.  \] Summing from $l=j$ to $j+k-1$ and then letting $k\to \infty $, using theorem 13.21.1 , yields \[  0\leq U(v_ j)-U(a_ j)\leq nM2^{1-j}.  \] Here $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has lower volume at least $\delta $, because $a_ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$; this also justifies the use of that theorem. Put $q_ j=P_\theta [v_ j]$. By theorem 13.19.5 , $q_ j$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v_ j$. The sequence $q_ j$ decreases, and each $q_ j$ has supremum zero. By normalized compactness, its decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $, so $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 13.21.2 , \[  q=P_\theta [q],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\lim _ j\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ j)\geq \delta , \qquad U(q_ j)\longrightarrow U(q).  \] Both $a_ j$ and $q$ lie below $q_ j$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (a_ j,q) & \leq \bigl (U(q_ j)-U(a_ j)\bigr )+\bigl (U(q_ j)-U(q)\bigr )\\ & \leq nM2^{1-j}+U(q_ j)-U(q)\longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] To treat the whole sequence, apply ( 13.22.6 ) with a late member $a_ j$ of the subsequence as the middle point. The Cauchy property makes the first term small for all sufficiently late members of the original sequence, while $d_\theta (a_ j,q)$ makes the other two terms small. Thus the original sequence converges to $q$. Uniqueness follows from proposition 13.22.5 , and the $L^1$ estimate in proposition 13.22.4 proves the last assertion. $\square$ The non-strict inequality $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta \geq \delta $ in the definition of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ is essential for completeness. Example 13.22.8 . AB2E8992474C Let $\theta $ be a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form of integral one on a compact Riemann surface, and let $0<\delta <1$. The ordinary models of mass strictly greater than $\delta $ do not form a complete space for $d_\theta $. Proof. Fix a point $x$, and let $g_ x\leq 0$ be the Green function used in theorem 20.3.10 , with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=\delta _ x-\theta $, where $\delta _ x$ is the Dirac measure at $x$. For $0\leq a<1$, put $q_ a=P_\theta [ag_ x]$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ag_ x)$ equals $a\delta _ x+(1-a)\theta $, with non-pluripolar mass $1-a$. Since the background is closed, both singularity volumes of $ag_ x$ equal this mass, and theorem 13.19.5 gives \[  q_ a=P_\theta [q_ a],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ a)=U(q_ a)=1-a.  \] Since $g_ x\leq 0$, the potentials $q_ a$ decrease as $a$ increases, and ( 13.22.2 ) gives $d_\theta (q_ a,q_ b)=|a-b|$. Choose $a_ j<1-\delta $ with $a_ j\uparrow 1-\delta $. The sequence $q_{a_ j}$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and every term has mass $1-a_ j>\delta $. By ( 13.22.2 ), any $d_\theta $-limit has upper volume $\lim _ j(1-a_ j)=\delta $. In this closed background the two volumes coincide, so no such limit has mass strictly greater than $\delta $. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.22.7
text: Theorem 13.22.7 . 62ECCE0A41E6 Every $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ converges for $d_\theta $ to a unique element of $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. Put $q_ j=P_\theta [v_ j]$. By theorem 13.19.5 , $q_ j$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v_ j$. The sequence $q_ j$ decreases, and each $q_ j$ has supremum zero. By normalized compactness, its decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $, so $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By theorem 13.21.2 , \[  q=P_\theta [q],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\lim _ j\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ j)\geq \delta , \qquad U(q_ j)\longrightarrow U(q).  \] Both $a_ j$ and $q$ lie below $q_ j$. Hence \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (a_ j,q) & \leq \bigl (U(q_ j)-U(a_ j)\bigr )+\bigl (U(q_ j)-U(q)\bigr )\\ & \leq nM2^{1-j}+U(q_ j)-U(q)\longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] To treat the whole sequence, apply ( 13.22.6 ) with a late member $a_ j$ of the subsequence as the middle point. The Cauchy property makes the first term small for all sufficiently late members of the original sequence, while $d_\theta (a_ j,q)$ makes the other two terms small. Thus the original sequence converges to $q$. Uniqueness follows from proposition 13.22.5 , and the $L^1$ estimate in proposition 13.22.4 proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Example 13.22.8
text: Example 13.22.8 . AB2E8992474C Let $\theta $ be a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form of integral one on a compact Riemann surface, and let $0<\delta <1$. The ordinary models of mass strictly greater than $\delta $ do not form a complete space for $d_\theta $. Proof. Fix a point $x$, and let $g_ x\leq 0$ be the Green function used in theorem 20.3.10 , with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ x=\delta _ x-\theta $, where $\delta _ x$ is the Dirac measure at $x$. For $0\leq a<1$, put $q_ a=P_\theta [ag_ x]$. The current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ag_ x)$ equals $a\delta _ x+(1-a)\theta $, with non-pluripolar mass $1-a$. Since the background is closed, both singularity volumes of $ag_ x$ equal this mass, and theorem 13.19.5 gives \[  q_ a=P_\theta [q_ a],\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q_ a)=U(q_ a)=1-a.  \] Since $g_ x\leq 0$, the potentials $q_ a$ decrease as $a$ increases, and ( 13.22.2 ) gives $d_\theta (q_ a,q_ b)=|a-b|$. Choose $a_ j<1-\delta $ with $a_ j\uparrow 1-\delta $. The sequence $q_{a_ j}$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy, and every term has mass $1-a_ j>\delta $. By ( 13.22.2 ), any $d_\theta $-limit has upper volume $\lim _ j(1-a_ j)=\delta $. In this closed background the two volumes coincide, so no such limit has mass strictly greater than $\delta $. $\square$

title: 13.23 Rooftops and capacity convergence
text: A small upper-volume deficit also controls the rooftop envelope of two potentials. For a finite family it suffices that the sum of the deficits stays below the lower volume of a common upper bound. Applying this criterion to stretched potentials gives increasing lower bounds for a suitable subsequence of models. Together with the decreasing upper bounds of the preceding section, they turn convergence for the volume comparison into convergence in capacity. Lemma 13.23.1 . 2B568CD72F9D Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ N,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $N\geq 1$ and $u_ i\preceq w$. If \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N\bigl (U(w)-U(u_ i)\bigr ) <\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w),  \] then the rooftop envelope $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)=P_\theta (\min _ iu_ i)$ is not identically $-\infty $. Proof. Whether a finite rooftop envelope is identically $-\infty $ does not change under bounded changes of its obstacles. By the definition of $U(u_ i)$, we can choose $v_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v_ i\sim u_ i$ whose masses satisfy \[  \sum _{i=1}^ N\left(U(w)-\int _ X\mu _{v_ i}\right) <\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w).  \] Translate so that $v_ i\leq w\leq 0$, and put \[  v_{i,k}=\max (v_ i,w-k),\qquad p_ k=P_\theta (v_{1,k},\ldots ,v_{N,k}).  \] The common competitor $w-k$ gives $w-k\leq p_ k\leq w$, so $p_ k\sim w$. The $p_ k$ decrease as $k$ increases, and a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic limit would be a competitor for $P_\theta (v_1,\ldots ,v_ N)$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $P_\theta (u_1,\ldots ,u_ N)\equiv -\infty $, so that $P_\theta (v_1,\ldots ,v_ N)\equiv -\infty $ as well. Then the $p_ k$ decrease to $-\infty $, and normalized compactness gives $\sup _ Xp_ k\to -\infty $. Fix $s>0$ and choose $k>s$ so large that $p_ k\leq -s$. Iterating proposition 16.28.6 , which bounds the measure of a rooftop by the measures of its obstacles on the contact sets, and using locality on $\{ v_ i>-s\} $, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (w) & \leq \int _ X\mu _{p_ k} \leq \sum _{i=1}^ N\int _{\{ v_{i,k}\leq -s\} }\mu _{v_{i,k}}\\ & \leq \sum _{i=1}^ N\left(U(w)-\int _{\{ v_ i>-s\} }\mu _{v_ i}\right). \end{split}  \] Here we used $v_{i,k}\sim w$, and $w-k<-s$, which gives $v_{i,k}=v_ i$ on $\{ v_{i,k}>-s\} =\{ v_ i>-s\} $. Let $s\to \infty $. The measures $\mu _{v_ i}$ are finite and put no mass on pluripolar sets, so the resulting inequality contradicts the choice of the $v_ i$. $\square$ To control the volume of a rooftop envelope, we first stretch each obstacle away from the maximum of the two, and then move both stretched potentials a fixed fraction back toward this maximum. By the lemma, the resulting potentials have a rooftop envelope that is not identically $-\infty $. Proposition 13.23.2 . 1542F41C8A51 Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, with $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)>0$, and suppose that $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. For all sufficiently large $j$, the rooftop envelope $p_ j=P_\theta (u_ j,u)$ is not identically $-\infty $, and \[  d_\theta (p_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p_ j) \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u).  \] Proof. Put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$, $m_ j=\max (u_ j,u)$ and $s_ j=d_\theta (u_ j,u)$. After discarding finitely many indices, choose $b_ j\to \infty $ with $b_ j>1$ and $b_ j^ ns_ j<\delta $. The upper-volume deficits of both $u_ j$ and $u$ from $m_ j$ are at most $s_ j$, while $m_ j$ has lower volume at least $\delta $. Thus lemma 13.18.1 shows that the stretching envelopes \[  G_ j=Q_{b_ j}(u_ j,m_ j),\qquad H_ j=Q_{b_ j}(u,m_ j)  \] are defined. Choose $a\in (0,1)$ with $2nMa<\delta $, and set \[  g_ j=(1-a)m_ j+aG_ j,\qquad h_ j=(1-a)m_ j+aH_ j.  \] These potentials lie below $m_ j$, because $G_ j\leq u_ j$ and $H_ j\leq u$. Addition and monotonicity give \[  2U(m_ j)-U(g_ j)-U(h_ j) \leq 2\bigl (1-(1-a)^ n\bigr )U(m_ j) \leq 2nMa<\delta .  \] Lemma 13.23.1 , with $w=m_ j$, therefore shows that $r_ j=P_\theta (g_ j,h_ j)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. For large $j$, put $t_ j=(ab_ j)^{-1}<1$. Since $r_ j\leq g_ j$ and $r_ j\leq h_ j$, the defining inequalities for $G_ j$ and $H_ j$ show that \[  (1-t_ j)m_ j+t_ jr_ j\leq u_ j,u.  \] The left-hand side is therefore a competitor for $p_ j$, so $p_ j\not\equiv -\infty $. For either volume, addition and monotonicity give \[  (1-t_ j)^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq (1-t_ j)^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (m_ j) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (p_ j) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u).  \] Since $t_ j\to 0$, this proves $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p_ j)\to \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$; and since $p_ j\leq u$, ( 13.22.2 ) gives $d_\theta (p_ j,u)=U(u)-U(p_ j)\to 0$. $\square$ For ordinary models, finite rooftop envelopes are again ordinary models. Their normalization prevents collapse when the number of obstacles tends to infinity. Theorem 13.23.3 . 7D5F8FB5CFAB Suppose $u_ j,u\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $d_\theta (u_ j,u)\to 0$. After passing to a subsequence and relabeling it, there are ordinary model potentials $v_ j,w_ j\in \mathcal M_{\delta /2}(\theta )$ such that \[  w_ j\leq u_ j\leq v_ j,\qquad w_ j\leq u\leq v_ j,  \] $v_ j$ decreases to $u$, $w_ j$ increases with $(\lim _ jw_ j)^*=u$, and \[  d_\theta (v_ j,u)+d_\theta (w_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The original sequence converges to $u$ in capacity. Proof. Step 1: upper bounds. For large $j$, the rooftop envelope $r_ j=P_\theta (u_ j,u)$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by proposition 13.23.2 . It is an ordinary model: since $r_ j\leq 0$ and the envelope is monotone, $r_ j\leq P_\theta [r_ j]\leq P_\theta [u_ j]=u_ j$ and likewise $P_\theta [r_ j]\leq u$, so $P_\theta [r_ j]$ is a competitor for the rooftop and equals $r_ j$. The sequence $u_ j$ is $d_\theta $-Cauchy by proposition 13.22.5 , and $d_\theta (r_ j,u)=U(u)-U(r_ j)\to 0$ by proposition 13.23.2 . Choose a subsequence so that \[  d_\theta (u_ j,u_{j+1})<\delta \, 2^{-(j+1)n},\qquad U(u)-U(r_ j)<\delta \, 4^{-(j+1)n}.  \] The tail-maximum construction in the proof of theorem 13.22.7 gives \[  v_ j=P_\theta \left[\left(\sup _{l\geq j}u_ l\right)^*\right] \searrow u,\qquad d_\theta (v_ j,u)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Indeed, that construction produces the unique $d_\theta $-limit, which here is $u$. The models $v_ j$ satisfy $v_ j\geq u_ j$ and $v_ j\geq u$, and have lower volume at least $\delta $. Step 2: lower bounds. By lemma 13.18.1 and the choice of the subsequence, the stretching envelopes \[  H_ l=Q_{4^ l}(r_ l,u),\qquad K_ l=Q_{2^ l}(r_ l,u)  \] are defined. Their defining inequalities show that $(1-2^{-l})u+2^{-l}H_ l$ is a competitor for $K_ l$ and that $K_ l\leq u$. Together with addition and monotonicity, this gives \[  (1-2^{-l})u+2^{-l}H_ l\leq K_ l\leq u, \qquad U(u)-U(K_ l)\leq nM2^{-l}.  \] Choose $j$ so large that $nM2^{1-j}<\delta $. For every $k\geq 0$, the sum of the deficits of $K_ j,\ldots ,K_{j+k}$ from $u$ is less than $\delta $, so lemma 13.23.1 shows that their rooftop envelope is not identically $-\infty $. Since $r_ l\leq u$, the stretching envelope $Q_ b(r_ l,u)$ decreases as $b$ increases; hence, for $l\geq j$, \[  Q_{2^ j}(r_ l,u)\geq K_ l.  \] Thus $R_ j^ k=P_\theta (Q_{2^ j}(r_ j,u),\ldots ,Q_{2^ j}(r_{j+k},u))$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The convex inequality for each obstacle gives \[  (1-2^{-j})u+2^{-j}R_ j^ k \leq w_ j^ k:=P_\theta (r_ j,\ldots ,r_{j+k})\leq u.  \] For either volume, 00C1CF12A199 13.23.4 \begin{equation}  (1-2^{-j})^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (w_ j^ k) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u). \end{equation} The argument used for $r_ j$ shows that $w_ j^ k$ is an ordinary model. For fixed $j$ it decreases in $k$ and has supremum zero, so normalized compactness shows that its limit $w_ j$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The lower-volume conclusion of theorem 13.21.2 passes the lower bound in ( 13.23.4 ) to $w_ j$. This bound is positive, so the upper-volume conclusion of the same theorem passes the bound for the upper volume as well. Step 3: convergence. The $w_ j$ increase, since each is defined by fewer obstacles than the previous one, and $w_ j\leq r_ j\leq u_ j$, $w_ j\leq u$. After discarding finitely many indices, they have lower volume at least $\delta /2$, and ( 13.23.4 ) gives $d_\theta (w_ j,u)\leq nM2^{-j}$. By proposition 13.22.4 , $w_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, so $(\lim _ jw_ j)^*=u$. The two monotone sequences $v_ j$ and $w_ j$ converge to $u$ in capacity by lemma 5.29.19 , and the bounds $w_ j\leq u_ j\leq v_ j$ give $u_ j\to u$ in capacity along the chosen subsequence. Since every subsequence of the original sequence has a further subsequence of this kind, the original sequence converges to $u$ in capacity. $\square$

title: Equation 13.23.4
text: 00C1CF12A199 13.23.4 \begin{equation}  (1-2^{-j})^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (w_ j^ k) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (u). \end{equation}

title: 13.24 Volumes of multiplier-ideal envelopes
text: Analytic regularizations recover the multiplier-ideal envelope, whose volumes may exceed those of the original potential. Continuity along decreasing models computes this excess, and a strict analytic potential absorbs the curvature error of the regularization, so that the comparison can be carried out entirely in the fixed background. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, write \[  \mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}),\qquad \mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})  \] for the two volumes of its ideal envelope. They depend only on the multiplier-ideal class of $u$. By proposition 18.5.1 and the gauge invariance of singularity volumes, they are also unchanged under a smooth change of decomposition $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$, $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Moreover, proposition 18.4.4 , theorem 13.17.1 give \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) \leq \mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u).  \] The ideal envelope is an ordinary model by corollary 18.4.4 , and its volumes are limits of the volumes of the dyadic analytic approximations. Corollary 13.24.1 . C72B68A062F4 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, fix a Hermitian form $h$, and let $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$, $\theta _ j=\theta +\epsilon _ jh$, be the dyadic analytic regularizations of $u$ of analytic type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ ju))$, with errors $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, as in ( 18.7.5 ). Then \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(a_ j) \searrow \mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u).  \] If $\mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u)>0$, then also \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta _ j}(a_ j) \searrow \mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u).  \] Proof. By theorem 18.7.6 , the analytic ordinary models $q_ j=P_{\theta _ j}[a_ j]$ decrease to $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and the backgrounds $\theta _ j$ decrease to $\theta $. Thus theorem 13.21.2 applies to the $q_ j$. Since $q_ j\sim a_ j$ by proposition 18.4.8 , the volumes of $q_ j$ and $a_ j$ agree. $\square$ When the ideal envelope has positive lower volume, the relative full-mass class detects whether $u$ and its ideal envelope have the same upper volume. Here $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ and $P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$ denote the ordinary and the multiplier-ideal envelopes with the constraint $h\leq F$ in place of $h\leq 0$ (definition 5.40.4 and section 18.8 ). Proposition 13.24.2 . 71B65CF5AD10 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and suppose that $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)>0$. Then the following conditions are equivalent: $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$; $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)=\mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u)$; $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,q)$; $P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$ for every $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. If they hold, then also $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)=\mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u)$. Proof. Recall that $q$ is an ordinary model and $u\preceq P_\theta [u]\leq q$. If (i) holds, then $P_\theta [u]=q$ has positive lower volume, and theorem 13.19.5 shows that both volumes of $u$ equal those of $q$; in particular (ii) holds, together with the final assertion. Conversely, (ii) and $u\preceq q$ give $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta ,q)$, and corollary 13.19.8 gives $P_\theta [u]=q$, which is (i). The same corollary shows that (i) is equivalent to (iii). By proposition 18.12.2 , (iii) implies (iv), and (iv) with $F=0$ is (i). $\square$ Under the hypotheses of the proposition, corollary 18.7.7 also identifies equality of the upper volumes with convergence of the dyadic ordinary envelopes $P_{\theta _ j}[a_ j]$ to $P_\theta [u]$. These envelopes live in the larger backgrounds $\theta _ j$. The next construction mixes the $a_ j$ with a strict analytic potential, which gives analytic approximants in the fixed background $\theta $ with the same limiting upper volume; their singularity types, however, need no longer be ordered. Theorem 13.24.3 . E9FC137BBE4E Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and suppose $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)>0$. There are analytic $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $b_ j\to u$ in $L^1$ such that the ordinary models $r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j]$ satisfy 34D208A53BBD 13.24.4 \begin{equation}  d_\theta (r_ j,q)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad d_\theta (r_ j,u)\longrightarrow \mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta }(u) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u). \end{equation} Their lower volumes converge to $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)$, and $r_ j\to q$ in $L^1$ and capacity. In particular $d_\theta (r_ j,u)\to 0$ if and only if $P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. Step 1: the approximants. Fix a Hermitian form $h$. Bigness and theorem 5.36.1 give an analytic $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq 0$ and a rational $\kappa >0$ such that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h$. Choose the dyadic regularizations $a_ j$ as in ( 18.7.5 ), enlarging their errors to positive rational numbers $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. Put \[  c_ j=\frac{\kappa }{\kappa +\epsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j+(1-c_ j)\rho .  \] Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq ((1-c_ j)\kappa -c_ j\epsilon _ j)h=0$. The coefficients are rational, so $b_ j$ has analytic singularities by proposition 5.34.1 . Since $a_ j\to u$ in $L^1$ and $c_ j\to 1$, also $b_ j\to u$ in $L^1$. Step 2: two-sided bounds. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$, and set \[  \widehat\theta _ j=\theta +(1+A/\kappa )\epsilon _ jh, \qquad t_ j=P_{\widehat\theta _ j}[a_ j].  \] These backgrounds decrease to $\theta $ and dominate $\theta +\epsilon _ jh$, so the $a_ j$ also satisfy ( 18.7.5 ) with the larger errors $(1+A/\kappa )\epsilon _ j$. Theorem 18.7.6 therefore gives $t_ j\searrow q$. Moreover \[  c_ j\widehat\theta _ j-\theta =(1-c_ j)(Ah-\theta )+c_ j\epsilon _ jh\geq 0.  \] By proposition 18.4.8 , $r_ j\sim b_ j$. Hence $r_ j/c_ j$ is a nonpositive $\widehat\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic function that is more singular than $a_ j$, because $b_ j\leq c_ ja_ j$; it is therefore a competitor for $t_ j$, and $r_ j\leq c_ jt_ j$. Also $q\leq t_ j\leq c_ jt_ j$. For a lower bound, recall that $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$, and $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j$ because $a_ j\geq u$. Addition and scaling preserve this order by theorem 5.37.3 , lemma 5.37.4 . Thus $c_ jq+(1-c_ j)\rho \preceq _{\mathcal I}b_ j$. This potential lies below zero, so envelope order and proposition 18.4.8 give \[  c_ jq+(1-c_ j)\rho \leq P_\theta [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}=r_ j \leq c_ jt_ j.  \] Step 3: volumes. For either singularity volume, homogeneity, addition and monotonicity now yield \[  c_ j^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (q) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\theta (\max (r_ j,q)) \leq c_ j^ n\operatorname {vol}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(t_ j).  \] The last comparison uses both $\theta \leq c_ j\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\max (r_ j,q)\leq c_ jt_ j$. By theorem 13.21.2 , the outer terms tend to $\operatorname {vol}_\theta (q)$. This proves the convergence of both volumes of $r_ j$ and the first limit in ( 13.24.4 ). In particular, after discarding finitely many indices, the ordinary models $r_ j$ and $q$ have a common positive lower-volume bound, so $r_ j\to q$ in $L^1$ and in capacity by proposition 13.22.4 , theorem 13.23.3 . For the second limit, translate $u$ so that $u\leq q$; this does not change $d_\theta (r_ j,u)$. Then \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,u)) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,q)).  \] Both bounds tend to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)$, so $d_\theta (r_ j,u)=2U(\max (r_ j,u))-U(r_ j)-U(u)$ tends to $U(q)-U(u)$, as claimed. The last equivalence follows from proposition 13.24.2 . $\square$ For a Hermitian background, the simpler rescaling in corollary 18.7.9 gives decreasing analytic models, with the same limits by theorem 13.21.2 . In a general big background, the strict correction above may introduce additional poles, but the volume comparison still measures exactly the excess of the ideal envelope. Theorem 13.24.5 . 8BB867A0263F Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic ordinary models $p_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$. More generally, if $p_ j=P_\theta [p_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ and $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. If $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$, apply theorem 13.24.3 with $u=p$. For the converse it suffices to prove the more general assertion, because analytic ordinary models are ideal models by proposition 18.4.8 . Put $q=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ and $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Choose $s_ j\in (0,1)$ tending to zero with $d_\theta (p_ j,p)<\delta s_ j^ n$, after discarding finitely many indices. For $m_ j=\max (p_ j,p)$ one has \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (m_ j)\geq \delta , \qquad U(m_ j)-U(p_ j)\leq d_\theta (p_ j,p).  \] By lemma 13.18.1 with $b=s_ j^{-1}$, there is $h_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $(1-s_ j)m_ j+s_ jh_ j\leq p_ j$. Set $H_ j=P_\theta [h_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. Since $m_ j\geq p$, monotonicity, addition and scaling of ideal envelopes (proposition 18.4.6 ) give \[  (1-s_ j)q+s_ jH_ j \leq P_\theta [(1-s_ j)m_ j+s_ jh_ j]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_\theta [p_ j]_{\mathcal I}=p_ j.  \] Consequently $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p_ j)\geq (1-s_ j)^ n\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q)\geq (1-s_ j)^ n\delta $ by addition and volume monotonicity, since $q\geq p$. The models $p_ j,p$ therefore lie in $\mathcal M_{\delta /2}(\theta )$ for large $j$, so proposition 13.22.4 gives $p_ j\to p$ in $L^1$. The $H_ j$ have supremum zero, so normalized compactness bounds $\int _ X(-H_ j)\, \mathrm{d}V$ by a constant $C_\theta $. Since $q\leq 0$, the convex inequality above gives $q-p_ j\leq s_ j(q-H_ j)\leq -s_ jH_ j$, and hence \[  \int _ X(q-p_ j)_+\, \mathrm{d}V \leq s_ j\int _ X(-H_ j)\, \mathrm{d}V \leq C_\theta s_ j\longrightarrow 0.  \] Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $q\leq p$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . The opposite inequality $p=P_\theta [p]\leq P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}=q$ holds by proposition 18.4.4 , so $p=q$. $\square$ Thus the ideal models of positive lower volume are exactly the $d_\theta $-limits of analytic ordinary models. On each $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ they form a closed set for this convergence and inherit Cauchy completeness from theorem 13.22.7 . The approximants constructed above have a common positive lower-volume bound, which need not equal the lower volume of the limiting model.

title: Corollary 13.24.1
text: Corollary 13.24.1 . C72B68A062F4 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, fix a Hermitian form $h$, and let $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$, $\theta _ j=\theta +\epsilon _ jh$, be the dyadic analytic regularizations of $u$ of analytic type $(2^{-j},\mathcal I(2^ ju))$, with errors $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, as in ( 18.7.5 ). title: 13.24.6 A countable divisorial positivity criterion
text:
A prescribed divisorial part can determine an ideal envelope's ordinary type even when it has infinitely many components. On the projective plane with a pluriclosed background, the smooth residual determines the mass of every representative of that type. This gives a positivity test directly from divisorial orders. Let $X=\mathbb P^2$, and let $\kappa $ be the Fubini–Study form with $\int _ X\kappa ^2=1$. Choose distinct hyperplanes $H_ j$ and coefficients $a_ j>0$ with $A=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j<\infty $. For unit defining sections $s_ j$, put \[  \ell _ j(Z)=\log  rac{|s_ j(Z)|^2}{\| Z\| ^2}\leq 0, \qquad u_0=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j\ell _ j, \qquad u=u_0-\sup _ Xu_0.  \] Let $	heta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	heta =0$ and $R=	heta -A\kappa >0$. Lemma 13.24.7 . 487BF774470F The series defines a quasi-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=S-A\kappa ,\qquad S=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j[H_ j],\qquad 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=R+S>0.  \] For every prime divisor $E$ on every smooth compact modification $\pi :Z	o X$, the convergent order profile is \[  b(E):=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j\operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*H_ j) =
u (u\circ \pi ,E).  \] Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell _ j=[H_ j]-\kappa $. Unitary invariance reduces its integral to the distribution of $x=|Z_0|^2/\| Z\| ^2$, whose density on $[0,1]$ is $2(1-x)$. Thus \[  \int _ X\ell _ j\kappa ^2=\int _0^1 2(1-x)\log x\, \mathrm dx=- rac32.  \] The decreasing series has finite $L^1$ norm and a common lower curvature bound $-A\kappa $. Its canonical limit is quasi-plurisubharmonic. Distributional convergence gives the current identities and strict positivity. Fix $\pi $ and $E$, and choose a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on the compact surface $Z$. For the tail $r_ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j\ell _ j$ of total coefficient $A_ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j$, the closed positive current \[  T_ N=A_ N\pi ^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(r_ N\circ \pi )  \] has trace mass $A_ N\int _ Z\pi ^*\kappa \wedge \gamma $, by distributional Stokes. The pullback of $r_ N$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, since $\pi $ is an isomorphism on a dense open set where $r_ N$ is finite almost everywhere. Divisorial removal gives \[  0\leq 
u (r_ N\circ \pi ,E) \leq A_ N rac{\int _ Z\pi ^*\kappa \wedge \gamma }{\int _ E\gamma }.  \] The denominator is positive and the ratio is finite. Finite additivity of Lelong numbers now identifies the partial profile with $
u (u\circ \pi ,E)$ up to an error tending to zero. This proves convergence and the asserted equality. $\square$ Proposition 13.24.8 . 20027E32C14E Let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. The conditions \[  
u (v\circ \pi ,E)=b(E)	ext{ for every }\pi ,E, \qquad v\sim _{\mathcal I}u  \] are equivalent. Under either condition, \[  q=P_	heta [v]_{\mathcal I}=P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}\sim u,  \] and every $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $w\sim q$ satisfies 027648EDCB33 13.24.9  egin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (w) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (q) =\int _ XR^2>0. \end{equation} The background is big and $X$ has the bounded mass property. Proof. Ideal profile and envelope. Choose an integer $C>A$ with $C\kappa \geq 	heta $. Both $u$ and $v$ are $C\kappa $-plurisubharmonic. The projective valuative characterization of all-weight ideal types applies in this closed background: generic orders on all smooth projective modifications recover point Lelong numbers by further point blowups, and equality of those numbers is equivalent to ideal equivalence. The stated profile therefore implies $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Conversely, ideal equivalence pulls back under every compact modification by lemma 5.43.23 ; the local valuative criterion theorem 5.37.3 then gives equality of generic coefficients on every such modification. The common factor between growth against $\log |z|$ and the book's $\log |z|^2$ convention does not affect these equalities. The potential $u$ has complex Hessian $S-A\kappa $. By corollary 18.4.9 , its ordinary and ideal envelopes agree and are ordinarily equivalent to $u$. Ideal equivalence identifies the defining families for the two ideal envelopes in the statement, proving the assertion about $q$. The inequality $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq R>0$ proves bigness. For any Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, choose $D$ with $D\kappa \geq h$. Bounded $h$-plurisubharmonic potentials are $D\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, and positivity of bounded mixed products bounds their masses by $\int _ X(D\kappa )^2=D^2$. This proves the bounded mass property. The bounded residual. Fix $w\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and put $T=C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$. Its base divisorial coefficients are $a_ j$, so divisorial removal and passage through increasing finite sums give \[  K=T-S=(C-A)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq 0,\qquad h=w-u.  \] The distributional difference has a canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, which is bounded by ordinary equivalence and almost-everywhere order. Thus $K$ has bounded local potentials, and its trace charges no pluripolar set. The current $S$ is carried by the actual pole union $ igcup _ jH_ j\subset \{ w=-\infty \} $. Thus $\langle Tangle =K$. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $L$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=0$, distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ X L\wedge \langle Tangle =(C-A)\int _ XL\wedge \kappa .  \] Closed top mass and smooth correction. Put $T_ u=C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=S+(C-A)\kappa $. For the finite partial sums $u_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j\ell _ j$, the closed non-pluripolar mass is $(C-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j)^2$: outside the finite divisor union the current is the smooth residual, and the measure gives that union zero mass. Since $u_0\leq u_ N$, closed-background mass monotonicity, the closed case of theorem 13.17.1 , gives \[  \int _ X\langle T_ u^2angle \leq \left(C-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ jight)^2.  \] For the reverse inequality, locally write $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$ with $b$ plurisubharmonic. The currents $(C-A)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (b,-k)$ have bounded local potentials and dominate $(C-A)\kappa $. Their squared products, restricted to $\{ b>-k\} $, therefore dominate $(C-A)^2\kappa ^2$ on that set. Letting $k$ increase and using the local truncation definition gives $\langle T_ u^2angle \geq (C-A)^2\kappa ^2$. The two bounds prove equality of total masses. Closed mass invariance under bounded changes then gives \[  \int _ X\langle T^2angle =(C-A)^2.  \] Set $L=C\kappa -	heta \geq 0$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=0$. Expanding the bounded products of $\max (w,-k)$ in the two backgrounds and restricting to $\{ w>-k\} $ gives, in the limit, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (w) =\langle T^2angle -2L\wedge \langle Tangle +L^2.  \] All correction measures are finite: the closed top measure has the mass just computed, the degree-one limit is $K$, and the smooth measure $L^2$ gives the pole set zero mass. The same truncations are used in both backgrounds, so this identity is an equality of Borel measures. Integrating yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (w) =(C-A)^2-2(C-A)\int _ XL\wedge \kappa +\int _ XL^2 =\int _ X(	heta -A\kappa )^2.  \] This holds throughout the ordinary type, proving both singularity-volume identities and their strict positivity. $\square$ Example 13.24.10 . E76D9C1B44B6 There is a nonclosed pluriclosed background on $\mathbb P^2$ with a nonanalytic ideal type satisfying 13.24.8 . Its prescribed divisors are not contained in a single pencil, and both singularity volumes of its ideal model are at least $1/16$. Proof. In a coordinate ball choose a smooth real cutoff $\chi $ equal to one near the origin, and extend $\alpha =\chi |z_2|^2\mathrm dz_1$ by zero. Put \[  	au =\partial \overline\alpha + ar\partial \alpha .  \] It is real and smooth, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	au =0$. Where $\chi =1$, \[  \mathrm d	au =\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d ar z_2 \wedge (\mathrm dz_1-\mathrm d ar z_1)
e 0.  \] Choose $\epsilon >0$ small enough that $	heta =\kappa +\epsilon 	au \geq \kappa /2$. Set $A=1/4$, $a_ j=A2^{-j}$, $t_ j=2^{-j}$ and \[  H_ j=\{ Z_0+t_ jZ_1+t_ j^2Z_2=0\} .  \] The Vandermonde determinant shows that any three defining linear forms are independent; hence the hyperplanes are not in one pencil. Here $R=	heta -A\kappa \geq \kappa /4$, so $\int _ XR^2\geq 1/16$. The preceding proposition gives the mass throughout the ordinary type and both singularity volumes. There are infinitely many positive base divisor coefficients. An analytic singularity on a compact manifold has only finitely many prime divisorial components, so no analytic potential has this ideal type. $\square$ Problem 13.24.11 . D0837305A3CF For a big nonclosed background $	heta $ on a manifold with the bounded mass property, find criteria for $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_	heta (P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I})>0$ in terms of restricted multiplier ideals or divisorial orders. When this lower volume vanishes, which implications between envelope equality and upper-volume equality, conditions (i) and (ii) of proposition 13.24.2 , remain valid? One implication fails: when the ideal envelope has zero lower volume, equality of the upper volumes of a potential and of its ideal envelope does not force equality of the envelopes. title: Lemma 13.24.7
text:
Lemma 13.24.7 . 487BF774470F The series defines a quasi-plurisubharmonic function, and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=S-A\kappa ,\qquad S=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j[H_ j],\qquad 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=R+S>0.  \] For every prime divisor $E$ on every smooth compact modification $\pi :Z	o X$, the convergent order profile is \[  b(E):=\sum _{j\geq 1}a_ j\operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*H_ j) =
u (u\circ \pi ,E).  \] Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell _ j=[H_ j]-\kappa $. Unitary invariance reduces its integral to the distribution of $x=|Z_0|^2/\| Z\| ^2$, whose density on $[0,1]$ is $2(1-x)$. Thus \[  \int _ X\ell _ j\kappa ^2=\int _0^1 2(1-x)\log x\, \mathrm dx=- rac32.  \] The decreasing series has finite $L^1$ norm and a common lower curvature bound $-A\kappa $. Its canonical limit is quasi-plurisubharmonic. Distributional convergence gives the current identities and strict positivity. Fix $\pi $ and $E$, and choose a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on the compact surface $Z$. For the tail $r_ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j\ell _ j$ of total coefficient $A_ N=\sum _{j>N}a_ j$, the closed positive current \[  T_ N=A_ N\pi ^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(r_ N\circ \pi )  \] has trace mass $A_ N\int _ Z\pi ^*\kappa \wedge \gamma $, by distributional Stokes. The pullback of $r_ N$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, since $\pi $ is an isomorphism on a dense open set where $r_ N$ is finite almost everywhere. Divisorial removal gives \[  0\leq 
u (r_ N\circ \pi ,E) \leq A_ N rac{\int _ Z\pi ^*\kappa \wedge \gamma }{\int _ E\gamma }.  \] The denominator is positive and the ratio is finite. Finite additivity of Lelong numbers now identifies the partial profile with $
u (u\circ \pi ,E)$ up to an error tending to zero. This proves convergence and the asserted equality. $\square$
